  • Any screen where users need confidence that content hasn't been selectively summarized or altered by the app's UI layer.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat, unstructured approach when:

  • The document is long enough that users would benefit from a table of contents, search-in-page, or section jump links — the lack of these here can frustrate users trying to find a specific clause (e.g., refund policy, dispute resolution).

  • You're presenting onboarding-critical consent flows, where a summarized, plain-language "highlights" version paired with a link to full legal text would drive better comprehension and informed consent (many apps now use this hybrid approach).

  • Accessibility is a priority — dense unstructured text without headers-as-navigation-landmarks or collapsible sections can be difficult for screen reader users to navigate efficiently.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 1
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is the critical first-impression screen following the splash/app launch, presenting the user with a fundamental fork in the road: create a new self-custody wallet or import an existing one. The layout is a classic centered "hero + two-CTA" pattern, optimized for extreme simplicity at a moment when the user's cognitive load must be minimized.

The visual hierarchy is deliberate: a large, glowing app icon sits at the vertical center, surrounded by a constellation of token/NFT art (dollar coin, diamond, arrows, a stylized character, a frog) floating in orbit. This creates a sense of an active, living ecosystem of assets before the user even has any — a "aspirational preview" technique. Sparkle accents reinforce a feeling of premium polish and magic/delight, softening what is otherwise a technically intimidating action (key generation, custody).

Below the hero, the button hierarchy is unambiguous: a solid white, high-contrast pill button ("Create new wallet") as the primary path, and a low-emphasis text-only link ("I already have a wallet") for returning users. This asymmetry nudges new users toward the primary, most common conversion path without hiding the secondary option, respecting both new and migrating users. The legal disclosure (terms/privacy) is compressed into a single inline sentence directly above the CTA, satisfying compliance without breaking flow.

The dark, near-black background maximizes contrast for the colorful token artwork and blue-accented branding, aligning with the "Rounded cards, Blue accents, Token art" look & feel of the broader app, while a page-control dash at the bottom hints this is one step within a larger onboarding sequence.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is warm, minimal, and welcoming ("Welcome to Coinbase Wallet") rather than technical or jargon-heavy, which is essential given crypto's reputation for intimidating terminology. The two CTAs are written in plain, action-oriented language ("Create new wallet" / "I already have a wallet") rather than crypto-native terms like "Generate seed phrase" or "Import wallet," lowering the barrier for non-technical, busy-urban users who want speed and clarity over precision.

Legal text is intentionally de-emphasized in size and placed as a single soft-toned line, with only the tappable "terms" and "privacy policy" words highlighted in the brand blue — satisfying regulatory requirements while not visually competing with the primary CTA.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Aspirational Asset Constellation: Surrounding the central wallet icon with vibrant token/NFT artwork before the user owns any assets creates emotional aspiration and previews the app's visual reward system.

  • Binary Decision Architecture: Reducing the entire onboarding fork to exactly two clearly weighted choices (primary solid button vs. secondary text link) eliminates decision paralysis.

  • Inline Legal Compliance: Terms/privacy links are woven into a single sentence directly above the CTA, meeting legal disclosure needs without adding friction or a separate screen.

  • Dark Canvas for Color Pop: The near-black background makes the colorful, gradient token icons and blue accents visually pop, reinforcing a premium, modern crypto-native aesthetic.

  • Sparkle Micro-Illustrations: Small sparkle glyphs add a sense of delight and "magic moment" framing around what is otherwise a high-stakes security action (key/wallet creation).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets both crypto newcomers and experienced users migrating wallets, but is tuned for the app's "Busy Urbans" persona — people who want to get set up fast without reading extensive documentation. The friendly illustration style and plain-language buttons reduce the intimidation factor that often causes drop-off in crypto onboarding funnels. The aspirational token art acts as a subtle motivational trigger (FOMO/curiosity about what assets can be held), while the clean, uncluttered layout respects the limited attention span and need for speed of on-the-go users.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern on the first substantive screen of any app requiring an account/identity bifurcation (new vs. returning user), especially for fintech, crypto, or security-sensitive products where trust and simplicity must be balanced. It's ideal when the primary action (new account creation) should be heavily favored while still surfacing a secondary path without hiding it in a menu.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when more than two entry paths are needed (e.g., SSO, multiple wallet import types), as cramming additional options into this minimal layout would break the clean hierarchy. It's also unsuitable for enterprise or B2B tools where users expect immediate access to detailed configuration rather than a marketing-style welcome moment. If legal/regulatory requirements demand more prominent, standalone consent screens, this compressed inline approach may not satisfy compliance teams.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 2
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen presents a binary choice architecture that determines how a user will authenticate into their crypto wallet — a critical fork in the onboarding/recovery flow. The design uses two large, tappable "tiles" rather than a dropdown or radio list, which reduces cognitive load and makes the decision feel deliberate and weighty (appropriate given the security implications of each path).

The layout is vertically stacked with generous spacing, a large bold headline, and a back arrow for escape, signaling this is a discrete step within a larger flow (likely wallet import/recovery in a Web3/crypto app such as Coinbase Wallet or similar). Each option card contains an icon, a bold title, and a two-line descriptive subtext explaining the underlying security mechanism — this is a strong pattern for technical products where users need context before making an irreversible or consequential choice.

The dark theme (near-black background, high-contrast white text, muted grey secondary text) is standard for crypto/finance apps, evoking a sense of security, sophistication, and reduced eye-strain for a power-user audience. The absence of a persistent CTA button implies the cards themselves are the tap targets — an efficient one-tap interaction model that removes an unnecessary confirmation step.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is direct, conversational, and framed as a question ("How do you sign in to your wallet?") rather than an imperative instruction, which reduces intimidation for a topic (crypto key management) that is often anxiety-inducing for users. Each card's description avoids jargon overload by naming familiar, trusted brands (iCloud, Google, Yubikey) to anchor the abstract concept of "passkey" in recognizable, trustworthy ecosystems.

The "Recovery phrase" option is described plainly as "your 12-word secret recovery phrase," reinforcing ownership ("your") and specificity (exact word count) to build confidence that the user is choosing the correct, familiar credential type rather than guessing.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Card-as-button pattern: Eliminates the need for a separate "Continue" button — selection is immediate, reducing friction and decision fatigue.

  • Contextual iconography: Distinct glyphs (person+key vs. asterisk-dot pattern representing a seed phrase) give instant visual differentiation between two similar-sounding security concepts.

  • Brand-anchored trust cues: Referencing iCloud, Google, and Yubikey within the passkey description leverages existing user trust in these platforms to de-risk a newer authentication method.

  • Minimalist dark UI: Reinforces a premium, security-focused brand tone appropriate for financial/crypto contexts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets crypto wallet users, ranging from newcomers migrating away from vulnerable seed-phrase-only storage to more security-conscious users adopting modern passkey standards (WebAuthn/FIDO2). The psychological driver here is reducing decision anxiety around asset security: by clearly bifurcating "modern/convenient" (Passkey) vs. "traditional/manual" (Recovery phrase) authentication, the app respects varying user sophistication and existing wallet setups. It also subtly nudges newer users toward the more secure, mainstream passkey option by listing it first and associating it with familiar, trusted providers.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a product must present a small number (2–4) of mutually exclusive, consequential paths — such as authentication methods, account recovery options, or account types — especially where each path requires brief explanatory context. It's ideal for security/fintech/crypto onboarding flows where trust and clarity are paramount, and where reducing choice-related anxiety through clear labeling and trusted brand references improves conversion and reduces support tickets.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this large-card single-choice pattern when there are many options (5+), as it would require excessive scrolling and diminish scanability — a list or dropdown would be more efficient. It's also unsuitable for low-stakes, frequently-repeated choices where the extra visual weight and descriptive copy would slow down power users; a more compact toggle or segmented control would be more appropriate in those cases.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 3
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen sits at a critical juncture in the wallet-import flow: the moment a returning user must prove ownership of an existing wallet by supplying their seed phrase. The design deliberately narrows the decision space to exactly two mutually exclusive paths, presented as large, equally-weighted tappable cards rather than buttons or a segmented control. This choice reduces cognitive load and touch-target ambiguity — critical in a flow where a mis-tap could send a user down the wrong (and possibly more tedious) path.

The top progress bar (two segments, first fully filled) sets expectations that this is a short, bounded process — a reassurance mechanic that combats the anxiety typically associated with handling irreplaceable financial credentials. The back arrow offers an obvious escape hatch, which is essential in security-sensitive flows where users often second-guess themselves.

Visually, the pure black background paired with high-contrast white typography and a single muted-blue accent link creates a serious, vault-like atmosphere appropriate for a crypto product handling private keys. Each card uses a simple icon (cloud vs. keyboard) to instantly communicate the mental model of the two paths without requiring the user to read dense copy — recognition over recall.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal, direct, and functional — typical of security/finance-grade fintech apps where trust is built through clarity rather than personality. "How do you want to enter your recovery phrase?" phrases the decision as a simple preference rather than a technical requirement, lowering perceived friction.

The inline "I need help" link is a subtle but important tonal choice: it acknowledges that recovery phrases are commonly forgotten or mismanaged, and preemptively offers support without cluttering the primary flow. This shows empathy for a notoriously stressful part of the crypto onboarding experience — losing or mismanaging a seed phrase can mean permanent loss of funds.

Card subtext ("Import your recovery phrase from your iCloud" / "Type in your recovery phrase") is purely descriptive and avoids marketing language, reinforcing a utilitarian, no-nonsense tone appropriate for handling sensitive credentials.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Binary card choice architecture: Only two large, icon-led cards are shown, eliminating decision paralysis at a high-stakes step.

  • Contextual help link embedded in the question itself rather than buried in a menu, reducing the chance a stuck user abandons the flow.

  • Segmented progress bar communicates a short, finite process, reducing anxiety before the user has even started entering sensitive data.

  • Cloud-first ordering: Placing "iCloud backup" above "Enter manually" nudges users toward the lower-friction, less error-prone recovery method first.

  • Dark, minimal visual language reinforces a sense of security and seriousness appropriate to financial custody actions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who already own a crypto wallet and are switching devices, reinstalling the app, or recovering access after uninstalling — a moment often loaded with stress and urgency since access to funds is at stake. The psychological drivers here are anxiety reduction and trust-building: the user needs to feel the process is safe, short, and reversible.

By offering an easy iCloud-based shortcut alongside the manual fallback, the design also targets less technical users who may not remember exact seed phrase order, while still respecting power users who prefer typing it manually for maximum control and paranoia around cloud storage of private keys.
screens.whereToUse: Use this two-path card selection pattern whenever a critical account-recovery or import action has exactly two distinct, mutually exclusive methods (e.g., cloud restore vs. manual entry, QR scan vs. code entry). It's ideal for security flows where users need confidence that they haven't been forced down a suboptimal path, and where a persistent progress indicator and inline help can meaningfully lower drop-off.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when there are more than 3-4 possible input methods, as large cards will force excessive scrolling; a list or segmented control would scale better. It's also unsuitable for low-stakes settings screens where the gravity of the dark, vault-like visual treatment would feel unnecessarily heavy or intimidating.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 4
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen represents the "recover existing wallet" path of onboarding, layered with a critical security interstitial. The base layer is a minimal, high-contrast dark screen with a two-segment progress bar, a clear heading ("Sign in with a recovery phrase"), a supporting explanation, a "Where can I find this?" help link, a mandatory Terms/Privacy checkbox, and a disabled "Continue" CTA that will only activate once the checkbox is ticked — a classic gating mechanism to force legal acknowledgment before proceeding.

Layered on top is a bottom sheet modal ("Beware of recovery phrase scams") that interrupts the flow before the user can even reach the phrase-entry field. This is a deliberate friction point: Coinbase Wallet trades a small amount of onboarding speed for a large reduction in social-engineering risk, since recovery-phrase phishing is the single most common attack vector in self-custody wallets. The sheet uses a vivid blue-to-teal gradient "Acknowledge" button to stand out against the otherwise monochrome dark UI, drawing the eye and making the required action unambiguous.

The stacking of two consent gates (checkbox agreement + acknowledge sheet) before the actual sensitive input field is a strong example of progressive disclosure of risk: the app doesn't overwhelm the user with warnings on the main screen but delivers them as an interruptive, unskippable layer exactly when it matters most.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is calm but authoritative, typical of financial/security-critical software. The base screen copy is plain and instructional ("This is a 12-word phrase you were given..."), avoiding jargon while assuming some prior context (the user already created a wallet elsewhere).

The bottom sheet shifts tone sharply into urgent, protective language: "Beware of recovery phrase scams" paired with a direct, unambiguous instruction — "Never enter a recovery phrase given to you by someone else, even if they're from Coinbase." This explicit callout of impersonation scams (including fake "Coinbase" support) demonstrates awareness of real-world attack patterns and directly inoculates users against social engineering, a copywriting technique borrowed from security/fraud-prevention best practices.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Disabled CTA until consent: The "Continue" button is visibly greyed out until the terms checkbox is checked, preventing users from skipping legal/security acknowledgment.

  • Forced security interstitial: A non-dismissible-looking bottom sheet interrupts the flow specifically before recovery phrase entry, targeting the exact moment of highest phishing risk.

  • Explicit anti-impersonation messaging: Calling out that even messages "from Coinbase" should never be trusted with a recovery phrase preempts a known scam vector.

  • High-contrast gradient CTA: The blue-teal "Acknowledge" button pops against the dark, otherwise low-saturation UI, signaling importance and driving action.

  • Progress indicator: The two-segment bar at top sets expectations that this is a short, bounded flow (likely: enter phrase → confirm), reducing perceived effort.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Coinbase Wallet's "busy urban" target users are often mainstream, non-technical crypto holders migrating from another wallet or a previous device. This flow is designed for someone in a state of moderate stress (recovering access to their funds) who may be vulnerable to shortcuts or scams promising to "help" them recover their wallet. The design deliberately slows this specific moment down with an unmissable warning, because self-custody means there is no customer support safety net if funds are stolen via a leaked seed phrase — the psychological cost of a mistake here is irreversible loss of money, unlike a typical app where errors are recoverable.
screens.whereToUse: Use this interruptive warning + gated consent pattern whenever a user is about to input or reveal a uniquely irreversible secret (private keys, seed phrases, recovery codes, API secrets, backup codes). It's ideal any time your product cannot undo the consequence of a leaked credential and where phishing/social engineering is a known threat vector for your user base.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-handed friction for low-stakes or reversible actions — e.g., editing a profile field or setting a preference — where an interruptive modal and disabled CTA would feel patronizing and increase drop-off without any real risk mitigation benefit. Also avoid stacking too many consent gates in flows where the user has already demonstrated trust/competence (e.g., repeat sign-ins), as it can create fatigue and desensitize users to future warnings ("warning blindness").

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 5
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen handles one of the highest-stakes interactions in any crypto product: restoring wallet access via a BIP-39 recovery phrase. The layout is deliberately minimal and distraction-free — a dark, near-black canvas with a single headline, one supporting sentence, and one contextual help link. There is no visible text input field in the visible viewport for the phrase itself yet, suggesting the actual word-entry fields appear below the fold or are revealed progressively (likely 12 discrete boxed inputs), while the keyboard is already docked and ready for input, signaling to the user that typing is the expected next action.

The two-segment progress bar at the top (one segment fully filled, one outlined) tells the user they are on step 1 of a short multi-step recovery flow, reducing anxiety about how long the process will take. A back arrow gives an obvious escape hatch back to the previous authentication choice screen (e.g., "create new wallet" vs "sign in").

Critically, the primary CTA ("Continue") is rendered in a disabled/greyed-out state until the mandatory legal checkbox — "I agree to the terms and privacy policy" — is checked. This is a deliberate gating mechanism: the app will not let a user proceed with a financially destructive, unrecoverable action (importing a seed phrase) without explicit acknowledgment of legal terms, which also doubles as a subtle liability shield for the product team.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is calm, direct, and reassuring rather than alarming, which is notable given how catastrophic a mistake with a seed phrase can be (loss of funds). The copy avoids jargon overload by defining the term immediately: "This is a 12-word phrase you were given when you created your previous wallet." This one sentence does the job of onboarding a returning user who may have forgotten the terminology.

The "Where can I find this?" link is a masterstroke of empathetic microcopy — it anticipates the single biggest point of user friction (forgetting where they stored the phrase) and offers help inline rather than forcing the user to abandon the flow to search externally or contact support.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Disabled CTA until consent: The "Continue" button stays visually inactive until the terms checkbox is ticked, preventing accidental legal exposure and reinforcing the seriousness of the action.

  • Inline contextual help: "Where can I find this?" pre-empts confusion at the exact moment of doubt instead of relying on a generic FAQ section.

  • Segmented progress indicator: Sets expectations for a short, bounded flow (2 steps), reducing perceived effort and abandonment risk.

  • Minimalist, high-contrast dark UI: Removes all non-essential elements so the user's full attention goes to correctly entering a sensitive, unrecoverable string of words.

  • Immediate keyboard readiness: The system keyboard is pre-docked, cutting one tap out of the input flow.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets returning crypto/wallet users who already own a self-custody wallet (e.g., MetaMask-style or a mobile-first wallet like Phantom/Trust Wallet) and need to restore access on a new device or after reinstalling the app. This is not a new-user acquisition screen; it assumes prior crypto literacy but still hand-holds on terminology since seed-phrase recovery is infrequent and highly error-prone.

Psychologically, the design leverages loss-aversion mitigation — because entering a wrong phrase or losing it entirely means permanent loss of assets, the UI compensates with reassurance (calm tone, clear step count) while simultaneously using friction-as-safety (mandatory consent checkbox) to slow the user down at a point where careless action is costly.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any recovery or import flow involving irreversible, high-consequence credentials: crypto wallets, hardware security keys, encrypted backup restoration, or enterprise SSO recovery codes. It's ideal whenever you need to combine minimal cognitive load with mandatory legal/safety gating.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-handed consent-gating and stripped-down layout for low-stakes, everyday sign-ins (e.g., standard email/password login) where it would add unnecessary friction. Also avoid docking the keyboard immediately if the form requires scanning, reviewing legal text, or multiple non-text inputs before typing, as it can crowd the viewport and hide important context (like the actual phrase input fields, which are pushed off-screen here).

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 6
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen initiates the self-custody recovery flow, a critical and high-stakes moment in the Coinbase Wallet experience. The layout is deliberately minimal and distraction-free: a top progress bar (two segments visible, indicating this is an early step in a multi-step flow) sits above a large, bold headline and a short, reassuring explanation. The back arrow affords easy exit without feeling trapped.

Notably, the actual input field for the 12-word phrase is not visible yet in this state — the keyboard is open but the input area is empty, suggesting the text entry field appears once the user taps into it (likely a secure, obscured multi-word input component below the fold or revealed on focus). This progressive disclosure keeps the initial screen calm and readable before the user is asked to handle sensitive data.

The legal checkbox ("I agree to the terms and privacy policy") is pre-checked, which reduces friction but is a debatable pattern from a consent-integrity standpoint. The primary CTA uses Coinbase's signature blue-to-teal gradient pill button, drawing the eye immediately and signaling the primary path forward. Overall information hierarchy is excellent: title → context → help link → legal → action, in a single vertical scan.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is calm, direct, and reassuring — critical for a moment that could otherwise trigger anxiety (users recovering a wallet often fear loss of funds). "Sign in with a recovery phrase" is plain-language, avoiding intimidating technical jargon like "seed phrase" or "mnemonic," which broadens accessibility for non-technical, busy urban users.

The supporting line clarifies exactly what is expected ("This is a 12-word phrase you were given when you created your previous wallet"), setting precise expectations and reducing the chance of user error or confusion. The "Where can I find this?" link acts as a safety net for users who may have misplaced or forgotten where they stored their phrase, addressing anxiety without cluttering the main flow with inline help text.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented progress bar at the top sets expectations that this is a multi-step, bounded process, reducing perceived effort.

  • Plain-language explanation demystifies the technical concept of a "recovery phrase" for a mainstream, non-crypto-native audience.

  • Inline contextual help link ("Where can I find this?") proactively answers a top user question without needing a separate FAQ screen.

  • Gradient CTA button reinforces brand identity while creating strong visual affordance for the primary action.

  • Pre-checked legal consent reduces friction to continue, trading off slightly on explicit opt-in ethics for speed.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Designed for "busy urbans" who may be switching devices, recovering a lost phone, or restoring access after an app reinstall. This audience values speed and clarity over deep technical explanation. The psychological trigger here is anxiety reduction: recovery flows are inherently stressful (users fear their funds are gone), so the interface leans on calm typography, minimal steps, and reassurance ("This is a 12-word phrase you were given...") to lower cognitive load and prevent drop-off or support escalations.

The pre-ticked terms checkbox also reflects a design choice optimized for conversion speed over friction, banking on the fact that most returning users have already accepted these terms in a prior session.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for high-stakes account recovery or re-authentication flows where users need clear, jargon-free instructions and reassurance. Ideal for fintech, crypto, or security-sensitive apps where a wrong entry has serious consequences (loss of funds/access). The segmented progress bar is valuable whenever a multi-step recovery or verification wizard needs to set expectations about remaining effort.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid pre-checking legal consent checkboxes in jurisdictions with strict opt-in consent laws (e.g., GDPR) — this can create compliance risk and should be an explicit user action instead. Also avoid this level of minimalism if the recovery phrase input requires complex validation (e.g., word-by-word autocomplete with error states) — in that case more inline guidance and real-time validation feedback should be surfaced directly on this screen rather than deferred.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 8
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a value-driven onboarding step that appears after wallet creation, designed to convert a cryptographically complex hexadecimal wallet address into a human-readable, brandable username (similar to an ENS domain). The layout follows a classic "illustration-headline-body-CTA" vertical rhythm common in mobile onboarding flows.

The centerpiece is a stylized illustration of a wallet/ID card holding an NFT avatar (a Bored Ape-style character), which cleverly visualizes the abstract concept of a "wallet identity" in a tangible, card-like metaphor. The gradient holographic card design borrows visual language from credit cards and driver's licenses, reinforcing the idea that this username acts as an official, ownable identity credential.

Below the fold, the interface uses a strict two-button hierarchy: a solid white, high-contrast primary button ("Claim my username") against a muted, low-contrast secondary button ("Maybe later"). This visual weighting nudges the user toward the desired action while still technically preserving optionality, a hallmark of ethical-but-persuasive onboarding design. A page control indicator at the very bottom signals this is one step within a larger multi-screen onboarding sequence.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is concise, benefit-led, and frictionless. "Claim your free username" uses the word "claim," which implies ownership and urgency (as if the username is already earmarked for the user and could be lost if not acted upon), paired with "free" to eliminate cost-based hesitation.

The supporting body text reframes a technical pain point ("remembering your wallet address") as the justification for adopting the feature, making the benefit feel practical rather than promotional. The CTA button uses first-person possessive language ("Claim my username") rather than a generic imperative ("Claim now"), which increases psychological ownership and conversion rates. The de-emphasized dismissal option "Maybe later" is intentionally soft and non-committal (versus a harder "No thanks" or "Skip"), reducing the perceived finality of opting out while still allowing progression.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Metaphorical Illustration: The wallet-as-ID-card visual instantly communicates an abstract Web3 concept (self-custody identity) through a familiar physical object metaphor.

  • Asymmetric Button Hierarchy: A stark contrast between the solid white primary CTA and the dark, muted secondary CTA visually funnels the user toward the desired action without removing choice.

  • Ownership-Framed Copy: Use of "Claim" and "my username" leverages loss-aversion and personal ownership psychology to boost adoption of an optional feature.

  • Non-Blocking Value-Add: Framed as an enhancement to an already-completed action (wallet creation) rather than a mandatory gate, keeping the onboarding funnel from feeling coercive.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets newly onboarded Coinbase Wallet users, particularly crypto newcomers who are unfamiliar with or intimidated by long alphanumeric wallet addresses (e.g., 0x71C...). By offering a free, human-readable username, Coinbase reduces onboarding friction for peer-to-peer transfers and social sharing, while also increasing platform stickiness (a claimed username creates a sunk-cost/identity investment in the Coinbase ecosystem specifically).

The NFT-avatar imagery also signals to a crypto-native audience (holders of profile-picture NFTs) that this wallet supports and celebrates digital identity/collectibles culture, subtly appealing to that community's values around personalization and status signaling.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when introducing an optional but high-value identity or convenience feature immediately after a core setup task (e.g., account creation, wallet generation) is completed. It's ideal for:

  • Turning technical/system-generated identifiers (IDs, hashes, URLs) into memorable, ownable handles.

  • Driving adoption of a free feature that increases platform lock-in or network effects (e.g., usernames, handles, custom URLs).

  • Any onboarding moment where you want to offer value without blocking progress, preserving a low-friction funnel.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, full-screen interstitial pattern for minor or low-value features, as it adds an extra step to onboarding and risks fatigue if used too many times in sequence. It's also inappropriate when the feature is mandatory for core functionality—framing something as an optional "claim" implies it's non-essential, so critical setup steps (like security backups or KYC) should use firmer, non-skippable UI instead. Additionally, this pattern should be skipped for expert/returning users who already understand and have configured their identity settings.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 7
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a critical security checkpoint within a crypto wallet's onboarding/authentication flow, specifically designed for the "restore existing wallet" path rather than "create new wallet." The layout is intentionally minimal and stripped of distraction — a dark, high-contrast background, a single bold headline, one line of supporting copy, and one primary action. This minimalism is not just stylistic; it signals to the user that they are entering a security-sensitive zone where focus and caution are paramount.

The top progress bar (two segments, with the first appearing complete/active) tells the user they are in a multi-step flow, reducing anxiety about how long the process will take. The back arrow provides an easy escape hatch, which is important since users recovering a wallet may have arrived here by mistake or want to switch methods (e.g., use a private key instead).

Notably, the actual input field for the 12-word phrase is not visible in this state — instead we see a loading spinner inside the primary CTA button, indicating the app is either validating a previously entered phrase, checking clipboard/biometric availability, or transitioning into the next step. This suggests the screen has multiple states: an initial input state (word entry grid) and this transitional/loading state captured here.

The mandatory legal checkbox ("I agree to the terms and privacy policy") is pre-checked but still visually present and interactive, ensuring compliance while reducing friction — a pattern common in fintech to satisfy legal requirements without overly slowing down power users who are re-importing an existing wallet.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is direct, reassuring, and utilitarian — typical of crypto-native products speaking to an audience that already understands the mental model of "recovery phrases" and self-custody. There's no hand-holding explanation of what a wallet or blockchain is; the tone assumes competence.

Key phrases like "This is a 12-word phrase you were given when you created your previous wallet" serve as a memory-jogging confirmation rather than an educational tutorial, reducing cognitive load for returning users while the "Where can I find this?" link acts as a safety net for those who forgot, without cluttering the main flow.

The legal microcopy is compressed into a single line with embedded links ("terms" and "privacy policy"), a standard low-friction compliance pattern that avoids interrupting the primary task with a separate legal screen.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented progress bar instead of a percentage or step counter — subtly communicates flow length without overwhelming a security-focused screen with extra UI chrome.

  • Deferred/contextual help link ("Where can I find this?") placed directly beneath the instructional text, addressing user uncertainty exactly where it arises rather than via a generic FAQ.

  • Loading state embedded in the CTA button itself (spinner replacing button label) rather than a separate full-screen loader, keeping the user anchored to the same visual context and reducing perceived wait time.

  • Pre-checked legal consent checkbox that still requires visual acknowledgment, balancing legal compliance with speed for repeat/expert users.

  • High-contrast dark theme with minimal color usage (blue reserved only for interactive/actionable elements) reinforces focus and signals this is a serious, security-critical action.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets existing crypto wallet holders who are migrating, reinstalling, or switching devices/apps and need to restore access using their self-custodied seed phrase — a technically literate audience already familiar with Web3 conventions. It is not aimed at first-time crypto users, which explains the terse, jargon-forward copy.

Psychologically, the design leverages trust-through-restraint: a clean, uncluttered dark UI mirrors the aesthetic of security-focused tools (password managers, hardware wallet apps), subconsciously reassuring users that their sensitive 12-word phrase is being handled in a serious, non-gimmicky environment. The immediate visibility of legal agreements taps into a sense of institutional legitimacy, important in a space often associated with scams.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any sensitive re-authentication or account-recovery flow — crypto wallets, password manager imports, or secure enterprise SSO recovery — where the user already possesses a secret credential and simply needs a focused, low-distraction entry point. It's ideal when the audience is assumed to have prior context (avoiding excessive explanation) and when legal/compliance acknowledgment must be captured without adding a separate screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal, jargon-forward approach for first-time or non-technical users, who would benefit from more explanatory scaffolding (e.g., visual diagrams of where to locate a recovery phrase, warnings about phishing). Also avoid a pre-checked consent checkbox in jurisdictions where regulations require explicit, unchecked opt-in for legal terms, as this could create compliance risk. Finally, embedding the loading state inside the button (without a fallback timeout message) can frustrate users if the validation process takes unusually long without feedback.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 9
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is the primary home/portfolio view of a self-custody crypto wallet application. The layout follows a strict hierarchy that mirrors banking app conventions to reduce cognitive load for users transitioning from traditional finance: identity selector at top-left (account switcher), global net-worth figure as the dominant hero element, primary transactional actions (Buy/Swap/Cash out) immediately below, and a segmented asset-class browser (Crypto/NFTs/DeFi) that organizes the user's entire on-chain net worth into digestible categories.

The dark theme is not merely aesthetic — it is the de facto standard for financial/crypto apps, reducing eye strain during frequent price-checking behavior and reinforcing a premium, 'serious money' tone. The gradient-filled primary CTA (Buy) uses color to create visual weight hierarchy against the two secondary pill buttons (Swap, Cash out), guiding new users toward the funding action first, since an empty wallet has no other meaningful actions available.

The single Bitcoin asset row with an almost-zero balance ($10.68) suggests this is either a fresh wallet, a QA/test account, or an onboarding-adjacent state — reinforcing the importance of the prominent Buy CTA as the natural next step. The bottom tab bar uses icon-only navigation (Home, Browser/dApp, Swap/Transfer, Activity, Wallet) which is standard for power-user crypto apps where horizontal space is precious and users learn icon meaning quickly through repeated use.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is minimal, numeric, and utilitarian — there is almost no explanatory copy, which is typical of tools built for an audience that already understands crypto terminology (Buy, Swap, Cash out, DeFi, NFTs). The percentage change is color-coded green with an upward arrow, tapping into familiar stock-ticker visual language that signals gains/losses instantly without requiring reading.

Labels are short, action-oriented verbs ("Buy", "Swap", "Cash out") rather than descriptive nouns, prioritizing speed of scanning over friendliness. There's no onboarding copy, tooltips, or empty-state messaging visible, which assumes user familiarity — a deliberate choice for a return-user dashboard rather than a first-run experience.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Balance-first hierarchy: The total dollar value ($10.68) is rendered in the largest type on the screen, immediately answering the user's #1 question ("how much do I have?") before anything else.

  • Three-action pill row: Buy/Swap/Cash out condenses the entire transactional surface area of a wallet into one thumb-reachable row, with the gradient Buy button visually prioritized as the default entry action for low/zero balance states.

  • Segmented asset taxonomy: Crypto/NFTs/DeFi tabs let a single wallet address represent multiple asset classes without cluttering the main list, scaling gracefully as portfolios grow more complex.

  • Network filter chip: "All networks" dropdown quietly solves one of the biggest pain points of multi-chain wallets (chain fragmentation) by defaulting to an aggregated cross-chain view.

  • Icon-only bottom navigation: Maximizes content space in a chart/number-dense app while relying on universally recognized wallet iconography.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This design targets self-custody crypto users — ranging from active DeFi/NFT participants to casual holders — who value speed, control, and data density over hand-holding. The lack of explanatory text and reliance on symbols (arrows, percentages, chain icons) signals a design decision to serve an already-literate audience rather than first-time crypto users.

Psychologically, the screen leverages loss/gain framing (green up-arrow percentage) to trigger dopamine responses tied to portfolio performance, a well-documented engagement driver in fintech apps. The prominent, high-contrast gradient Buy button exploits the path-of-least-resistance principle: with a near-empty balance, funding the wallet is the only rational next action, so the interface funnels attention there through color and positioning rather than copy.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for financial dashboards, wallets, brokerage, or portfolio-tracking apps where a single aggregate number is the most important piece of information a returning user needs. It's ideal when the product supports multiple asset types/categories that benefit from a lightweight tab/segment switcher, and when the primary actions are few and highly repeatable (buy, sell, transfer).

Also effective for multi-chain or multi-account products needing an "All networks/accounts" aggregation pattern to reduce fragmentation anxiety.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimal, jargon-heavy approach for first-time user onboarding or consumer-facing apps targeting non-expert audiences — the lack of labels, explanations, or empty-state guidance would confuse users unfamiliar with terms like "Swap" or "DeFi." Also unsuitable for information-dense enterprise dashboards where users need multiple data points (charts, historical trends) visible simultaneously rather than a single hero balance.

If the product anticipates predominantly zero-balance or churned users, a more directive empty-state with explanatory copy and a stronger single CTA would outperform this three-button pattern.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 17
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen functions as a merchandising hub within the "Cards" tab of the Venmo app, designed to upsell users on financial products they haven't yet activated. Rather than presenting a single card, it uses a vertically stacked list of large, high-contrast promotional tiles, each dedicated to a distinct product (Credit Card, Debit Card, Teen Debit Card).

The layout leverages a strong visual split-card pattern: the left side of each tile uses neutral light-gray background with dark text for readability of the value proposition, while the right side uses a vibrant, on-brand color block (mint green, Venmo blue) that mimics the physical card's texture/design (QR-code-like dot pattern, chip icon, contactless icon, and the Venmo wordmark). This creates an immediate mental association between the marketing copy and the physical card being offered, despite no actual photograph of the card being used.

Each primary tile includes a circular arrow CTA button embedded directly in the colored card graphic, which affords tap interaction while keeping the layout clean and uncluttered. The third entry (Teen Debit Card) is visually demoted to a simpler horizontal banner with an icon and text, using a pink "announcement" icon to signal it's a promotional callout for a niche audience segment rather than a primary product.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copywriting is benefit-first and objection-handling. Each headline names the product plainly ("Venmo Credit Card:", "Sign up for the Venmo Debit Card") while the subtext proactively addresses the biggest psychological barriers to applying for financial products:

  • "No impact to your credit bureau score if declined" — directly neutralizes fear of rejection hurting credit score, a major friction point in credit card applications.

  • "Automatic cashback offers. No monthly fee. No credit check." — stacks three risk-reducing, cost-free benefits in a punchy staccato rhythm.

  • "Flexibility for teens, visibility for adults." — a clever dual-audience pitch that speaks to both the teen user's desire for independence and the parent's desire for control/oversight in a single line.

The tone throughout is confident, reassuring, and low-pressure, avoiding aggressive sales language in favor of factual, trust-building statements.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Objection-handling microcopy: Leading with "No impact to credit score if declined" tackles the #1 psychological blocker to credit applications before the user even considers tapping.

  • Split-tile visual metaphor: Using color blocks with chip/contactless icons and dot-matrix patterns evokes the physical card's aesthetic without needing a rendered photo, keeping the design abstract yet recognizable.

  • Tiered visual hierarchy: The two primary products get large, colorful, CTA-forward cards while the niche Teen Card gets a lighter-weight banner treatment, correctly matching visual weight to expected audience size/priority.

  • Embedded circular CTA: Placing the arrow button directly on the brand-colored side of the tile creates a natural focal point that guides the eye without needing a separate button below the text.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets existing Venmo users who already trust the peer-to-peer payment app but have not yet adopted its banking/card products. The design assumes users are price-sensitive and risk-averse, likely younger or credit-cautious demographics who may have been previously denied credit or are wary of hard credit inquiries.

Psychologically, the screen relies on loss-aversion mitigation (removing fear of credit score damage), fee-transparency trust-building (no monthly fee, no credit check), and familial trust dynamics for the Teen card (appealing to parents' need for oversight while giving teens autonomy). The cross-sell placement within an already-engaged app session (user came to view/manage their cards) capitalizes on contextual relevance and low-friction discovery.
screens.whereToUse:
• Multi-product fintech or banking apps offering tiered financial products (credit, debit, family/teen accounts) that need to cross-sell without overwhelming the user.

  • Screens where reducing application anxiety (credit checks, fees, rejection) is critical to conversion.

  • Any hub screen consolidating several related but distinct offers, where visual differentiation by product color/branding helps users self-select the right option quickly.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern when a user already owns all available products — showing empty promotional cards to already-converted users creates clutter and signals poor personalization.

  • Not suitable for single-product apps where cross-sell isn't relevant; the split-tile treatment adds unnecessary visual complexity for a single CTA.

  • Should be avoided if the underlying offers are time-sensitive or urgent, as the calm, reassuring tone here undersells urgency-driven conversions.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 19
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a single step within a multi-step parental onboarding flow for setting up a Venmo Teen Account. It follows a classic "value-prop" educational pattern: a large, human, lifestyle photograph at the top (a hand holding a phone showing the Venmo app UI next to a handwritten notebook/ledger) paired with a large bold headline and a short explanatory paragraph below.

The layout is vertically stacked and single-column, minimizing cognitive load — there is only one primary decision point (the "Get started" CTA) and one secondary escape hatch ("Learn more"). A back chevron in the top-left allows the parent to revisit the prior step, and a page-control/progress bar at the very bottom of the screen (visible as a short black pill) signals that this is one step in a longer sequence, setting expectations for the length of the flow.

Legal/compliance copy (Mastercard issuer disclosure, eligibility requirements) is pushed below the fold in smaller, lower-contrast gray type, correctly de-prioritizing it while still keeping it accessible for FDIC/regulatory compliance without cluttering the primary narrative.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is warm, permissive, and reassuring, targeted at parents rather than teens. The headline "Access to the app (if you want)" is deliberately conversational and uses a parenthetical qualifier to immediately signal parental control and optionality — this is not a mandatory step, alleviating anxiety that parents are being forced to give up control.

The body copy uses clear, benefit-oriented language ("view the current balance, track their spending, add payment methods, and pay friends") that maps directly to the fears/desires of a parent overseeing a minor's finances: transparency and financial literacy.

The legal disclosure block shifts tone entirely into formal, compliance-driven language (issuer details, FDIC membership, age eligibility 13-17), which is a necessary tonal contrast for a regulated financial product.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Parenthetical reassurance in the headline ("if you want") directly addresses parental control anxiety and reduces perceived commitment before the user even reads the body text.

  • Authentic lifestyle photography instead of a sterile illustration — showing a real hand, a real phone, and a handwritten notebook — builds trust and relatability, subtly implying "budgeting/financial responsibility" without saying it outright.

  • Dual-tier information architecture: consumer-friendly value prop up top, legally required fine print below, clearly separated by a divider so neither dilutes the other.

  • Low-commitment secondary action ("Learn more") placed beneath the primary CTA gives cautious parents an offramp to gather more information without abandoning the flow entirely.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
The primary audience is parents or legal guardians (not the teen) who are setting up a supervised financial account for a 13-17 year old. This demographic is motivated by a desire to teach financial responsibility while retaining oversight, but is also wary of privacy, security, and unwanted financial exposure for their child.

Psychologically, the screen leverages autonomy-supportive framing (the "if you want" qualifier) to reduce reactance — parents are more likely to proceed when they feel in control of the pace and scope of access granted. It also uses social/relatable imagery (handwritten ledger, casual home setting) to invoke trust and everyday practicality rather than a cold banking-app aesthetic.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when onboarding a "primary" user (parent, admin, team owner) into a flow that will eventually grant delegated access to a secondary/dependent user (teen, employee, family member). It's ideal for:

  • Multi-step setup wizards where trust and control need to be established before permissions are granted.

  • Regulated financial or health products requiring both persuasive marketing copy and mandatory legal disclosures on the same screen.

  • Any flow introducing a feature that could be perceived as relinquishing control, where reassurance language ("optional," "if you want") can reduce drop-off.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy educational/legal pattern for simple, low-stakes toggles or non-regulated features — the dense disclosure text and full-screen real estate would feel disproportionate and slow down the flow unnecessarily. It's also not appropriate for expert/power-user flows where the audience already understands the feature and just needs a quick confirmation, or for screens where the user is the actual end-consumer (the teen) rather than the intermediary decision-maker, since the tone here is specifically calibrated for a supervisory parent.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 18
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen functions as a dedicated feature-marketing splash within the onboarding/settings flow, introducing Venmo's Teen Account product to a parent user. The layout follows a classic top-to-bottom persuasion funnel: a large hero visual (a device mockup showing the actual product UI) establishes credibility and concreteness, followed by a bold emotional headline, a supporting rational sub-headline, a benefit bullet list, and finally a dual-CTA footer (primary solid button + secondary text link).

The use of a literal in-app screenshot inside a phone bezel (rather than an abstract illustration) is a deliberate trust-building device — it shows the parent exactly what they're getting, reducing ambiguity about the feature before they commit to tapping through. The page-control dash at the very bottom signals this is one card in a multi-step explainer carousel/sequence, setting expectations that more context follows before final commitment (likely leading into a Setup Wizard for adding the teen).

Visual hierarchy is strong: the cobalt-blue hero block anchors attention immediately, the black bold headline is scannable in under two seconds, and the CTA is impossible to miss thanks to full-width pill styling and high contrast. The back chevron in the top-left preserves user control, letting the parent bail out to prior screens without friction.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy speaks directly to the parent's emotional state rather than the teen's. "Your teen gets Venmo. You get peace of mind." is a masterful two-clause reframe: it immediately answers the implicit objection ("Is it safe to give my kid a payment app?") before it's even asked, using the reassuring phrase "peace of mind" — a classic trigger phrase in parental-control and safety products.

The sub-headline, "The independence they want, the control you want (plus a few added bonuses)," is structured as a balanced trade-off statement, acknowledging both parties' needs in one sentence — a subtle negotiation/mediation tone that positions Venmo as the neutral facilitator between teen autonomy and parental oversight.

The bullet copy ("Keep an eye on their activity via the app and real-time alerts") uses concrete, benefit-driven language rather than technical feature description, emphasizing surveillance-as-care rather than surveillance-as-control.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Product-accurate hero mockup: Using a real screenshot of the teen's balance/profile view inside a device frame builds tangible trust versus a generic illustration.

  • Dual-audience copywriting: The headline simultaneously validates the teen's desire for independence and the parent's desire for control in a single sentence, disarming objections before the CTA is even reached.

  • Low-friction secondary path: The "Learn more" text link beneath the primary CTA respects users who need more information before committing, avoiding a hard forced choice.

  • Progress dot indicator: Signals this is part of a short, finite sequence rather than an open-ended flow, reducing perceived commitment anxiety.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets parents/guardians of teenagers within Venmo's "Busy Urban" demographic — adults who are already comfortable with digital payments and want to extend financial tools to their children without losing oversight. The psychological trigger at play is loss-of-control anxiety mitigation: parents fear giving teens unsupervised financial access, so the copy and real-time-alert bullet directly neutralize that fear. Simultaneously, it appeals to the parent's desire to be seen as a "modern," enabling parent who supports their teen's growing independence rather than restricting it, tapping into an aspirational parenting identity.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when introducing a sensitive, dual-stakeholder feature (e.g., family sharing, parental controls, joint accounts, guardian dashboards) where one user configures a tool on behalf of another. It's ideal for feature announcement or upsell moments where trust and reassurance must precede any setup flow. Also effective for any B2C2C (business-to-consumer-to-consumer) product introducing a new persona type into an existing single-user app.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy narrative/marketing screen format for simple, low-stakes feature toggles or settings changes — it would feel bloated and slow down power users who just want to flip a switch. It's also inappropriate for repeat visits; once a parent has seen this pitch, it should not resurface, or it will feel like nagging. Additionally, this format is risky if the screenshot mockup doesn't perfectly match the live product (breaks trust the moment inconsistency is spotted).

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 20
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a critical step in a Know Your Customer (KYC) flow, likely for a fintech, banking, or crypto app. The layout uses a clean, single-column structure that isolates two distinct document upload tasks (ID proof and SSN/ITIN proof) into separate tappable tile modules with camera icon placeholders, immediately signaling "tap here to photograph a document."

The visual hierarchy is strong: a large, friendly headline ("We need a few more details") softens what could otherwise feel like an invasive request for sensitive personal documents. The body copy immediately follows with a clear instruction on image quality expectations ("clear, well-lit photos"), preemptively reducing failed submissions and re-uploads.

Each requirement is paired with a square photo-upload placeholder on the left and descriptive text on the right, explaining exactly which document types are acceptable (passport, driver's license, government ID / SSN card, W2, paystub). This dual-format acceptance list reduces user anxiety about not having the "right" document on hand.

A progress bar at the very bottom of the screen indicates this is one step within a larger multi-step onboarding or verification wizard, reassuring the user of forward momentum. The "Requirement details" link offers a low-friction path to more information without cluttering the primary view, adopting a progressive disclosure pattern.

The close (X) button in the top-left allows users to exit without being trapped, though in real implementations this often triggers a confirmation dialog to prevent unintentional drop-off during a compliance-critical step.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is calm, reassuring, and conversational — "We need a few more details" reframes a legally mandated identity check as a small, cooperative favor rather than a bureaucratic hurdle. This choice of words avoids intimidating terms like "verification," "compliance," or "KYC" that could raise user apprehension about privacy or security.

The instructional copy is concise and actionable, using imperative-lite phrasing ("Help confirm your information by submitting clear, well-lit photos") that guides users toward a successful first-attempt upload, reducing back-and-forth error correction later in the process.

Section labels ("Name and Date of Birth", "SSN or ITIN") are functional rather than emotional, clearly mapping the abstract data being verified to the concrete physical document required, which reduces cognitive load for users unfamiliar with compliance jargon.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Empathetic reframing: Turns a mandatory regulatory checkpoint into a friendly, collaborative request, lowering perceived friction.

  • Document flexibility: Offering multiple acceptable document types (passport, license, ID / SSN card, W2, paystub) per requirement reduces abandonment from users lacking one specific document.

  • Visual affordance clarity: Camera icon placeholders inside bordered tiles unmistakably communicate "tap to capture/upload photo" without requiring additional labels.

  • Progressive disclosure: The "Requirement details" link keeps the primary screen lightweight while still offering deeper explanation for cautious or confused users.

  • Progress transparency: The bottom progress bar sets expectations that this is a finite, multi-step process, not an open-ended demand.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users onboarding into a regulated financial product (neobank, payments app, crypto exchange, or lending platform) where identity verification is legally required under KYC/AML regulations. The audience spans a broad demographic, so the design leans on plain language rather than legal terminology to remain accessible to less financially sophisticated users.

Psychologically, the screen leverages trust-building through transparency — by explicitly stating why the data is needed and what will satisfy the requirement, it reduces the anxiety and suspicion often associated with being asked for government ID and SSN, which are frequent targets of fraud. The structured, itemized checklist format also taps into the completion/closure motivation, showing users a clear, finite set of tasks standing between them and account access.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an app must collect sensitive identity documents for regulatory compliance (banking, lending, crypto, insurance, gig-economy driver/worker verification). It's ideal when:

  • Multiple document types can satisfy a single requirement, and you want to communicate flexibility upfront.

  • Users need reassurance about photo quality before they attempt an upload, to reduce failed OCR/verification attempts.

  • The step is part of a longer onboarding flow and progress indication will reduce perceived effort.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, form-like presentation for low-stakes or optional profile completion tasks — it may feel disproportionately serious. Also avoid bundling too many document requirements onto a single screen; if more than 2-3 uploads are required, consider breaking them into separate steps within a wizard to prevent overwhelming the user. Additionally, don't use vague photo placeholders without accompanying example images/guidelines for users in regions where document formats vary widely, as this can increase upload errors.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 1
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen is the entry point into Cleo's actual product experience — the Chat tab — captured mid-load, with a typing indicator suggesting Cleo is about to send an opening message (likely a personalized greeting following the "Unleash Cleo" completion screen from the prior onboarding sequence). The oversized, low-contrast repeating "CHAT / CLEO" wordmark watermark filling the background is a distinctive branding choice — rather than a blank or loading-skeleton background, Cleo fills empty conversational space with its own identity, reinforcing brand presence even before any real content (messages) exists on screen. This confirms what earlier screenshots established: Chat is one tab among several (Spend, Budget, Chat, Save, Borrow), not the entirety of the app, correcting any assumption that Cleo is a chat-only interface.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven; visible text is limited to a date marker and repeating brand wordmarks, with no actual conversational copy yet loaded (the typing indicator suggests Cleo's first message hasn't rendered at the moment of capture).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Branded empty state instead of blank space — filling an otherwise sparse loading screen with a large decorative wordmark keeps the brand present and avoids a jarring blank-white loading gap (perceived performance / brand consistency).

  • Typing indicator sets expectation — the three-dot bubble is a well-understood convention signaling "a response is coming," reducing uncertainty during the load (visibility of system status).

  • Date marker for conversational context — showing "January 31, 2024" mirrors real messaging-app conventions (like iMessage or WhatsApp), reinforcing Chat's identity as a genuine conversation thread rather than a static screen.

  • Chat as one of several first-class destinations — the five-tab structure confirms Cleo's Chat is peer to Spend/Budget/Save/Borrow, not a wrapper around the whole app.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• ChatGPT mobile app — uses a similar three-dot typing indicator convention while awaiting a generated response.

  • WhatsApp / iMessage — both use date-marker separators identical in function to the "January 31, 2024" label seen here.

  • Replika — an AI companion app that similarly treats its chat interface as the product's home base with heavy brand-identity styling behind the conversation.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (typing indicator + date marker + branded background) fits any AI-conversational product interface where the chat itself is a first-class, persistent feature the user returns to repeatedly, and where reinforcing brand identity during load states adds value without obstructing usability.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for purely transactional or utility chat interfaces (e.g., customer support widgets) where a large decorative brand watermark would be visual noise competing with functional content, rather than a meaningful identity reinforcement.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 2
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen solves the classic "blank chat box" cold-start problem: rather than dropping a first-time user into an empty text field with no guidance on what Cleo can actually do, it offers five concrete, tappable starting points that double as a lightweight feature tour (spending control, cash advance, credit score, general exploration, transaction visibility). Including "I don't know 🦄" as an explicit option is a thoughtful design choice — it validates uncertainty as a legitimate starting state rather than forcing the user to have a clear goal before engaging, and gives Cleo latitude to guide an undecided user rather than leaving them stuck. The reaction GIF and celebratory copy carry emotional momentum directly over from the "ARE YOU READY? / Unleash Cleo" completion screen, so the first real in-app moment continues that same high-energy tone rather than resetting to something flat or transactional.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The greeting is warm, familiar, and personality-forward: "I've been expecting you here 👋" and "You've just walked into the best decision of your fabulous life" lean fully into affirming, almost over-the-top flattery — consistent with Cleo's established sassy, confident brand voice throughout the onboarding sequence. "Knew you could do it ✨" (paired with the reaction GIF) treats simply arriving in the app as an accomplishment worth celebrating, which is a deliberate choice to make the user feel good at the exact moment they're most likely to be evaluating whether they made the right download decision. The quick-reply chips mix functional labels with playful emoji that don't always literally match the text (e.g., a stopwatch/clock emoji next to "cash advance," a unicorn next to "I don't know") — a small but consistent design quirk that reinforces whimsy over literal-mindedness throughout Cleo's visual language.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Solving the cold-start problem with guided chips — offering concrete starter prompts instead of a blank input field reduces the "what do I even say" friction common to first-time chatbot interactions (reducing user's cognitive load at first contact).

  • Validating uncertainty as a valid path — including "I don't know" as an equal-weight option alongside specific goals respects that not every new user arrives with a defined task, avoiding a forced-choice dead end.

  • Emotional continuity from onboarding completion — carrying the celebratory tone directly from the previous "ARE YOU READY?" screen into the first real chat message avoids a jarring tonal reset right after the user's biggest commitment moment (downloading/completing setup).

  • Multimedia reinforcement of personality — embedding a reaction GIF in the chat thread (rather than only text) is a distinctive way to convey Cleo's character quickly and memorably, beyond what copy alone could do.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• ChatGPT / Replika — both use quick-reply suggestion chips at the start of a fresh conversation to guide users unfamiliar with what to ask.

  • Duolingo — similarly opens with a celebratory, personality-driven welcome message immediately after onboarding completes, mirroring Cleo's tonal continuity choice.

  • Snapchat's chatbot features — use embedded GIFs/stickers within chat threads to convey personality and reaction, similar to Cleo's use of the reaction GIF here.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (personality-driven welcome message + reaction media + guided quick-reply chips including an "I don't know" option) fits any conversational AI product's first real interaction screen, especially where the product wants to demonstrate its distinct voice immediately and reduce first-message anxiety for new users.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for utility-focused or enterprise chatbots (e.g., IT support, banking fraud reporting) where excessive personality and celebratory tone could undermine perceived seriousness or trustworthiness at a moment users expect efficient, businesslike help.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 3
screens.uxAnalysis: Selecting "control my spending" from the prior screen's quick-reply chips routes the user into a short, explicitly-framed Personalization Quiz rather than jumping straight into generic budgeting advice. Cleo sets expectations plainly — "5 qs," addressed by name ("Trisha"), with a clear stated reason ("The more I know, the better I can help you") — which is a good practice for quiz-style data collection: users tolerate being asked personal questions more readily when the exchange value is explicit and the scope is bounded (5 questions, not open-ended). Reducing the next action to a single "let's go 💃" chip (rather than multiple options, as seen in the previous screen) signals a shift from open exploration to a focused, linear task the user has now committed to.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The copy continues Cleo's established sassy, familiar voice — using the user's first name directly ("Be honest in the next 5 qs, Trisha") personalizes the request in a way that feels more like a friend's ask than a form's instruction. Framing honesty as something the user is being coached toward ("Be honest...The more I know, the better I can help you") is a subtle but effective persuasion technique: it reframes data collection as being in the user's own interest, improving the reliability of self-reported answers by explicitly incentivizing candor rather than assuming it. The "let's go 💃" chip keeps momentum high with an upbeat, low-friction call to action rather than a plain "Continue" or "Next," maintaining tonal consistency with the celebratory energy carried over from onboarding.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Bounded scope reduces perceived commitment — explicitly stating "5 qs" up front lets the user mentally commit to a small, known task rather than an open-ended one, reducing quiz abandonment risk.

  • Personalized addressing builds rapport — using the user's actual name mid-conversation reinforces the sense of individualized coaching rather than generic scripted output.

  • Explicit incentive for honest input — telling the user why honesty matters ("the better I can help you") is a deliberate design choice to improve data quality at the source, rather than assuming users will self-report accurately by default.

  • Progressive commitment through single-chip continuation — narrowing from multiple choice chips to one clear "let's go" chip mirrors the user's own narrowing intent (they picked a specific goal), keeping the interaction focused.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo — uses a similarly framed personalization quiz early in a chosen learning path, explaining why answers matter before asking.

  • Noom — frames its onboarding habit questions with comparable "the more you tell us, the better we can help" incentive language before a multi-question personalization sequence.

  • Headspace — personalizes onboarding copy with the user's name and bounds question sets to a known, small number to reduce perceived friction.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (explicit scope + named personalization + honesty incentive + single-CTA continuation) fits any product moment where a short, bounded data-collection sequence will directly improve the personalization or accuracy of subsequent recommendations, and where user trust in the "why" of the ask affects response quality.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for lengthy or open-ended data collection — bounding expectations to "5 questions" works because it's true and manageable; using this same reassuring framing before a much longer or vaguer survey would erode trust once the user discovers the scope was understated.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 4
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen asks a genuinely sensitive question — how much of your income you spend versus save — using a graded, ordinal scale rather than requiring the user to type or select an exact percentage. Framing the options through weather metaphors (sunny → stormy) is a distinctive design choice: it externalizes what could otherwise feel like a judgment-laden confession ("I spend everything I earn") into a lighter, less personally loaded visual language, making it psychologically easier to answer honestly. The clarifying parenthetical about what counts as "income" (paychecks, government support, student loans) is inclusive and non-assumptive — it doesn't presume a single traditional employment income source, which matters for a financial app serving a broad range of users including those without traditional paychecks.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "Think back over the last 6 months" anchors the question to a concrete, bounded timeframe rather than asking for a vague generalization, which tends to produce more accurate self-reported answers. The explanatory aside "(This is any money that comes in. Like paychecks, government support, student loans, and more)" is notably non-judgmental and broad in scope — a small but meaningful inclusivity choice for a financial app, since narrowly assuming "income = paycheck" would alienate or confuse users on benefits, loans, or irregular income. The weather-metaphor answer options ("not much ☀️" through "all of it, and then a lot more ⛈️") let the copy stay light and non-clinical even while asking about a topic (overspending, living paycheck to paycheck or beyond) that can carry real shame for users — a thoughtful tonal choice consistent with Cleo's broader "supportive, not judgmental" positioning seen in earlier onboarding screens.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Ordinal scale reduces precision-reporting burden — offering five graded categories instead of requiring an exact percentage or number lowers the cognitive and emotional cost of answering (recognition over recall, reduced input friction).

  • Metaphorical framing de-stigmatizes a sensitive answer — using weather severity rather than blunt financial language ("I overspend") makes admitting financial strain feel less like a confession and more like a light self-assessment.

  • Inclusive definition of income — explicitly naming non-traditional income sources (government support, student loans) avoids alienating users whose financial situation doesn't fit a default "salaried employee" assumption.

  • Bounded recall window — anchoring to "the last 6 months" rather than an open-ended "generally" question improves the reliability of the self-reported answer.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Noom — uses similarly non-clinical, metaphor-based response scales (rather than raw numeric input) when asking users to self-assess sensitive habits.

  • Cleo's own broader pattern — consistent with the "Swear Jar" and challenge-based tone observed in earlier product research, reinforcing that Cleo systematically avoids blunt, judgmental framing around money behavior.

  • Headspace — uses graded, illustrated response scales (rather than plain text options) for self-reported emotional/behavioral check-ins, a similar design logic applied here to financial behavior.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (ordinal graded scale + metaphorical/non-clinical labeling + bounded recall window + inclusive definitions) fits any self-assessment question touching a potentially sensitive or shame-prone topic (finances, health habits, mental wellbeing) where honest self-report is more valuable than precise numeric data.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit where precise, actionable numeric data is actually required for a downstream calculation (e.g., an actual budget needs real dollar figures eventually) — a qualitative weather-scale answer alone wouldn't suffice if Cleo's budgeting engine needs concrete numbers rather than a general spending disposition.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 5
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen shows the quiz progressing conversationally rather than through a static form — the user's previous answer appears as a genuine sent chat bubble, and Cleo's next question follows directly from it, maintaining the illusion of a responsive, adaptive conversation even if the underlying question sequence is likely fixed. Narrowing from the prior screen's five-option graded scale to a binary choice here ("on top of them" vs. "on top of me") suits a naturally dichotomous question — bill management tends to have two real states (in control or behind) rather than a spectrum, so the interaction format appropriately matches the nature of each specific question rather than reusing one uniform answer-scale style throughout the quiz.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "What are you like with bills?" is short, casual phrasing — closer to how a friend would ask than a form field label ("Bill payment status" would be the generic alternative).
