The paired crab/scorpion emoji options ("I'm on top of them 🦂" vs. "they're on top of me 🦀") extend the whimsical animal/nature-emoji motif seen in the prior screen's weather icons, using a playful visual pun (literally "on top of" as a physical position, echoed by small creatures) rather than plain checkmarks or neutral icons. This keeps a question that could otherwise feel like a mild "gotcha" (admitting you're behind on bills) light and non-judgmental, continuing the same de-stigmatizing tonal strategy observed in the previous spending question.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Answer format matches question structure — using a binary choice for an inherently two-state question (rather than forcing a five-point scale everywhere) shows appropriate interaction-design judgment rather than template reuse.

  • Conversational continuity reinforces engagement — displaying the user's own prior answer as a real sent message (rather than silently advancing) maintains the feeling of an actual back-and-forth conversation, not a disguised form.

  • Consistent de-stigmatizing tone — extending the playful emoji-metaphor pattern from the previous spending question maintains a uniform emotional register across the whole quiz, rather than shifting tone question to question.

  • Casual phrasing reduces perceived formality — "What are you like with bills?" invites a more honest, less guarded answer than a clinical survey-style question would.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Noom — similarly varies its self-assessment question formats (scales vs. binary choices) based on what best fits each specific question's natural structure, rather than uniform templating.

  • Headspace — uses casual, friend-like phrasing in its own personalization quiz questions, matching Cleo's conversational register here.

  • Duolingo — displays user answers as persistent chat-style bubbles during its own placement/personalization flow, reinforcing the same "this is a real conversation" illusion.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (binary or scaled choice matched to the question's natural structure, displayed within a persistent conversational thread) fits any multi-question personalization sequence where maintaining engagement and honest self-report matters more than rigid format consistency across questions.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit if the underlying data actually needs to be precisely comparable across users in a structured database (e.g., a clinical intake form) — varying answer formats per question (binary here, five-point scale previously) can complicate downstream data analysis compared to a single standardized response type.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 6
screens.uxAnalysis: The quiz closes with a notably different question format from the earlier graded-scale and binary questions: a playful fill-in-the-blank ("This was less painful than...") that shifts from pure data collection into pure entertainment, since the actual content of the answer ("getting my wisdom teeth out") has no obvious bearing on Cleo's ability to generate financial advice. This is a deliberate engagement/rapport-building beat inserted at the end of an otherwise functional questionnaire — a "fun tax" the user pays that reinforces Cleo's personality before transitioning into the payoff. Cleo's closing lines ("Cause now I've got enough ammo / To set your worst habits on fire") reframe the entire quiz retroactively: what felt like casual Q&A was actually explicitly building toward a "roast," which the final "roast me Cleo 🔥" chip confirms as the next deliberate, consented-to step.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "K, final thing" is deliberately casual, almost text-message-shorthand phrasing that signals closeness to the end without breaking immersion in the chat-with-a-friend format. The "less painful than..." fill-in-the-blank format invites genuine wit from the user rather than a straightforward answer, functioning as a light bonding moment rather than a data point — the user is being asked to be funny, not honest, which is a notable tonal pivot from the more sincere prior questions. Cleo's payoff line — "I've got enough ammo to set your worst habits on fire" — is aggressive, confrontational language reframed as playful anticipation rather than genuine hostility, consistent with Cleo's established "sassy roast" persona; explicitly offering "roast me Cleo 🔥" as an opt-in chip (rather than just launching into critique) respects user consent even within a comedic, confrontational format.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Entertainment beats reinforce brand personality mid-task — inserting a non-data-driven, purely fun question at the close of a functional quiz builds emotional engagement without compromising the quiz's actual purpose.

  • Retroactive reframing builds anticipation — revealing that the quiz was "ammo" for a roast only after the fact creates a small narrative payoff, making the preceding functional questions feel more purposeful in hindsight.

  • Explicit consent before confrontational content — offering "roast me Cleo" as a distinct, tappable choice (rather than auto-launching into critique) respects the principle that even playful negative feedback should be opted into, not sprung on the user.

  • Format variety sustains engagement across a multi-question sequence — shifting from graded scale, to binary, to fill-in-blank across three consecutive questions prevents the repetitive fatigue a uniform format would risk over even a short 5-question quiz.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo — closes early quiz/placement sequences with a lighter, personality-driven closing beat before transitioning into its main app experience, similar to Cleo's fill-in-blank closer.

  • BuzzFeed-style personality quizzes — commonly use fill-in-the-blank or free-response questions as an engagement device distinct from the data-gathering questions around them.

  • Noom — offers a comparable "we'll use this to help you" framing after a habits questionnaire, though without Cleo's distinctive roast/confrontational payoff style.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (entertainment-only closing question + retroactive reframing + explicit opt-in to a confrontational payoff) fits products with a strong, established comedic or personality-driven brand voice, where a moment of genuine fun can be inserted into an otherwise functional flow without undermining trust in the surrounding data collection.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for products without an already-established permissive, jokey brand relationship with users — introducing "roast me" style confrontational content without the extensive tonal groundwork Cleo lays throughout its onboarding would risk feeling mean-spirited or presumptuous rather than charming.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 7
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen delivers the payoff of the entire quiz sequence: rather than silently generating a budget artifact and dropping the user into it, Cleo narrates what was just built ("Your overview's ready... an overview of where your money's going") and, in response to the user's own clarifying question ("how does it work?"), explains the mechanic in plain, scannable bullets before the user ever opens it. This front-loaded explanation reduces the chance of the user opening the overview and being confused by an unfamiliar daily-spending-limit concept — a real product mechanic (not just a report) is being introduced here, so setting expectations conversationally first lowers the risk of the feature feeling unexplained or intrusive once encountered.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Cleo's voice reaches peak intensity and informality here — "You check your damn phone to stay on track" and especially "Trisha. Let's fucking do this thing 👇" mark the strongest departure from neutral/corporate language seen anywhere in this flow so far, including actual profanity. This is a deliberate escalation consistent with the "roast me" consent given on the prior screen — the user opted into a more aggressive, unfiltered tone, and Cleo's copy here delivers on that expectation rather than reverting to safer language. The three-bullet explanation ("We see what's coming in and out / I give you a daily spending limit / You check your damn phone to stay on track") is notably concise and mechanic-focused rather than benefit-focused, prioritizing clarity about how the feature works over selling why it's good — appropriate at this stage since the user has already opted in ("I can do this 🌶️") and needs functional understanding, not further persuasion.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explain the mechanic before the user encounters it — describing how the daily spending limit and check-in behavior work before opening the overview reduces confusion at first contact with a new, ongoing product feature.

  • Escalating tone matched to explicit consent — the shift into unfiltered, casual-profanity language directly follows the user's own "roast me Cleo" opt-in, respecting that the tone shift was invited rather than imposed.

  • Concise, scannable feature explanation — three short bullet points (rather than a paragraph) make a genuinely new mechanic digestible in a chat-bubble format that wasn't designed for long-form text.

  • Deferred entry point — placing "My overview 👀" as a distinct link only after the explanation, rather than immediately upon quiz completion, ensures the user has context before landing in the actual feature.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo — similarly explains a new mechanic (e.g., the XP/streak system) in plain bullet form immediately after onboarding, before the user first encounters it live.

  • Noom — generates a personalized program summary after its own habits questionnaire, explaining how ongoing tracking will work before the user opens their plan.

  • Robinhood — introduces new account features (e.g., recurring investments) with a similar short mechanic explanation before linking to the live feature.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (result-ready confirmation + on-demand mechanic explanation + deferred link to the actual feature) fits any flow where a personalization process produces an ongoing, interactive feature (not just a static report), and where understanding the mechanic in advance meaningfully improves first-use comprehension.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for features that are simple, static, or self-explanatory on sight (e.g., a one-time summary page) — inserting an explanatory bulleted breakdown before something the user could understand instantly just by looking at it would add unnecessary friction.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 8
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen closes the loop on the spending-limit explanation from the prior chat exchange with a single, highly memorable visual metaphor: coins poured like salt from a shaker, paired with a punny proverb ("A spend limit a day keeps the overdraft away," riffing on "an apple a day keeps the doctor away"). Rather than a plain confirmation screen, Cleo uses wordplay and a custom illustration to make an abstract financial concept (a daily spending cap) memorable and slightly humorous, continuing the pattern established throughout onboarding of translating dry financial mechanics into visual and verbal wit. The small brain-emoji avatar beneath the message bubble is a distinctive touch — likely signaling this specific tip/tagline as a piece of "financial wisdom" or insight, visually distinct from Cleo's own chat avatar seen elsewhere.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "YOU'RE ALL SET" is short, declarative, and confidence-building — a clean sign-off after a fairly information-dense sequence of quiz questions and mechanic explanations. The proverb-style tagline ("A spend limit a day keeps the overdraft away") is a clever wordplay device that repackages a real financial consequence (overdraft fees) into something closer to a nursery rhyme than a warning — light enough to be memorable and shareable, while still communicating genuine stakes. This continues Cleo's consistent strategy across the entire flow: taking topics that could otherwise feel punitive or anxiety-inducing (spending limits, overdrafts) and wrapping them in playful, non-threatening language.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Metaphor aids retention — the coin-salt-shaker visual and proverb wordplay make an abstract mechanic (daily spend limit) more memorable than a plain text explanation would.

  • Consequence framed without alarm — referencing "overdraft" (a real financial penalty) inside a lighthearted proverb format keeps the stakes present without inducing anxiety, consistent with Cleo's established tone strategy.

  • Clear closure signal — "YOU'RE ALL SET" gives an unambiguous sense of completion after a multi-step explanation sequence, useful for orienting the user before the next screen/action.

  • Distinct avatar for tips/wisdom content — using a different icon (brain emoji) than Cleo's standard chat avatar may help visually distinguish "insight/tip" moments from regular conversational turns, aiding scannability in a chat-based interface.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo — uses similarly punny, proverb-style microcopy to reinforce app mechanics (e.g., streak reminders) in a memorable, non-threatening way.

  • Headspace — closes feature-explanation sequences with short, confidence-building confirmation screens ("You're all set") before returning the user to the main app.

  • Mint (Intuit), historically — used comparable illustrated metaphors to explain budgeting mechanics in a visually engaging, non-clinical way.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (proverb-style wordplay + custom illustration + clear "all set" closure) fits any product moment introducing a new ongoing mechanic with real financial or behavioral stakes, where making the concept memorable and non-threatening improves the odds the user actually internalizes and uses the feature.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for regulatory or compliance-critical disclosures where precise, unambiguous language matters more than memorability — wordplay and metaphor risk obscuring exact terms in contexts requiring legal clarity (e.g., actual fee structures or terms of a cash advance).

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 9
screens.uxAnalysis: This is the full, scrolled version of the previous screenshot, revealing that the salt-shaker proverb was only the first of a three-part extended metaphor: spend limit → harness → tornado protection. Building out the metaphor across multiple beats (rather than stopping at the proverb) reinforces the concept through repetition and escalation — a "harness" reframes the limit from a restriction into protective equipment, and "financial chaos 🌪️" gives the abstract downside (uncontrolled spending) a vivid, almost cinematic image. This layered explanation approach mirrors how the earlier onboarding "heads up" disclosure screen structured bad news, but here it's building anticipation and buy-in for a genuinely new, ongoing feature rather than softening a limitation — the multi-beat pacing lets the concept land progressively rather than all at once.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The extended metaphor sequence — spend limit as salt shaker, then reframed as a "harness," then explicitly protecting against "financial chaos 🌪️" — builds a coherent, escalating narrative rather than three disconnected one-liners. "Think of it as a harness..." followed by "There to protect you from financial chaos" reframes what could read as restrictive (a spending limit) into something protective and supportive, directly addressing a likely objection (nobody wants to feel controlled) before it's raised. This is a subtle but effective persuasion technique: naming the feature's downside interpretation and pre-emptively reframing it, rather than only describing the feature's mechanics as seen in the earlier explanation screen. The CTA "See updated budget 👀" (rather than a plain "Continue" or "Done") maintains anticipation and curiosity right up to the final tap, consistent with Cleo's established pattern of avoiding generic button copy at genuinely significant transition points.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Escalating metaphor builds conceptual buy-in — layering salt shaker → harness → tornado protection across three beats reinforces the idea more effectively than a single explanatory sentence would, using narrative pacing to aid retention.

  • Proactive reframing of a restrictive feature — explicitly naming the limit as protective ("harness," "protect you from financial chaos") pre-empts the natural objection that spending limits feel controlling, addressing it before the user forms that impression on their own.

  • Curiosity-driven closing CTA — "See updated budget 👀" maintains engagement and anticipation through the very last tap, rather than defaulting to neutral confirmation language.

  • Clear transition signal — this screen explicitly bridges from feature explanation into the live budget view, giving the user a concrete sense of "next, you'll see the real thing" rather than an abstract sense of completion.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Headspace — uses similarly extended, layered metaphors (e.g., "training your mind like a muscle") across multiple onboarding beats to build conceptual buy-in for an abstract practice.

  • Noom — reframes restrictive-sounding features (calorie budgets) as supportive tools using comparable protective/harness-style language before the user encounters them live.

  • Duolingo — closes feature-introduction sequences with curiosity-driven CTAs rather than generic "Continue" labels, matching Cleo's "See updated budget 👀" approach.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (multi-beat escalating metaphor + proactive reframing of a restrictive feature + curiosity-driven closing CTA) fits any onboarding moment introducing a feature that could otherwise feel limiting or controlling, where building emotional buy-in before the user encounters the feature live meaningfully improves adoption and reduces resistance.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for features that are unambiguously positive or require no persuasion (e.g., "here's your account balance") — layering an extended metaphor onto something the user already wants would slow the flow without adding value.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 10
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen introduces a distinct feature — bill tracking — using the same chat-bubble explanatory format and bold display-type headline established throughout Cleo's onboarding and feature-introduction screens, maintaining strong visual consistency even as it's likely presented at a different point in the user's journey (possibly triggered after some usage, not strictly during first-run onboarding). The color shift to purple background and mint-green CTA (versus the blue/indigo palette dominant elsewhere) may signal this is a distinct feature module or contextual entry point rather than the core onboarding flow, though the underlying interaction patterns (headline + explanatory bubbles + single CTA) remain identical to prior screens. Framing bill verification as something Cleo will do "for you" once confirmed reduces the perceived burden of manual bill tracking — the user's role is just confirmation, not ongoing data entry.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "Bills suck, but I can make them suck less" leads with blunt, relatable validation before pivoting to the value proposition — acknowledging the tedium of bill management rather than pretending the feature makes it delightful, which is a more credible, less oversold framing than typical marketing copy would use. "Confirm your bills here so I can track 'em for you 👇" is casual and direct, using contraction ('em) and an emoji pointing toward the action, maintaining the same familiar, low-formality register established throughout the app. This continues Cleo's consistent strategy of acknowledging the genuinely unpleasant aspects of personal finance (bills, overdrafts, overspending) honestly rather than glossing over them, which likely builds more credibility than relentless positivity would.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Honest acknowledgment builds credibility — "Bills suck" validates a real negative feeling before offering help, which tends to land as more trustworthy than pure positive-spin marketing copy.

  • Low-burden framing of the ask — "so I can track 'em for you" reframes bill verification as delegating a chore rather than adding a task, reducing perceived friction.

  • Consistent visual grammar across distinct features — reusing the headline + chat-bubble + single-CTA structure from prior onboarding screens for what's likely a different feature module reinforces a coherent design system across Cleo's broader product surface, not just its first-run flow.

  • Distinct CTA color for a distinct action type — the mint-green "Verify bills" button (versus the blue CTAs elsewhere) may help users visually distinguish confirmation/verification actions from standard navigation actions, though this can't be fully confirmed without seeing more of the app's color system.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Rocket Money — uses similarly blunt, relatable copy ("we hunt down your forgotten subscriptions") when introducing bill/subscription-tracking features.

  • Mint (Intuit), historically — introduced bill-tracking and reminder features with comparable illustrated, headline-driven interstitials before requiring user confirmation of detected bills.

  • Truebill/Rocket Money — matches the "confirm what we found" interaction pattern, where the user's role is verification rather than manual entry.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (validating a real pain point + low-burden confirmation framing + consistent visual grammar) fits any feature-introduction screen for an automation-style feature (the app does detection/tracking, the user just confirms), especially where the underlying task (like bill management) is widely perceived as tedious.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for features requiring extensive manual setup rather than simple confirmation — framing something as low-effort ("so I can track 'em for you") when it actually requires significant user input would create a mismatch between promised and actual effort, undermining trust.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 10
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a critical security checkpoint in the wallet onboarding flow, specifically for encrypting a cloud backup of the user's secret recovery phrase. The layout follows a strict single-column, single-task pattern: a clear back navigation, a bold headline ("Create Password"), a concise explanatory paragraph, a single password input, a mandatory acknowledgment checkbox, and a primary CTA. This minimal-choice architecture reduces cognitive load and funnels the user toward one action only.

The disabled/dimmed state of the "Continue" button is a deliberate progressive-disclosure technique — it visually communicates that the form is incomplete until both the password field is filled and the checkbox is ticked, preventing premature submission. The eye-icon toggle within the text field allows users to reveal/hide their password, balancing security (masking by default) with usability (verification before submission).

The dark theme with high-contrast white typography against a near-black background reinforces a "vault-like," serious, security-focused atmosphere appropriate for a financial/crypto product. The generous whitespace between the description and the input isolates the risk warning, ensuring it isn't skimmed past.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is direct, unembellished, and deliberately alarming where necessary — "We can't reset it if you lose it, so keep it safe" and "I won't be able to access my backup...losing all the crypto in my wallet" use blunt, consequence-driven language rather than soft reassurance. This is intentional: in self-custody crypto products, ambiguity about recovery leads to catastrophic loss, so the tone prioritizes clarity and legal/psychological accountability over friendliness.

The checkbox copy functions as an informed-consent contract, embedding legal links (terms, privacy policy) inline within the acknowledgment text rather than as separate footer links, tying legal consent directly to the security warning for maximum context.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explicit risk acknowledgment gate: Users must actively check a box confirming they understand irreversible loss consequences — this is a deliberate friction point that shifts responsibility and reduces support burden from "I lost my password" complaints.

  • Disabled CTA until requirements met: The visually muted "Continue" button acts as an implicit validation cue without needing explicit error messaging.

  • Password visibility toggle: Standard but essential affordance letting users confirm accuracy before committing to an unrecoverable secret.

  • Inline legal consent: Bundling terms/privacy acceptance with the security disclaimer streamlines compliance without adding a separate screen.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users (Coinbase Wallet) who are setting up encrypted cloud backups of their seed phrase — a mix of crypto-native and mainstream users who may not fully grasp the irreversibility of losing a non-custodial password. The psychological trigger here is loss aversion: by front-loading the catastrophic consequence of forgetting the password, the design leverages fear to increase attentiveness and encourage users to store the password securely (e.g., in a password manager) rather than treating it casually like a typical app password.

The forced checkbox also serves a commitment and consistency psychological principle — having users actively affirm understanding increases perceived personal responsibility and reduces blame-shifting behavior later.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when building any flow involving irreversible actions with high-stakes consequences — private key/seed phrase encryption, non-recoverable account deletion, or backup encryption for end-to-end encrypted data. It's ideal wherever standard "forgot password" recovery flows are impossible and users need explicit priming before proceeding.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this level of friction and alarming language for low-stakes or recoverable actions (e.g., standard app login, everyday settings) as it will feel unnecessarily intimidating and increase drop-off. Also avoid disabling the CTA without clear visual/text feedback explaining why it's disabled — if there's no secondary hint (like field validation state or a tooltip), users may feel confused about what's blocking progress.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 11
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a critical security checkpoint within the wallet creation flow, specifically for encrypting a cloud backup of the user's secret recovery phrase. The layout follows a strict single-column, single-task pattern: a back arrow and contextual header ("Confirm backup password"), a large bolded H1 ("Create Password") to reinforce the primary action, explanatory body copy, two password fields (create + confirm), a mandatory legal/risk acknowledgment checkbox, and a single full-width primary CTA.

The dark, near-black background paired with high-contrast white typography creates a serious, high-stakes atmosphere appropriate for a financial security action — this is not a playful screen, and the visual tone communicates that to the user subconsciously. The two stacked text fields with obscured/masked eye icons are visually identical in styling, reducing cognitive load since the user already understands password field conventions.

Critically, the primary "Continue" button is rendered in a muted/disabled-looking blue (low contrast text) because the checkbox has not yet been checked and/or fields are empty — this is a deliberate state-gating mechanism that prevents progression until the user has explicitly acknowledged the risk. The page control dots at the bottom indicate this is one step in a longer multi-step onboarding sequence, setting expectations for progress.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is direct, cautionary, and unambiguous. Phrases like "We can't reset it if you lose it, so keep it safe" and "I won't be able to access my backup, which could mean losing all the crypto in my wallet" use blunt, consequence-driven language rather than softening the stakes. This is intentional: crypto wallets deal with irreversible, self-custodied assets, so the tone must eliminate any illusion of a safety net (e.g., no "forgot password" flow exists).

The checkbox copy doubles as both a comprehension check and a legal consent mechanism (linking out to Terms and Privacy Policy), efficiently combining risk acknowledgment with compliance requirements in a single interaction rather than spreading it across multiple screens.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explicit risk framing before action: Rather than burying the "no recovery" warning in fine print, it's placed front-and-center in both the header description and the checkbox copy, ensuring informed consent for an irreversible action.

  • Gated CTA via mandatory checkbox: The Continue button's disabled/low-emphasis state until the checkbox is ticked acts as a forcing function, guaranteeing the user cannot accidentally skip past critical risk disclosure.

  • Password reveal toggles: The masked eye icon on both fields lets users visually verify what they've typed before committing to a password that, if forgotten, causes permanent asset loss — reducing typo-induced lockouts.

  • Double entry confirmation pattern: Requiring the password twice (create + confirm) prevents fat-finger errors from locking a user out of an unrecoverable encrypted backup.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets both crypto-curious newcomers and experienced self-custody users setting up a Coinbase Wallet (a non-custodial wallet, distinct from the custodial Coinbase exchange app). The psychological trigger at play is loss aversion combined with responsibility transfer: the app explicitly disclaims responsibility ("We can't reset it if you lose it") to set correct mental models about self-custody, preventing future support tickets and user frustration. The heavy warning language also serves a legal/liability purpose, protecting the company by ensuring informed consent is documented via the checkbox interaction.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever an application requires the user to create credentials or perform an action that is genuinely irreversible and has severe consequences — e.g., encryption keys, recovery phrases, wallet backups, or one-way account deletion. It's ideal when standard "forgot password" safety nets do not exist and the user must be made acutely aware of that fact before proceeding.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-handed warning approach for low-stakes password creation (e.g., a standard app login) as it will feel alarmist and increase abandonment unnecessarily. Also avoid disabling primary CTAs without clear visual/textual feedback explaining why the button is inactive — some users may not immediately understand the checkbox is a hard gate, so pairing it with inline validation or a tooltip is recommended for lower-friction implementations.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 12
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a critical security checkpoint within the wallet onboarding flow, specifically for encrypting a cloud backup of the user's secret recovery phrase. The layout follows a strict single-column, single-task structure to minimize cognitive load during a high-stakes action.

The visual hierarchy is deliberate: a bold H1 ("Create Password") anchors the screen, followed by a concise explanatory paragraph in muted gray to reduce visual noise while still delivering critical risk information. Two stacked password fields (password + confirmation) enforce input accuracy without needing a separate "success" state, since the Continue button gating occurs at the checkbox/agreement level. The eye-icon toggle inside each field is a well-established affordance for verifying sensitive text.

Crucially, the primary CTA ("Continue") is styled as a vibrant blue-to-teal gradient pill, contrasting sharply with the pure black background — this draws the eye immediately and signals forward progress, but it is functionally blocked until the mandatory checkbox is acknowledged. The progress bar at the bottom (thin white pill) subtly signals the user is mid-flow, providing reassurance that the task is scoped and finite.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy tone is direct, sober, and consequence-driven rather than celebratory — appropriate for a self-custody crypto wallet. Phrases like "We can't reset it if you lose it" and "could mean losing all the crypto in my wallet" are intentionally blunt, avoiding euphemism to ensure the user cannot claim ignorance of the risk later.

The checkbox copy functions as an explicit, legally-informed acknowledgment (akin to a liability waiver) rather than a simple terms-of-service checkbox, reinforcing personal responsibility in a non-custodial system. Embedded hyperlinks ("terms" and "privacy policy") are color-coded in blue to stand out from the surrounding gray-white text without needing separate buttons.
screens.keyHighlights:

  • Double password entry: Confirms intent and reduces typos for a credential that has no recovery mechanism.

  • Checkbox-gated CTA: Forces active, conscious consent (not just a passive scroll) before enabling the high-stakes "Continue" action, functioning as a psychological commitment device.

  • High-contrast gradient CTA on black canvas: Creates a premium, security-vault aesthetic consistent with crypto/fintech branding while keeping visual focus on the single next action.

  • Reveal/hide password toggle: Reduces input errors for a critical, unrecoverable credential.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users, ranging from crypto-native power users to newcomers migrating from custodial exchanges. Because losing this password results in permanent, irreversible loss of funds, the design leans heavily on loss aversion and explicit informed consent psychological triggers rather than persuasive/marketing techniques used elsewhere in the app. The stark black background and serious tone are intended to snap the user out of "casual app" mode and into a heightened state of attention, mirroring patterns used in legal/financial disclosure screens.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a user is about to set a credential or complete an action with severe, irreversible consequences — e.g., wallet seed phrase backups, account deletion, encryption keys, or financial transfers. It's ideal any time you need documented, active user acknowledgment of risk before enabling a destructive or high-stakes irreversible action.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-handed, risk-laden approach for low-stakes or reversible actions (e.g., changing an app theme or a recoverable account password), as it will feel alarmist and increase drop-off/friction unnecessarily. Also avoid stacking multiple full paragraphs of risk copy on flows where the user is already fatigued (e.g., deep into a 10+ step onboarding), as comprehension will drop — consider chunking into a dedicated warning screen instead.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 13
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen manages one of the highest-stakes interactions in any crypto product: displaying and safeguarding a 12-word seed phrase. The layout prioritizes clarity and caution over speed. A status indicator ("Backed up to iCloud") sits prominently at the top, immediately reassuring the user that the critical failure mode—loss of funds due to a lost phrase—has already been mitigated.

The recovery phrase itself is presented in a blurred/obscured card, a deliberate shoulder-surfing and screenshot-leak mitigation pattern. The user must intentionally reveal or copy the content, adding friction that guards against accidental exposure in public or recorded contexts (e.g., screen recording, screen sharing).

Actions are hierarchically color-coded: the neutral "Change backup password" button uses a muted dark tone, while the destructive "Delete iCloud backup" action is rendered in alarming red at the very bottom, separated spatially to reduce the chance of an accidental irreversible tap. This visual hierarchy reinforces which actions are safe versus dangerous, guiding user behavior through color psychology alone.

The generous whitespace and single-column vertical flow reduce cognitive load, letting the dense security warnings breathe and be read carefully rather than skimmed.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is direct, imperative, and urgent without being alarmist: "Never share these words," "Coinbase will never ask you for them." This directly counters common phishing/social-engineering attacks by pre-emptively educating the user on what a legitimate request looks like.

The explanatory paragraph uses plain language ("This phrase lets you recover your wallet if you lose your device") to demystify a technically complex concept (BIP-39 mnemonic phrases) for a non-technical audience, reinforcing trust through transparency rather than jargon.

The dual recommendation—"Back it up on iCloud (recommended) or write it down. Or both."—offers flexible options while nudging toward the safer, redundant path, respecting user autonomy while still guiding best practice.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Blurred/obscured seed phrase display prevents passive shoulder-surfing or accidental screen-recording leaks until the user deliberately interacts.

  • Status badge confirmation ("Backed up to iCloud") gives immediate peace of mind and reduces anxiety about data loss.

  • Color-coded action hierarchy: neutral gray for reversible actions vs. red for destructive/irreversible ones (Delete iCloud backup), leveraging color psychology to prevent costly mistakes.

  • Explicit anti-phishing messaging baked directly into the security copy, proactively inoculating users against social engineering.

  • Copy to clipboard shortcut reduces transcription errors when moving the phrase to a password manager or paper backup.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users—ranging from crypto-native power users to newcomers onboarded via Coinbase's ecosystem—who bear full personal responsibility for asset security. The design leans heavily on loss aversion and fear-based motivation (irreversible fund theft) balanced with reassurance (backup confirmation) to keep users engaged rather than panicked. It also exploits the authority/trust heuristic by explicitly stating "Coinbase will never ask you for them," building brand-level trust that outlasts the interaction itself and helps users recognize scams elsewhere.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an application must surface highly sensitive, unrecoverable secrets (seed phrases, API keys, 2FA backup codes, encryption keys). It's ideal for:

  • Self-custody wallets and password managers exporting master credentials.

  • Any flow where a single leaked string can cause irreversible financial or security damage.

  • Situations requiring a mix of soft reassurance (backup status) and hard warnings (irreversible loss/theft language).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-handed security framing for low-stakes data (e.g., regular account settings, non-sensitive preferences)—it would create unnecessary anxiety and friction. Also avoid displaying sensitive secrets in plaintext by default; always default to an obscured state to prevent accidental exposure in screenshots, recordings, or over-the-shoulder viewing. Don't use alarming red destructive buttons for actions that are easily reversible, as this dilutes the signal for genuinely dangerous actions elsewhere in the app.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 17
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen presents a binary decision point during crypto wallet creation, asking the user to choose their preferred wallet security/backup mechanism. The layout uses two large, tappable card tiles stacked vertically, each representing a distinct security paradigm: Passkey (modern, device-based biometric/cloud authentication) versus Recovery phrase (traditional, self-custodied 12-word seed phrase).

The dark, minimal theme with generous whitespace reduces cognitive load, allowing the two options to be the sole focus. Each card uses a consistent structure: an icon, a bold title, and a short descriptive subtitle explaining the underlying mechanism and its trust anchors (iCloud, Google, Yubikey vs. self-held 12 words). This structure supports quick scanning and comparison without needing to tap into either option to understand the trade-off.

Notably, the "Passkey" option is positioned first (top), signaling it as the recommended/default modern path, aligning with the industry-wide push toward passwordless, passkey-based authentication as the friendlier onboarding choice for less crypto-savvy users. The Recovery phrase option is preserved below for power users or those wary of custodial/cloud dependencies.

The back arrow in the top-left maintains user control and reversibility, critical in a flow as consequential as wallet security setup.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is concise, technical-but-accessible, and avoids jargon overload. "Secured by a passkey in iCloud, Google, Yubikey, password managers, and more" educates the user on multi-platform compatibility in a single line, building confidence that they won't be locked into one ecosystem.

The Recovery phrase description is deliberately terse — "Secured by your 12-word secret recovery phrase" — reflecting that this is the well-known, legacy crypto standard that needs little explanation to its target audience.

The title "Create wallet" is direct and functional, setting a task-oriented tone rather than a marketing one, appropriate for a security-critical setup step rather than a promotional screen.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Progressive disclosure via comparison cards: Both security paths are shown side-by-side (stacked) with just enough detail to make an informed choice without overwhelming the user with cryptographic detail.

  • Passkey-first ordering: Placing the more modern, lower-friction Passkey option above the traditional Recovery Phrase nudges new/mainstream users toward an easier, less error-prone security setup, reducing onboarding drop-off and support tickets from lost seed phrases.

  • Icon language reinforcement: The key/person icon and the asterisk/seed icon visually differentiate the two mental models (identity-based vs. secret-based) at a glance.

  • Neutral dark canvas: Removes visual distraction, appropriate for a decision that carries real financial/security stakes.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets both crypto-native users who expect and trust the traditional 12-word recovery phrase standard, and mainstream/new users onboarding into Web3 who may be intimidated by seed phrases and prefer familiar biometric/passkey flows they already use for banking or social apps.

Psychologically, this leverages the familiarity heuristic — presenting Passkey using recognizable brand names (iCloud, Google, Yubikey) reduces perceived risk and taps into trust already established with those platforms. For the Recovery Phrase option, it appeals to autonomy and self-custody values prized by crypto purists who don't want reliance on third-party cloud providers.

Offering a choice rather than forcing one method also respects varying risk tolerances and technical literacy, which increases completion rates in onboarding funnels.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when onboarding users into systems with multiple valid security/backup mechanisms (e.g., crypto wallets, password managers, secure note apps) where the trade-offs (convenience vs. self-custody control) are significant enough to warrant explicit, informed user choice rather than a forced default.

Also effective when trying to widen the on-ramp for both technical and non-technical audiences within the same product, by presenting the lower-friction/modern option prominently while still preserving the legacy/expert option for continuity.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern if the choice is inconsequential or fully reversible later, as it introduces unnecessary friction into onboarding — in such cases, a single smart default should be used instead of forcing a decision upfront.

Also avoid presenting two security paradigms as equally weighted, unlabeled options if one is strictly better/safer for most users; consider adding a "Recommended" badge to reduce decision paralysis and prevent security-naive users from choosing a riskier path (e.g., self-storing a seed phrase insecurely) without proper warnings.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 14
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen employs a layered modal pattern where a bottom sheet confirmation overlays a dimmed background screen (the actual "Back up your wallet" instructional content). This visual hierarchy is a deliberate psychological technique — the background text is grayed out/blurred to signal it is temporarily inaccessible until the user resolves the foreground task, reducing cognitive load by focusing attention on a single decision point.

The bottom sheet uses a self-custody security "gate" pattern common in Web3 wallets: before the user can proceed, they must explicitly attest via a checkbox that they've completed a critical, irreversible security task (saving their 12-word seed phrase). The primary CTA ("Complete backup") is visually present but functionally gated by the checkbox — a classic progressive disclosure / commitment gate that prevents users from skipping an essential security step out of impatience.

The illustration (a stylized key with a checkmark) reinforces the metaphor of "securing access" and lends a moment of visual reward/reassurance amid an otherwise anxiety-inducing security task. The secondary "Cancel" button is present but de-emphasized (gray, low contrast) to nudge users toward completion rather than abandonment.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is serious, direct, and protective — appropriate for an irreversible financial security action. Phrases like "Never share these words. Anyone who learns them can steal all of your crypto" use vivid loss-aversion language to underscore stakes without being alarmist.

Coinbase proactively builds trust and combats phishing by stating "Coinbase will never ask you for them" — a defensive copy pattern designed to inoculate users against social engineering attacks that impersonate the brand.

The checkbox label doubles as a legal consent mechanism, bundling the security acknowledgment with Terms and Privacy Policy agreement — an efficient pattern that reduces friction by combining two required confirmations into one gesture, while still remaining legally binding via explicit affirmative action.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed background layering: Creates focus and hierarchy, visually "locking" prior content until the current task is acknowledged.

  • Gated primary action via checkbox: Forces explicit user attestation before allowing progression, reducing support tickets from users who lost access due to skipped backups.

  • Combined legal + safety consent: Merges terms/privacy agreement with the security confirmation into a single checkbox, minimizing extra steps.

  • Reassuring iconography: The key + checkmark illustration transforms a stressful security task into a moment of visual accomplishment.

  • De-emphasized escape hatch: "Cancel" is available but styled to be subordinate, discouraging drop-off without fully blocking it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users, many of whom are new to managing private keys and are highly vulnerable to loss-of-funds scenarios due to lost or unrecorded seed phrases. The design leverages fear of irreversible loss (loss aversion bias) to motivate careful action, while the explicit checkbox leverages the commitment and consistency principle — once a user affirms they've saved the phrase, they're more likely to have actually done so, and Coinbase gains a documented record of user acknowledgment for liability protection.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any irreversible, high-stakes action where user negligence could cause catastrophic loss (e.g., crypto key backup, account deletion with data loss, disabling 2FA). It's ideal when you need a documented, explicit user attestation before allowing progress, and when combining legal consent with safety confirmation streamlines the flow without diluting importance.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-handed gating pattern for low-stakes or reversible actions — it adds unnecessary friction and can frustrate users completing routine tasks. Also avoid bundling unrelated consents (e.g., marketing opt-ins) into a security checkbox, as this can create legal ambiguity or erode trust. Do not use if the underlying action doesn't warrant the anxiety this UI intentionally provokes.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 15
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen uses a layered modal (Bottom Sheet) pattern to confirm a critical, irreversible security step within a self-custody crypto wallet setup flow. The background screen ("Back up your wallet") is dimmed and pushed back, while a bottom sheet slides up to demand explicit confirmation before proceeding. This layering visually reinforces that the user must complete a sub-task (acknowledging the phrase was saved) before the parent flow can continue.

The visual hierarchy is deliberately structured: a reassuring illustration (a shield/key motif in brand gradient colors) sits above a direct yes/no-style question, followed by a mandatory checkbox that bundles two distinct commitments (saving the phrase + agreeing to legal terms) into one interaction. This checkbox-gating pattern is a classic friction-by-design choice — it slows the user down at the single most dangerous point in the entire onboarding flow: losing/leaking a seed phrase means permanent, irrecoverable loss of funds with no customer support recourse.

The primary CTA "Complete backup" uses a vibrant blue-to-teal gradient that contrasts sharply against the near-black background, drawing the eye and signaling forward progress, while "Cancel" is rendered as a low-emphasis dark gray pill, deprioritized but still easily accessible — respecting user agency without encouraging exit.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is direct, urgent, and unambiguous — deliberately avoiding softening language given the severity of the consequences ("Anyone who learns them can steal all of your crypto"). This is a rare instance where a fintech product intentionally uses fear-based language rather than reassurance-first copy, because the cost of user complacency is catastrophic and irreversible.

The question "Did you save all 12 words?" is phrased as a direct, personal checkpoint rather than a generic disclaimer, increasing the user's sense of individual accountability. The checkbox label smartly combines a security acknowledgment with legal consent ("terms" and "privacy policy" as inline links), reducing screen count while maintaining compliance coverage.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Two-layer confirmation architecture: Stacking a confirmation sheet on top of the informational backup screen visually and functionally separates "read the warning" from "confirm you understood it," reducing accidental dismissal.

  • Combined checkbox for security + legal consent: Efficiently merges an active-acknowledgment step with T&Cs/privacy agreement, minimizing extra steps without diluting the seriousness of the security warning.

  • Asymmetric button treatment: High-contrast gradient CTA vs. muted "Cancel" pill clearly communicates the intended path while preserving an easy way out.

  • Brand-consistent illustration used to soften a high-anxiety moment: The abstract shield/checkmark/key graphic injects a moment of calm and trust into an otherwise high-stakes security checkpoint.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users, ranging from onboarding crypto newcomers to experienced holders, at the exact moment they take on full personal responsibility for their private keys. The design leans heavily on loss-aversion psychology — emphasizing catastrophic, irreversible consequences ("steal all of your crypto") to override the natural tendency to skip security steps during onboarding.

The mandatory checkbox exploits the commitment and consistency principle: by physically checking a box affirming "Yes, I saved my recovery phrase," users are nudged toward genuinely completing the backup rather than clicking through blindly, which reduces support tickets and irrecoverable fund loss down the line — a major business risk for a non-custodial wallet provider like Coinbase Wallet.
screens.whereToUse:
• Any flow involving generation or display of irreproducible secrets (seed phrases, private keys, one-time backup codes) where the consequence of loss is permanent and severe.

  • Legal/compliance moments where explicit, logged user consent is required before proceeding (e.g., terms acceptance bundled with a critical security action).

  • High-stakes destructive or irreversible actions where you want to add deliberate friction to prevent careless taps (e.g., wallet deletion, account closure, financial transfers).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy-handed, anxiety-inducing pattern for low-stakes or easily reversible actions — it will feel excessive and erode trust through unnecessary alarm.

  • Don't bundle unrelated consents (e.g., marketing opt-in) into a security checkbox; it dilutes the seriousness of the message and can create compliance ambiguity.

  • Avoid stacking multiple modal layers for routine confirmations, as excessive layering fatigues users and can lead to blind rapid-tap dismissal, undermining the very safeguard being designed.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 16
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen tackles one of the highest-stakes moments in the self-custody crypto onboarding flow: securing the seed phrase. The layout is intentionally sparse and linear, removing all distractions so the user's full attention is directed at the security warning, the sensitive data, and the single required action.

The information hierarchy is deliberate: a status badge ("Not backed up to iCloud") sits at the top like a persistent warning label, followed by two distinct paragraphs of body copy that separate the "danger" message from the "instructional" message. This chunking prevents cognitive overload by not mixing warnings with mechanics in a single wall of text.

The recovery phrase itself is rendered in a bordered card with the text blurred/obscured by default — a shoulder-surfing and screenshot-mitigation pattern that forces a deliberate reveal action (implied) before the words are exposed. A small icon in the card likely toggles visibility. Below the card, a low-emphasis "Copy to clipboard" text-link offers a secondary, less risky path than manual transcription.

The primary CTA, "Back up on iCloud," uses a vivid gradient (blue-to-teal) that visually pops against the otherwise monochrome black-and-grey interface — a clear visual weight signal that this is the recommended, safest path. The back arrow at top-left preserves the ability to exit without commitment, respecting user autonomy in a moment that could otherwise feel coercive.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy tone is authoritative and protective, almost like a security briefing. Phrases such as "Never share these words" and "Coinbase will never ask you for them" are classic anti-phishing conditioning lines, designed to inoculate the user against future social-engineering attacks by setting a firm behavioral norm early.

The writing avoids technical jargon (no mention of "BIP-39" or "entropy") and instead frames the recovery phrase functionally: "This phrase lets you recover your wallet if you lose your device." This benefit-first framing helps non-technical users understand *why* they should care, not just *what* to do.

The status label "Not backed up to iCloud" is intentionally alarming (red dot/X icon) to create urgency without being a full error state — it's informational but colored to provoke action.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Blurred sensitive data by default: The seed phrase is obscured until explicitly revealed, protecting against shoulder-surfing, screen recording malware, and accidental screenshots.

  • Dual backup pathways: Offering both "Back up on iCloud" (primary, effortless) and "Copy to clipboard" (secondary, manual) respects different user risk tolerances and technical comfort levels.

  • Persistent status indicator: The "Not backed up to iCloud" badge acts as a lightweight progress/warning signal that can likely change state once the backup completes, giving the user closure.

  • High-contrast gradient CTA: The single vivid button on an otherwise dark, neutral screen unmistakably directs the eye toward the recommended safe action.

  • Explicit anti-phishing messaging: "Coinbase will never ask you for them" preemptively defends users against future scam attempts referencing the wallet's own brand authority.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets both crypto newcomers setting up their first self-custody wallet and experienced users who still need a guided, low-error backup flow. The design leans heavily on loss-aversion psychology — by foregrounding the catastrophic risk ("Anyone who learns them can steal all of your crypto") before showing the actual phrase, it primes users to treat the following screen with appropriate gravity.

The blur-by-default mechanic also reduces liability for Coinbase: it discourages careless screenshotting, which is a leading cause of seed-phrase theft via cloud photo-sync services or malware. The offering of iCloud backup as "recommended" nudges users toward a recoverable path (reducing support tickets and lost-wallet complaints) while still preserving the self-custody ethos by allowing manual copy as an alternative.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an application must present highly sensitive, unrecoverable, one-time-view credentials — such as crypto seed phrases, API secret keys, 2FA backup codes, or encryption recovery keys. It's ideal for:

  • Self-custody wallet onboarding or wallet migration flows.

  • Developer platforms issuing one-time API secrets.

  • Password manager master-key or recovery-kit generation.

The blur-then-reveal plus dual backup-method approach is especially valuable when the cost of exposure (theft, screenshot leaks) is severe and irreversible.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy warning treatment for low-stakes or easily-recoverable data — excessive alarm fatigue will erode trust if applied to routine settings changes or non-destructive actions. Do not use blurred reveal-on-tap patterns for data users need to reference repeatedly during a flow, as it adds friction; and avoid pushing a single third-party backup method (like iCloud) as the sole "recommended" option in privacy-sensitive contexts where users may prefer fully offline custody, as this could conflict with self-sovereignty expectations of crypto-native audiences.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 22
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen captures the Coinbase Wallet home/dashboard with a Wallets bottom sheet modal overlaid on top, triggered by tapping the "Address 1" selector in the top-left. The sheet uses a partial-height drawer pattern, letting the underlying home screen (balance, watchlist, trending swaps) remain visible and dimmed, which reinforces context and reduces the feeling of a jarring context switch.

The sheet itself is organized as a clean stacked list, grouping identities under "WALLET 1" and "WALLET 2" labels. Each wallet row uses an avatar (an NFT/emoji-style profile picture), a human-readable ENS-style name (alexsmithmobbin.cb.id) or generic label (Address 1), and a USD balance — prioritizing recognizability over raw hex addresses, a critical usability win for a product where addresses are otherwise long, error-prone strings.

A checkmark badge clearly marks the currently active address, giving unambiguous system status feedback. The sticky footer CTA "Add & manage wallets" with a gear icon anchors the sheet, providing an obvious, always-visible escape hatch to deeper wallet management without cluttering the primary list.

The drag handle at the bottom edge signals further interaction affordance (dismiss via swipe), consistent with native iOS/Android sheet conventions.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy is minimal, functional, and confidence-inspiring: "Wallets," "Total: $0.00," "Add & manage wallets." There is no unnecessary jargon or crypto-native slang that could intimidate a mainstream "busy urban" user. Balances are shown in familiar USD rather than raw token units, lowering cognitive load for people who are not deeply versed in crypto denominations.

The all-caps section labels ("WALLET 1", "WALLET 2") create clear visual hierarchy and scannability, letting users quickly locate the specific wallet/account they want without reading full sentences — ideal for someone glancing at their phone between meetings or while commuting.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Human-readable identity resolution: Displaying "alexsmithmobbin.cb.id" instead of a 42-character hex address dramatically improves trust and reduces the risk of sending funds to the wrong place.

  • Non-blocking modal context: The bottom sheet only covers ~60% of the screen, keeping the home dashboard peeking through above, so users retain spatial orientation.

  • Explicit active-state indicator: The blue checkmark next to "Address 1" removes any ambiguity about which wallet is currently in use before performing a transaction.

  • Persistent management CTA: "Add & manage wallets" is pinned at the bottom, always reachable regardless of list length, following the thumb-zone ergonomics best practice for one-handed mobile use.

  • Aggregate total balance: Showing "Total: $0.00" at the sheet header gives an at-a-glance portfolio snapshot across all wallets before drilling into any single one.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets busy urban professionals who likely manage multiple crypto identities (a personal wallet, a work/DAO wallet, an NFT-flexing ENS identity) and need to switch between them rapidly and confidently while on the go. The design leans on the psychological principle of reducing choice friction — by surfacing avatars and human names instead of addresses, it triggers faster System-1 recognition rather than slow, effortful System-2 verification of long strings.

The checkmark and balance-per-wallet also tap into loss-aversion and safety reassurance: self-custody users are highly anxious about sending assets from/to the wrong address, so this screen's clarity directly mitigates a top source of crypto-native anxiety.
screens.whereToUse: Use a bottom sheet wallet/account switcher pattern whenever an app supports multiple identities, profiles, or accounts that a user must frequently toggle between (multi-wallet crypto apps, multi-account banking apps, team/workspace switchers in SaaS tools). It's ideal when the switch action is frequent but shouldn't warrant a full-screen navigation, and when preserving background context aids orientation.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if there are more than 8-10 accounts, since an unpaginated flat list in a sheet becomes hard to scan and would benefit from search/filter instead. It's also unsuitable for irreversible, high-stakes account switches (e.g., switching a live trading session) without an additional confirmation step, since a simple tap in a sheet may be too frictionless for consequential state changes. Additionally, avoid stacking too much financial complexity (fees, gas, chain indicators) inside this compact layout, as it can quickly overload the minimal design.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 18
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen represents the first step in a critical, high-stakes onboarding flow for a crypto wallet application. The layout follows a strict single-column, single-purpose structure that minimizes cognitive load while priming the user for the security responsibility they are about to undertake.

The segmented progress bar at the top immediately sets expectations that this is a multi-step process (3 steps), reducing abandonment anxiety by showing the user exactly how much commitment is required. The dark, near-black background is a deliberate choice common in fintech/crypto apps—it signals sophistication, security, and reduces eye strain, while allowing the vibrant abstract illustration (a stylized "key" or "puzzle" motif in blue/yellow/cyan) to pop as the visual focal point.

The information hierarchy is clean: large bold headline, decorative illustration, explanatory body copy, and a single high-contrast gradient CTA button. There is no clutter, no competing actions, and no secondary navigation—forcing the user's full attention onto understanding the concept of a "secret recovery phrase" before proceeding. The back arrow in the top-left preserves user control without disrupting the linear flow.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is direct, reassuring, and educational rather than technical or jargon-heavy. "Create a new wallet" is an active, ownership-oriented headline that feels empowering rather than intimidating.

The body text uses plain language ("Your new wallet will be secured by...") instead of crypto-native terminology alone, briefly explaining the concept of a secret recovery phrase for newcomers. The imperative safety instructions—"write it down and don't share it with anyone"—are short, punchy, and unambiguous, leveraging urgency and authority to ensure critical security behavior is not skipped or glossed over.

The "Learn more" link is a low-commitment escape valve for curious or cautious users who want more detail without breaking the primary flow, respecting different user knowledge levels.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented progress indicator: Clearly communicates flow length and current position, reducing perceived effort and abandonment risk in a sensitive setup process.

  • Single dominant CTA: The gradient "Continue" button is the only actionable element, eliminating decision paralysis at a moment requiring full user attention.

  • Abstract, non-literal illustration: Avoids scary technical imagery (like seed phrases or private keys) in favor of a friendly, colorful abstract motif that keeps the tone approachable despite the high-stakes subject matter.

  • Plain-language security education: Translates a complex crypto concept (recovery phrase) into simple, actionable instructions before the user even sees the phrase itself, priming correct behavior in advance.

  • Deferred detail via "Learn more": Keeps the primary path lightweight while still offering an out for users who need reassurance or more information.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets first-time or newly onboarding crypto wallet users, particularly those who may be unfamiliar with self-custody concepts like seed phrases. The design leans on priming and expectation-setting psychology: by explaining the security model before showing the actual recovery phrase, it reduces panic or confusion at the critical moment and increases the likelihood that users will actually write down and safeguard their phrase.

The dark theme and premium gradient button also target a tech-savvy, design-conscious audience that expects a polished, "Web3-native" aesthetic similar to leading wallets (e.g., Rainbow, MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet). The step indicator leverages the Zeigarnik effect—users are more likely to complete a task once they've started and can see visible progress toward completion.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any high-stakes, security-critical onboarding step where the user must be educated before performing an irreversible or sensitive action (e.g., generating encryption keys, backup codes, account recovery setup). It's ideal for multi-step wizards where each step isolates a single concept, and works well whenever you need to set behavioral expectations (like "don't share this") ahead of revealing sensitive data.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, isolated single-concept-per-screen approach for low-stakes or frequently repeated flows, as the extra step and full-screen explanation would feel like unnecessary friction. It's also not ideal for expert/power users who already understand the concept and would benefit more from a condensed or skippable flow. Additionally, avoid vague abstract illustrations if your audience needs highly literal, trust-building imagery (e.g., a lock icon) to feel secure.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 21
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a critical checkpoint in a crypto wallet's onboarding flow, appearing immediately after a user has been shown their 12-word secret recovery phrase. Rather than simply trusting the user clicked "I saved it," the app forces an active recall test: tap the 1st word, then the 12th word, from a shuffled word bank (implied by the grid area below the instructions).

The layout is deliberately minimal and high-contrast (dark background, single focal instruction) to eliminate distraction during a moment that requires full attention. A 3-segment progress bar at the top signals this is step 2 or 3 of a short, finite onboarding sequence, reducing anxiety about how much work remains. The back arrow allows users to return to the phrase if they failed to save it — a crucial escape hatch given the catastrophic consequences of losing wallet access.

The single, full-width gradient CTA ("Continue") is disabled or inert until the verification logic is satisfied elsewhere on screen (in the word-grid area, currently rendered blank/placeholder in this capture), enforcing task completion before progression.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The headline "You saved it, right?" is conversational, almost cheeky, breaking from the sterile, technical tone typical of security flows. This humanizes a high-stakes moment and reduces intimidation for non-technical users entering the crypto space.

The supporting copy is precise and instructional: it tells the user exactly what to do ("tapping the first (1st) then last (12th) word") with numeric reinforcement (1st, 12th) to avoid ambiguity. This is copy written for zero-tolerance error scenarios — there is no room for the user to misinterpret the task.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Active recall over passive confirmation: Instead of a checkbox ("I saved my phrase"), the app requires the user to prove retention by identifying specific words, dramatically reducing the number of users who lose funds due to unsaved seed phrases.

  • Conversational microcopy: "You saved it, right?" injects personality and urgency without being alarming, softening an otherwise high-anxiety security step.

  • Segmented progress bar: Gives users a clear sense of finite, short remaining effort, which is especially important during friction-heavy security setup.

  • Escape hatch via back navigation: Lets users who didn't actually save the phrase return and fix their mistake rather than being trapped or forced to guess.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new crypto wallet users, many of whom are unfamiliar with self-custody and the irreversible nature of losing a seed phrase. The design leans on the psychological principle of the testing effect (retrieval practice improves retention far better than re-reading), ensuring the user has genuinely internalized or physically recorded their recovery phrase before they can proceed.

It also mitigates a well-documented support burden for wallet providers: users who skip past the seed-phrase screen without saving it, then lose access permanently. By gating progression behind a verification quiz, the product protects both the user and its own support/reputation costs.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a user is issued a piece of information that is irrecoverable if lost and non-transmittable by the app itself (e.g., recovery codes, encryption keys, master passwords, backup codes for 2FA). It's ideal anywhere the cost of user error is catastrophic and silent (no error message will ever fire later — the user just loses access one day).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavier verification friction for low-stakes or easily recoverable data (e.g., a username or a preference setting) — it will feel like unnecessary busywork and increase drop-off. Also avoid it if the underlying system can recover the credential another way (e.g., email-based password reset), since the security theater isn't justified by real risk.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 19
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a critical security checkpoint within a multi-step wallet creation flow, indicated by the segmented progress bar at the top. The layout follows a strict linear hierarchy: a bold headline, an explanatory two-paragraph body, a visually obscured "reveal" container for the sensitive data, a secondary "Copy to clipboard" action, and finally two mutually exclusive CTAs for completing the backup.

The most important interaction design decision is the default blurred/obscured state of the 12-word recovery phrase. This acts as a passive security gate — even though the user is alone, the app defaults to shoulder-surfing protection, forcing an explicit tap-to-reveal gesture (implied by the eye/diamond icon) before the sensitive credential is exposed. This adds friction intentionally, which signals to the user the gravity of the content.

The choice architecture at the bottom is also deliberate: the high-contrast, gradient-filled "Back up on iCloud" button is visually dominant, nudging users toward the easier, lower-abandonment cloud backup path, while "Back up manually" is styled as a flat, muted secondary button for power users who prefer self-custody of the phrase (e.g., writing it on paper). This is a classic default-bias pattern that reduces support tickets from users who lose a manually recorded phrase, while still preserving the non-custodial ethos of crypto wallets by not forcing cloud dependency.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is calm, direct, and slightly cautionary without being alarmist — appropriate for a high-stakes financial security moment. Phrases like "used to recover your crypto if you lose your phone" clearly state the functional purpose, while "never share them with anyone" injects an urgent security warning in plain language rather than jargon.

The tone avoids technical terms like "BIP-39 mnemonic," opting instead for the friendlier "12 words" and "secret recovery phrase," which lowers cognitive load for non-technical or first-time crypto users. The instructional framing ("Save these 12 words in a secure location, such as a password manager") also proactively guides best practices instead of assuming user knowledge.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Obscured-by-default secrets: The recovery phrase is blurred until explicitly revealed, preventing accidental exposure via screen recording, screenshots, or shoulder surfing.

  • Dual backup paths with visual hierarchy: A prominent gradient CTA nudges most users toward the safer, low-friction iCloud backup, while a muted secondary option preserves manual self-custody for advanced users.

  • Progress indicator: The segmented bar at the top sets expectations that this is one of several onboarding steps, reducing perceived effort and abandonment risk.

  • Copy-to-clipboard affordance: Reduces transcription errors when users choose to paste the phrase into a password manager.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new crypto wallet users during account creation — a mix of crypto-native users who understand self-custody risks and mainstream users onboarding into their first non-custodial wallet. The psychological trigger at play is loss aversion: the copy and obscured phrase emphasize the catastrophic, irreversible consequence of losing this phrase ("used to recover your crypto if you lose your phone"), motivating careful action.

The design also leverages the default effect / path of least resistance by visually emphasizing the iCloud backup option, capitalizing on many users' trust in existing cloud ecosystems (Apple iCloud) to reduce the drop-off common with manual seed-phrase backups.
screens.whereToUse:
• Any flow requiring users to safeguard highly sensitive, non-recoverable credentials (crypto seed phrases, encryption keys, 2FA backup codes).

  • Onboarding flows where you want to offer both a "friction-free" managed backup and a "manual/expert" self-custody path.

  • Situations where you need to build user trust by demonstrating that sensitive information is protected by default (blur/obscure pattern).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy warning/friction pattern for low-stakes data (e.g., a username or bio) where excessive caution would feel patronizing.

  • Don't default to cloud backup prominence if your product's value proposition is strictly self-custody/zero-knowledge — this could contradict brand promises around privacy and decentralization.

  • Avoid obscuring content that users need to reference repeatedly during the same flow, as constant re-authentication to reveal it can frustrate rather than protect.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 20
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is the critical verification checkpoint within a crypto/Web3 wallet's onboarding flow, positioned immediately after the user has been shown their 12-word secret recovery (seed) phrase. Rather than simply asking "did you save it?" with a yes/no confirmation, the app enforces an active recall verification: the user must locate and tap the 1st and 12th words from a shuffled word grid (implied by the empty/placeholder grid area below the copy).

The layout is deliberately minimal and high-contrast (dark background, single focal message) to reduce cognitive load and signal the gravity of the task — this is not a casual UI moment, it's a security gate. The segmented progress bar at the top confirms the user is in step 2 of a 3-step setup flow, giving a sense of momentum and finite effort remaining.

The primary CTA "Continue" is rendered in a muted/disabled-looking purple, subtly implying it may only activate once the verification tapping is completed correctly — a form of blocking progression until the security-critical task is honestly performed.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The headline "You saved it, right?" is conversational, informal, and almost cheeky — using second-person direct address and a rhetorical question to create a moment of friendly accountability. This tone choice is intentional: it disarms the intimidating, high-stakes nature of cryptographic key management by wrapping it in casual, human language rather than dry technical jargon.

The supporting instruction is precise and procedural ("tapping the first (1st) then last (12th) word"), ensuring zero ambiguity about the required action despite the casual headline. This pairing of casual tone + precise instruction balances approachability with the need for exact user comprehension in a task where mistakes are costly (loss of funds).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Active recall over passive confirmation: Instead of a checkbox "I saved my phrase," the app forces the user to physically locate and tap specific words, which meaningfully increases the likelihood they actually recorded the phrase correctly.
