  • Bookend verification strategy: Requiring only the 1st and 12th words (rather than all 12) is a clever UX compromise — it verifies the user has the full, correctly-ordered list without the friction of re-entering the entire phrase.

  • Segmented progress indicator: Reinforces that this friction is temporary and finite, reducing abandonment risk during a necessarily tedious security step.

  • Tone contrast: Playful headline paired with unambiguous procedural instructions balances emotional friction reduction with functional clarity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new self-custody crypto wallet users (e.g., MetaMask, Phantom, Rainbow-style apps) who are often crypto novices unfamiliar with the severity of losing a seed phrase. The design leverages the psychological principle of the generation/testing effect — active retrieval of information (tapping specific words) cements memory and behavior far more effectively than passive acknowledgment.

It also exploits a light accountability/social-contract trigger in the copy ("right?") — implicitly asking the user to be honest with themselves, discouraging the common bad habit of blindly clicking "I saved it" without actually doing so.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a user must retain a piece of information critical to account recovery or irreversible security (seed phrases, backup codes, recovery keys, master passwords). It's ideal for:

  • Non-custodial wallet setup flows

  • 2FA backup code confirmation

  • Any "point of no return" step where support cannot recover lost credentials
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavier verification friction for low-stakes or easily recoverable information (e.g., email preferences, non-critical settings) where it would feel like unnecessary busywork. Also avoid casual/playful copy tone ("right?") in contexts involving regulated financial custodial services or enterprise/B2B audiences who may expect more formal, professional language for security procedures.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 11
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen appears during Cleo's account-linking onboarding flow, immediately after the user connects their bank account. Rather than presenting a raw transaction dump, Cleo has already run its categorization engine to auto-detect recurring payments and surfaces them as a pre-filled, editable list for user verification. This is a classic "confirm, don't create" pattern that drastically reduces the cognitive load of manual budget setup.

The layout uses a bottom-sheet/modal card rising from a bold blue backdrop, with a large, high-contrast condensed headline that dominates the top third of the screen. Each bill is represented as a stacked list row with a custom icon, merchant/category name, frequency + due date subtext, and a right-aligned amount with a stylized typographic treatment (large integer, small decimal). This hierarchy lets users scan and verify data in seconds rather than reading dense paragraphs.

The interaction model is explicitly explained in the subheader ("Tap to edit or swipe to remove"), preemptively teaching a gesture-based editing pattern without needing a tutorial overlay. A single sticky primary CTA ("Next") anchors the bottom, keeping the flow linear and reducing decision fatigue. The close (X) icon gives an escape hatch, and the progress pill at the very bottom signals this is one step within a longer setup wizard.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The headline "ARE THESE YOUR BILLS?" is phrased as a direct, casual question in bold all-caps display type — consistent with Cleo's blunt, conversational personality even outside the chat interface. It personalizes the data ("your bills") to build trust that the AI has done real work on the user's behalf, rather than presenting generic categories.

The supporting copy is short, plain-English, and instructional: it defines "bills" in layman's terms ("any recurring or fixed payments") and gives explicit micro-guidance on the interaction pattern. There's no financial jargon, no dashboards, and no lengthy disclaimers — just a quick, low-friction confirmation task framed conversationally.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Auto-detected pre-fill: Instead of asking users to manually input recurring bills, Cleo does the heavy lifting via transaction analysis and asks for a lightweight yes/no-style confirmation, converting a tedious form task into a quick review task.

  • Embedded interaction hint: The subheader copy ("Tap to edit or swipe to remove") teaches the gesture vocabulary inline, avoiding a separate coach-mark overlay and reducing onboarding friction.

  • Custom playful iconography: Whimsical icons (a winged dollar coin, a bank building) for each bill category reinforce Cleo's fun, mascot-driven brand identity even in a purely functional financial screen.

  • Typographic price hierarchy: Large integer + smaller decimal formatting for amounts improves scannability and mirrors familiar receipt/pricing conventions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users onboarding onto Cleo who have just linked a bank account, likely younger, mobile-first consumers (Gen Z/Millennial) who are put off by traditional budgeting apps' manual entry requirements. The psychological trigger here is reduced effort + delegated authority: by having the AI pre-populate bills, Cleo signals competence and does the "boring" work, letting the user simply validate rather than labor through data entry, which increases completion rates for the onboarding funnel. The editable/removable list also builds trust and a sense of control, mitigating anxiety about an AI misreading personal financial data.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever an app can algorithmically infer structured data (subscriptions, contacts, calendar events, expenses) on a user's behalf during onboarding or data import. It's ideal for finance, subscription-tracking, or CRM apps where confirming pre-filled data is far less taxing than manual entry, and where building early trust in automated intelligence is a core value proposition.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the underlying detection/categorization accuracy is poor, as showing wrong data erodes trust immediately at first use. It's also unsuitable when the dataset is very large (dozens of transactions), since a simple list without search/filtering or bulk actions would become unwieldy — a batch review or table view would be more appropriate. Additionally, if users have no context on why data was detected this way, the lack of an explanation/source citation could feel intrusive or "creepy."

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 12
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen functions as a milestone celebration interstitial, breaking up the flow of a multi-step budget setup process. Rather than a plain "Success" confirmation, Cleo interrupts the utilitarian task (customizing a budget) with a full-bleed, high-energy visual reward. The layout uses a single dominant focal point—the oversized "LIKE A BOSS." typography—paired with playful donut illustrations that bleed off the edges of the screen, creating a sense of abundance and celebration.

The chat bubbles beneath the headline maintain continuity with Cleo's core conversational identity even in a full-screen takeover moment, reassuring the user that this is still "Cleo talking to them" rather than a generic system modal. The single, high-contrast CTA button ("Take a look 👀") sits at the bottom thumb-zone, providing an unambiguous, low-cognitive-load next step. The page indicator dot at the very bottom signals this is one step within a larger flow, managing expectations that more content follows.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is irreverent, hype-driven, and distinctly un-bank-like. "LIKE A BOSS." is bold slang copy that reframes a mundane admin task (finishing a budget form) as an empowerment win. Pairing this with "Nice job 👌" and casual, lowercase-style phrasing continues Cleo's persona as a blunt, funny best-friend rather than a formal financial institution.

The CTA "Take a look 👀" uses an emoji instead of a sterile "Continue" or "Next," reinforcing curiosity and lightness. The copy is deliberately terse — "You've fully customised your budget." — delivering the functional confirmation only after the emotional payoff, prioritizing feeling over information.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Emotional Reward Before Data: Leads with a dopamine-triggering celebration screen instead of dumping the user straight into a budget dashboard, making a boring finance task feel like an achievement.

  • On-Brand Mascot Illustration: Uses whimsical, oversized donut illustrations (a nod to indulgent spending/reward) bleeding off-canvas to create scale and joy, avoiding generic checkmark/confetti clichés.

  • Persistent Chat Metaphor: Even in a full-screen celebratory moment, the confirmation is delivered via chat bubbles, keeping the entire app experience conversational and consistent.

  • Single, Curiosity-Driven CTA: One button with playful emoji copy reduces decision fatigue and nudges forward momentum.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets younger, digitally-native users (Gen Z/Millennials) who are fatigued by traditional, dry banking UX and respond better to meme-adjacent, humor-forward interfaces. The psychological trigger here is the Peak-End Rule: by inserting a high point of delight at the end of a setup task, Cleo ensures users remember the budgeting process positively, increasing the likelihood they'll complete future onboarding steps or engage with the app again. The "Like a Boss" framing also taps into self-affirmation and identity reinforcement, making financial responsibility feel cool and validating rather than restrictive.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern after a user completes a moderately effortful, potentially tedious task (form completion, budget setup, goal creation) within onboarding or key flows. It's most effective when the underlying task is functional/dry and needs an injected moment of levity to prevent drop-off or negative sentiment before continuing to the next step.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, full-screen celebratory treatment for minor, frequent micro-actions (e.g., every single toggle change), as it will quickly become obtrusive and slow down power users. It's also inappropriate for enterprise, B2B, or highly formal financial products where overly casual tone or slang ("Like a Boss") could undermine perceived trust or professionalism.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 13
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen translates a traditionally dry financial report (a monthly budget summary) into a visually playful, illustrative narrative. Instead of bar charts or line graphs, Cleo uses stacked "coin towers" to represent Income ("In"), Spending ("Out"), and the ghosted outline of the user's self-imposed "Limit". This metaphor is instantly parsable — taller stack of coins = more money — without requiring any data-literacy.

The layout follows a clear vertical hierarchy: a header contextualizes the time period (Feb 1-29) and burn-down (11 days left via a progress bar), the hero visualization sits in the middle third, and a white card "below the fold" breaks the dark canvas to surface the two hardest-working numbers (total spent-to-date and daily budget) in large, high-contrast typography. This card also cleverly uses the visual weight of a bottom sheet/pull-up card to signal "here's your actionable data" against the "here's your visual story" section above.

Horizontal swipe arrows on the far left/right edges indicate this is one card in a carousel of month-by-month or category breakdowns, allowing lateral time-travel through budget history without cluttering the screen with a date picker.

The mascot's speech-bubble at the bottom ("Been 2 weeks of budgets. Thoughts?") re-engages the user conversationally, reinforcing Cleo's chat-first identity even on a data screen, and gives a low-friction entry point back into the chat interface.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is short, punchy, and casual — "11 days left," "Been 2 weeks of budgets. Thoughts?" — mimicking a friend checking in rather than a bank statement. The all-caps header "FEBRUARY'S BREAKDOWN" adds an energetic, tabloid-headline feel that matches Cleo's blunt personality.

The floating thumbs-up illustration acts as a wordless verdict/reaction to the user's performance, giving instant emotional feedback (approval) before any numbers are even read — a technique borrowed from social media 'reaction' mechanics.

The final banner poses a direct, informal question ("Thoughts?") rather than a passive notification, inviting a two-way conversation and subtly funneling the user toward the Chat tab.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Metaphorical Data Visualization: Replacing bar/line charts with a "coin stack" illustration makes raw financial data feel tactile, gamified, and less intimidating.

  • Emotional Reaction Overlay: The purple mascot thumb floating in front of the chart delivers an instant qualitative judgment on financial behavior, adding personality where a normal fintech app would show a neutral chart.

  • Layered Information Density: The dark "story" zone (visual/emotional) and light "data" zone (precise numbers) are cleanly separated by a rounded card, letting users choose how deep they want to go.

  • Editable Goal Inline: The "until $1,463" edit pencil lets users adjust their spending ceiling directly inline without navigating to a settings screen.

  • Conversational Re-engagement Banner: A dismissible chat-bubble nudge at the bottom of a data screen pulls users back into Cleo's core AI-chat loop.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially anxious or budget-averse users (often younger, Gen Z/Millennial) who find traditional banking dashboards boring, shameful, or overwhelming. By using humor, mascot reactions, and playful iconography instead of stark red/green deficit charts, Cleo lowers the emotional barrier to checking one's own finances regularly.

Psychological triggers at play include: Loss aversion softened by humor (a thumbs-up mascot makes even a review of spending feel non-judgmental), the Zeigarnik effect (the "11 days left" progress bar creates a sense of an unfinished task driving return visits), and social-style feedback loops (mascot commentary mimics receiving a text from a friend rather than a bank).
screens.whereToUse: Use this illustrative, narrative-driven data pattern when the goal is to encourage habitual engagement with otherwise dry or emotionally sensitive data (budgets, health metrics, screen time). It's ideal for apps with a strong mascot/brand voice trying to differentiate from clinical competitor dashboards, and for periodic (weekly/monthly) summary screens meant to be swiped through like a story or carousel.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this approach for power users, accountants, or B2B financial tools where precision, comparability, and data density matter more than charm — illustrative metaphors like coin stacks scale poorly for detailed multi-category comparisons. Also avoid if brand tone is meant to convey stability/trust (e.g., mortgage or investment platforms), since playful mascot commentary can undercut perceived seriousness for high-stakes financial decisions.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 23
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen shows a crypto wallet's Settings page with a contextual Bottom Sheet overlay triggered by tapping "Legal." The base layer uses a grouped list pattern (Security, Display, Connect to Coinbase, Notifications, Help, Legal) with leading icons, descriptive subtitles, and trailing chevrons/external-link glyphs to signal navigation depth or context switching (in-app drill-down vs. external browser).

The modal itself is a minimal, focused bottom sheet exposing exactly two legal sub-links (Privacy policy, Terms of service) with a drag handle affordance at the top, reinforcing that it's dismissible via swipe. The background is dimmed and slightly blurred/darkened, maintaining spatial context so users don't lose their place in Settings while making a lightweight, low-stakes choice.

Visual hierarchy is achieved through a strict two-line pattern: bold primary label + muted gray secondary description, which lets users scan quickly without reading dense paragraphs. This is a dark-mode-first design (fitting a finance/crypto app), reducing eye strain and reinforcing a premium, "vault-like" security aesthetic.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy is terse, utilitarian, and functional — typical of financial/security settings where clarity and trust outweigh personality or playfulness. Labels are noun-based ("Security," "Display," "Notifications") paired with plain-English subtitles that preview exactly what's inside each section (e.g., "Passcode, backup, Face ID"), reducing the need to tap in blindly.

The legal sheet uses standard, expected terminology ("Privacy policy," "Terms of service") with no embellishment — appropriate for compliance-driven content where users expect standard legal boilerplate, not marketing tone.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Descriptive subtitles on every row: Each settings item previews its contents (e.g., "Dark mode, currency, balances, language") so users don't need to tap-and-check, saving time and reducing navigation anxiety.

  • Differentiated affordances: Chevron arrows indicate in-app drill-down, while the diagonal arrow icon on "Help" clearly signals it opens an external browser/support center — a subtle but important expectation-setting detail.

  • Lightweight bottom sheet for low-complexity choices: Rather than navigating to a full new screen for two links, the app surfaces them in a compact sheet, minimizing navigation depth and preserving context.

  • Search bar at the top of Settings: Acknowledges that as feature-rich apps grow, users prefer typing over hunting through nested menus.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday users of a crypto/finance wallet app (likely Coinbase Wallet or similar) who need to configure security and privacy settings — a population that is often anxious about fund safety and data privacy. Grouping "Security" first and giving it a lock icon builds immediate trust and signals that the app prioritizes asset protection.

The Legal bottom sheet caters to compliance-conscious or skeptical users who want quick access to Privacy Policy/Terms without friction, and to the platform's own regulatory obligation to surface these documents discoverably without cluttering the main settings list.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for settings/preferences screens where legal, help, or secondary informational links need to be grouped without dedicating a full screen. Ideal for:

  • Financial, healthcare, or regulated apps needing quick access to Privacy Policy/ToS.

  • Any settings hub with a mix of high-frequency (Security, Notifications) and low-frequency (Legal) actions, where the bottom sheet keeps low-frequency items decluttered.

  • Apps with deep settings trees that benefit from an in-page search bar for quick filtering.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when legal documents are lengthy and require full reading/scrolling — a bottom sheet with only links is fine, but rendering full ToS text inside a sheet is poor UX (use a full screen or in-app browser instead). Also avoid using a bottom sheet for items requiring complex multi-step interaction; sheets work best for short, binary-choice or link lists like this one.

screens.name: Incognito Mode
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen reuses the exact search-sheet layout from the standard new-search overlay but recolors it entirely in dark tones and adds explicit labeling ("Incognito," footprint icon, "You're browsing Incognito"), creating an unmistakable visual mode-switch that's hard to confuse with regular browsing even at a glance. Dark theming as the primary differentiator is a well-established convention for private/incognito modes across browsers, so users can rely on prior mental models rather than learning something new. The explicit confirmation text goes beyond just changing color — it verbally reassures the user the mode is active, which matters for a privacy feature where the user needs confidence the setting actually took effect before they proceed to search.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "You're browsing Incognito" is a direct, reassuring statement written in second person, functioning purely as status confirmation rather than persuasion — there's no need to sell the feature here since the user deliberately chose to enter it. This is appropriately restrained: unlike onboarding screens that build a case for a feature, this is a mode the user already opted into, so the copy's only job is to confirm, not convince.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Distinctive Mode Signaling — full dark theming plus explicit labeling creates an unambiguous, hard-to-miss visual distinction from standard browsing mode.

  2. Consistency (Jakob's Law) — reusing dark theme plus footprint iconography follows an established cross-browser convention for private browsing, reducing learning cost.

  3. Visibility of System Status — the explicit "You're browsing Incognito" text removes any doubt about whether the mode switch succeeded.

  4. Trust Through Explicit Confirmation — pairing a visual cue (dark theme) with a written statement (not just color alone) reduces the risk of a user misunderstanding their privacy state.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Chrome (Incognito mode) — uses the same dark theme plus explicit "You've gone Incognito" messaging and a spy/mask icon as its mode indicator.

  2. Safari (Private Browsing) — similarly shifts to a dark UI theme with explicit labeling when private mode is active.

  3. DuckDuckGo (default private browser) — reinforces its always-private nature with consistent dark/muted theming and privacy-focused messaging.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any feature requiring an unambiguous mode switch with real user consequences (privacy, safety, data handling), where a strong, consistent visual signal (theme change) paired with explicit text confirmation reduces the risk of the user being unaware of their current state.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for low-stakes preference toggles where a full theme change would be an outsized, disruptive visual response to a minor setting adjustment.

screens.name: Site Settings
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen confirms the Site Settings modal can expand to full-screen height (likely via a drag gesture on its handle), revealing the previously truncated "App Settings" row in full and removing any visibility of the underlying page. This progressive expansion — from a partial sheet peeking over the page to a full-screen modal — follows the standard iOS sheet-detent pattern, letting users choose how much of the settings panel they want visible without forcing a full-screen takeover by default. With the "App Settings" row now fully visible and unobstructed, its function as a link to broader, non-site-specific configuration is confirmed, distinct from the google.com-scoped toggles above it.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Labels remain plain and functional (Block Ads, Block Cookie Banners, Block Trackers, Pinch to Summarize, Collapse Bottom Bar, Swipe to Navigate) with no persuasive framing, appropriate for a settings surface where clarity matters more than motivation — users arriving here already know what they want to check or change, so the copy's only job is unambiguous labeling.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Progressive Sheet Expansion — allowing the modal to grow from a partial to full-screen presentation (standard iOS sheet-detent behavior) gives users control over how much context they want to see at once.

  2. Clear Escape from Scoped to Global Settings — the "App Settings" row, now fully visible, offers an obvious, separate path to broader configuration beyond the current site's scope.

  3. Consistency (Jakob's Law) — the expand/collapse drag-handle behavior matches standard iOS sheet conventions, requiring no new learning.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Brave Browser's per-site Shields panel — offers an almost identical grouped set of per-site privacy toggles (ad blocking, tracker blocking, cookie handling) scoped to the current site.

  2. Safari's per-website settings (Reader, content blockers) — provides comparable site-specific toggles accessible from a similar settings sheet.

  3. 1Blocker / AdGuard's per-site rules — group ad, tracker, and cookie-banner blocking as distinct toggles scoped to individual domains, matching this panel's structure.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits browsers offering granular, per-site control over privacy and interaction features, where users benefit from adjusting settings for a specific troublesome site without changing global app-wide defaults.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for settings that are inherently global and don't make sense scoped per-site (e.g., account-wide preferences), where offering a per-site override would create confusing, hard-to-track inconsistencies across different sites.

screens.name: App Icon Change 01
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen confirms the app-icon customization introduced during onboarding remains accessible afterward via Settings, echoing the earlier finding that onboarding features aren't one-time-only experiences. Notably, this picker's format differs meaningfully from the onboarding version: onboarding used a static 3×3 grid with radio buttons beneath each tile, while this Settings-accessed picker uses a horizontally scrollable single-row carousel resting on a simulated home-screen dock — a design choice that visually previews how the selected icon would actually look on the user's home screen, rather than just displaying it in isolation. This dock-preview context is a meaningful UX improvement over the onboarding version for a settings-revisit scenario, since the user is making a more deliberate, considered choice here (not a first-run default) and benefits from seeing the icon in its real destination context.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "App Icon" as a header is plain and functional, appropriately neutral for a settings sub-screen reached deliberately by the user, contrasting with the more playful "Pick an icon for your home screen" framing used during onboarding — the settings context needs less persuasive framing since the user actively navigated here to make this exact change.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Contextual Preview — showing icon options resting on a simulated dock lets users evaluate a choice in its real-world visual context, rather than as an isolated icon tile.

  2. Format Adaptation by Context — using a carousel here (versus onboarding's static grid) suggests the interface adapts its presentation to the browsing context — a scrollable format works well for a focused, single-purpose revisit, while a full grid suited the more exploratory first-run moment.

  3. Post-Onboarding Feature Access — confirming this customization option remains available and easily reachable after onboarding reinforces that first-run features aren't disposable, one-time-only choices.

  4. Low-Friction Exit — the prominent "X" dismiss button ensures users can back out without committing to a change if none of the visible options appeal.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Instagram/Telegram's in-app icon picker (Settings) — similarly offers icon customization from within app settings, often with a dock or home-screen preview context.

  2. iOS's own "Home Screen Customization" (alternate app icons) — uses comparable preview treatments showing how an icon would appear once selected.

  3. Spotify's icon/theme customization within Settings — offers a similar post-onboarding, deliberate revisit path for a personalization choice first introduced during setup.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any personalization choice (like app icon) that's worth offering both during onboarding (for first impressions) and later via settings (for users who want to reconsider), with the settings version benefiting from contextual preview (like a dock mockup) since the choice here is more deliberate.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit to duplicate the exact same static-grid presentation from onboarding in settings without adapting to context — a carousel-with-dock-preview format (as shown here) provides more real-world context appropriate for a considered, deliberate revisit rather than a fast first-run decision.

screens.name: Global Site Settings 02
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen resolves the earlier ambiguity about "Swipe to Navigate" being a value-display row rather than a binary toggle: it's a two-option selector, letting users choose between the more permissive "From Anywhere" (swipe starting anywhere on screen triggers back-navigation) and the more conservative, iOS-standard "From Screen Edges" (swipe must start at the screen edge, avoiding conflicts with in-content gestures). The checkmark clearly indicates the current selection ("From Screen Edges"), and presenting this as a compact in-place popover — rather than navigating to a separate screen — keeps the interaction lightweight for a setting with only two possible values. This detail also explains the app's earlier "swipe anywhere to go back" feature highlighted in onboarding: it's evidently not the default behavior, but an opt-in alternative to the more conservative default, giving users the choice between convenience (swipe anywhere) and gesture-conflict safety (edge-only).
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — plain, functional option labels ("From Anywhere," "From Screen Edges") with no persuasive framing, appropriate for a straightforward binary-choice settings control.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Clear Selection Indication — a checkmark unambiguously shows which of the two options is currently active, avoiding any doubt about the setting's present state.

  2. Lightweight In-Place Selection — using a compact popover rather than a full navigation to a new screen keeps the interaction efficient for a setting with only two possible values.

  3. Trade-off Transparency Through Naming — the option names themselves ("From Anywhere" vs. "From Screen Edges") communicate the underlying trade-off (convenience vs. gesture-conflict avoidance) without needing additional explanatory text.

  4. Resolving Prior Ambiguity — this screen provides the missing context for a setting whose display-only value ("From Screen Edges" / "From Anywhere") appeared in two earlier screens without showing how it was actually changed.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. iOS system-level "Swipe from edge" gesture settings — offer a very similar edge-only vs. anywhere-based interaction choice for back-navigation gestures.

  2. Android's system-wide gesture navigation settings — provide a comparable binary choice between edge-triggered and more permissive gesture zones.

  3. Reddit's mobile app "swipe to navigate" preference — offers a similar two-option selector for customizing swipe-back gesture sensitivity.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits binary or small-option-set settings where a compact, in-place popover with a clear checkmark indicator is more efficient than navigating to a dedicated sub-screen, especially for settings whose two options represent a clear, nameable trade-off.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for settings with many possible values or those requiring additional explanatory context, where a compact popover wouldn't have room to adequately describe each option's implications, and a dedicated screen with more detail would serve users better.

screens.name: Change Default Browser 01
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen is a significant reveal for the app's overall positioning: "Browse for Me" — Arc's own AI-powered feature — is listed as a selectable default search engine alongside major third-party providers (Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo) and other AI-native competitors (Perplexity, Kagi), meaning users can choose to make Arc's own AI search the actual default for every query, not just an optional toggle accessed via the earlier Arc/Google switcher UI. Positioning "Browse for Me" first in the list (above Google, which is currently checked) subtly nudges toward it as the "preferred" or intended choice, even though Google remains the actual current default in this state. Including competitors like DuckDuckGo, Ecosia, Perplexity, and Kagi — several of which are themselves privacy-focused or AI-native alternatives — signals a genuinely open, non-locked-in browser philosophy, letting users pick a search provider that matches their own values (privacy, environment, AI-search preference) rather than being funneled toward one default.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — plain, functional engine names with no persuasive copy, appropriate for a straightforward provider-selection list where the names themselves carry all necessary information.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Self-Referential Option Placement — listing "Browse for Me" first, ahead of the actual current default (Google), subtly promotes the app's own differentiated feature without forcing it as mandatory.

  2. Genuine Provider Choice — offering a range of philosophically distinct engines (privacy-focused DuckDuckGo, environmental Ecosia, AI-native Perplexity/Kagi) respects that different users have different search priorities beyond just "which engine is biggest."

  3. Clear Current-State Indication — a single checkmark unambiguously shows which engine is presently active, avoiding confusion in a list where any option could plausibly be selected.

  4. Extensibility — the "Add Search Engine" option signals this list isn't a closed, fixed set, allowing power users to add custom or niche search providers beyond the pre-populated options.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's Default Search Engine settings — offers a comparable list of major providers (Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo, Ecosia) for users to choose from, though without an AI-native option like "Browse for Me."

  2. Brave Browser's search engine picker — includes both traditional and privacy-focused engines, plus a custom "add search engine" capability, closely matching this screen's structure.

  3. Opera's search engine settings — similarly lists multiple third-party engines with a checkmark-based single selection, though typically without a browser's own AI feature listed as a selectable "engine."
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits browsers wanting to offer genuine search-provider choice while still promoting their own differentiated AI or search feature as a legitimate first-class option among established competitors, rather than hiding it as a secondary toggle.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit if a browser's AI feature isn't yet reliable enough to serve as every query's default — presenting it as a full peer alongside Google or Bing sets an expectation of comprehensive search capability that an early-stage AI feature might not consistently meet.

screens.name: Notifications Permission
screens.uxAnalysis:
This closes the earlier alerts loop. Flighty first shows the value of notifications, then asks for OS permission—at a moment when the flight is airborne and the changing data makes the benefit immediately relevant.

The underlying flight data is especially strong: the original time, revised time, delay/early delta, recency, and countdown are all visible, making changes transparent without requiring calculation.

The main flaw is placement. The permission dialog covers the “Alerts Off” control—the exact state it is asking the user to change and the control they may need if they decline.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The dialog is Apple's; everything behind it is Flighty's, and the contrast is instructive.

"Notifications may include alerts, sounds, and icon badges." — system boilerplate, unmodifiable, and notably vaguer than what Flighty already told the user. The in-app card showed a specific delay alert with a replacement gate; this describes generic mechanics. That's precisely why priming matters: by the time this appears, the user is answering the question do I want delay alerts, not what is a notification. Flighty supplied the meaning the system prompt can't.

"Lands in 30m" — the app's most important string, and it changes verb with phase. Pre-departure it read "Gate Departure in 1h 5m"; airborne it reads "Lands in 30m". The countdown always answers the next question the user has, not a fixed field.

"Flight is En Route" — a status sentence rather than a label, and the capitalisation of "En Route" treats it as a defined state in the app's vocabulary, consistent with "On Time".

"8:45" struck through · "9m early" — the strikethrough is copy as much as styling. It preserves what was promised alongside what happened, which is how a user calibrates trust in a data source over time. An app that silently overwrote 8:45 with 8:36 would be equally accurate and considerably less credible.

"38m ago" — relative rather than absolute, correct for a value the user reads at a glance. And it quietly confirms the data is fresh, which for a live tracker is a claim worth making implicitly.

"10m early" at OOL — the arrival prediction, and this is where the product's actual proposition sits. Anyone can report a departure that happened; forecasting an early arrival mid-flight is the pilot-grade claim being cashed.

Green throughout, for early as well as on-time. The app has one positive colour and applies it consistently.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Prime before you prompt — the OS dialog is a one-shot resource, and spending it only after demonstrating a concrete alert is the single highest-leverage decision in the notification flow.

  2. Ask when the value is visible — an airborne flight with revised times is the strongest possible backdrop for a permission request about status changes.

  3. Show the revision, not just the result — strikethrough plus delta plus timestamp lets users audit the data rather than trust it blindly.

  4. Countdowns that change question with phase — "Gate departure in" becomes "Lands in", so the headline number always answers what's next.

  5. Dialog occludes the related control — the "Alerts Off" chip is hidden behind the prompt governing it, which is exactly where a refusing user would look next.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Uber / DoorDash — prime with a concrete example of a status alert before triggering the system prompt, at the moment an order or ride is active.

  2. Apple Wallet / airline apps (flight change display) — struck-through original times beside revisions, the convention this borrows and executes cleanly.

  3. Citymapper (live journey) — countdown reframing by phase, from "departs in" to "arrives in", following the journey state.
screens.whereToUse: Best where notifications carry genuinely time-critical information and the value can be demonstrated before the OS prompt is spent. Ask during an active instance of the use case, not at onboarding, so the request arrives with evidence behind it.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit at first launch or before any use, where the prompt is spent on a user with no basis to answer. Also wrong when the prompt covers the control or content that motivated it, since a declining user is left without the affordance to reconsider.

screens.name: Settings
screens.uxAnalysis: The screen serves the Preference Center flow by grouping settings into clearly labeled sections — Streaming, Preferences, and Stay in touch — so users can scan by category rather than parse a flat list. Placing the Apple Music upsell at the top prioritizes monetization within a utility screen, betting that users in a settings mindset are receptive to a subscription pitch. The mix of drill-down rows, such as iCloud Sync and Notifications, and inline toggles, such as Identify songs on app start and Autoplay Videos, appropriately separates settings that need dedicated screens from simple binary preferences, reducing unnecessary navigation.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven. (The Apple Music card's copy — "Get up to 2 months free. Play full songs in Shazam. Add songs to playlists." — is benefit-framed and concrete, but it's a small supporting element rather than the dominant purpose of this settings screen.)
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Recognition over recall: chevrons consistently mark rows that navigate to a sub-screen, while switches mark inline binary settings, letting users predict behavior without tapping.

  2. Visibility of system status: toggle states (off/on) are immediately visible via color and knob position, confirming current configuration at a glance.

  3. Grouping / chunking (Gestalt: proximity): settings are clustered into Streaming, Preferences, and Stay in touch sections with header labels, easing scanning in a long list.

  4. Contextual monetization placement: surfacing the Apple Music upsell at the top of Settings (rather than interrupting core app flows) targets users already engaged in configuration without disrupting music discovery/listening tasks.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Spotify (Settings screen with Premium upsell banner at top) — same pattern of leading a settings list with a subscription upsell card before functional preferences.

  2. Duolingo (Settings with grouped preference sections and toggles) — comparable sectioned list mixing drill-down rows and inline switches.

  3. Instagram (Settings and Activity screen) — similar "Stay in touch"-style section linking out to social/rating actions alongside core preference toggles.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any app's central settings/preferences hub where a mix of account, permission, and behavioral toggles need to be organized, especially when there's also a subscription or upsell opportunity to surface without interrupting the core product flow.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for a first-run or onboarding context, where bundling a monetization upsell among routine preference toggles would feel premature and could undermine trust before the user has experienced core value.

screens.name: Settings 2
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen supports the Enabling & Disabling flow by confirming and explaining a setting managed at the OS level rather than offering an in-app toggle. The illustration and plain-language headline, "iCloud Sync is on," make a technical background process easy to understand, while the "Last Sync" timestamp provides concrete proof that syncing is active. The closing note sets expectations clearly by explaining that deeper control, such as revoking or granting access, happens in system Settings.
screens.tonalityAndContent: This is a largely copy-driven confirmation screen: interactive machinery is minimal (just a back button), so the illustration, headline, and subtext carry the communication. The tone is reassuring and plain-spoken — "iCloud Sync is on" is stated as a direct fact rather than a technical status code, and the subtext explains the benefit ("keep your songs up to date across devices") rather than the mechanism, which suits the lever that matters here: trust that a background process is functioning correctly. Showing a concrete "Last Sync" timestamp reinforces this trust with verifiable evidence rather than just a static "on" label. The footnote redirecting to system Settings is appropriately brief and doesn't overpromise in-app control the feature doesn't have.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of system status: the "Last Sync" timestamp gives concrete evidence the background process ran recently, beyond just stating a binary on/off state.

  2. Recognition over recall: the checkmark-cloud icon is an immediately familiar visual shorthand for "cloud sync working," reducing the need to read carefully to understand status.

  3. Plain language over jargon: "iCloud Sync is on" and the benefit-focused subtext avoid technical sync terminology, making a backend process approachable.

  4. Appropriate scoping of in-app control: rather than faking a toggle it can't fully control, the screen honestly defers deeper account/permission management to system Settings, avoiding a misleading affordance.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Photos ("iCloud Photos" status screen) — same pattern of a status illustration, on/off headline, and last-sync-style detail, deferring full control to system Settings.

  2. Apple Notes (iCloud sync status page) — comparable confirmation screen explaining background sync state in plain language.

  3. 1Password (iCloud/sync status screen) — similar reassurance pattern showing sync is active with a timestamp for trust.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits well for confirming the state of background, infrastructure-level features (sync, backup, connectivity) where users need reassurance and a timestamp of last activity, but don't need granular in-app controls.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when the user actually needs to toggle or configure the setting directly in-app — a purely informational confirmation screen without an actionable control would frustrate users expecting to change the setting from this same screen.

screens.name: Lock Screen Permission
screens.uxAnalysis: This resolves the unlabelled lightning chip from earlier — it's the Live Activity control, and the menu explains itself right at the point of decision: the header names the surfaces (Lock Screen, Dynamic Island), the scope ("this flight"), and the timing ("starting 3 hours prior") in one line. Per-flight scoping is the right call — a frequent traveller doesn't want every tracked flight cluttering the Lock Screen, and the toolbar placement keeps the decision contextual. The chip's greying is ambiguous, reading as inactive despite "Show" being checkmarked — plausibly "pending" since the flight is 8h24m out and the activity starts at 3h, but it's never explained. The data below has a clear defect: "Total 20m · 421 mi" for a 5:45–6:05 flight is Mach 1.7 — the same route showed "Total 1h 20m" earlier, so an hour's gone missing somewhere.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Three strings, and the header is the one carrying weight.

"Show this flight on your Lock Screen and Dynamic Island starting 3 hours prior." — a complete explanation in one sentence, and the ordering is deliberate: action, surfaces, scope, timing. Naming the OS features by their proper names rather than saying "on your phone" respects a user who knows what a Dynamic Island is, and teaches one who doesn't by association with Lock Screen. "3 hours prior" is the specific commitment that makes the setting predictable — vague alternatives like "before your flight" would leave the user unable to plan around it.

"Show" / "Don't Show" — a matched verb pair, which is better than the common "On/Off" because it describes what happens rather than a state. The negative option repeats the verb rather than offering an unrelated word like "Hide" or "Disable", so the two rows are legible as a single choice rather than two separate actions.

Lightning and lightning-slash icons — the slash convention for the negative, matching the bell-slash used for "Alerts Off" on the earlier detail screen. The app has a consistent internal grammar for negation.

"Alternatives" and "More" — the toolbar chips are nouns, not verbs, correctly signalling destinations rather than actions. "More" with an ellipsis glyph is the standard overflow affordance.

What's missing is any statement of whether this setting persists to future flights. A per-flight control with no indication of default behaviour means a user must decide anew each time, or discover the default by observation.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Explain the setting at the point of decision — surfaces, scope and timing in one sentence beats a settings screen the user must go find.

  2. State the schedule, not just the behaviour — "3 hours prior" makes the feature predictable and pre-empts the clutter objection.

  3. Scope to the object, not the app — per-flight control matches how a traveller actually thinks about which flight matters.

  4. Consistent negation grammar — the slash glyph for "off" states matches the bell-slash used elsewhere, so the visual language is learned once.

  5. Data defect — "Total 20m · 421 mi" is internally impossible and contradicts the same route's 1h 20m elsewhere in the app.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple (Live Activities in Maps, Fitness) — per-activity opt-in with a plain statement of which surfaces are affected.

  2. Uber (trip Live Activity) — automatic activation tied to a time window before the event, the same scheduling model.

  3. Apple Podcasts / Timers (Dynamic Island controls) — per-item rather than global control over persistent status display.
screens.whereToUse: Best where a persistent OS-level display should apply to one item rather than everything the app tracks, and where the activation window needs stating so users can predict it. Explaining timing in the menu itself suits any feature whose behaviour is deferred.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit when the setting is genuinely global, where a per-item control multiplies decisions unnecessarily. Also wrong when the control's own visual state contradicts the menu's selection, as the greyed chip arguably does here.

  4. Appropriate scoping of in-app control: rather than faking a toggle it can't fully control, the screen honestly defers deeper account/permission management to system Settings, avoiding a misleading affordance.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Photos ("iCloud Photos" status screen) — same pattern of a status illustration, on/off headline, and last-sync-style detail, deferring full control to system Settings.

  2. Apple Notes (iCloud sync status page) — comparable confirmation screen explaining background sync state in plain language.

  3. 1Password (iCloud/sync status screen) — similar reassurance pattern showing sync is active with a timestamp for trust.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits well for confirming the state of background, infrastructure-level features (sync, backup, connectivity) where users need reassurance and a timestamp of last activity, but don't need granular in-app controls.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when the user actually needs to toggle or configure the setting directly in-app — a purely informational confirmation screen without an actionable control would frustrate users expecting to change the setting from this same screen.

screens.name: App Settings 01
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen functions as the app's central settings hub, reachable specifically from the site-level settings panel, and it directly echoes several features taught during onboarding — "Set Arc as Default Browser," "Change App Icon," and implicitly ad/tracker blocking (moved to Global Site Settings) — confirming these onboarding-taught features remain accessible and adjustable after initial setup, not just presented once during first use. The grouping logic separates identity/branding actions (default browser, icon, home screen) from content/language preferences (search engine, languages) from behavioral toggles (auto-open keyboard, archive timing, link-opening behavior), giving the settings screen a a fairly conventional taxonomy despite covering a wide range of concerns. "Raise to Call Arc" is a notable, distinctive setting not covered anywhere earlier in this analysis set — it implies a phone-raise gesture can trigger the voice assistant ("Call Arc") feature demonstrated in earlier screens, extending that feature's activation methods beyond just tapping a button.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Labels remain consistently plain and functional throughout (Set Arc as Default Browser, Change App Icon, Search Engine, Clear Browsing Data), matching the neutral register expected of a comprehensive settings screen; no persuasive or brand-voice copy appears here, appropriately, since users navigating this deep into settings already know what they're looking for.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Feature Continuity Post-Onboarding — surfacing "Set as Default Browser" and "Change App Icon" here confirms features introduced during onboarding remain accessible for later reconsideration, not one-time-only prompts.

  2. Logical Grouping by Concern — separating identity/branding, content preferences, and behavioral toggles into distinct card sections aids scanability across a long settings list.

  3. Value-Revealing Rows — showing current values inline (Google, After 1 day, Native App) lets users understand current state at a glance without opening each sub-page.

  4. Novel Gesture Discovery — "Raise to Call Arc" introduces a previously unseen activation method for the voice assistant feature, expanding on the tap-based invocation shown in earlier screens.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. iOS Settings app (grouped preference sections) — uses a comparable card-grouped structure separating different categories of app behavior, closely matching this screen's organization.

  2. Chrome's Settings (Default browser, search engine, privacy) — groups similar categories of settings (browser identity, search preferences, browsing behavior) in a comparable structure.

  3. Safari's Settings (Auto-Fill, Search Engine, Privacy) — offers a similar range of app-wide preference categories accessible from one central settings screen.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any app needing a comprehensive, well-organized settings hub covering diverse concerns (branding, content preferences, behavior toggles), where grouping by functional category helps users navigate a long list efficiently.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for apps with only a handful of settings, where this level of categorization and grouping would be unnecessary structural overhead for a short, simple list that could be presented flatly.

screens.name: App Settings 02
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen reveals two notable features: "Sync with Arc Desktop" requiring sign-in confirms the cross-device promotion seen earlier in the tab switcher connects to a genuine account-based sync feature, not just a marketing banner. More distinctively, "Show Onboarding" lets users voluntarily re-trigger the entire onboarding sequence analyzed throughout this conversation — a thoughtful inclusion that treats onboarding as a resource users might want to revisit (e.g., to rediscover a forgotten gesture like Pinch to Summarize) rather than a one-time, disposable experience. The "Gift Arc to a friend" banner uses a distinct gradient treatment to stand out from the otherwise neutral gray settings rows, positioning referral prominently within settings rather than relegating it to a rarely-visited "About" page. Rounding out the screen with standard support/legal rows (Contact the Team, Privacy Policy, Open Source Licenses) and a version number footer follows conventional app-settings-screen structure.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Most labels remain plain and functional (Contact the Team, Privacy Policy, Open Source Licenses), but "Gift Arc to a friend" breaks from that register with warmer, more personal phrasing — consistent with the app's broader tendency (seen in onboarding) to inject a bit of warmth into otherwise transactional moments. This small tonal shift, paired with the distinct visual treatment, appropriately signals it as a discretionary, feel-good action rather than a core utility, differentiating it from the neutral settings rows around it.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Revisitable Onboarding — "Show Onboarding" treats the first-run tour as an on-demand resource rather than a one-time gate, respecting that users may want to rediscover features later.

  2. Visual Differentiation for Promotional Content — the gradient "Gift Arc to a friend" banner stands apart from neutral settings rows, appropriately signaling it as an optional, non-utility action.

  3. Standard Settings Screen Conventions — grouping support/legal rows (Contact, Privacy Policy, Licenses) with a version footer at the bottom follows familiar app-settings patterns, aiding predictability.

  4. Account-Gated Sync Confirmation — showing "Sign in" under "Sync with Arc Desktop" clarifies this is a genuine account feature requiring authentication, not a passive or automatic sync.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo's Settings ("Restart tutorial") — similarly allows users to voluntarily re-trigger onboarding content from within settings.

  2. Any referral-driven app's Settings ("Invite a friend" banner) — uses a comparable visually-distinct promotional row within an otherwise neutral settings list.

  3. Standard iOS app Settings screens (Contact Us, Privacy Policy, version footer) — follow the same closing structure seen at the bottom of this screen.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits comprehensive settings screens where account/sync features, referral promotions, and support/legal information all need a home — grouping and visually differentiating each category (toggle behaviors, sync, promotional banner, support links) keeps a long list navigable.
