  3. Spotify Canvas / YouTube Shorts — Short looping vertical music video in a stepped or scrolled sequence, comparable in using brief clips as a discovery hook toward the full catalogue.
screens.whereToUse: This fits short-form vertical media in a bounded set, where a segmented indicator can honestly promise a small number of items and the user's session is a quick browse rather than a deliberate watch.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit for long-form video, where a stories bar misrepresents commitment, and for content the user needs to identify or act on — a format with no title, no metadata, and no visible controls is wrong wherever the content itself is the thing being chosen.

screens.name: Home Screen 23
screens.uxAnalysis: This section expands beyond Shazam's core ecosystem in two notable ways. The Video card uses YouTube's native play control, making it the first destination in the flow that leads outside Apple services. While this broadens access to content, the interface relies on users recognizing the YouTube branding rather than explicitly stating where the tap will lead. Below it, Highlights introduces portrait-oriented short-form videos with visible duration badges, giving users a clear expectation of viewing time—something the audio previews earlier in the flow did not consistently provide. By this point, the experience has shifted from the originally identified song to broader artist exploration, making the connection to the user's initial intent progressively weaker.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven. Its strings are section headings, track titles, artist credits, and duration labels.

Worth noting that "Highlights" is the least predictive heading in the flow. "Top Songs", "More Albums", and "Video" each name their contents plainly; "Highlights" could mean clips, moments, career milestones, or editorial picks, and the user only learns it means 30-second vertical videos by looking at the thumbnails. One clip title truncates before its parenthetical resolves, continuing a pattern visible across most shelves on this screen.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Duration disclosed on the item — Clip length shown on the thumbnail sets expectation before the tap, which is exactly the disclosure the audio previews elsewhere in this flow never provided.

  2. Format signalled by shape — Portrait thumbnails immediately distinguish short vertical clips from the landscape video above, so two video types coexist without a label doing the work.

  3. Third-party destination by brand mark alone — The YouTube control is instantly recognisable but unlabelled; leaving the ecosystem is signalled by logo rather than by text.

  4. Diminishing relevance with depth — Sections progress from the identified song outward to general artist content, so the link back to the user's original question weakens the further they scroll.

  5. Vague section naming — "Highlights" fails the test its sibling headings pass: it does not predict its contents.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (artist page video shelves) — Featured video above shorter clip carousels with duration badges; the component grammar is inherited from the parent product.

  2. Spotify (Canvas and artist clips) — Short vertical video attached to tracks within an otherwise horizontal-media layout, comparable in mixing formats on one artist surface.

  3. YouTube Music (music video plus Shorts shelves) — Same pairing of a full-length video with a shelf of short vertical clips, and the same reliance on aspect ratio to distinguish them.
screens.whereToUse: This fits deep sections of a content-rich result page where video of different formats can be offered together, and where per-item duration badges let users judge the commitment before tapping.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the user's original query was narrow and time-boxed, since sections this far removed from the question serve browsing rather than answering, and wherever an unlabelled third-party destination would surprise the user — leaving an app should be legible from text, not only from a logo.

screens.name: Google Pay Watching Video 1
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a full-bleed vertical video player, likely embedded within a social media feed (e.g., Instagram/TikTok Reels or YouTube Shorts) used to promote a theatrical film release. The layout is intentionally cinematic and minimal: a letterboxed video frame is sandwiched between two solid black bars at the top and bottom of the viewport, mimicking a traditional widescreen aspect ratio within a native vertical mobile canvas.

The top black bar houses the film title in a bold, technical/utilitarian typeface split across three lines on the left, balanced by a right-aligned call-to-action ("IN CINEMAS 24 MARCH") that anchors the release date without competing for visual weight against the title. The bottom bar contains a small, low-contrast legal disclaimer ("*RATING TO BE ADVISED"), which is intentionally de-emphasized so as not to distract from the marketing message while still satisfying regulatory/compliance requirements.

There is no visible chrome (no scrubber, play/pause icons, or progress indicator visible in this frame), reinforcing an "ambient content" viewing experience typical of autoplaying social video ads where the video itself is the primary interactive surface and controls are hidden until tapped.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
"

The copywriting is stripped down to essential marketing information: film title, release date, and a legal caveat. The tone is authoritative and confident, using all-caps, bold, condensed typography that echoes the film's own abstract, chaotic branding. There is no persuasive sales copy, no hashtags, no emoji—the messaging trusts the visual intrigue of the dark, ambiguous scene to do the emotional/curiosity-driven work, while the text purely handles logistical info (when and where to watch).

The asterisked disclaimer ("*RATING TO BE ADVISED") is a compliance-driven microcopy pattern common in film advertising, added in small, muted type so it satisfies legal requirements without diluting the trailer's dramatic tone.

"
screens.keyHighlights:
• Cinematic Letterboxing: Using black bars top and bottom on a vertical mobile canvas signals "premium film content" and differentiates the post from native, user-generated vertical video.

  • Information Hierarchy via Placement: Title on the left, date on the right — a classic poster/billboard convention adapted for a small screen, allowing key facts to be scanned in under a second.

  • Minimal Compliance Footer: The rating disclaimer is present but visually subordinate, satisfying advertising standards without breaking immersion.

  • No Player Chrome Clutter: Absence of visible scrubbers/buttons keeps focus entirely on mood and atmosphere, leveraging the ambiguity of the dark scene to spark curiosity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets social media scrollers (likely on Instagram, Facebook, or TikTok) being retargeted with movie marketing content ahead of a theatrical release. The audience is broad "moviegoers" segment being reached via paid or organic social video ads.

Psychologically, the pattern leverages curiosity gaps — the frame shown is intentionally dark, abstract, and hard to parse (looks like the inside of a washing machine or a distorted reflective surface), which triggers a need to keep watching to resolve the visual ambiguity. The letterboxed, "film-like" framing also invokes authority/quality signaling: it looks like cinema-grade content rather than an amateur ad, increasing perceived credibility and desire to see it on the big screen. The fixed date ("24 March") layered with cinema imagery creates mild urgency/anticipation without being aggressively salesy.
screens.whereToUse:
Adapt this pattern for any teaser/trailer content distributed on social feeds where the goal is brand/film awareness and date-driven conversion (buy tickets, set reminder). It's ideal when:

  • The visual content itself is intriguing enough to not need heavy text overlays.

  • You need to convey a release date/CTA quickly within the first 1-2 seconds of an autoplaying, sound-off video.

  • Legal/regulatory disclaimers need to be present but should not dominate the creative.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimal-chrome, letterboxed approach when:

  • The content requires immediate interactivity (e.g., shopping, in-app deep actions) — the lack of visible controls/CTAs would hurt conversion.

  • The audience is unfamiliar with the film/brand and needs more explanatory context; pure mood-based imagery without any synopsis text could confuse or fail to convert cold audiences.

  • Accessibility is a priority — low-contrast, small-caption legal text and no captions/subtitles for dialogue would fail hearing-impaired or low-vision users.

screens.name: Google Pay Watching Video 2
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a full-bleed, vertically-oriented video advertisement (rotated to fill a mobile viewport) promoting a theatrical film release. It is not a native app screen but rather a paid social/video ad unit likely surfaced inside a feed (e.g., Instagram Reels, TikTok, or YouTube Shorts) or a video player experience. The layout prioritizes the cinematic still/clip above all else, with minimal chrome: a subtitle/caption overlay at mid-frame, a movie title lockup, a release-date call-to-action line, and a small compliance disclaimer ("Rating to be advised") tucked into a corner.

The design leans entirely on the source material's own visual language rather than app-native UI patterns — there's no navigation bar, no buttons, no interactive controls visible in this frame. The only "interface" elements are typographic overlays: a caption line mimicking closed captions/subtitles, and a bold, stacked all-caps title treatment for branding recall.

The composition uses a classic environmental portrait (a laundromat) with shallow depth of field to keep focus on the actor's emotionally loaded expression, while a diegetic subtitle ("Mrs. Wang, Mrs. Wang") anchors the narrative moment. This is a marketing artifact optimized for silent autoplay feeds — captions ensure comprehension without sound.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is quiet, intimate, and slightly melancholic — contrasting sharply with the film's own frenetic, high-concept reputation. This is a deliberate teaser strategy: instead of showcasing the multiverse action/comedy elements, the ad isolates a small, human, emotionally vulnerable beat (a name being called out, tears welling) to hook viewers on character and emotion rather than spectacle.

Typography is bold, condensed, all-caps sans-serif for the title and CTA ("IN CINEMAS 24 MARCH"), following standard film marketing conventions — high contrast white-on-black outside the video frame keeps the branding legible regardless of the underlying footage's color palette. The disclaimer text ("*Rating to be advised") is intentionally small and unobtrusive, satisfying legal/regulatory requirements without distracting from the emotional pull of the creative.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Sound-off storytelling: Embedded subtitle-style captions allow the emotional beat to land even when the video autoplays muted in a feed — critical for social/paid media performance.

  • Emotional hook over plot hook: Choosing a quiet, vulnerable close-up instead of an action set-piece differentiates this ad from typical genre-trailer noise and builds curiosity through restraint.

  • Minimal branded chrome: Only title, date, and disclaimer are overlaid — nothing competes with the actor's performance, maximizing watch-through and emotional retention.

  • Regulatory compliance integrated unobtrusively: The ratings disclaimer is present but visually deprioritized, balancing legal needs with creative integrity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This ad targets general social media/streaming audiences being retargeted with film marketing — likely adults 18–45 scrolling short-form video platforms. The psychological trigger is curiosity-gap storytelling: showing a highly specific, emotionally charged micro-moment (a character being repeatedly called by name in a mundane setting) without context compels the viewer to want narrative resolution, driving them toward ticket purchase or trailer click-through. The subdued, humanizing frame also serves to broaden appeal beyond genre/sci-fi fans to viewers seeking character-driven drama, widening the addressable audience for the theatrical release.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for film, streaming, or long-form content marketing on social/video platforms where sound-off consumption is the default. It's effective when a title has a strong emotional core to lead with, or when you want to counter-position against audience expectations set by genre or prior trailers. Also appropriate for any teaser/announcement unit that needs to work as a silent autoplay asset while still conveying a full emotional beat via captions.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal-caption, no-CTA-button approach for performance-driven ads that need direct, trackable interaction (e.g., app installs, e-commerce) since there's no tappable element visible in-frame — conversion relies entirely on platform-level swipe-up/link mechanics. It's also unsuitable for products or films where the core selling proposition is spectacle/action, as an overly quiet creative could undersell the tone and attract the wrong audience or fail to differentiate in a crowded action-trailer market.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Uploading & Downloading 4
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen follows a well-established crypto wallet pattern for receiving funds, prioritizing accuracy and trust above all else since a single character error in a wallet address can result in permanent loss of funds. The layout is a single-purpose, distraction-free canvas: a large, high-contrast QR code sits front and center as the primary interaction method, with the plain-text address serving as a redundant, human-verifiable fallback.

The use of a Segmented Control ("Segwit" / "Legacy") at the top lets advanced users switch address formats without leaving the screen or triggering a new flow, while defaulting to Segwit (the more modern, lower-fee standard) as a smart default for less experienced users. The truncated address display (bc1qfl2...6ud9jkzc8h) reduces visual clutter and cognitive load, while the prominent gradient "Copy" button provides a low-friction alternative to manual QR scanning or typing.

The dark theme with a vivid orange Bitcoin-branded QR marker creates strong visual hierarchy — the eye is drawn immediately to the code without ambiguity. The bottom-anchored, full-width "Share" button offers an alternative distribution channel (e.g., messaging apps) for the address, acknowledging that not all receiving contexts happen in person via camera scan.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal, functional, and reassuring rather than promotional — appropriate for a financial transaction screen where trust and clarity trump marketing. The microcopy "Transactions may take a few minutes to complete" proactively manages user expectations around blockchain confirmation times, reducing anxiety-driven support requests or repeated refreshing.

The "Learn more about Segwit vs Legacy" link acknowledges that the terminology may be unfamiliar to less technical users, offering an escape hatch to education without cluttering the primary flow with lengthy explanations.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-format redundancy: QR code and plain-text address are both presented, accommodating both scan-based and copy/paste-based receiving workflows.

  • Smart default selection: Segwit is pre-selected as the recommended, lower-fee format, guiding novice users toward best practice without requiring a decision.

  • Truncated address with one-tap Copy: Reduces error-prone manual transcription and visual noise while keeping the full address accessible via clipboard.

  • Expectation-setting microcopy: Proactively informs users that blockchain confirmations take time, preempting confusion or premature support tickets.

  • Contextual education link: "Learn more" bridges the knowledge gap for the Segwit/Legacy distinction without overwhelming the primary task.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets both crypto-native users and newcomers within a Bitcoin wallet or exchange app. Experienced users benefit from the address-type toggle and copy/share affordances for efficiency, while newcomers are protected by smart defaults and reassuring timing copy. The psychological driver here is trust and error-prevention — financial apps dealing with irreversible transactions must minimize any chance of misreading or mistyping an address, which is why the QR code (near-zero error rate) is visually prioritized over the text string.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any peer-to-peer or wallet-to-wallet value transfer flow where an identifier (address, account number, IBAN, username) needs to be shared to receive funds or content. It's ideal when precision matters and multiple sharing channels (scan, copy, share-sheet) should be supported simultaneously.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, QR-centric layout for low-stakes or frequently repeated transactions (e.g., in-app tipping between known contacts) where a simpler username-based system suffices. Also avoid showing multiple address format options to fully novice audiences without an educational nudge, as it can create decision paralysis or confusion about which to use.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Uploading & Downloading 1
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen solves the classic crypto UX challenge of receiving funds, which requires exposing a technically complex, unforgiving data point (a wallet address) to non-technical users. The layout follows a clear top-to-bottom hierarchy: navigation context ("Receive Bitcoin"), format selection (Segwit/Legacy tabs), a large scannable QR code as the primary visual anchor, and a truncated address string with a one-tap "Copy" action.

The most important interaction design decision here is the contextual education layer: rather than assuming users understand the difference between address formats, the app proactively surfaces a bottom sheet explaining "SegWit vs. Legacy" the moment the user lands on a screen where that choice matters. This prevents a potentially fund-losing mistake (sending to/generating the wrong address type for a counterparty's wallet) at the exact decision point, rather than burying the explanation in a help center.

The QR code is rendered large and high-contrast against the dark background, optimized for camera scanning in varied lighting conditions, while the truncated address (bc1qfl2...6ud9jkzc8h) with a dedicated Copy button acknowledges that manual re-typing of a 42-character string is unrealistic and error-prone.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is deliberately plain-language and reassuring, avoiding jargon overload despite the technical subject matter. Phrases like "Try using SegWit first, and if that doesn't work, use Legacy" translate a protocol-level distinction into a simple, actionable fallback instruction rather than a technical explanation of bech32 vs. base58 encoding.

The microcopy "Your Bitcoin address" is a plain label with zero embellishment, keeping focus on the data itself. The bottom sheet title "SegWit vs. Legacy" uses a direct comparison framing that primes the user to expect a decision-support explanation, and "Got it" as the dismiss CTA is casual and low-friction, signaling comprehension rather than commitment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Just-in-time education: The SegWit vs. Legacy explainer appears exactly when the ambiguity is introduced (two tabs), rather than as a static help article the user must seek out.

  • Fallback-oriented guidance: Instead of explaining the technical tradeoffs, the copy gives a simple decision heuristic ("try X first, then Y"), reducing cognitive load for non-technical users.

  • Dual redundancy for address sharing: Providing both a scannable QR and a copyable text string accommodates both in-person (camera) and remote (paste) receiving scenarios.

  • Truncated address display: Showing only the first and last characters of the address keeps the UI clean while the full string is preserved for the copy action, reducing visual noise and error-prone reading.

  • Segmented control for address type: Clearly separates SegWit and Legacy as mutually exclusive states with an active underline indicator, mirroring familiar tab UX.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets both newcomers to cryptocurrency wallets and experienced holders who need to receive funds from an exchange, another wallet, or a peer. Newer users are the primary psychological target of the explainer sheet: crypto novices are highly risk-averse about "getting it wrong" because mistakes with blockchain transactions are often irreversible, so proactively de-risking the address-format decision builds trust and reduces support tickets/abandonment.

The dark, minimal, high-contrast aesthetic with a blue-to-teal gradient CTA taps into fintech/crypto design conventions that signal security, seriousness, and technical sophistication, appealing to a demographic that associates dark UIs with "pro trading tools." The large QR code caters to the very common in-person or cross-device transfer scenario (e.g., scanning from a hardware wallet or another phone).
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever an app must present a shareable identifier (wallet address, event check-in code, Wi-Fi credentials, contact info) that benefits from both a scannable and copyable format. The contextual bottom-sheet explainer is ideal any time a UI introduces a binary choice with real consequences that the user may not understand (e.g., file format exports, currency/network selection, shipping method tradeoffs) — surface the explanation adjacent to the choice rather than in a separate help section.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid stacking an unsolicited educational bottom sheet on every visit — it should be dismissible permanently (or shown only on first encounter) to avoid becoming an annoying, repetitive interruption for returning users. Also avoid this pattern if the choice being explained doesn't actually carry irreversible risk; over-explaining trivial UI toggles will feel patronizing and add unnecessary friction to simple tasks.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Uploading & Downloading 2
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen follows the near-universal pattern for cryptocurrency deposit flows, prioritizing accuracy and trust over visual flourish. The layout is a strict vertical hierarchy: navigation, address-type selector, a large scannable QR code, the copyable address, contextual education, and a primary share action.

The Segmented Control (Segwit/Legacy) sits directly beneath the header, letting technically-savvy users switch address formats without leaving the screen. Placing it above the QR code makes the causal relationship clear — the code and address below update in response to this toggle.

The QR code is oversized and centrally framed with generous negative space, acknowledging that this is the primary interaction target (most transfers happen via a second device scanning this code, not manual entry). The Bitcoin logo watermark in the center reinforces asset context at a glance without harming scan integrity (a common technique with high error-correction QR generation).

The address itself is truncated (bc1qfl2...6ud9jkzc8h) with a dedicated, high-contrast gradient Copy button — reducing the risk of manual transcription errors, which in crypto are irreversible and costly. A muted disclaimer about transaction timing and an inline "Learn more" link manage expectations and offer progressive disclosure for less experienced users without cluttering the primary flow. The full-width dark Share button anchors the bottom, offering an alternate distribution method (sending the address via message/email) for scenarios where scanning isn't feasible.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal, functional, and reassuring rather than promotional. "Receive Bitcoin" is a direct, unambiguous title. The microcopy "Transactions may take a few minutes to complete" preemptively defuses anxiety during the wait for blockchain confirmation — a critical trust-building moment in fintech/crypto UX where users are conditioned to expect instant feedback.

"Learn more about Segwit vs Legacy" acknowledges that the terminology is jargon-heavy for mainstream users, offering an escape hatch to education rather than forcing comprehension inline. The tone throughout is utilitarian and confidence-inspiring, avoiding playful or casual language that would feel inappropriate when handling financial transfers.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented address-type control placed above the QR code so the causal link between selection and generated output is immediately legible.

  • High-contrast, oversized QR code with sufficient quiet zone and a centered brand watermark, balancing scannability with brand reinforcement.

  • Truncated address + one-tap Copy pairing eliminates the need for risky manual transcription of a long alphanumeric string.

  • Dual distribution paths (QR scan and Share button) accommodate both in-person and remote receiving scenarios.

  • Expectation-setting microcopy about confirmation delays reduces support inquiries and user anxiety mid-transaction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets cryptocurrency holders and traders, ranging from casual users receiving a small transfer from a friend to more advanced users who understand the Segwit/Legacy address distinction. The dark theme and orange Bitcoin accent cater to the crypto-native aesthetic that signals security and modernity to this audience.

Psychologically, the design leans on error prevention and loss aversion — because blockchain transactions are irreversible, every design choice (large QR, copy button, truncated-but-verifiable address) is engineered to minimize the catastrophic risk of sending funds to a mistyped address. The reassurance copy about processing time also targets user anxiety, since crypto users are highly sensitive to transaction status due to past experiences with stuck or delayed transfers.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any deposit, wallet-funding, or address-sharing flow in crypto, banking, or peer-to-peer payment apps. It's ideal whenever a user needs to communicate a complex identifier (wallet address, bank routing info, event ticket ID) to another system or person, especially where transcription errors carry real financial or logistical cost. The segmented format toggle is reusable anywhere multiple technical variants of the same credential need to coexist without separate screens.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, QR-centric layout for low-stakes or simple identifiers (e.g., sharing a username) where a QR code adds unnecessary friction. Also avoid exposing technical distinctions like "Segwit vs Legacy" to novice-only audiences without very strong default selection and education — surfacing this choice prematurely can create confusion or decision paralysis for users who don't understand the implications of picking the wrong format.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Uploading & Downloading 3
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a dedicated "Receive" utility view within a cryptocurrency wallet application, designed to facilitate incoming Bitcoin transactions with maximum clarity and minimal error potential. The layout follows a strict vertical hierarchy: navigation, address-type selector, the dominant visual asset (QR code), the copyable text data, contextual disclaimers, and a final action.

The QR code is given the most visual real estate and is placed dead-center, immediately signaling its primary role as the fastest, most error-proof way to transfer an address (via camera scan) compared to manually typing a 34-character string. The branded Bitcoin logo embedded in the center of the QR code reinforces asset recognition and adds a touch of premium polish, while the vibrant blue-to-purple gradient dot pattern breaks from the typical stark black-and-white QR aesthetic to align with the app's dark, tech-forward branding.

Below the QR sits a bordered card containing the truncated address string and a high-contrast gradient "Copy" button — a clear affordance for the secondary transfer method for advanced users who prefer pasting into another exchange or wallet. The truncation (13rJ1J9...bs34qoAuDR) reduces visual clutter and cognitive load while still allowing verification via first/last character matching.

The Segwit/Legacy segmented control at the top is a critical but understated inclusion, letting technically savvy users pick their preferred address format without overwhelming novice users with jargon front-and-center. The dark theme throughout reduces eye strain and matches crypto-native app conventions, while generous whitespace and large touch targets ensure this high-stakes financial action (where mistakes are irreversible) feels calm and controlled rather than rushed.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal, functional, and reassuring rather than promotional — appropriate for a financial transaction screen where trust and precision matter more than persuasion. "Your Bitcoin address" is plainly labeled with no embellishment, and the microcopy "Transactions may take a few minutes to complete" proactively manages user anxiety about blockchain confirmation delays, preventing support tickets or repeated refresh-checking behavior.

The inline "Learn more about Segwit vs Legacy" link is an excellent piece of progressive disclosure — it acknowledges that most users won't know the difference between address formats but provides an escape hatch for curious or cautious users without cluttering the primary flow with an explanation nobody asked for.

The tone is neutral and instructional, avoiding hype-driven crypto marketing language, which builds credibility and signals that this is a serious financial tool rather than a speculative gamified experience.
screens.keyHighlights:
• QR-first hierarchy: Placing the scannable QR code as the visual centerpiece over the raw text address optimizes for the fastest, least error-prone transfer method.

  • Branded QR code: Embedding the Bitcoin logo and using on-brand gradient colors within the QR code turns a purely functional element into a polished, recognizable brand touchpoint.

  • Address truncation with Copy button: Reduces cognitive overload from a 34-character string while still offering one-tap precision copying, eliminating manual transcription errors entirely.

  • Address-format segmented control: Surfaces advanced functionality (Segwit vs Legacy) without forcing novice users to understand it, paired with a "Learn more" link for those who want depth.

  • Proactive latency messaging: Setting expectations about confirmation delays upfront reduces user anxiety and support burden.

  • Native Share action: The full-width Share button lets users push their address into messaging apps or other wallets instantly, extending the receive flow beyond just this screen.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves both crypto novices and experienced holders who need to receive funds — a moment of high emotional stakes since a wrong address or wrong network format can result in permanently lost funds. The design leverages the psychology of trust-through-simplicity: by minimizing text, maximizing the scannable QR, and using a bordered "safe zone" card around the address, the interface visually communicates "this is the one correct, verified thing to copy or scan."

The segmented Segwit/Legacy control caters specifically to power users and those receiving from exchanges with specific format requirements, while the "Learn more" link caters to intermediate users leveling up their crypto literacy. The overall psychological driver is anxiety reduction — irreversible blockchain transactions demand an interface that feels authoritative, uncluttered, and confidence-inspiring rather than experimental or playful.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any peer-to-peer or wallet-to-wallet asset transfer flow where an address, code, or identifier must be shared precisely — cryptocurrency receive screens, contactless payment QR sharing, event ticket QR passes, or Wi-Fi network sharing. It's ideal whenever the primary conversion goal is "get this exact string into another device" and errors are costly or irreversible.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy QR-centric layout for casual or low-stakes sharing (e.g., sharing a social profile link) where a simple share sheet suffices and a full-screen QR would feel like overkill. Also avoid exposing technical toggles like Segwit/Legacy to fully mainstream consumer audiences without a clear default and explanation, as it can introduce confusion or decision paralysis for first-time crypto users who don't understand the implications of choosing the wrong format.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Uploading & Downloading 5
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen solves a classic crypto UX challenge: helping a non-technical user safely receive funds without manually typing an error-prone 26-42 character alphanumeric string. The design leans heavily on redundancy of format — offering both a scannable QR code (fast, error-free for camera-equipped senders) and a copyable text string (for pasting into another app or exchange) — so no matter the sender's context, there's a frictionless path.

The Segwit/Legacy segmented control at the top is a critical but easily overlooked detail for power users: Bitcoin has multiple address formats, and defaulting to Segwit (the modern, lower-fee standard) while still surfacing Legacy for compatibility with older wallets/exchanges shows thoughtful accommodation of the protocol's fragmentation without overwhelming novice users — it's tucked away as a simple tab rather than a confusing dropdown of technical jargon.

The truncated address (bc1qfl2...6ud9jkzc8h) paired with a full-width tap target and a persistent 'Copied' state change on the button is a strong micro-interaction: it gives immediate, unambiguous confirmation that the clipboard action succeeded, which is essential when the content being copied is invisible/opaque to the user (they can't 'see' their clipboard).

Layered confirmation (button label changes to 'Copied' AND a toast/snackbar reading 'Copied to clipboard' appears near the bottom) is slightly redundant but intentional — this is a case where redundancy is a feature, not a bug, given the catastrophic cost of a failed or unnoticed copy (sending funds to the wrong address or address never being pasted).
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal, functional, and reassuring rather than promotional. Microcopy like "Transactions may take a few minutes to complete" preempts anxiety and support tickets by setting expectations about blockchain confirmation times before the user starts worrying about a 'missing' deposit.

"Learn more about Segwit vs Legacy" is a well-placed contextual education link — it doesn't force a lengthy explanation on-screen (which would clutter a transactional flow) but offers an escape hatch for curious or confused users, respecting the diverse literacy levels of a crypto app's audience (from beginners to advanced holders).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-format address delivery: QR code + copyable text string covers both scanning and manual-entry/paste use cases.

  • Address type segmentation (Segwit/Legacy): Exposes advanced blockchain functionality without technical overload, defaulting to the safer/cheaper modern standard.

  • Multi-signal copy confirmation: Button text swaps to "Copied" (green, high-contrast) plus a floating toast, doubling the assurance for a high-stakes clipboard action.

  • Expectation-setting microcopy: Proactively addresses the common "where's my deposit?" anxiety with a simple timing disclaimer.

  • Share action: Native share sheet integration lets users send the address via messaging apps instead of manual copy/paste, widening the ways a transaction can be initiated.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves both crypto newcomers and experienced holders within a self-custody or exchange wallet app. Newcomers benefit from the visual simplicity of "just scan this code," while experienced users benefit from the Legacy/Segwit toggle and the ability to copy/share the raw address for use in other software.

Psychologically, the design mitigates the loss-aversion terror unique to crypto transactions — unlike a bank transfer, sending Bitcoin to a wrong or malformed address is often irreversible. Every design choice (large QR, truncated-but-verifiable address, redundant copy confirmation, Bitcoin-orange branded QR center icon) is aimed at building certainty and reducing the chance of costly human error.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any "receive funds/data" flow where the underlying payload (an address, ID, or key) is too long/complex for reliable manual transcription — crypto wallets, bank account/routing number sharing, Wi-Fi password sharing, or B2B API key distribution. Also apply the layered confirmation (label change + toast) pattern anytime a copy-to-clipboard action is critical and its result isn't immediately visually verifiable to the user.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid multiple address-format tabs (Segwit/Legacy) if your product's users are exclusively beginners for whom this distinction adds confusion without benefit — consider hiding it behind an "Advanced options" disclosure instead. Also avoid stacking a toast AND a button-state change for low-stakes copy actions (e.g., copying a promo code), where a single lightweight confirmation is sufficient and less visually busy.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Uploading & Downloading 6
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a bottom sheet modal layered on top of the wallet home/dashboard, triggered from the "copy/receive" icon in the top navigation bar. The design uses progressive disclosure: the main dashboard stays dimmed and visible behind the sheet, reinforcing spatial context and letting the user dismiss via swipe-down without losing their place.

The content hierarchy is deliberately layered by complexity and frequency of use. The top-most, most prominent card is the user's human-readable ENS-style identity (alexsmithmobbin.cb.id) — abstracting away hex addresses for a friendlier onboarding experience. Below it, the raw Ethereum address is offered as a fallback with a truncated hex string, a QR code option, and a row of small network badges (Optimism, Avalanche, BNB, Polygon) signaling multichain compatibility without cluttering the layout with four separate cards.

The "Receive with US bank" tile handles fiat on-ramping, geographically localized, and is visually de-emphasized (icon + chevron) since it's a secondary, less-frequent path. An "Other assets" chevron row is a collapsed drill-down for less common tokens, keeping the primary sheet lightweight.

Behind the sheet, the $0.00 balance and disabled-looking Swap/Cash out buttons make it clear this is a new/empty wallet, and the flow naturally funnels a first-time user toward funding the wallet — the copy icon and QR affordances reduce friction for peer-to-peer crypto transfers or exchange withdrawals.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The copy is short, plain-language, and action-oriented ("Share address to receive crypto or messages", "Get your US bank information"). It deliberately avoids crypto jargon like "public key" in favor of consumer-friendly framing, aligning with Coinbase's mission to demystify Web3 for a busy, non-technical mainstream audience. The human-readable ".cb.id" identity is foregrounded above the intimidating hexadecimal address, softening the technical nature of blockchain addresses.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Human-readable identity first: Surfacing the ENS-like .cb.id name above the raw hex address dramatically lowers cognitive load and error risk when sharing an address.

  • Consolidated multichain address: A single Ethereum address card with small network chip icons communicates EVM-compatibility across L2s/sidechains without needing five redundant cards.

  • Dual affordances (copy + QR): Offering both a one-tap copy button and a QR scan option serves both remote (send from exchange) and in-person (peer-to-peer) receiving contexts.

  • Progressive disclosure via "Other assets": Keeps the primary sheet focused on the two most common receive methods while not hiding less-common ones entirely.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Designed for busy urban professionals who are likely new or casual crypto users needing to quickly onboard funds without navigating blockchain complexity. The psychological trigger here is friction reduction and trust-building: by leading with a friendly username instead of an intimidating string of hex characters, users feel more confident sharing their "address" the way they'd share a Venmo handle or email, reducing anxiety around irreversible crypto transfer mistakes.
screens.whereToUse: Use a layered bottom sheet with a "receive" pattern like this whenever an app needs to present multiple deposit/funding methods (crypto address, bank transfer, QR) without navigating away from the main dashboard. Ideal for fintech, wallet, and payment apps that must balance simplicity for beginners with power-user options (multichain, raw addresses) via progressive disclosure.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the underlying data/action set is simple (e.g., a single-currency wallet) since the extra layering and multiple card options would be unnecessary complexity. Also avoid leading with an abstracted identity (like .cb.id) without a very clear, prominent fallback to the raw address for power users or when interoperability with third-party wallets that don't resolve custom domains is critical — clarity must never be sacrificed for cuteness in irreversible financial transactions.

screens.name: Lesson Quiz 15
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is a well-constructed check because the answer cannot be reasoned from words. The four options are diagrams differing only in where the second point sits, so the learner must read the geometry — which is exactly the skill the preceding exploration built. A text-based version of this question would be nearly impossible to phrase and trivially guessable; the visual format makes it neither.

The distractors are also carefully graded rather than arbitrary. One shows the second point very close to a, producing a steep secant that hugs the curve. One shows it far left with a shallow line. One shows a horizontal secant through two symmetric points — a configuration where the secant slope is zero while the curve at a is clearly rising, which is the most instructive wrong answer since it looks tidy but is maximally wrong.

The correct answer is arguably the top-left option, where the points are closest together — but the selected option is top-right, where they are further apart. Whether that reflects a learner's mistake or a different intended answer cannot be determined without the result state; the phrasing "best approximates" implies closest-points, which favours top-left.

"Start over" reappears here, in a question where tapping another card is the reset — the same redundancy noted on the earlier numeric-entry exercise.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Sparse, with the question carrying the entire verbal load.

"Which secant best approximates the curve at (a, f(a))?" — "best approximates" is the operative phrase, and it is doing careful work. It does not ask which is correct, because all four are legitimate secants. It asks which is closest, which is the actual concept: the approximation improves as the points converge. That framing prepares the learner for a limit without naming one.

"Secant" is used without underlining here, unlike the exposition screens where it carried a definition affordance. The term is now assumed known.

No option labels. The four cards carry no A/B/C/D markers, no captions, no descriptions — the diagrams speak entirely for themselves. That is right for a question testing visual reading, though it makes the options harder to discuss or report.

"Start over" and "Check" are consistent with the earlier exercise, though the former has little to reset here.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visual question for a visual skill — the answer cannot be reasoned from wording, so the check genuinely tests what the exploration taught.

  2. Graded distractors — each wrong option represents a distinct degree of approximation, including one that looks tidy but is maximally wrong.

  3. "Best approximates" prepares the limit — asking for the closest rather than the correct answer frames convergence without naming it.

  4. Unlabelled diagrams — no captions means the geometry does all the work, at the cost of making options hard to reference.

  5. Redundant reset — "Start over" adds nothing on a single-select grid where tapping another card resets the answer.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Khan Academy — visual multiple choice for graph-reading skills, with diagram-only options.

  2. Desmos — comparison-based questions where the learner selects among configurations.

  3. Brilliant's own pattern — this mirrors the explore-then-check structure used with the microscope sequence.
screens.whereToUse: Best where the skill being tested is visual interpretation, and where distractors can be graded along a meaningful dimension rather than being arbitrary.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit where thumbnails are too small to distinguish reliably, and poor fit when the difference between the best and second-best option is finer than the rendering resolution.

screens.name: Lesson Quiz 16
screens.uxAnalysis:
This resolves the ambiguity from the previous frame — the selection has changed to the bottom-right horizontal secant, which is marked wrong. That is the most instructive of the four distractors: a flat line through two symmetric points has zero slope while the curve at a is clearly rising, so it is maximally wrong despite looking tidy.

The error treatment is consistent with the numeric exercise seen earlier: same amber sheet, same "See answer" secondary and "Try again" primary, same flag. One learned pattern covers every wrong answer in the app.

But there is a notable inconsistency in the error colour. The earlier numeric exercise marked its wrong answer with an amber cross matching the sheet. Here the cross is red while the sheet remains amber. That is a real deviation — the earlier screen's amber-throughout treatment was a deliberate softening of failure, and red on the badge partially undoes it. Either the colour is question-type-dependent or one of the two is a defect.

The dimming of the three unselected options is also worth noting: they fade to near-invisible, which means the learner cannot easily compare their wrong choice against the alternatives while reading the hint.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven, and the hint is the weakest seen in this lesson.

"Select the line that best approximates the graph." This is a near-verbatim restatement of the question, not a hint. Compare the earlier numeric exercise, whose wrong-answer sheet reframed the problem entirely — "What is the derivative when t = 1?" — offering a genuinely different route to the answer. Here the learner is told again what they were already asked, with no new information.

For a learner who selected the horizontal secant, the useful hint is specific and available: the curve is rising at a, but your line is flat. That single observation would correct the misunderstanding. Restating the question corrects nothing.

"Graph" replaces "curve" between the question and the hint, a small vocabulary inconsistency in two sentences that otherwise say the same thing.

No statement that the answer is wrong, consistent with the earlier error state — the marker carries the verdict and the copy moves to help, even though the help here is thin.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Hint restates rather than reframes — repeating the question gives the learner nothing new, unlike the earlier exercise's genuinely different angle.

  2. Error colour inconsistent with the earlier exercise — red cross here versus amber cross previously, against an identical amber sheet.

  3. Recovery structure consistent — same sheet, same button hierarchy, same flag as every other wrong-answer state.

  4. Dimming impedes comparison — the three alternatives fade too far to be usefully weighed while reading the hint.

  5. Specific correction available but unused — "the curve is rising but your line is flat" would fix this exact misunderstanding in one sentence.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo — bottom-sheet error feedback with continue and report, though with more specific per-answer explanations.

  2. Khan Academy — hints escalate in specificity across attempts rather than repeating the prompt.

  3. Brilliant's own numeric exercise — the earlier error state in this same lesson reframed the question rather than restating it, so the app is capable of better here.
screens.whereToUse: The sheet structure and button hierarchy are sound and worth keeping; the hint content is what needs to differ per distractor.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit wherever a hint merely repeats the question — a learner who did not understand the prompt the first time gains nothing from reading it again.

screens.name: Lesson Quiz 23
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is the lesson's final assessment and it inverts the direction of every prior exercise. Earlier questions gave a function and asked for the rate; this gives data and asks the learner to build the function. That is a genuine step up — reading a slope off a line is recognition, deriving one from scattered points is construction.

The equation template is the key design decision. Rather than an open field, the learner fills a single blank in p(t) = ___ t + 20. The intercept is supplied, the structure is supplied, and only the coefficient is asked for. That isolates exactly what is being tested — the rate — while removing the risk of failing on notation, form, or a misremembered intercept. It is the same principle as fixing the unit outside the numeric field in the first exercise.

Notably there is no movable point and no live preview. Every prior graph exercise in this lesson gave the learner a manipulable instrument; this one gives a static plot. That is consistent with a terminal assessment — the scaffolding is withdrawn and the learner must read the data unaided. It also removes the trial-and-error route that the live-preview exercises permitted.

The points sit at clean intervals with readable values, so the arithmetic is tractable: the rise across the visible range divides evenly.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven only in the instruction, and it is minimal.

"Enter the rate of change for the function." Imperative, no scaffolding, no reminder of method. Consistent with the other section assessments, which also stripped the supportive framing used during instruction.

"Rate of change" persists to the final screen. Across an entire calculus lesson — animation, microscope, secants, three assessments — the word "derivative" has appeared exactly once, inside an error hint. That is a remarkable and sustained deferral. Whether it is deliberate staging for a later lesson or an omission cannot be determined from here, but a learner completing this lesson would not know the formal name for what they have spent it learning.

The equation template is the real instruction. p(t) = ___ t + 20 tells the learner the function is linear and where the blank sits, without a sentence explaining either.

No units anywhere, consistent with the second section's bare numerals and unlike the first exercise's ml/s.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Direction inverted at the final check — building a function from data is harder than reading a rate from one, an appropriate terminal difficulty.

  2. Template isolates the tested variable — supplying structure and intercept means only the coefficient is assessed.

  3. Scaffolding fully withdrawn — no movable point, no live preview, no guides; the learner reads static data unaided.

  4. Trial-and-error route removed — without a preview, the answer cannot be found by adjustment.

  5. Formal vocabulary never introduced — "derivative" remains absent from the lesson's entire instructional path.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Khan Academy — fill-in-the-template equation exercises that isolate a single parameter.

  2. Desmos — regression and line-fitting exercises from scatter data.

  3. Brilliant's own earlier exercises — the same lesson used live-preview instruments, so their absence here is a deliberate assessment choice.
screens.whereToUse: Best as a terminal check where the learner should construct rather than recognise, with a template that removes irrelevant failure modes.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit if the data points are hard to read against the axes, since arithmetic error would then masquerade as conceptual failure.

screens.name: Lesson Quiz 17
screens.uxAnalysis:
This confirms the correct answer is the top-left option — the two points closest together — which validates the reading of "best approximates" as favouring convergence. The learner reached it on a second attempt after the horizontal-secant error, so the recovery loop worked as designed.

The success treatment is identical in structure to the earlier text-based question: green sheet, party emoji, +15 XP, "Why?" secondary, Continue primary, flag. Two different question types — numeric entry, text multiple choice, visual multiple choice — all resolve into the same feedback component. That consistency is the app's strongest structural quality in the lesson experience.

The XP award is flat at 15 regardless of the wrong attempt. There is no reduction for a second try, no bonus for first-time correctness. That is a deliberate choice consistent with the app's forgiving posture — a learner who struggled and recovered earns the same as one who breezed through — though it does mean XP measures completion rather than mastery.

The dimming of the three wrong options is heavier here than useful. Having just chosen the horizontal secant and been corrected, the learner might benefit from comparing it against the winner, but at this contrast the comparison is hard to make.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven, and identical to the earlier success state — which is the notable fact.

"Correct!" with a party popper and an exclamation mark is the same celebration used on the text question. Success is named and marked; failure, two frames earlier, was never verbally acknowledged. That asymmetry is now confirmed as systematic across question types.

"Why?" is more valuable here than on the earlier question. This learner got it wrong once, then right — so they may have arrived by elimination rather than understanding. An explanation of why closest points give the best approximation would consolidate the concept. The button being available, demoted, and identically placed across every question means a learner develops a habit around it.

"+15 XP" remains unexplained. Several exercises in, XP has accumulated with no visible total, no stated purpose, and no connection made to the Leagues tab or the header lightning bolt.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. One feedback component across question types — numeric, text, and visual questions all resolve into the same sheet, so the pattern is learned once.

  2. Flat XP regardless of attempts — consistent with a forgiving posture, though it means points measure completion rather than mastery.

  3. "Why?" most valuable after a recovery — a learner who was wrong then right may have guessed, and the explanation is exactly what they need.

  4. Asymmetric tone confirmed — success is celebrated verbally, failure is never named, across every question type in the lesson.

  5. Heavy dimming limits comparison — the just-rejected wrong answer is hard to weigh against the correct one.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo — identical green success sheet with XP and continue across all exercise types.

  2. Khan Academy — offers explanations on correct answers, particularly valuable after a prior miss.

  3. Brilliant's own text question — the earlier success state in this lesson is structurally identical, confirming the component is shared.
screens.whereToUse: Best wherever a learning product has multiple exercise formats — a single shared feedback component means the outcome experience is consistent regardless of question type.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit where a points system carries no stated purpose, and poor fit if dimming prevents the learner from comparing their error against the correct answer at the moment they are most receptive.

screens.name: Lesson Quiz 18
screens.uxAnalysis:
The header finally explains the three dots. The progress bar has filled completely and the first dot now carries a ring — so the bar tracks progress within a section, and the dots mark sections. A learner who wondered what the dots meant for the entire lesson now has the answer through observation rather than explanation.

The exercise itself is the lesson's synthesis. It returns to the water-bottle function from the opening screens, but instead of asking the learner to read the coefficient off the equation, it gives them a graph, a movable point, and dashed guides showing the coordinates at that point. The learner can position the marker, read off a value pair, and compute the rate — or recognise the slope directly. Both routes work, which accommodates learners who reasoned differently through the lesson.

The tool provided is exactly the one the lesson built. Three separate interactions — the animated bottle, the microscope, the secant — all trained reading a rate off a graph, and this question requires it.

Offering four discrete options rather than free numeric entry is a notable softening. The earlier version of this same question used the maths keyboard and an open field; here the answer space is bounded, which lowers difficulty and rules out formatting errors.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven only in the question, and it is deliberately unadorned.

"What is the rate of change for the function?" — no scaffolding, no reminder of the method, no hint about using the point. After a lesson that carefully framed every concept, this question offers nothing beyond the ask. That is appropriate for an assessment: the support was the lesson, and this measures whether it landed.

"Rate of change" persists. The lesson has now used this phrase across every screen — animation, exposition, secants, and now assessment — while "derivative" has appeared exactly once, inside an error hint. The formal term is still being withheld this deep into a calculus course.

The options are bare numerals, no units. The earlier version of this question required ml/s; here the unit is dropped entirely, which slightly weakens the connection between the number and what it measures.

No instruction to move the point, consistent with every interactive control in this lesson.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. The dots are finally explained by observation — a filled bar plus a ringed first dot reveals the two-level progress structure without any text.

  2. Assessment uses the tool the lesson built — reading a rate off a graph is precisely what three prior interactions trained.

  3. Bounded options lower the difficulty — four choices instead of open numeric entry removes formatting failure and narrows the answer space.

  4. Support withdrawn at assessment — no hints or scaffolding, correctly distinguishing a check from instruction.

  5. Units dropped — bare numerals weaken the link between the value and the quantity it describes.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo — section-level progress marked by discrete indicators above a within-section bar.

  2. Khan Academy — assessment items that reuse the interactive tool from the preceding instruction.

  3. Brilliant's own earlier exercise — the same question asked with open numeric entry, so this is a deliberately easier variant.
screens.whereToUse: Best as an end-of-section check that requires the exact skill the section taught, with the supporting tool available but the scaffolding removed.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit when the options are guessable by elimination — four round numbers where one matches an obvious slope is answerable without the graph.

screens.name: Lesson Quiz 20
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is a materially different error state from the two seen earlier in the lesson, and the differences look deliberate rather than accidental.

The correct answer is revealed immediately. Previous wrong answers offered "Try again" and withheld the solution; here the right option is marked and the learner cannot retry. That fits an end-of-section assessment — this question checks whether the section landed, so a second attempt would compromise the measurement.

"Why?" is promoted to primary. On every prior screen it was the muted secondary. Here it is the black button and Continue is demoted. With no retry available, understanding the explanation is the only remaining value in the screen, and the hierarchy says so.

The sheet is grey, not amber. The earlier wrong-answer sheets were amber with a softening intent; this is neutral grey with a thinking-face emoji rather than a party popper. The register has shifted from encouragement to matter-of-fact.

The overall effect is a genuine tonal distinction between practice and assessment. Practice forgives and invites another go; assessment records the outcome and offers the explanation. That is coherent design — though it also means the app now has three different wrong-answer treatments (amber cross with amber sheet, red cross with amber sheet, red cross with grey sheet), which is more variation than the underlying distinction requires.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven, and this is the first time the app names failure.

"Incorrect" appears for the first time in the entire lesson. Both earlier wrong answers used only a marker and moved straight to help — no verbal acknowledgment of being wrong. Here the word is stated plainly, without softening and without apology.

That is defensible in an assessment context, where the learner needs to know the result unambiguously. But it is a sharp break from a lesson that spent every prior error state carefully avoiding the word.

The thinking-face emoji replaces the party popper used on success. It reads as considered rather than disappointed, which takes some edge off the plainness.

No hint accompanies "Incorrect." Unlike the earlier errors, which offered a reframed question or a restated instruction, this sheet offers only the label and the buttons. The explanation lives behind "Why?" rather than being surfaced.

"Why?" as the primary label is well chosen — it frames the next action as curiosity rather than remediation, even at the moment of being told you were wrong.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Assessment behaves differently from practice — no retry, correct answer revealed, explanation promoted to primary.

  2. Hierarchy follows what remains useful — with retry removed, "Why?" becomes the only action with instructional value and is styled accordingly.

  3. Register shifts with stakes — grey sheet and a thinking face replace amber and celebration, matching a check rather than a coaching moment.

  4. First naming of failure — "Incorrect" appears after an entire lesson of avoiding the word, a deliberate but abrupt tonal change.

  5. Three wrong-answer treatments now exist — amber/amber, red/amber, red/grey — more variation than the practice-versus-assessment distinction needs.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo — distinguishes practice feedback from test feedback with different retry rules and tone.

  2. Khan Academy — mastery checks reveal the answer without retry, unlike practice sets.

  3. Brilliant's own earlier errors — the two prior wrong-answer states in this lesson both offered retry and withheld the answer, confirming this is a distinct assessment treatment.
screens.whereToUse: Best on end-of-section checks where a retry would invalidate the measurement, and where the explanation is the only remaining instructional value.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit in practice contexts, where removing retry converts a learning opportunity into a verdict, and poor fit if the tonal shift is not signalled — a learner may not know they have entered an assessment.

screens.name: Lesson Quiz 25
screens.uxAnalysis:
Comparing the three input states — empty, 2, and now 25 — shows the preview bracketing the answer from both sides. At 2 the line was far too shallow, passing below every point; at 25 it is far too steep, clearing the top of the graph before t = 3. The learner has now seen the failure mode in both directions, which is more informative than either alone: the correct value lies between, and the visual gap tells them roughly where.

This also demonstrates the preview updating per keystroke rather than on commit. Appending "5" to "2" produced an immediate and dramatic replot, so the learner gets feedback while typing rather than after finishing.

The overshoot is handled gracefully. The line simply exits the plot area at the top rather than rescaling the axes, which is the right choice — rescaling would keep the line visible but destroy the fixed reference the data points provide. Holding the view constant means "off the top" reads unambiguously as "too big."

The mechanical-adjustment concern remains, and this frame illustrates it clearly: a learner bracketing between 2 and 25 could converge on 5 by bisection without ever computing rise over run. But bracketing is itself a legitimate numerical method, and for a fitting task the visual judgement is part of the skill.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
No new copy, and the equation template continues to do the communicating.

p(t) = 25 t + 20 reads as a complete, well-formed function, and its plot is visibly wrong. The learner is looking at correct notation producing an incorrect model, which is a useful thing to see — being able to write a function is not the same as writing the right one.

Nothing signals error. No message, no colour change, no warning that the line has left the visible range. Consistent with every interactive screen in this lesson, the geometry carries the verdict.

The "5" key is highlighted blue, tracking the most recent keypress — so the highlight follows the last input rather than persisting across the entry.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Bracketing from both sides — having seen too-shallow and too-steep, the learner knows the answer lies between and roughly where.

  2. Per-keystroke updating — feedback arrives while typing rather than on commit.

  3. Fixed axes on overshoot — refusing to rescale keeps the data points as a stable reference and makes "too big" legible.

  4. Correct notation, wrong model — the template shows that well-formed does not mean right.

  5. Bracketing as legitimate method — converging by adjustment is closer to real practice on a fitting task than it would be on slope-reading.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Desmos — per-keystroke replotting with fixed viewport unless the user zooms.

  2. GeoGebra — parameter entry with immediate visual consequence on a fixed frame.

  3. Brilliant's own earlier frames — the same component at 2 and at empty, confirming continuous update.
screens.whereToUse: Best where overshoot and undershoot are both instructive, and where holding the viewport fixed preserves a reference the learner is judging against.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit where the line leaving the frame gives no information — here it does, but a plot that rescales automatically would lose the signal entirely.

screens.name: Lesson Quiz 27
screens.uxAnalysis:
This resolves the ambiguity flagged on the previous frame. At 4 the line sat just below the later points and could plausibly have been read as a fit; at 5 it passes cleanly through every point, and the difference between the two states is legible once seen. The concern that visual validation cannot discriminate near the answer turns out to be overstated for this particular data set — the points sit exactly on the line at the correct value, so "close" and "correct" do look different.

That works because the data is noiseless. Every point lies exactly on p(t) = 5t + 20, so the correct answer produces a perfect fit rather than a best fit. Had the points carried any scatter, 4 and 5 would both have produced near-misses and the visual check would genuinely fail to discriminate. The exercise is well constructed for its tool.

The five input states together — empty, 2, 25, 4, 5 — form a complete demonstration of the component. The learner bracketed from both extremes, closed in, and landed on an unambiguous result. That progression is the exercise working exactly as designed.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
No new copy, and the graph delivers the confirmation the text does not.

Nothing states that the answer is correct. The app offers no confirmation message, no colour change, no check mark — the line passing through every point is the signal. Consistent with every interactive screen in this lesson, geometry carries the verdict.

That restraint works better here than on the previous frame. At 4 the silence left the learner uncertain; at 5 the visual is decisive enough that a message would be redundant.

The template reads p(t) = 5 t + 20, a complete function whose plot demonstrably describes the data. Notation and geometry agree, which is the same dual-representation principle the lesson opened with.

The "5" key is highlighted, tracking the latest keypress, consistent throughout.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Exact fit resolves the ambiguity — noiseless data means the correct answer produces a perfect fit, so visual validation does discriminate here.

  2. Data construction enables the tool — points lying exactly on the line is what makes the preview a reliable check rather than an approximate one.

  3. Bracketing to resolution — five input states show the learner narrowing from both extremes to an unambiguous result.

  4. Silence justified at the endpoint — no confirmation message is needed when the visual is decisive.

  5. Notation and geometry agree — the completed template and its plot are the same function verified two ways.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Desmos — exact-fit exercises with noiseless data rely on the same visual confirmation.

  2. GeoGebra — parameter-matching tasks constructed so the correct value produces a clean fit.

  3. Brilliant's own earlier frames — the same component at 2, 25, and 4, isolating what changes at the correct value.
screens.whereToUse: Best where data is constructed to lie exactly on the target function, so visual fit is a genuine check rather than an approximation.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit with noisy or real-world data, where no coefficient produces a perfect fit and adjacent values look identical — a residual measure would then be required.

screens.name: Lesson Quiz 28
screens.uxAnalysis:
This confirms the submission flow: dismissing the keyboard restores the full layout and reveals Check, now enabled. It also confirms the awkwardness noted across all five input frames — the keyboard covers the primary action, so completing this exercise requires typing, dismissing, then tapping, rather than a single continuous gesture. A "Check" action placed in the keyboard accessory row beside "Done" would collapse those three steps into two.

The unfocused field has reverted to a grey border, so the input's resting state is visually distinct from its focused state. Small, but it means the learner can tell at a glance whether the field is live.

With the question text visible again alongside the fitted line and the completed equation, the screen presents the whole problem and its solution in one view. That is the right final state before submission — the learner can verify the instruction, the data, the function, and the fit together.

Across the full lesson, this exercise is the culmination: it inverts the direction of every earlier question, withdraws multiple-choice support, requires construction rather than recognition, and provides a tool whose feedback is genuine rather than merely suggestive. It is the strongest single exercise in the sequence.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
No new copy; the restored question text is the only addition.

"Enter the rate of change for the function." Reappearing at the moment of submission means the learner can confirm what was asked before committing — a small but real benefit of the keyboard dismissing rather than the layout scrolling permanently.

"Rate of change" concludes the lesson. Across every screen — animation, exposition, microscope, secants, three section assessments — the formal term "derivative" has appeared exactly once, in a hint after a wrong answer. A learner finishing this lesson has built the concept thoroughly and does not know its name. That is either careful staging for a subsequent lesson or a notable omission; the lesson itself does not indicate which.

The template stands complete as p(t) = 5t + 20, with its plot as verification.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Whole problem visible before submission — question, data, function, and fit together let the learner verify everything at once.

  2. Keyboard obscures the primary action — a three-step type-dismiss-tap flow that a keyboard-row Check would reduce to two.

  3. Field state legible when unfocused — grey border versus blue distinguishes resting from live input.

  4. Culminating exercise — construction rather than recognition, with genuine rather than suggestive feedback.

  5. Formal vocabulary never introduced — the lesson ends without naming the derivative.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Khan Academy — places submit actions in the keyboard accessory row to avoid the dismissal step.

  2. Desmos — expression entry with the action available without dismissing input.

  3. Brilliant's own earlier numeric exercise — the same three-step submission pattern, so this is consistent rather than a one-off.
screens.whereToUse: Best as a terminal assessment where the learner constructs a model from data and can verify the result visually before committing.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit where the submit action remains hidden behind the keyboard — the dismissal step is avoidable friction at the moment of completion.

screens.name: Lesson Quiz 29
screens.uxAnalysis:
This closes the lesson, and the header tells the story: all three dots solid, bar full. Two levels of progress complete simultaneously, and the CTA changes from "Continue" to "Finish" — the first time in roughly twenty lesson screens that the button label has changed. That single word is the entire completion signal within the exercise flow.

The success treatment is otherwise identical to every prior correct answer: green sheet, party popper, +15 XP, "Why?" demoted. Notably the app does not escalate for the final question — no bigger celebration, no bonus, no summary. The celebration presumably lives on the screen after "Finish."

The flag is absent from this sheet, unlike every earlier feedback state. Reporting a content problem is available throughout the lesson but not on its last question, which looks like an oversight rather than a decision.

Across the full lesson the structure now reads clearly: three sections, each ending in an assessment, with instruction and practice between. The final assessment required construction from data, the hardest task in the sequence, and the learner reached it having bracketed their way to the answer with a tool that made the fit verifiable.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven in the sheet, and one word carries the weight.

"Finish" replaces "Continue" for the first time in the lesson. It is unambiguous — the learner knows this was the last question without any separate announcement. Changing a single label to mark completion is economical and effective.

"Correct!" with the party popper and +15 XP is unchanged from every prior success, so the flat reward structure holds to the end: no first-try bonus, no final-question multiplier.

"Why?" remains available on the last question, which is consistent and appropriate — a learner who bracketed to 5 rather than computing rise over run may want the reasoning before leaving.

"Rate of change" ends the lesson. The instruction text on this final screen uses the same phrase the lesson opened with, and "derivative" was never introduced. Whatever the pedagogical intent, a learner completing this lesson has the concept without its name.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Completion signalled by one label change — "Finish" replacing "Continue" marks the end without a separate screen or announcement.

  2. Both progress levels resolve together — full bar and three solid dots make completion unambiguous.

  3. Flat reward to the end — no bonus for the final or hardest question, consistent with XP measuring completion rather than difficulty.

  4. "Why?" retained at the finish — the explanation stays available for a learner who arrived by adjustment rather than calculation.

  5. Reporting affordance missing — the flag present on every other feedback state is absent here.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo — changes its final-question CTA to signal lesson end before a summary screen.

  2. Khan Academy — marks mastery completion through progress indicators rather than a distinct celebration within the exercise.

  3. Brilliant's own earlier success states — structurally identical, isolating "Finish" as the only change.
screens.whereToUse: Best as a terminal state where a single label change communicates completion, with the celebration reserved for a following summary.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit if no summary follows — "Finish" implies something completes, and a learner returning straight to the course map without acknowledgment would find the ending abrupt.

screens.name: Lesson Quiz 33
screens.uxAnalysis:
Structurally this mirrors the Calculus lesson's opening exactly — illustration above, title, framing paragraphs, Continue, with the same three-dot section structure. The lesson template is confirmed as consistent across courses.

What differs is the illustration. Where the Calculus lesson opened with an abstract bar chart and the derivative lesson with a filling bottle, this opens with a social scene: two people on a sofa, a match on television, a drink. That is a deliberate register shift. Probability is the branch of maths people already reason about informally — anyone who has said "they're definitely losing this" has estimated a probability — so anchoring in a familiar situation rather than a diagram is well matched to the subject.

The illustration style is also new. Flat, angular, high-contrast figures with cropped framing, closer to editorial illustration than the geometric diagrams used elsewhere in the app. It signals a different kind of lesson before a word is read.

The empty progress bar and three inactive dots confirm this is a fresh lesson of comparable length to the Calculus one.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven, and the opening is warmer than the previous lesson's.

"Whether you love or hate televised sports, they are a great way to see probability in action."
