screens.uxAnalysis: This screen closes the result experience by returning to the identified song and presenting its factual details—album, label, year, genre, and the time it was recognized. The Recognized timestamp transforms the entry from catalog data into a personal record, making the adjacent location prompt feel like a way to complete a memory rather than collect unnecessary information. Positioning the empty location field directly beneath the completed timestamp naturally communicates its value without additional explanation. The final Share Song CTA receives the same visual emphasis that Play Full Song had at the top of the page, shifting the closing action from commercial to social. After multiple subscription prompts throughout the flow, ending with sharing feels appropriately restrained and aligned with users who have chosen to keep exploring instead of subscribing.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven in the table — the labels are terse, and the one persuasive string is a link.

The metadata labels use trailing colons and single words, which suits a reference table where scanning down the left column matters more than reading. "Recognized" is the standout label because it is the only row describing the user rather than the record; everything above it is catalogue data, and this one is autobiography. Choosing "Recognized" over "Shazamed" is slightly odd given the app's habit of using its own name as a verb, but it is clearer for a first-time user.

"Enable Location" does the work of an entire priming screen in two words, because the row's label supplies the rest of the sentence. It is an imperative rather than a question, which is more assertive than the flow's usual register, but the placement makes the benefit obvious enough that a longer pitch would be redundant. Rendering it as a blue link rather than a button also keeps it optional-feeling — a user scanning the table reads it as a row that could be filled in, not as a demand.

"Share Song" is plain and correctly scoped. It names the object, which distinguishes it from the header's generic share glyph that might share the screen, the artist, or the album.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Permission priming by adjacency — Placing the location ask next to a filled timestamp row lets the surrounding data explain the benefit, so no explanatory copy is needed.

  2. Contextual timing over launch-time asking — Requesting location deep in a result the user chose to explore, rather than at first run, means the ask arrives when its purpose is visible.

  3. Metadata as memory — The "Recognized" timestamp converts a catalogue record into a personal log entry, which is the foundation of the app's library value.

  4. Optional framing through visual weight — The location prompt is a text link rather than a button, so it reads as an available action rather than a required one.

  5. Restraint at the terminus — Ending on a teal share action rather than another Apple Music CTA respects a user who has already scrolled past several asks.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Photos and Camera (location metadata) — Location attached to a captured item as context rather than as a feature, with the same framing that place completes a record which already has a time.

  2. Google Maps Timeline / Google Photos — Comparable in treating where-and-when as the pair that makes a log entry memorable, and in asking for the permission where the resulting value is displayed.

  3. Last.fm scrobble history — A listening log where per-item metadata and timestamps are the product; a fair comparison for why Shazam surfaces recognition time at all.
screens.whereToUse: This fits the foot of a detail screen where reference metadata belongs, and where an optional permission can be requested beside data that already demonstrates what it would add.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit for a first-run or launch-time permission ask, where no surrounding data makes the benefit legible, and for screens where the metadata is not the user's own — a table of pure catalogue facts does not motivate a location grant.

screens.name: Home Screen 28
screens.uxAnalysis: This artist page prioritizes In My Music above the broader catalog, making the user's own history with the artist the first thing they see. For Shazam, that inversion is appropriate, as the app's unique value lies in recording what users have discovered rather than simply presenting an artist's discography. The hero follows familiar music-app conventions with artwork, playback, name, and genre, while the biography is truncated with an inline More action to keep the first screen compact. The editorial voice introduced earlier also returns, giving the page a richer, magazine-like feel. Two minor inconsistencies remain: the hero play control switches to orange instead of the flow's usual teal, and the same orange accent is reused for the More link, giving one color multiple interface meanings.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven in the About section — this is the second appearance of Apple Music's editorial voice in the flow, and here it has room to demonstrate itself.

The biography opens with the same florid construction seen truncated on the carousel card, and at four lines its register is clearer: metaphor-forward, enthusiastic, willing to make aesthetic claims. It reads as a critic writing for readers who already care, which is appropriate for a page a user reaches deliberately rather than passes through. Naming a decade in the third sentence anchors the artist in time, useful for a catalogue figure a younger user may not place.

Section headings are the flow's most inconsistent element. "ABOUT" and "IN MY MUSIC" are set in all caps, where every other section on the result screen used sentence case ("Top Songs", "More Albums", "You May Also Like"). Two heading conventions in one product, reachable within a tap of each other.

"IN MY MUSIC" is nonetheless the most interesting string on the screen. First-person possessive is rare in interface copy — Apple's own guidance generally prefers "your" — and it makes the section sound like the user's own filing rather than the app's categorisation. Whether that reads as warm or as slightly twee depends on the reader, but it is a deliberate voice choice, not an accident.

"MORE" as an expand link is terse and clear, though all-caps and coloured identically to the hero play control, which blurs the distinction between a playback action and a text expansion.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Personal history above catalogue — Leading with the user's own Shazams differentiates the page from a generic artist entry and reinforces what the app uniquely holds.

  2. Progressive disclosure of prose — Truncating the biography to four lines with an inline expand keeps the page scannable while making depth available.

  3. Hero borrowed from a known template — Portrait, play, name, genre requires no learning because it matches Apple Music and every other music service.

  4. First-person voice as ownership signal — "In My Music" frames the section as the user's rather than the app's, a small register choice with a real effect on how the list reads.

  5. Heading convention drift — All-caps section labels here against sentence case one tap away is the clearest typographic inconsistency observed across the flow.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (artist pages) — Hero portrait, play control, genre subtitle, and expandable editorial bio; the template is inherited wholesale from the parent product.

  2. Spotify (artist page with "About" and library sections) — Comparable structure, and comparable in surfacing a user's own saved items from that artist within the page.

  3. Last.fm artist pages — A listening-history service placing the user's own play data alongside artist reference material, the closest analogue to what "In My Music" is doing here.
screens.whereToUse: This fits artist or entity pages in products that hold personal history, where leading with the user's own record differentiates the page from a generic catalogue entry.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the user has no history with the entity, since a personal section would sit empty at the top of the page, and where the page's job is purely reference — foregrounding personal data delays the facts a reference-seeking user came for.

screens.name: Home Screen 30
screens.uxAnalysis: The artist page prioritizes the user's personal history before the broader catalog, but this ordering becomes less effective when that history is sparse. With only one recognized track, In My Music occupies a prominent position while adding little beyond repeating the song the user just identified. The duplication becomes more noticeable because Army Dreamers also appears in Top Songs, using the same artwork and visual treatment, making the two entries feel redundant rather than representing different relationships to the track. This reflects a broader pattern in the flow, where independently assembled sections repeatedly surface the current item. The sticky header adds a minor usability issue by partially obscuring the About label, reducing the clarity of the section structure while leaving its content visible.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven. Its strings are section headings, track titles, and artist credits, all carried over from surfaces already analysed.

Worth restating: "IN MY MUSIC" and "TOP SONGS" are set in all caps here, while the result screen used sentence case for the same kind of headings ("Top Songs", "More Albums"). The identical heading text rendered two different ways one tap apart is the clearest evidence yet of two competing typographic conventions inside one product. "MORE" remains all-caps and orange, overlapping the text it truncates.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Personal history foregrounded — Leading with the user's own recognitions differentiates this from a generic artist page and reinforces what the app uniquely holds.

  2. Empty-ish sections at prime position — A personalization section that will be sparse for most users still occupies the top slot, so the payoff is deferred to heavy users.

  3. Duplication across independently composed sections — The same track appearing twice in one viewport under different headings reads as an error because nothing marks the two contexts as distinct.

  4. Consistent shelf grammar — Paging, badging, and centred play overlays repeat from the result screen, so no new interaction model is introduced at this depth.

  5. Heading convention drift — All-caps here against sentence case on the result screen, with identical heading text in both places.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (artist pages with library sections) — Identical structure of personal library items above catalogue shelves; inherited directly from the parent product.

  2. Spotify (artist page showing liked songs by that artist) — Comparable in surfacing the user's own saved items within an artist context, and in facing the same duplication when a liked track is also a top track.

  3. Last.fm artist pages — A listening-history service placing personal scrobble data alongside catalogue reference, the closest analogue to "In My Music".
screens.whereToUse: This fits artist or entity pages in products that hold meaningful personal history, where the user's own record differentiates the page and is likely to contain several items.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where personal history will typically hold zero or one item, since a nearly empty section above the catalogue delays the content most users came for, and wherever the same item can appear in adjacent sections without visual differentiation.

screens.name: Skeleton Loading
screens.uxAnalysis:
This loading state is correctly differentiated from the earlier random-flight loader. Instead of a decorative animation, it uses skeletons matching the final row layout, setting expectations for the incoming results.

The three skeleton rows also frame Alternatives as a shortlist rather than a search engine. Pre-filled filter chips make the default experience zero-input: users immediately see relevant alternatives for the current route, while editable chips support different dates or airports.

Strategically, this feature completes Flighty’s value proposition. The app has mostly shown what is happening; Alternatives helps users act on it, turning early flight awareness into something practical.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Three strings, all working.

"Alternatives" — one word, precisely chosen. Not "Other Flights" (vague), not "Rebook" (implies a transaction Flighty can't perform), not "Search" (implies the user must supply something). "Alternatives" presumes a problem with the current flight without naming it, which is tactful: the user arriving here may be stressed, and the title neither dramatises the situation nor pretends nothing is wrong.

"Tap to add to My Flights and view details" — a single line doing two jobs. It sets the interaction model (rows are tappable) and, more importantly, sets the consequence: tapping adds the flight to your list. That's a state change, and telling the user before they tap rather than surprising them after is the right order. It also quietly clarifies scope — Flighty is not booking anything, it's tracking something else. Given the emotional context, being explicit that this is a tracking action and not a purchase avoids a genuinely dangerous misreading.

The phrasing "add to My Flights" also reuses the app's own scope name rather than a generic "your list", so the sentence connects to the home screen the user already knows.

"SYD" / "OOL" / "Sep 06, 2023" — chips as labels, no field names. The airport codes need no explanation on a screen reached from a flight; spelling out "From: Sydney" would be noise. The date format is unambiguous, unlike the "9/6/2023" in the plain-text share artifact — the app is inconsistent between surfaces on exactly the format where ambiguity matters most.

What's absent: no result count, no sort control, and no statement of what happens if there are no alternatives. The last is the important one — the empty state for this screen is the moment a stranded traveller most needs guidance, and nothing here indicates it's been designed.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Loading treatment should match stakes — skeletons for a consequential query, animation for a playful one, and the same app correctly using both.

  2. Skeletons that model the real layout — matching row structure and count means the wait teaches the user what's coming rather than just occupying it.

  3. Prefill collapses the query to zero input — inheriting route and date from the current flight makes the common case instant and leaves the chips for the exception.

  4. State changes stated before the tap — telling users the row adds a flight, rather than letting them discover it, respects a user who may be acting quickly under stress.

  5. Feature completes the proposition — this is the first screen that converts knowing about a delay into doing something about it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Flights / Kayak (alternative flights on a route) — same prefilled route-and-date query, though those are booking surfaces where this is a tracking one.

  2. Citymapper (alternative routes) — offering substitutes at the moment a planned journey degrades, with filters inherited from the original.

  3. Apple News / App Store (skeleton loading) — row-shaped placeholders matching the incoming layout, the platform convention this follows.
screens.whereToUse: Best where a user arrives with a problem and the correct query is already known from context, so results can load with no input. Skeleton loading fits whenever the result layout is predictable and the user benefits from knowing the shape and rough count in advance.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit where result counts vary unpredictably, since a fixed skeleton count sets a false expectation. Also wrong for playful or optional actions, where a literal placeholder wastes a moment that could carry personality — as this same app demonstrates elsewhere.

screens.name: Leaderboard
screens.uxAnalysis: This is the fullest expression of Shazam's proprietary data, and the four chart types are the most interesting part. "Top 200" measures volume, while "Viral" and "Discovery" surface velocity and first-time identification — signals streaming services cannot derive because streams measure listening, while Shazams measure not knowing. "Cities" extends that signal geographically. Presenting all four as peer tabs turns one dataset into four distinct questions. The weaker detail is country selection: "Top 200 Spain" appears in the header while a separate "SPAIN" selector repeats it below, with only one being interactive. The hero card is also unusual, promoting the number-two entry while the ranked list begins at one, causing the same track to appear twice in different treatments.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Not applicable in the persuasive sense — this screen is interaction-driven. But the tab labels carry meaning.

"Viral" and "Discovery" are doing real definitional work with one word each. "Viral" implies velocity rather than volume; "Discovery" implies first-time finds. Neither is explained anywhere on screen, so both rely on the user inferring what distinguishes them from the default — a reasonable bet for "Viral", less so for "Discovery".

"The top songs in Spain this week" scopes geography and time in one line, matching the Search tile's "The week's top songs around the world" and confirming a weekly refresh.

Tab labels are all caps while the hero heading and subhead are sentence case, so two conventions appear within one header block.

Long artist credits truncate mid-name on the chart rows, cutting collaborator lists.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Chart types exposing a unique signal — Viral and Discovery measure identification behaviour rather than listening, metrics no streaming competitor can produce.

  2. Four questions from one dataset — Peer tabs let the same data answer volume, velocity, novelty, and geography.

  3. Time and place scoped in one line — The subhead states both the region and the refresh cycle without a second element.

  4. Country stated twice, editable once — Header title and selector bar duplicate the country with only one interactive.

  5. Hero promoting the second-ranked entry — The featured card shows #2 while the list beneath starts at #1, duplicating a track in one viewport.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Spotify Charts — Regional chart pages with Top and Viral variants; the closest structural comparison.

  2. Apple Music (city and country charts) — Comparable country selection and chart-type tabs, and the source of this component styling.

  3. Billboard — The originating convention of ranked regional charts with multiple methodologies presented as peers.
screens.whereToUse: This fits chart products where one dataset supports several distinct methodologies, so peer tabs can present them as different questions rather than variations.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where tab labels cannot be understood without explanation, and where a featured card would duplicate an entry already visible in the list beneath it.

screens.name: Alternative Results
screens.uxAnalysis:
The row component is efficiently reused, with the countdown gutter replaced by a status gutter. But the first row exposes a bug: “0 MINUTES” appears alongside a departure from 15h 30m ago, creating a clear contradiction.

The colour system is strong. Green and red are applied per endpoint, showing where a flight actually gained or lost time rather than flattening status across the whole journey.

The bigger issue is the purpose of the list. Since every visible flight has already departed, Alternatives currently reads more like route performance history than a rebooking tool. For a stranded traveller, the list should prioritise the next available departure, not the first flight of the day.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Dense, factual, and one string doing something unusual.

"23 RESULTS" — a count where the loading state gave none, and it does real work. It tells the user the route is busy, which is itself the answer to the implied question: if your flight is cancelled, there are options. On a thin route the same string would communicate the opposite, equally usefully.

"SHOW CODESHARES" — genuinely expert vocabulary, and the decision to default it off is the notable one. Codeshares would inflate 23 results into a list padded with duplicates of the same aircraft under different flight numbers. Hiding them by default means the list shows distinct physical flights, which is what a traveller actually needs, while the toggle serves the user who booked through a partner airline and needs to find their own number. That's domain fluency expressed as a default rather than a feature.

"Dep. due 15h 30m ago" — the abbreviation is out of character for an app that elsewhere writes "Departs" and "Gate Departure" in full. More importantly, the phrasing is awkward for a completed event: a departure that was "due" 15 hours ago either happened or didn't, and this row doesn't say which, unlike every other row's explicit "Arrived" or "Landed".

"Arrived 3m late" / "Arrived 10m early" / "Arrived 31m late" — past tense with a signed delta, consistent with the strikethrough treatment on the live detail screen. The app's convention throughout is state plus magnitude, never state alone, and it holds here.

"ARRIVED" vs "LANDED" in the status gutter — two words for what appears to be the same outcome, on adjacent rows. If these encode a real distinction (wheels down versus at gate), nothing on screen explains it; if they don't, it's an inconsistency in a column designed for scanning.

Truncated route names — "Sydney to Coolangatta (Gold C…" on every single row. The parenthetical that was a courtesy on the detail screen becomes noise here, since all 23 rows share the same route. Dropping the destination entirely on a route-filtered list would free the line for something differentiating.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Component reuse across contexts — the same row from the home screen, with the countdown gutter repurposed for status, means no relearning across twenty-three rows.

  2. Per-endpoint colour — colouring departure and arrival independently reveals where time was lost, not just that it was.

  3. Expert defaults — hiding codeshares by default shows distinct aircraft rather than a padded list, and the toggle serves the minority who need it.

  4. Result count as an answer — "23 RESULTS" tells a worried traveller the route is well served before they read a single row.

  5. Wrong default anchor — a list of alternatives that opens on 5:45 AM when it's 9:41 PM makes the user scroll past the whole day to reach anything actionable.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. FlightAware / Flightradar24 (route history) — same-route listings with per-flight status, though generally framed as history rather than alternatives.

  2. Google Flights (date grid / same-route list) — chronological same-route comparison with airline filtering, on a booking surface rather than a tracking one.

  3. Citymapper (alternative departures) — a list of substitutes anchored to now, which is the anchoring this screen appears to lack.
screens.whereToUse: Best where a user needs to compare many instances of the same thing on one axis, and where the comparison rows can reuse a component the user already knows. Filtering defaults that reflect domain expertise — like suppressing codeshares — pay off most on lists long enough that noise is costly.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit when the list opens at a point far from the user's actual position in time, since the value of an alternative decays entirely once it has departed. Also wrong when every row shares the same repeated content, which crowds out the fields that actually differentiate.

screens.name: Product Details
screens.uxAnalysis: The most compelling aspect of this screen is how it reframes Apple Music as part of the concert experience rather than a separate upsell. Instead of promoting full-song playback as an alternative to identification, it suggests preparing for a concert the user has already committed to, making the recommendation feel genuinely useful. Featuring the Essentials playlist is an effective choice, as a curated collection better reflects what users are likely to hear live than a complete discography. The weaker point is the section that follows. Listen to Rose Gray begins with a recent remix single rather than the artist's core releases, making it a less suitable starting point for concert preparation. As a result, the two sections overlap in purpose without clearly explaining why users should engage with both.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven in the headings, and the framing choice is where the work is.

"Get Ready for the Show" is the flow's best-framed commercial heading. It names a user goal rather than a product ("Listen on Apple Music", "Play Full Song"), and it makes the content's purpose obvious without stating a benefit or an offer. Crucially it presumes attendance, which is appropriate immediately after a save action — the copy is addressed to someone who has decided, not someone being persuaded.

"Listen to Rose Gray" is plainer and does less. It is an instruction rather than a purpose, and coming after a heading that framed content around the user's plan, it reverts to the generic register used elsewhere. Two sections of near-identical content sit under one motivated heading and one unmotivated one.

Nothing here mentions a subscription, a trial, or a price. After a flow that stated the two-month offer on at least four surfaces, its absence at the point of highest alignment is notable — arguably a missed placement, arguably restraint.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Upsell framed as preparation — Aligning the commercial content with a goal the user already holds is the most defensible placement of Apple Music anywhere in this flow.

  2. Object matched to purpose — A curated Essentials playlist approximates a live set better than a discography, so the content fits the stated task.

  3. Goal-named heading — "Get Ready for the Show" describes what the user wants rather than what the product is.

  4. Second section without a distinct purpose — "Listen to Rose Gray" repeats the first section's function under a weaker heading.

  5. Merchandising mismatched to task — Leading the release shelf with a remix single serves neither preparation nor catalogue orientation.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Spotify (concert pages with artist playlists) — Comparable in pairing event listings with a curated playlist framed as preparation.

  2. Bandsintown — Offers artist playlists alongside tour dates for the same reason: attendees want to know the material.

  3. Apple Music (Essentials playlists) — The playlist object and its banner treatment are inherited directly from the parent product.
screens.whereToUse: This fits post-commitment contexts where catalogue content genuinely serves the user's next step, so a commercial placement can be framed as preparation rather than as an alternative to what they were doing.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit before commitment, where "get ready" presumes a decision the user has not made, and where the surfaced content does not actually serve the stated preparation — a remix single does not help someone learn a set.

screens.name: Search Alternatives
screens.uxAnalysis:
The match highlighting is the standout detail. Bolded search terms across the airport name, IATA code, and city make fuzzy matches immediately understandable, especially when unexpected results appear.

Showing IATA, ICAO, and city also supports expert users without adding much visual weight.

The hierarchy is clear: the selected result gets full emphasis while others recede, and the return icon makes it easy to restore the previous selection.

The inline expansion is equally strong. The chip becomes a search field without removing the other filters, preserving context and making the edit feel lightweight.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Almost no authored copy; the design is in what's displayed rather than what's written.

"SYD · YSSY · Sydney" — three identifiers, dot-separated, in a fixed order: IATA, ICAO, city. The ordering is deliberate — the code most users know first, the code specialists use second, the human name last as disambiguation. Note that rows without an ICAO simply drop it rather than showing a placeholder, so the pattern degrades cleanly.

"Au-Rose Bay Airport" — the one string that isn't clean. The "Au-" prefix is almost certainly a country-code artifact leaking from the data source into the display name, and it sits directly above a row that renders "Sydney West Airport" correctly. On a screen otherwise notable for careful data presentation, it's a visible seam in the underlying feed.

Flags as country markers — emoji flags rather than text country names, which is compact and scannable but carries the usual costs: they render inconsistently across platforms, they convey nothing to a screen reader beyond the country name, and a user who doesn't recognise the Danish flag learns nothing from it. A grey country name in the metadata line would have been more robust and would have fit the existing dot-separated pattern.

"next" on the keyboard return key — the system key, but its label tells the user this field is one of a sequence. A small confirmation that committing here advances to the destination field rather than dismissing the whole edit.

No placeholder text is visible since the field holds a value, and no empty-state or no-results copy can be assessed from this frame.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Show why each result matched — bolding the query fragment across name, code and city makes an otherwise baffling result set self-explanatory.

  2. Serve the expert in the metadata line — ICAO codes cost one line of grey text and are exactly what a knowledgeable user reaches for.

  3. Preselection as a safe exit — highlighting the current value with a return affordance means an accidental tap costs nothing.

  4. Edit in place, keep the context — expanding the chip rather than pushing a screen preserves the relationship between the three filters.

  5. Data hygiene shows — "Au-Rose Bay Airport" is a feed artifact surfacing in a product whose whole claim is data quality.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Flights (airport picker) — the closest analogue: fuzzy matching across name, code and city with the matched fragment emphasised.

  2. Apple Maps (search suggestions) — inline typeahead beneath an expanded field, with the current or likely result promoted to the top.

  3. Kayak / Skyscanner (origin fields) — multi-identifier airport rows serving both casual and expert users, though generally without the match highlighting.
screens.whereToUse: Best where a query can plausibly match several fields and results might otherwise look arbitrary — airports, stations, tickers, any domain with codes alongside names. Inline chip expansion suits filter sets small enough that the unedited filters should stay visible.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit when results are few and exact, where a plain picker beats a search field. Also wrong when the underlying data isn't clean enough to display raw, since typeahead surfaces every naming inconsistency in the source directly to the user.

screens.name: Leaderboard List
screens.uxAnalysis: Rank numbers sit outside the artwork in a dedicated left column, which is the right choice for a chart — position is the organising fact, and the gutter lets the eye scan ranks without parsing the rest of the row. It is a justified departure from the app's other lists, where thumbnails lead. The generous spacing and separate Apple Music badge make each row tall, with only about six visible per screen. For 200 entries, that creates substantial scrolling with no index, jump-to-rank, or section markers. The vertical ellipsis is also inconsistent with the horizontal one used elsewhere. Play overlays remain centred on artwork, partially obscuring the sleeves that are the main recognition cue for unfamiliar entries.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven. Its strings are rank numbers, titles, and artist credits.

Two artist credits truncate mid-name on collaborations, cutting the very information that distinguishes a multi-artist release. On a chart where several entries are collaborations, that is a recurring loss.

Spanish-language titles and artist names render correctly with accents, and the chart is genuinely regional rather than a translated global list — the fourth, sixth, and seventh entries are Spanish-market releases.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Rank in its own column — Position gets a dedicated gutter so the numbers can be scanned independently of the rows' content.

  2. Layout departing from the app's convention where justified — Every other list leads with artwork; a chart correctly leads with rank.

  3. Regional data genuinely regional — Local releases appear alongside global hits, so the country selector produces a real difference.

  4. No navigation aids for a 200-row list — No index, jump, or interval markers, at roughly six rows per screen.

  5. Overflow glyph inconsistent with the rest of the app — A vertical ellipsis here against horizontal everywhere else.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Spotify Charts — Ranked regional lists with position in a leading column; the closest structural comparison.

  2. Apple Music charts — Comparable row composition and the source of this component styling.

  3. Billboard — The originating convention of rank-led chart rows with artwork secondary.
screens.whereToUse: This fits ranked lists where position is the organising fact, so a dedicated rank column lets users scan by number rather than by content.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit for long ranked lists without navigation aids, since 200 entries at six per screen is a substantial scroll with no way to jump, and where per-row spacing could be tightened without loss.

screens.name: Empty State - Alternatives
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen, flagged earlier as undesigned, turns out to be one of the more considered ones in the app. Instead of a generic "try again," it offers three ranked hypotheses for the failed search — route-doesn't-operate (leading, with the exact query restated), wrong-airport (London's classic failure mode), and multi-segment (rarest, and an honest admission that Flighty only searches single legs). "Edit Search" and "New Search" stay separate since a wrong date and a wrong mental model need different fixes, and with filter chips still visible, there are three ways back. The standout is "Tell us what's wrong" at the foot — treating an empty result as a possible data gap, asked for at the exact moment the user can explain it.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The most carefully written screen in the set, and the register is deliberately flat.

"No Flights Found" — factual, past tense, no apology and no exclamation. Compare the app's other empty states: "Let's Fly Somewhere" was invitational because that emptiness was an opportunity; this emptiness is a problem, and the copy correctly drops the charm. A product that used the same playful voice here would read as tone-deaf to a user who may be stranded.

Note the phrasing is about the search, not the route — "No flights found" leaves open that flights exist and weren't found, which is honest given the multi-segment limitation admitted two rows below. "This route doesn't operate" would have been a stronger and less defensible claim.

"Double check that STN → LPL operates on September 07." — the arrow glyph does the work three words would, and echoing the exact query values means the user can spot their own error without re-reading the chips. "Double check" places the burden gently: it doesn't say you got this wrong, it says this is worth verifying.

"Some cities have multiple airports, check that you searched the correct airport." — general knowledge stated as a hint rather than an accusation. It's also the one row that teaches something a user might not know, which is the right thing to spend a row on.

"If your flight has multiple segments, search for them one-by-one." — a limitation disclosed as guidance. The product could have said nothing and let the user conclude the route doesn't exist; instead it names its own boundary and provides the workaround. That's expensive honesty and it builds more trust than a fourth reassurance would.

"Edit Search" vs "New Search" — two verbs distinguishing preserve from discard. Precise labelling on recovery actions, where most products offer one ambiguous button.

"Tell us what's wrong" — first person plural, informal contraction, and crucially it assumes something is wrong rather than asking the user to justify a complaint. It also implicitly accepts that the app may be at fault, which is a small act of accountability at exactly the right moment.

The one inconsistency: "September 07" with a zero-padded day in prose, where prose would normally read "September 7". The chip's "Sep 07" format has leaked into a sentence.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Diagnose, don't apologise — three ranked causes with matching recoveries turn a dead end into a troubleshooting flow.

  2. Rank hypotheses by likelihood — leading with the most probable cause means most users are helped by the first line they read.

  3. Distinguish preserve from discard — "Edit Search" and "New Search" name two genuinely different recoveries rather than offering one ambiguous button.

  4. Disclose your own limitations — admitting the single-segment constraint costs nothing and prevents a user concluding the data is wrong.

  5. Treat empty results as a possible data failure — inviting a report at the point of failure collects the best-quality signal a data product can get.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Flights (no results) — offers nearby airports and adjacent dates as concrete recoveries rather than a bare message.

  2. Google Search (zero results) — ranked suggestions for reformulating the query, the diagnostic-list convention this follows.

  3. Citymapper (no route found) — states the constraint causing the failure and offers a reformulation path, with a report affordance.
screens.whereToUse: Best where a query can fail for several distinguishable reasons and the product can rank them, so the empty state teaches rather than stonewalls. Offering a feedback path fits any data product where zero results may indicate a coverage gap rather than user error.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit where the failure cause is singular and obvious, since three hypotheses then add noise to a one-line answer. Also wrong when suggestions can't be acted on from the screen — diagnostic copy without matching recovery links is just an explanation of failure.

screens.name: Discover Search
screens.uxAnalysis: Focusing the field changes very little, which is the notable part. The Discover tiles remain instead of being replaced by recent searches or suggestions, letting users reconsider without dismissing the browse destinations. This is gentler than the Library's scoped search, which replaced the header and chips row entirely — two search modes serving different contexts. The difference is defensible: the Library's controls were irrelevant once searching, while these tiles remain valid destinations. The weakness is the lack of assistance: no recent searches, trending queries, or suggested artists appear. The field simply waits while the tiles sit partially occluded by the keyboard, despite the app having enough data to make this space more useful.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Not applicable in the persuasive sense — this screen is interaction-driven, and no strings change on focus.

The placeholder "Lyrics, Songs or Artists" persists, continuing to demonstrate scope across three fields. It remains the app's strongest placeholder and the only surface where lyrics search is disclosed.

The Discover tiles' titles and subheads are unchanged and now partially occluded by the field and keyboard, with the Concerts subhead cut mid-line.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Non-destructive focus state — Keeping the browse tiles visible means tapping the field is reversible without dismissing anything.

  2. Two focus behaviours across one app — Library search replaced its chrome entirely; global search preserves it, justified by what that chrome contains.

  3. Placeholder persisting through focus — Scope remains stated while the user decides what to type.

  4. No assistance offered on focus — No recents, suggestions, or trending terms populate the moment between focus and input.

  5. Occlusion without replacement — The field and keyboard cover the tiles they left in place, so the retained content is partly unreadable.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music search — Retains browse categories on focus rather than replacing them; the platform convention this follows.

  2. Spotify search — Comparable in keeping browse tiles visible when the field is focused, though typically adding recent searches.

  3. Apple App Store search — Same model, but populates the focus state with recent and trending terms.
screens.whereToUse: This fits global search where the surrounding content remains a valid alternative path, so focusing the field need not clear the screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where retained content would be substantially occluded without being usable, and where the product has recent-query or suggestion data that could fill the focus state more usefully.

screens.name: Product Details 2
screens.uxAnalysis: This section reuses the result screen's familiar structure—a featured item followed by a horizontally paged shelf—creating continuity across the artist and concert experiences. The pattern is efficient because returning users do not need to learn a new browsing model. However, the content selection conflicts with the Get Ready for the Show framing above it. A remix single and a collaboration led by Kesha are poor fits for someone trying to prepare for the artist's live set, suggesting the shelf is driven by recency or popularity rather than concert relevance. The featured card also introduces a basic metadata inconsistency: it is labeled Album while the title identifies the release as a Single, undermining confidence in the content hierarchy.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Not applicable in the persuasive sense — this screen is interaction-driven. Its strings are a section heading, titles, and credits.

"Listen to Rose Gray" is an instruction rather than a purpose, and coming immediately after "Get Ready for the Show" the drop in framing is conspicuous. The earlier heading told the user why the content was there; this one tells them what to do with it, which they could already infer from a play control on every row.

The type label "Album" above "April (Daniel Avery Remix) - Single" is the clearest metadata error in the flow — the label and the title state different formats about the same item.

One track title truncates mid-parenthetical, continuing a pattern visible across nearly every shelf in this app.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Structural reuse across contexts — The same featured-plus-shelf pattern appearing on a result screen and a concert page means one learned model serves both.

  2. Destination disclosed before the tap — Apple Music badging on every item keeps the paywall visible in advance.

  3. Framing and contents out of step — A section headed as show preparation is populated by remixes and guest features rather than the artist's core material.

  4. Metadata contradicting itself — "Album" labelling an item titled "Single" undermines the type system in the most prominent slot.

  5. Occlusion of artwork — Play controls centred on thumbnails hide the focal area of each sleeve, consistent with every other shelf in this app.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (artist page release shelves) — Featured release above a paged track shelf; the component grammar is inherited directly.

  2. Spotify (concert pages with artist tracks) — Comparable in appending catalogue content to an event listing.

  3. Bandsintown — Offers artist tracks alongside tour dates, though typically weighted toward material likely to appear in a set.
screens.whereToUse: This fits catalogue shelves appended to event or result pages where a consistent structure can serve multiple contexts, and where badging keeps each item's destination legible.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where a section's heading promises a curated purpose the contents do not fulfil — preparation framing demands material selected for that purpose, not a generic popularity or recency feed.

screens.name: Playlist 2
screens.uxAnalysis:
The two menu options are valuable because both are explicitly scoped to the library. Search in Library is meaningfully different from the global search in the tab bar: one searches the catalogue, the other searches the user's own identification history. Keeping it inside the menu avoids competing search affordances, though it also makes the scoped function invisible until the menu is opened.

Select is the more consequential addition because it introduces the app's only bulk-action pathway. Until this point, every library action has been per-item, making large-scale cleanup unnecessarily repetitive. A user managing dozens or hundreds of identifications needs a way to remove multiple entries at once. Hiding that capability behind an ellipsis is conventional, but its discoverability is weak for a feature that becomes increasingly important as the library grows.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Borderline — two labels, and their scoping is the point.

"Search in Library" is precisely disambiguated. "In Library" is what distinguishes it from the global search sitting in the tab bar, and dropping those two words would make the row indistinguishable from the app-wide search a user already knows about. The specificity is doing real work.

"Select" is the platform-standard label for entering a multi-select mode, and it correctly names the mode rather than any particular batch action. What it does not do is indicate what becomes possible once selected — delete, share, add to a playlist — so the user enters the mode to find out.

Both labels are verb-first, consistent with the app's habit, and the menu carries no section header, which is appropriate at two rows and a welcome contrast to the over-scoped "Listen On:" seen on the item-level menus.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Scoped versus global search kept distinct — Naming the scope in the label prevents confusion with the tab bar's app-wide search.

  2. Bulk mode as the only escape from per-item actions — This is the sole route to multi-item operations in an app otherwise entirely per-row.

  3. No header where none is needed — Two rows carry no section label, avoiding the over-scoping seen on the item menus.

  4. Discoverability cost of an unlabelled trigger — Both features are invisible until an ellipsis is opened, which for bulk management in a growing log is deep placement.

  5. Mode named without its consequences — "Select" enters a mode without indicating what batch actions follow.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music and Photos — Screen-level overflow menus offering scoped search and a select mode; the platform convention and component source.

  2. Apple Mail and Files — Comparable in placing multi-select behind an overflow rather than a persistent edit control.

  3. Last.fm — Listening histories that grow indefinitely and need scoped search, illustrating why in-library search matters as the log accumulates.
screens.whereToUse: This fits collection screens where a scoped search must be distinguished from a global one, and where bulk operations are occasional enough to live behind an overflow rather than in persistent chrome.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where bulk management is frequent, since burying it behind an unlabelled trigger adds friction to a routine task, and where a scoped search would be better served by a persistent field.

screens.name: Dark Mode Profile & Account
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen supports a Searching & Finding flow by giving users deeper context on an artist beyond just song metadata, structuring facts (hometown, birth date) as clearly labeled fields for quick scanning, followed by a narrative biography for users who want more depth. The verified checkmark badge signals this is an authoritative, curated artist profile rather than user-generated content, reinforcing trust in the accuracy of the details shown. This kind of enrichment content turns a simple song-identification result into a richer discovery moment, encouraging engagement with the artist beyond the single track that was Shazamed.
screens.tonalityAndContent: This is a copy-driven screen: apart from structural labels (Hometown, Born), its entire value comes from the written biography. The tone is engaging and editorial rather than dryly factual — it uses vivid, magazine-style language to characterize the artist's voice and career rather than a flat list of facts, which suits the discovery/engagement lever this screen serves: making an artist bio feel like an inviting read rather than a Wikipedia-style reference dump. This editorial voice likely comes from a licensed music-metadata/biography provider rather than being written in-house, consistent with how many music apps source artist bios.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Progressive disclosure: structured quick-facts (Hometown, Born) appear before the longer narrative bio, letting users get key details fast without committing to reading the full paragraph.

  2. Trust signaling: the verified checkmark badge reassures users this is an authoritative profile, not unverified or user-submitted content.

  3. Scannable field labeling: small caps labels ("HOMETOWN," "BORN") paired with clear values follow standard profile-card conventions, aiding quick recognition.

  4. Editorial voice for engagement: a lively, narrative biography (rather than a bare fact list) increases the likelihood users read and engage with artist content beyond the identified track.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (Artist "About" page with bio and quick facts) — same combination of structured fields (hometown, born) plus an editorial-style biography.

  2. Spotify (Artist bio section) — comparable pattern of a short artist bio surfaced alongside music discovery, sourced from licensed metadata providers.

  3. Genre database apps like Discogs (Artist profile pages) — similar structured-plus-narrative artist information format, though typically less editorial in tone.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any music-discovery app wanting to deepen engagement after a song identification or search result by surfacing rich, structured-plus-narrative artist context.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for a lightweight, transactional lookup where the user just wants to confirm a song/artist match quickly — a lengthy biography would add unnecessary friction to a simple identification task.

screens.name: Timeline & History 2
screens.uxAnalysis: Entering search replaces the header, count, sort control, and chips with a single focused field, committing the screen fully to one task rather than layering search over the browse chrome. Keeping the full library visible beneath it is the stronger choice: the mode never feels empty, users can still browse while deciding what to type, and results narrow from a known starting point. The keyboard appearing immediately also makes the expected interaction obvious without instruction. The remaining weakness is the placeholder, which describes the field rather than demonstrating what it accepts — for example, a song title, artist, or both.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Borderline — one string, and it is doing scoping work.

"Search in Library" repeats the overflow menu row that opened this mode verbatim, so the path from trigger to destination is verbally continuous — the same consistency seen between "Location" and its sheet, and between "Find Concerts" and its screen. It also keeps the scope explicit while the user is inside the mode, which matters because a bare "Search" placeholder would be indistinguishable from the app-wide search in the tab bar.

What it does not do is indicate what fields are searched. A user cannot tell from the placeholder whether typing an artist name will match, or only titles. A demonstrative placeholder — an example title or artist — would have shown both the scope and the accepted input in the same space, which is the improvement the Location sheet also needed.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Mode commits the chrome — Replacing the header and chips rather than layering search over them removes competition for a task the user entered deliberately.

  2. Content visible before input — Keeping the unfiltered list beneath means the mode never reads as empty and results narrow from a known set.

  3. Verbal continuity from trigger to mode — The placeholder repeats the menu row's exact wording, so the destination confirms the path.

  4. Scope stated inside the mode — "in Library" distinguishes this from the tab bar's global search while the user is typing.

  5. Placeholder describes rather than demonstrates — Nothing indicates whether titles, artists, or both are searchable.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music library search — Scoped search replacing library chrome with the full list retained beneath; the platform convention and component source.

  2. Apple Mail and Notes — Comparable in showing existing content beneath an empty search field rather than a blank state.

  3. Spotify library search — Same model of a scoped field distinct from the app-wide search, with the collection visible while typing.
screens.whereToUse: This fits scoped search over a collection the user already has, where showing the unfiltered set beneath the field gives context and makes narrowing legible.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the searchable set is not already loaded or visible, and where a placeholder cannot convey what the field matches — an example is more useful than a restatement of the label.

screens.name: No result
screens.uxAnalysis: Search is confirmed to be live-filtering: the list clears immediately without requiring a submit action, which is appropriate for a small local library. The weakness is the resulting empty state. A moment earlier the full 24-item collection provided context; after a non-match, that context disappears entirely, leaving only two generic lines. Showing partial matches or retaining some collection context would make the failure less abrupt. The reuse of “No results / Try searching again” also exposes a missed opportunity for contextual guidance: in this screen, the useful information would be whether the search covers song titles, artists, or both. A scoped library search could make that explicit instead of relying on generic recovery copy.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven — two lines, both reused verbatim from an earlier screen.

"No results" remains the correct headline: plain, scoped to the search, and not blaming the input.

"Try searching again." is the same filler observed in the Location sheet, and it is weaker here because the context permits something better. In a library the user personally built, the app knows exactly what it contains — an empty state could name the searchable fields, offer the collection size as reassurance ("nothing in your 24 songs matches"), or simply restore the list. Instead it restates the only available action.

The reuse itself is worth flagging as a pattern rather than a one-off: the app's strongest empty state, "No Concerts Here", named the cause and offered a targeted escape, which shows the team can write these well when the context is treated specifically rather than generically.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Search-as-you-type confirmed — Results clear without submission, appropriate for filtering a small local collection.

  2. Context lost on non-match — Clearing the visible library is a harsh response when the collection is small and already known to the user.

  3. Generic empty state reused across contexts — The same two lines serve both a location picker and a library filter, so neither is specific.

  4. Opportunity for specificity unused — The app knows the library's size and fields but offers neither in the failure message.

  5. Query retained for editing — The entered value stays in the field with a clear control, so correction is an edit rather than a retype.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music library search — Returns a comparable no-results state with the query retained; the platform convention.

  2. Apple Notes and Mail — Comparable scoped searches that clear results on non-match while keeping the query editable.

  3. Spotify library search — Same model, though typically retaining a partial-match section rather than clearing entirely.
screens.whereToUse: This fits scoped search over collections where instant filtering is expected and a clear no-match signal prevents the user from assuming a slow response.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the collection is small and already visible, since clearing it removes context the user was relying on, and where a generic message is reused in a context that permits a specific one.

screens.name: Search Result
screens.uxAnalysis: This confirms that library search matches the artist field as well as song titles, supports partial strings, and filters live without requiring submission. The day grouping remains intact, preserving the library's framing as a personal log rather than a flat search result — useful when the user cares about when a song was found as much as what it was. However, the row template becomes less efficient under search: when multiple results share the same matched artist and were identified within minutes of each other, the repeated artist and timestamp provide little additional information. The title is the key differentiator, but the surrounding metadata is largely redundant once the search has established the common attribute.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Not applicable in the persuasive sense — this screen is interaction-driven. Its strings are the query, titles, artist credits, and timestamps.

Worth noting: no result count appears. The unfiltered library showed "24 songs" and the artist-chip filter showed "3 songs", but the search mode replaced that header entirely, so a user filtering by search has no number telling them how many matches exist. The chip filter and the search filter therefore give different feedback for functionally similar operations.

No matched-text highlighting appears either — the string "Kate" is not emphasised within the artist lines it matched, which the Location picker's suggestion list did do with its grey-prefix, bold-completion treatment. The same app solves this two ways.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Multi-field matching, undisclosed — Artist matching works and is what most users would want, but nothing in the placeholder or empty state said so.

  2. Incremental filtering — Results narrow on partial input with no submission, appropriate for a small local collection.

  3. Log framing preserved under search — Day grouping survives filtering, so results remain a history rather than a flat list.

  4. Row template redundant under search — When the query establishes the shared attribute, repeating it on every row spends two lines to no effect.

  5. No result count in search mode — The chip filter reports how many matched; search does not.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music library search — Multi-field incremental matching with grouping retained; the platform convention and component source.

  2. Apple Photos search — Comparable in matching across derived fields while preserving date grouping in results.

  3. Spotify library search — Same model of instant filtering across title and artist within a personal collection.
screens.whereToUse: This fits scoped search over a personal collection where multiple fields are worth matching and the collection's native grouping remains meaningful in results.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the row template cannot adapt to a filtered context — repeating the matched attribute on every row wastes the space — and where users need a match count to judge whether the query was specific enough.

screens.name: Discover Search 2
screens.uxAnalysis: These are query completions rather than entities — tapping one runs a search instead of opening an artist page — unlike the Location picker's selectable place suggestions. Yet both use the same visual treatment, making the distinction unclear. The completions are well chosen: an artist, artist-plus-song, and song-plus-artist, with the third demonstrating matching beyond the typed prefix — "505" appears before the query. The grey-and-black treatment explains the logic without labels: black is typed, grey is suggested, and its position shows where the match occurred. The main weakness is placement: the suggestions sit at the top while the field remains at the bottom, forcing the eye to travel almost the entire screen between typing and reading.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Not applicable in the persuasive sense — this screen is interaction-driven. But the typographic treatment is doing the communication.

"Suggestions" as a panel heading matches the Location picker's heading exactly, so the same word covers two different kinds of row — selectable places there, runnable queries here.

The grey-black split inverts the Location picker's convention. There, the typed prefix was grey and the completion bold; here the typed portion is black and the addition grey. Two opposite treatments of the same idea appear in one app, and the version used here is arguably the weaker one, since it emphasises what the user already knows over what the system is offering.

The query is entered with a capital A while all three suggestions are lowercase, so the field does not normalise case in either direction.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Completions rather than entities — Suggestions run searches instead of opening items, a different model from the Location picker despite identical styling.

  2. Match position made visible — Typographic weight shows where the typed string landed within each completion, including mid-phrase matches.

  3. Non-prefix matching demonstrated — "505 arctic monkeys" proves the system matches anywhere in the phrase.

  4. Emphasis inverted from the app's other typeahead — Typed text is emphasised here, completions there; two opposite conventions in one product.

  5. Suggestions distant from the caret — Panel at the top, field at the bottom, so the eye crosses the full screen between input and output.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music search — Query completions in a suggestions panel with typographic differentiation; the platform convention.

  2. Spotify search — Comparable in offering completions before results, with the typed portion emphasised.

  3. Google search suggestions — The originating convention for non-prefix matching displayed with weight differentiation.
screens.whereToUse: This fits global search where the query space is large and completions help users express what they want before results are fetched.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where suggestion rows would be visually indistinguishable from entity results despite behaving differently, and where the panel's distance from the input makes the connection hard to follow.

screens.name: Searching By Voice 04
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen confirms the "Browse for Me" loading pattern is consistent regardless of how the query was entered — voice ("Call Arc") or typed text both funnel into the identical "Reading N web pages" loading state with a fading source-domain list, as seen with the earlier "best new movies 2025" query. The specific domains shown (food52.com, allrecipes.com, athome.starbucks.com, thepioneerwoman.com) are topically appropriate to a coffee recipe query, reinforcing that source selection is genuinely query-relevant rather than generic. This continuity between input methods (voice vs. text) means the user experiences one unified feature regardless of how they choose to interact, reducing the learning curve if they switch between typing and speaking across sessions.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — this screen's only text is the operational status label ("Reading 9 web pages") and reused system domains, already covered in the analysis of the equivalent typed-query loading screen; the tone remains the same plain, transparent, process-labeling style.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Consistency Across Input Modalities — using the identical loading pattern for both voice and text queries reduces cognitive load when switching between input methods.

  2. Visibility of System Status — naming specific, topically relevant sources continues to build trust and transparency during the loading period.

  3. Trust Through Transparency — recognizable domains relevant to the coffee recipe query (Starbucks, Pioneer Woman, AllRecipes) reinforce that the AI's source selection is meaningfully tailored to the query.

  4. Unified System Model — the persistent Arc/Google toggle and bottom toolbar remain fixed regardless of entry method, reinforcing one coherent mental model of the app.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Perplexity AI (voice and text search parity) — surfaces the identical "reading sources" loading treatment regardless of whether a query was typed or spoken.

  2. Google Assistant → Search results — voice queries transition into the same visual search results loading pattern used for typed queries.

  3. Bing Chat / Copilot — unifies voice and text input into one consistent "searching the web" loading experience.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits multi-modal search products where maintaining one consistent loading and results experience across input methods (voice, text, etc.) is important for reducing user confusion and reinforcing a single mental model of the feature.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit if voice and text queries genuinely warrant different follow-up experiences (e.g., voice results optimized for audio playback vs. text results for reading), where forcing identical visual treatment across modalities could obscure meaningful functional differences.

screens.name: Searching By Voice 05
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen reconfirms that the "Browse for Me" answer-page template is fully reusable across very different query types — a subjective ranked-opinion query ("best movies") and a how-to/recipe query ("coffee recipe") both render into the same carousel-plus-sources-plus-write-up structure, with only the content itself changing to fit context (an instructional labeled infographic instead of movie posters, recipe steps instead of ratings). Notably, the recipe entries use ingredient/method descriptions rather than percentage ratings, since a coffee recipe has no equivalent to a Tomatometer score — showing the template flexibly adapts its content type (quantities, steps) to whatever's actually relevant to answering the specific query, without forcing every query into an identical data shape.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The write-up shifts from the earlier critic-style prose (movies) into instructional, ingredient-and-method language appropriate for a recipe query — "combines coarsely ground coffee, dark brown sugar, and ground cinnamon, steeped overnight" reads like a condensed recipe headnote rather than a review. This is a meaningful content-and-clarity finding: the AI-generated voice adapts its register to the query's genre (evaluative for movies, procedural for recipes) while keeping the same title-plus-emoji-plus-description structural shell, which is what makes the underlying template feel purpose-built for each answer type rather than generically templated.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Content-Adaptive Templating — the same visual and structural shell (carousel, sources, emoji-labeled entries) flexes its content type (ratings vs. ingredients/steps) to fit the query's genre.

  2. Progressive Disclosure — visual (infographic/photos) → credibility (source icons/cards) → substance (recipe write-up) layering repeats the pattern established for the movie query.

  3. Scannability — emoji markers (coffee cup, snowflake) again let users quickly differentiate entries (hot vs. iced) before reading full descriptions.

  4. Trust Through Transparency — recognizable culinary/brand sources (Starbucks, Food52, AllRecipes) anchor the AI-generated recipe content in credible, familiar publishers.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Pinterest recipe pins / roundups — use similarly labeled infographics alongside recipe steps and source attribution, matching this page's visual-plus-instructional structure.

  2. Google's AI Overview for recipe queries — surfaces a similar image-plus-source-plus-synthesized-steps format for how-to and recipe searches.

  3. Perplexity AI (recipe/how-to answer pages) — adapts its answer template's content type (steps/ingredients vs. ratings) based on query genre, exactly as shown here.
screens.whereToUse: This adaptive template fits any AI-synthesized answer product handling diverse query types, where a consistent visual shell paired with genre-appropriate content (ratings for opinions, steps for how-tos) keeps the experience familiar without forcing irrelevant data into every answer.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit if the underlying content genre is too varied to fit a repeated title-emoji-description shell at all (e.g., a query needing a single numeric answer, a map, or a calculation) — forcing those into this list-style template would misrepresent the actual answer format needed.

screens.name: Event
screens.uxAnalysis: The closing block performs the same structural role as the Library's "Want more?" panel: it ends a finite feed with an onward action rather than letting the scroll simply stop. Its placement is unobtrusive because the recommendations are already exhausted. Unlike the Library, though, the action is non-commercial, leading to the app's own concert search rather than a subscription pitch — notable given how often this flow monetises its terminal positions. The clustered avatar illustration also communicates variety and abundance more effectively than the flat grid above. Meanwhile, the final tile introduces an aggregated date format ("Oct 10–11") with a "2 events near you" subline, marking the first time the grid groups events rather than listing individual dates.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven in the closing block — three strings, and they avoid the commercial register the flow's other terminal blocks used.

"See the Shows You Want" is possessive and outcome-framed. "You Want" presumes desire rather than creating it, which reads as continuation of a session already spent browsing rather than as a pitch. It also implies the search will honour intent, which is a claim the filters on "Find Concerts" can actually support.

"Find your next concert on Shazam" names the product, which is unusual — the app rarely refers to itself outside the recognition flow. Here it works as a positioning line, staking a claim that concert discovery is part of what Shazam does, which for a song-identification app is a genuine reframe.

"Find a Concert" as the CTA is very close to "Find Concerts" used on three other surfaces. The singular differs from the plural everywhere else, so a phrase the app had used consistently now has a fourth variant.

"2 events near you" on the tile above compresses a multi-date run into one entry with a count, which is more scannable than two separate tiles for the same artist.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Terminal block that is not a pitch — The end of a finite feed offers a functional next step rather than a subscription ask, unlike the flow's other end-of-scroll positions.

  2. Illustration arguing abundance — Overlapping avatars at varied scales suggest breadth in a way the uniform grid above cannot.

  3. Outcome-framed CTA copy — "Shows You Want" presumes intent rather than manufacturing it, matching a user who has been browsing.

  4. Self-naming as positioning — "on Shazam" claims concert discovery as part of the product's identity.

  5. Fourth variant of one label — "Find a Concert" against "Find Concerts" used elsewhere.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Bandsintown — Closes discovery feeds with a search prompt rather than a monetised block; the category convention.

  2. Apple Music (end-of-shelf browse prompts) — Comparable in offering an onward navigation action at the end of a finite feed.

  3. Dice — Same model of terminating a recommendation grid with an entry to full search.
screens.whereToUse: This fits the end of finite discovery feeds where a search entry point is the natural next step, and where an illustration can suggest breadth beyond what was scrolled.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit for infinite or paginated feeds where a terminus never arrives, and where the CTA's wording would diverge from a label the product uses consistently elsewhere.

screens.name: Search Top Results
screens.uxAnalysis: The results are organised by entity type with a "Top Results" panel above, a sensible structure for a heterogeneous catalogue where a query could mean either an artist or a song. The visual distinction is strong: square album art identifies songs while circular portraits identify artists, making each row's type clear before reading. This is an improvement over the suggestion list, where every row used the same search glyph. Chevrons also clearly signal navigation, distinguishing these results from the runnable queries shown earlier. The main weakness is the horizontally paged Songs card: it introduces a second gesture axis inside a vertical results page, while three visible rows and no pager leave the total number of results unclear.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Not applicable in the persuasive sense — this screen is interaction-driven. Its strings are section headings, titles, and artist credits.

"Top Results" is the conventional label and correctly implies cross-type ranking rather than a category. "Songs" and "Artists" are the plainest possible type names.

The section headings are sentence case, matching the Library's Explore sheet and the Concerts tab, and differing from the artist page's all-caps equivalents — the app's heading-convention split persists.

Artist credits repeat identically beneath every song row, which is expected for an artist-scoped query but means the second line carries no differentiating information in this particular result set.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Ambiguity hedged by a top panel — Offering both an artist and a song above the typed sections avoids forcing the user to guess which section holds their intent.

  2. Entity type readable from shape — Square artwork for songs, circular portraits for artists, so kind is legible pre-attentively.

  3. Navigational rows clearly marked — Chevrons distinguish these from the runnable query suggestions shown a tap earlier.

  4. Second gesture axis inside a scroll — The Songs card pages horizontally within a vertically scrolling page, with no pager or count.

  5. Redundant second lines — Artist credits repeat identically on every song row for an artist-scoped query.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music search results — Top Results above typed sections with shape-differentiated entities; the platform convention and component source.

  2. Spotify search — Comparable top-result panel followed by songs, artists, albums, and playlists sections.

  3. YouTube Music — Same structure of a cross-type top result above categorised results.
screens.whereToUse: This fits search across heterogeneous catalogues where a query's intended entity type is ambiguous, and where shape can distinguish result kinds without labels.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where introducing horizontal paging inside a vertical results page adds a gesture the user did not ask for, and where section contents are too few to justify their own card.

screens.name: Find Concerts
screens.uxAnalysis: Reached directly from the Concerts tab, this screen becomes a local listings board rather than an artist-specific tour list, and the proximity data finally delivers on the earlier Concerts Near You promise. Every event is within a few miles, making the distance figures immediately useful rather than discouraging. The Location chip also reflects how the filter was set: Near Me here versus a specific city in the artist-scoped view. The search placeholder is another clear improvement, with Artists or Bands demonstrating what the field accepts instead of merely naming it. The remaining weakness is discoverability: every row carries a plus and ellipsis without labels, leaving users to infer which saves the event and which opens additional actions.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Not applicable in the persuasive sense — this screen is interaction-driven. But the placeholder is worth noting as a correction.

"Artists or Bands" names the two things the field matches, so a user learns the scope before typing. That is the demonstrative approach the Location sheet's "Enter Location" lacked, and it means the same app now shows both the weak and the strong version of the same pattern.

"Near Me" on the chip reuses the phrasing from the Location sheet and the Concerts tab, so proximity is expressed one way across three surfaces — better consistency than "See All" versus "View All Dates" elsewhere.

The Date chip remains unset and unlabelled with a value, consistent with its behaviour on the artist-scoped version of this screen.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Proximity finally load-bearing — Distances of a mile or two make the metric genuinely decision-relevant for the first time in this flow.

  2. Same screen, different purpose by entry point — Without an artist query this is a local listings board; with one it is a tour list, using identical components.

  3. Placeholder demonstrating rather than describing — "Artists or Bands" teaches the field's scope, correcting the weakness of "Enter Location".

  4. Consistent proximity vocabulary — "Near Me" means one thing across the filter sheet, the Concerts tab, and this chip.

  5. Two unlabelled row controls — Plus and ellipsis on every row with nothing distinguishing save from menu.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Bandsintown / Songkick — Local listings boards with proximity filters and per-row tracking; the category convention.

  2. Dice — Comparable in presenting nearby shows as a browsable list with save-from-list triage.

  3. Eventbrite — Same model of a location-scoped event feed with a persistent search for narrowing by name.
screens.whereToUse: This fits event discovery where proximity is the primary constraint and users browse before searching, with a search field available to narrow rather than to initiate.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the same screen serves two materially different purposes without signalling which mode is active, and where row controls carry no labels to distinguish their functions.

screens.name: Discover
