screens.uxAnalysis: An empty search screen has nothing to show, and this one fills the space with three destinations rather than recent searches or trending terms — a defensible choice for an app where users mostly identify rather than search, making query history less useful. Two tiles also surface Shazam's own aggregate data: Charts and Radio Spins exist because millions of people have identified songs, turning the Library's individual behaviour into collective discovery. That is a genuine product asset, and giving it prominence here makes sense. The tile visuals reinforce the distinction — world map for charts, signal bars for radio, crowd photography for concerts — while the "Lyrics, Songs or Artists" placeholder is unusually informative, naming three searchable fields and introducing lyric matching for the first time in this flow.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven in the tiles — three title-and-subhead pairs, each doing scoping work.

"Shazam Charts" is the only place the brand names its own data product, and "The week's top songs around the world" scopes both the time window and the geography without a second line.

"Radio Spins" is the least self-evident title in the app — "spins" is industry vocabulary for broadcast plays — and the subhead has to carry the whole explanation. It does so accurately, but a user who does not read it will not know what the tile contains.

"Concerts" with "Find live music events" duplicates a destination already present in the tab bar, so the same feature is reachable two ways from one screen. The subhead is nonetheless the plainest of the three.

"Lyrics, Songs or Artists" is the app's best placeholder. It demonstrates scope across three fields rather than restating the label, and it is the only mention of lyrics search anywhere in this flow — a capability the Library's own search never disclosed.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Empty state filled with destinations — Browsable entry points serve a search screen better than recent queries in an app where searching is not the primary action.

  2. Proprietary data given top billing — Charts and Radio Spins are the collective form of what the app collects individually, and no competitor has the equivalent.

  3. Tiles differentiated by imagery — Map, signal texture, and crowd photography make three same-shaped cards distinguishable pre-attentively.

  4. Placeholder demonstrating scope — Three named fields, including a lyrics capability surfaced nowhere else in the app.

  5. Industry vocabulary in a title — "Radio Spins" requires its subhead to be understood at all.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (Browse) — Full-width discovery tiles above a search field; the component and layout convention.

  2. Spotify Search — Comparable in filling the pre-query state with browsable categories rather than history.

  3. Billboard and Last.fm charts — The aggregate-data-as-product model that Shazam Charts and Radio Spins participate in.
screens.whereToUse: This fits search destinations in apps where searching is secondary to a primary action, so the resting state can carry browsable entry points and proprietary data products.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where recent searches would be more useful than curated destinations, and where a tile's title requires its subhead to be comprehensible at all.

screens.name: Searching 03
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen deepens the loading experience from the previous "empty canvas" state into a transparency moment: instead of just showing that something is happening, it names exactly which sources ("Reading 20 web pages," with the specific domains fading in) the AI is drawing from to build the answer. This does double duty as both a progress indicator and a lightweight trust-building device — seeing recognizable, credible outlets (Forbes, Rotten Tomatoes, Vulture) reassures the user the eventual summary is grounded in real journalism rather than an opaque black box. The domains are rendered in a fading gradient of opacity (top ones solid, later ones lighter), which visually implies sequential reading rather than all sources appearing at once.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "Reading 20 web pages" is written in the app's consistent plain, present-tense, process-labeling style — matching the earlier "Summarizing for you..." status text from onboarding. It's not persuasive copy; it's operational transparency, and that fits its role in the trust lever for an AI-answer feature: naming a concrete number of sources ("20") is more credible than a vague "gathering information" message, since specificity itself signals rigor even without the user reading every domain.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of System Status — naming the exact number and identity of sources being processed goes beyond generic loading feedback, giving real insight into what's happening.

  2. Trust Through Transparency — surfacing recognizable, reputable domains during the loading state pre-builds credibility for the eventual AI-synthesized answer.

  3. Progressive Disclosure — the list reveals sources incrementally (implied by the fading opacity) rather than dumping all 20 at once, keeping the loading state readable.

  4. Consistency (Jakob's Law) — the query heading, toolbar, and Arc/Google toggle remain in the same position as the prior loading screen, so this reads as a continuation of the same moment rather than a new screen.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Perplexity AI (source-reading loading state) — shows a near-identical "reading N sources" list with fading source names while an AI answer is being compiled.

  2. Bing Chat / Copilot (searching-the-web state) — displays which sites are being consulted during an AI-generated answer's loading phase for the same transparency purpose.

  3. You.com (AI search loading) — surfaces a scrolling or fading list of sources being read as part of its multi-step search-and-synthesize loading sequence.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any AI-synthesis loading state where naming real, credible sources during processing meaningfully builds trust in the eventual output, especially for research-style or fact-based queries.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when the underlying sources are numerous but low-value or undifferentiated (e.g., scraped forum posts with no recognizable authority), where listing them would add noise without building the intended credibility.

screens.name: Searching 04
screens.uxAnalysis: This is the fully realized version of the answer page previewed in onboarding: a scannable, magazine-style layout that opens with visual appeal (movie posters) before establishing credibility (recognizable publisher icons and "Read 20 web pages") and finally delivering the synthesized content itself. Structuring each movie entry with a bolded title, an emoji marker, and a concrete stat (Tomatometer percentage) gives the AI-generated text just enough structure to feel edited and skimmable rather than like a raw paragraph dump. The floating Arc/Google toggle persists from the loading state, keeping the fallback-to-traditional-search option available even once the AI answer has rendered, reinforcing that this is one mode among options rather than a locked-in destination.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The write-up mixes plain factual reporting (percentages, ratings) with light editorial color ("bittersweet storytelling," "masterful blend of gore and subversion"), giving the AI-generated content a voice closer to a film-critic roundup than a neutral encyclopedia entry. This tonal choice supports the content-and-clarity goal directly: readers get both the "what" (ratings, genre) and the "why it's good" in the same sentence, so they don't need to click into a full article to get a usable recommendation — which is the entire value proposition "Browse for Me" was built to deliver.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Progressive Disclosure — the page layers visual (posters) → credibility (source icons/cards) → substance (synthesized write-up), letting users stop scrolling as soon as they have what they need.

  2. Social Proof — recognizable outlet logos (Rotten Tomatoes, Forbes, IMDb) and specific rating percentages lend third-party credibility to AI-generated recommendations.

  3. Scannability — emoji markers and bolded titles let users skim multiple entries quickly rather than reading dense prose top to bottom.

  4. Persistent User Control — keeping the Arc/Google toggle visible even after the answer loads ensures the fallback option isn't buried once its "urgency" (during loading) has passed.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Perplexity AI (finished answer page) — uses the same image-carousel-plus-cited-write-up structure once a query finishes processing.

  2. Rotten Tomatoes' own "Certified Fresh" roundup articles — the emoji-and-rating format for individual movie entries closely mirrors this kind of curated critic listicle.

  3. Google's AI Overview (finished state) — similarly surfaces source logos and linked cards above a synthesized summary once an AI-generated answer completes.
screens.whereToUse: This layout fits any AI-synthesized answer for a subjective, ranked-list-style query (best movies, top restaurants, recommended products) where visual media, credible sourcing, and concise editorial framing together make the answer more useful than a plain link list.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for factual, single-answer queries (e.g., "what year did X happen") where a rich, multi-section magazine layout would be overkill for content that could be answered in one line.

screens.name: Searching 06
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen shows the answer page organizing itself into clear topical sections rather than remaining one long undifferentiated list — after the ranked movie entries, a new "Notable Performances" heading signals a shift in angle (actors rather than films), which helps a long AI-generated page stay navigable as it grows. The underlined actor names read as inline links, implying each name is tappable (likely to a source, filmography, or further detail), extending the page's interactivity beyond the earlier plain-text movie titles. A pull-quote box beginning to peek in at the bottom, marked with an opening quotation mark, signals the page is about to shift again into a directly-cited excerpt — a different content type from the paraphrased descriptions used so far.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The entries follow a name–em-dash–sentence structure similar to the movie list, but the content itself shifts to performance-specific praise ("showcasing her range in a complex role," "brings charisma and depth") — critic-style language appropriate for evaluating acting rather than a whole film. This consistency of sentence rhythm across very different sub-topics (films, then performances) reinforces that the entire page, despite drawing from 20 different sources, reads with one unified authorial voice rather than stitched-together excerpts — a deliberate synthesis choice that supports the content-and-clarity goal of the page.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Chunking with Sub-Headings — introducing a new "Notable Performances" heading partway down a long answer breaks the page into digestible topical sections rather than one continuous scroll.

  2. Affordance Signaling — underlining actor names as links signals they're interactive, inviting deeper exploration without cluttering the page with buttons.

  3. Consistency Across Sub-Sections — reusing the emoji-marker-plus-bolded-name-plus-description format from the movie list keeps the new section visually familiar despite the topic shift.

  4. Content Layering — transitioning toward a directly quoted excerpt (visible at the bottom) after several paraphrased sections suggests the page varies its content type to keep a long answer from feeling monotonous.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. IMDb "Notable Performances" or awards-season roundup articles — use the same structure of underlined actor names with brief evaluative blurbs.

  2. Rotten Tomatoes editorial roundups — commonly segment a longer piece into named sub-sections (e.g., "Best Films" then "Best Performances") exactly as this page does.

  3. Wikipedia-style long-form AI answers (e.g., Perplexity's "Pro Search") — use inline linked names and topical sub-headings to organize an otherwise long synthesized response.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits long AI-synthesized answers covering multiple related but distinct angles on one topic (e.g., films and their performances), where topical sub-headings help users jump to the specific facet they care about.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for short, single-fact answers where introducing multiple sub-sections would add unnecessary structural overhead to content that doesn't naturally divide into separate topics.

screens.name: Searching By Voice 01
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen captures a mid-transition moment: the user has triggered a new search (likely by tapping the search icon in the bottom toolbar or a similar entry point) while still on the previous "best new movies 2025" results page, and the new empty search sheet is animating up and over the old content rather than navigating to a completely separate screen. The dimmed, faded visibility of the prior page's carousel and search bar behind the new sheet preserves spatial context, reassuring the user their previous results are still there and one tap away, rather than being discarded. This layered-sheet approach lets searching feel lightweight and iterative — closer to opening a new tab than performing a full page navigation — consistent with the "fast, low-friction" identity established throughout onboarding.
screens.tonalityAndContent: This is a transient interaction state with no original app copy beyond the placeholder "Search..." text.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Continuity of Context — keeping the previous page dimly visible behind the new search sheet reassures the user their prior results haven't been lost.

  2. Minimal Interruption — layering a new search sheet over existing content (rather than a full-screen replace) keeps the interaction feeling fast and non-disruptive.

  3. Visibility of System Status — the raised keyboard and focused cursor make it immediately clear the app is ready for new input.

  4. Progressive Disclosure — presenting an empty search field first, before any suggestions or results, keeps the entry point simple and unopinionated.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Search app (new search overlay) — uses a similar sliding sheet that layers a fresh search bar over previous results rather than fully navigating away.

  2. Spotlight Search on iOS — presents an overlay search sheet on top of dimmed background content, closely matching this layered transition pattern.

  3. Notion's quick-find overlay — similarly slides a search input over existing content while keeping the underlying page faintly visible for context.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits enabling rapid, repeated searching within a session, where preserving visual continuity with prior results (rather than a hard navigation) helps users feel they can search again without losing their place.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when a new search represents a genuinely distinct task or context switch, where dimming rather than fully clearing the previous content could create confusion about whether the old results are still relevant or active.

screens.name: Find Concerts Dark Mode
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen supports a Searching & Finding flow for live events, letting users browse all tour dates for a searched artist ("Rose Gray") while narrowing results by Location or Date. The consistent row structure — date, artist, venue, city, distance — makes multiple shows easy to scan and compare, while the standalone "+" provides a lightweight save action without opening each concert's detail page. Showing distance for every entry, including far-flung options like Bondi Beach at 7,414 mi, also suggests the list prioritizes full tour visibility over proximity by default, leaving location filtering to the user.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Scannable repeated layout (Gestalt: similarity): identical row structure across all four+ entries lets users quickly compare dates, venues, and distances without re-parsing format each time.

  2. Lightweight save without full commitment: the standalone "+" affordance lets users bookmark a date directly from the list, reducing friction compared to requiring a full detail-page visit first.

  3. Progressive filtering: Location and Date chips let users narrow a potentially long list without leaving the results view, keeping the search loop tight.

  4. Persistent search context: keeping the search bar populated with "Rose Gray" at the bottom (rather than hiding it after the initial search) makes it easy to refine or clear the query without navigating back.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Bandsintown (artist search results with multiple tour dates and a save/track button) — same pattern of a scrollable list of an artist's upcoming shows with quick-save actions per row.

  2. Songkick (concert search results filtered by location/date) — comparable filter-chip-plus-list structure for browsing an artist's tour schedule.

  3. Ticketmaster (event search results with filters and quick-add) — same combination of Location/Date filtering and per-row save/add actions in a concert search context.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any event-discovery search flow where users need to browse and compare multiple instances of the same or similar events (tour dates, showtimes, sessions) and want a lightweight way to save options before committing to view full details.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when there's typically only one or a small number of results per search (e.g., a single scheduled webinar), where a full list-with-filters UI would be overkill compared to surfacing the single relevant result directly.

screens.name: Alternatives - No Results
screens.uxAnalysis: Two empty states exist for the same screen, and they don't match up. The STN → LPL case (a valid but unmatched query) got three ranked diagnostics, two labelled recovery links, and a feedback path. This one — reached from a malformed airport code — gets a headline, a hint about an unrelated mechanic, and a party trick. That's backwards: "SYDxd" is unambiguously invalid, the app knows it, and should just say so, rather than nudging the user to tap Next or leaving the bad chip unmarked and uncorrectable. The real issue is upstream — the airport field has typeahead but apparently lets free text commit without a valid selection, so invalid input reaches the results stage at all. "Shake for random flight" is the odd inclusion here: a delightful easter egg, but misplaced on a failed search, and now exposed through a second, inconsistent mechanic (text vs. the tappable link on the home empty state).
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Three strings, and the mismatch between them is the story.

"No Results" — shorter and flatter than the other empty state's "No Flights Found", and less informative. "Flights" named what was missing; "Results" is generic and could describe any query. Two labels for the same condition on the same screen is an inconsistency, and the app picked the weaker one for the case that needed more clarity.

"Searching by Route? Enter one airport, then tap Next" — a question-and-instruction pair, and the question is doing intent-detection: is this what you were trying to do? That's a reasonable rhetorical move, but the answer here is no. The user did enter two airports; one is simply invalid. The hint diagnoses a mechanic problem when the actual problem is a data problem, so it reads as the app guessing wrong about what went awry.

There's also a mechanical mismatch: "tap Next" refers to the keyboard's return key, which isn't visible on this screen. The instruction describes a state the user isn't in.

"Shake for random flight" — playful, and it does teach a hidden gesture that would otherwise go undiscovered. But placing gesture education in a failure state means the app is spending the user's attention on delight at the moment they need utility. The shake glyph is also the first motion-based icon in the app, unlabelled beyond the text.

What's missing is the obvious sentence: "SYDxd" isn't a recognised airport. One line naming the invalid value would resolve the failure completely, and the app already knows enough to write it.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Match diagnosis depth to ambiguity — the ambiguous failure got three diagnostics; the unambiguous one got none, which is inverted.

  2. Validate at the field, not the results — an airport picker with a curated list shouldn't accept a string that matches nothing.

  3. Name the invalid value — the app knows which chip is malformed and could say so in one sentence.

  4. One condition, one label — "No Results" and "No Flights Found" describe the same state on the same screen.

  5. Delight belongs outside failure states — a hidden-gesture hint is charming on an idle screen and misplaced when the user's task has just failed.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Flights (invalid airport) — rejects unmatched input at the field rather than allowing it through to a results query.

  2. Apple Maps (no results) — names the searched term back to the user, so an unrecognised query is visibly the cause.

  3. Google Search ("did you mean") — offers a correction for a near-miss string rather than a generic empty result.
screens.whereToUse: Best where a query can fail for a single, identifiable reason the system can name — then the empty state should name it and offer the fix. Gesture hints suit idle or exploratory states where the user has attention to spare.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit when a system knows exactly why a query failed and declines to say. Also wrong when guidance addresses a hypothetical different problem, since a user whose actual issue isn't mentioned concludes the app doesn't understand the failure.

screens.name: Dark Mode Discover 2
screens.uxAnalysis: This Search screen blends direct query search with editorial discovery, recognizing that users may arrive without a specific song in mind. Leading with a "Discover" section of large, visually distinct cards positions browsing curated content as an equally valid entry point to typing a query, serving both intentional searchers and casual explorers. Placing the search field at the bottom is also notable: it keeps the primary input within the thumb-reachable zone while giving the taller discovery cards more visual prominence above.
screens.tonalityAndContent: This screen has light copy support: each card pairs a short, punchy title (Shazam Charts, Radio Spins, Concerts) with a one-line description clarifying its content ("The week's top songs around the world," "Songs getting the most radio plays worldwide," "Find live music events"). The tone is plain and informative rather than persuasive, appropriately treating these as straightforward content categories rather than something requiring a sales pitch. The search placeholder "Lyrics, Songs or Artists" is notably functional copy — it communicates multiple valid search input types in three words, helping users understand the search bar accepts more than just song titles.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Discovery-first layout for ambiguous intent: placing curated content cards above the search field accommodates users who want to browse rather than search with a specific query in mind.

  2. Distinct visual coding per category: using different color gradients and imagery for each card (blue/map for Charts, blue/waveform for Radio Spins, orange/crowd for Concerts) aids quick visual differentiation even before reading labels.

  3. Multi-input search affordance: the placeholder text ("Lyrics, Songs or Artists") sets accurate expectations about what kinds of queries the search bar supports, reducing failed search attempts.

  4. Thumb-zone consideration: positioning the search input near the bottom of the screen aligns with natural one-handed mobile reach patterns.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Spotify (Search tab with Browse categories above the search field) — same pattern of curated discovery cards taking visual priority over a query-first search bar.

  2. Apple Music (Search tab featuring Browse/Charts categories) — comparable structure combining direct search with editorial content categories like charts.

  3. YouTube Music (Explore tab with Charts, New Releases, Moods cards) — same principle of multiple distinct editorial cards for different discovery angles alongside search.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any content-discovery app where a meaningful portion of users browse without a specific query in mind, benefiting from curated entry points (charts, trending, events) alongside direct search.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for utility-focused search experiences where users almost always arrive with a specific, known query (e.g., a file search tool), where prioritizing editorial browsing cards above the search field would add unnecessary friction to the primary task.

screens.name: Dark Mode Top Results
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen structures search results by content type, leading with a condensed "Top Results" summary that combines the strongest song and artist matches before expanding into dedicated Songs and Artists sections. This layered approach supports both quick decisions and deeper browsing: users can act on the Top Results immediately or scroll through the full catalogue. Consistent row formatting — artwork, title, subtitle, and chevron — also keeps the mixed content types easy to scan within a single results view.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Result prioritization (Top Results first): surfacing the single best song and artist match at the top saves effort for users with high search intent confidence, before offering deeper category browsing.

  2. Consistent row affordances (Master–Detail): uniform chevron-led rows across all sections signal that every result leads to a dedicated detail page, reducing uncertainty about what tapping will do.

  3. Categorical chunking (Gestalt: proximity): splitting results into Songs and Artists sections with clear headers helps users locate the specific result type they're looking for within a broader query.

  4. Distinct iconography per content type: waveform icons for songs versus circular avatar photos for artists/people provide quick visual differentiation between result types even before reading labels.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Spotify (Search results segmented into Top Result, Songs, Artists, Albums) — same pattern of a prioritized top match followed by type-specific result sections.

  2. Apple Music (Search results with Top Hit and categorized sections) — nearly identical structure of a best-match summary plus sectioned browsing by content type.

  3. YouTube Music (Search results with Top Result and category rows) — same principle of leading with a best-guess match before offering categorized full results.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any search experience spanning multiple content types (songs, artists, albums, etc.) where users benefit from both a fast best-match answer and the ability to browse comprehensively by category.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for narrow, single-content-type search experiences (e.g., searching only within one's own library for songs), where segmenting into multiple type-based sections would be unnecessary structure for a naturally homogeneous result set.

screens.name: Empty State
screens.uxAnalysis: The hardest problem here is that a flight tracker with no flights has nothing to track, and the design solves this by refusing to look empty. The map fills the frame with something visually rich and thematically relevant, making the product feel capable rather than blank. Beneath it, three escalating paths cover different starting points: enter a flight number, check another list, or "view a random flight." The third is the smartest — instead of requiring users to already have flight data, it lets them experience the product first, turning a dead end into a demo. The ordering is also deliberate: search remains fixed near the header, while the guidance sits lower in the sheet and disappears once flights exist, preserving muscle memory without permanently adding clutter.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The voice is warm, first-person-plural and unhurried — a striking tonal contrast with the instrument-panel restraint of the rest of the product.

"Let's Fly Somewhere" — an invitation, not an apology. The default failure mode of empty states is negation ("No flights yet," "Nothing here"), which tells the user the app is broken or they are behind. This headline instead names the pleasant thing the space is for, and the inclusive "let's" positions the app as a travel companion rather than a database awaiting input. It sets emotional tone before it sets task.

"Use the search bar or view a random flight" — plain, instructional, and correctly ordered by likelihood: the intended action first, the escape hatch second. The phrasing does one clever thing — it names the search bar rather than pointing at it, which works because the bar is visible in the same viewport. Had the copy said "tap above," it would break the moment the sheet scrolled.

"view a random flight" — the most interesting three words on the screen. "Random" is honest about the fact that this flight has nothing to do with you, which preserves trust, but it also does real motivational work by appealing to curiosity rather than utility. A user with no trip planned has a reason to tap. Compare a more conventional "see a demo," which announces a sales artifact and invites dismissal; "random flight" promises a real aircraft in the air right now, which is both truer and more enticing.

"Search to add flights" — the placeholder is a verb phrase stating outcome, not a field label. It answers "what do I type here" implicitly by answering "what will happen."

The lever is activation, and the copy pulls it by lowering the entry requirement from having a trip to being curious. The tonality's only cost is a slight mismatch: "Let's Fly Somewhere" is the voice of a leisure travel app, while the product's substance is delay forecasting for people who fly often and reluctantly. It's charming, and it may set a marginally softer expectation than the app delivers.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Empty states as onboarding — the highest-leverage moment in the app is when it has no data, and this screen treats it as a teaching opportunity rather than a status report.

  2. Reducing the cost of first action — offering a zero-input path ("random flight") removes the single largest activation barrier: needing a trip booked before the app is useful.

  3. Aesthetic-usability effect — the satellite basemap makes an empty product feel substantial and premium, buying patience the interface would not otherwise earn.

  4. Progressive disclosure and spatial stability — guidance occupies space the flight list will later claim, so the layout teaches without creating a layout the user must unlearn.

  5. Contrast under a variable backdrop — the map-layer button's translucent chrome sits over imagery that ranges from near-black ocean to bright city lights. It's legible here; over a bright region it would be marginal, and the same risk applies to the status bar's dark glyphs.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Citymapper — map-canvas home with a persistent bottom sheet holding search and saved items; empty state points at search while the map carries the visual load. Nearly identical structural bet.

  2. Flightradar24 — same domain and same zero-data problem, solved by dropping the user straight onto a live traffic map. A useful contrast: it shows data immediately, where Flighty deliberately shows your data and offers a sample only on request.

  3. Duolingo / Headspace onboarding — different domain, same "let them experience one real unit of the product before asking for commitment" activation tactic that "view a random flight" implements.
screens.whereToUse: Best where the product's value is invisible until the user supplies personal data, and where a representative sample can be shown without any input — live-data products in transit, weather, markets and sports fit especially well. The map-plus-sheet structure suits apps whose content is inherently spatial, so the empty list still has something meaningful to sit on.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit where no honest sample exists — anything personal, private or generated (messages, health records, documents), since a "random" example is either fabricated or someone else's. It also misfires when the empty state is the normal steady state rather than a first-run condition, because a permanent invitation to explore reads as the app failing to do its job.

screens.name: Loading & Connecting
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen turns an unavoidable network wait into part of the experience rather than treating it as dead time. The radar sweep gives latency a domain-specific metaphor — the app appears to be actively searching for aircraft on the user's behalf — making the wait feel purposeful rather than slow. The caption then uses that guaranteed attention to reinforce value while the user has nothing else to do.

The main omission is a cancel or timeout state. Indeterminate loading without an escape is acceptable only when the operation is reliably brief; if the network stalls, the overlay becomes a trap. There is also a subtle mismatch in the metaphor: radar implies searching nearby, while the app is actually selecting an arbitrary flight anywhere in the world. Charming and relevant, but not entirely truthful to the underlying operation.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Two lines, doing entirely different jobs, and the split is the interesting part.

"Scanning…" — a single word chosen for atmosphere over accuracy. "Loading" would be honest and forgettable; "Searching" would be accurate and flat. "Scanning" borrows the vocabulary of air traffic control and pairs with the radar visual to keep the user inside the product's fiction for the duration of the wait. The ellipsis follows platform convention for in-progress states correctly. It is a small word doing real work: it makes a network call feel like an instrument operating.

"Random flights include Flighty Pro free of charge" — this is a monetization message wearing a loading state's clothing, and it is placed with some care. Three things it accomplishes in nine words. It removes a barrier by pre-empting the suspicion that the sample flight will be a crippled, upsell-riddled preview. It sets the reference frame that Pro is the normal experience and free is the reduced one, so the user's first encounter with the product is the good version. And it plants the tier name at a moment of zero resistance, since a user waiting for something they requested is not defending against a pitch.

The tonality is matter-of-fact rather than promotional — "free of charge" is transactional phrasing, not celebratory, and there is no exclamation mark or CTA. That restraint is what keeps it from reading as an ad in a loading screen. Compare a version like "Enjoy Flighty Pro on us!" which would be the same information delivered in a way that invites dismissal.

The lever is conversion via anchoring, executed during a moment the user has no reason to resist. It is the third distinct Pro mention across these screens — onboarding gift, comparison table, and now loading caption — each pitched differently and none of them a hard sell. Cumulatively that is a well-sequenced funnel.

One small clarity gap: "Random flights include Flighty Pro" doesn't say whether the grant is per-random-flight and perpetual, or a one-off. A user could reasonably read it as an ongoing free channel into Pro features, which may or may not be intended.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Perceived performance — a domain-native animation makes an identical wait feel shorter and purposeful, which is the cheapest performance win available.

  2. Productive waiting — the one moment of guaranteed undivided attention is used for a value message rather than left blank.

  3. Objection pre-emption — telling the user the demo isn't crippled removes the main reason to distrust a free sample.

  4. Anchoring the premium tier as default — experiencing Pro first makes the free tier read as a reduction, which is the strongest position a freemium product can establish.

  5. No cancel path — the screen's real defect. Indeterminate loading without an escape hatch or stated timeout leaves the user stranded if the request hangs.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Uber (matching a driver) — an indeterminate wait dressed in a domain-specific animation, with reassurance copy filling the interval. Same conversion of latency into narrative.

  2. Shazam (listening) — a branded, thematically exact loading state that makes waiting feel like the product working rather than stalling.

  3. Spotify / YouTube Premium trial prompts during playback interstitials — naming the paid tier at a moment of low resistance rather than at a decision point. Same placement logic, different surface.
screens.whereToUse: Best where a short, unavoidable wait has a natural real-world metaphor in the product's own domain, and where the user has explicitly requested the operation so the wait is expected. It also fits when there is a genuinely useful, non-promotional-feeling thing to say about what they're about to receive.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit where the wait is long or unpredictable, since a charming animation without progress or cancel becomes an unexplained hang. It also backfires when the message is a pure upsell with no bearing on the operation in progress — users read an ad shown during a wait they cannot skip as hostile rather than helpful.

screens.name: Searching 02
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen captures the brief in-between moment after a "Browse for Me" query is submitted but before the synthesized answer page has populated — the query text itself becomes a large, prominent heading (echoing the onboarding demo's title-first structure), while the rest of the canvas stays empty, signaling work in progress without an explicit spinner or percentage. The Arc/Google source toggle floating in the bottom right suggests the user can switch between Arc's own AI-summarized approach and a traditional Google search for the same query, giving a fallback if the AI answer isn't what they want. The minimized toolbar (tabs, new tab, collapse) stays consistent with the earlier three-button minimal-chrome design established as core to the app's identity.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven (a loading transition), not copy-driven; the only text present is the user's own query, not app-authored messaging.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of System Status — displaying the submitted query prominently while the rest loads reassures the user their input was received, even without a traditional spinner.

  2. Minimal Interruption — keeping the loading state visually quiet (empty gradient, no heavy loading animation) matches the app's broader "stay out of the way" design philosophy noted in earlier onboarding screens.

  3. User Control & Freedom — the Arc/Google toggle gives users an explicit way to bypass the AI-generated answer in favor of a standard search if desired.

  4. Consistency (Jakob's Law) — the bottom three-button toolbar remains unchanged from the app's default browsing chrome, keeping the loading state visually anchored to the rest of the app.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Perplexity AI (query-submitted loading state) — similarly displays the user's query as a heading while the AI-generated answer is still being assembled.

  2. Google Search (Search Generative Experience loading) — shows the query at the top with a placeholder/loading area before the AI overview renders.

  3. ChatGPT (prompt-submitted state) — echoes the user's input prominently before the response streams in, similar to this heading-first loading treatment.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any AI-generated or synthesized-answer feature where processing takes a few seconds, and reassurance that the query was received is more important than a detailed progress indicator.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for longer processing times, where an empty canvas without a spinner, skeleton loader, or progress cue risks feeling broken or unresponsive rather than "in progress."

screens.name: Searching By Voice 02
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen represents Arc Search's voice-assistant mode ("Call Arc," referenced in earlier product research), overlaying a friendly, minimal smiley-face avatar and conversational greeting on top of the existing results page, which stays dimly visible beneath it just as the text-search overlay did. The live waveform beneath the greeting gives real-time visual confirmation that the microphone is actively capturing speech, which is essential feedback for a voice interface where there's no typed text to visually confirm input. The orange dot in the status bar's call-indicator pill signals an active session, similar to how iOS marks an ongoing phone call or recording, reinforcing that this is a live, continuous interaction rather than a one-off command.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "Hi! How can I help?" is warm, casual, and conversational — deliberately written as spoken dialogue rather than a UI label, since the entire interaction is voice-first. This matches the brand's consistent friendly, approachable tone seen throughout onboarding, but shifts here into a more overtly personified register (a literal greeting with a smiling face) appropriate for a voice-assistant context, where users expect to be spoken to conversationally rather than instructed.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Anthropomorphism / Personification — the smiley-face avatar and greeting give the voice feature a friendly, approachable "character" rather than presenting it as a bare technical function.

  2. Visibility of System Status — the live waveform and status-bar call indicator together confirm the assistant is actively listening, critical feedback for a voice interface with no visible typed input.

  3. Continuity of Context — dimming rather than fully replacing the previous results page keeps the user oriented to what they were doing before invoking voice search.

  4. Conversational Design — greeting the user with a spoken-style prompt ("Hi! How can I help?") sets expectations for natural language input rather than keyword-style queries.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Siri (iOS voice assistant overlay) — uses a nearly identical full-screen overlay with an animated orb/avatar and waveform to indicate active listening.

  2. Google Assistant — similarly greets users conversationally and shows a real-time waveform while listening, dimming background content behind the overlay.

  3. Alexa app (voice interaction screen) — uses a friendly greeting plus live audio visualization to confirm the assistant is actively receiving speech input.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any voice-assistant entry point layered over existing app content, where a friendly greeting plus live waveform feedback reassures the user their voice is being captured, especially when invoked mid-task from another screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for silent or background voice capture (e.g., always-listening wake-word detection before invocation), where a full-screen animated overlay would be an unnecessary interruption before the user has confirmed intent to speak.

screens.name: Searching By Voice 03
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen is the direct continuation of the previous "Hi! How can I help?" listening state, now showing the payoff of that listening: real-time speech-to-text transcription displayed as a pill-shaped label ("Coffee recipe") directly beneath the avatar. This is a critical trust and usability checkpoint for voice interfaces — the user can visually confirm the assistant heard them correctly before the search executes, catching potential misrecognition errors before they lead to a bad result. The waveform's changed appearance (more structured, evenly spaced bars versus the busier pattern in the listening state) may subtly signal a shift from "actively listening" toward "processing/about to submit," though this distinction is inferred rather than explicitly labeled.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — the only text present, "Coffee recipe," is a direct transcription of the user's own spoken words rather than authored app copy.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of System Status — displaying the transcribed query lets the user confirm the assistant correctly understood their speech before any search executes.

  2. Error Prevention — showing transcribed text as an intermediate step (rather than jumping straight to results) gives the user a chance to notice and correct a misheard query.

  3. Continuity of Interaction — reusing the identical avatar and layout from the listening screen keeps this feeling like one fluid voice interaction rather than a separate step.

  4. Recognition over Recall — the user doesn't need to remember what they said; it's echoed back to them directly on screen.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Siri (query confirmation) — displays the transcribed spoken request on screen before or while executing the search, matching this pattern closely.

  2. Google Assistant (voice search transcription) — shows recognized text beneath the listening animation as a confirmation step.

  3. Alexa app (voice query display) — echoes transcribed speech on screen as part of its voice-interaction flow, serving the same error-prevention purpose.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any voice-input flow where confirming correct speech recognition before acting on the query meaningfully reduces the cost of a misunderstood command, especially for open-ended or free-form spoken queries.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for extremely short, low-stakes voice commands (e.g., "next," "stop") where the action is reversible and the overhead of an explicit transcription-confirmation step would slow down an otherwise instant interaction.

screens.name: Searching 01
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen is functionally identical to the previous one, with the only meaningful difference being the search bar's focus state: a blinking text cursor is now visible at the start of the field, indicating the keyboard is actively engaged and the user is positioned to type. This subtle state change confirms the hint is being shown at the exact moment of active search intent — right as the user is about to type a query — rather than as a passive, disconnected tip. Everything else (the tooltip copy, arrow, highlighted button, suggestion list, keyboard) carries over unchanged, reinforcing that this is the same coach-mark moment captured at a slightly different interaction state.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — the copy is unchanged from the previous screen ("Tap Browse for Me for a faster answer"), so the tonal analysis carries over directly: it remains a direct, outcome-focused instruction suited to a just-in-time hint shown mid-task.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Just-in-Time Guidance — the active text cursor confirms the hint appears exactly as the user is engaging with the search field, maximizing relevance.

  2. Visibility of System Status — the blinking cursor is a small but clear signal that the field is focused and ready for input, distinct from the unfocused state in the prior screen.

  3. Von Restorff Effect — the single colored "Browse for Me" button remains isolated against three gray duplicates, continuing to direct attention.

  4. Consistency — reusing the identical tooltip, arrow, and layout from the previous screen keeps the hint experience coherent regardless of the exact focus state captured.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Gmail (Smart Compose hints) — shows contextual tooltips as the user is actively typing, not just when a field is idle.

  2. Notion (slash-command hints) — surfaces guidance the moment the text cursor becomes active in a relevant field.

  3. YouTube (live coach marks) — ties hints to the exact interaction state (e.g., focused search field) rather than a generic screen view.
screens.whereToUse: Same as the previous screen: fits reinforcing a feature already introduced during onboarding via a hint shown on the live interface at the moment of active engagement.
screens.whereNotToUse: Same as the previous screen: a poor fit if shown repeatedly after first engagement with the feature.

screens.name: Searching 05
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen confirms the write-up pattern established earlier scales consistently across multiple entries: each item follows the identical title–percentage–description formula, making the list easy to skim even without re-reading the structure each time. The varied, expressive emoji per entry (🎬 for a baseball dramedy, 👑 for a fairy-tale horror film, 🕵️ for an espionage thriller, 💔 for a romantic drama, 😂 for a dark comedy) act as quick visual genre cues, letting a user's eye jump to whichever tone matches their mood before reading the text. The persistent floating Arc/Google toggle staying anchored in place while the page scrolls underneath it confirms it's a fixed overlay control rather than part of the scrolling content, keeping the fallback option always within reach regardless of scroll position.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The consistent sentence structure — bolded italic title, em-dash, rating percentage, then a one- or two-sentence critical assessment — reads like a tightened, AI-condensed version of a "best of" listicle, mixing concrete data (percentages, director and cast names) with brief editorial framing ("celebrated for its sleek design and dry wit," "explores the complexities of love and desire"). This consistency across all five entries reinforces the earlier finding: the tone stays informative-but-colorful throughout, prioritizing quick usefulness over exhaustive detail, which suits a scannable answer page rather than a full review.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Consistency (Jakob's Law) — identical formatting across all entries lets the user's reading pattern become automatic after the first one or two items.

  2. Scannability — varied, meaningful emoji per entry let users visually differentiate genre/tone at a glance before committing to reading the text.

  3. Persistent Controls — the Arc/Google toggle remaining fixed in place while content scrolls ensures the fallback search option is always accessible without needing to scroll back up.

  4. Chunking — breaking a "top movies" answer into individually bounded entries (rather than one continuous paragraph) makes a long-form AI response digestible in a mobile context.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Rotten Tomatoes' own "Certified Fresh" roundups — use the same rating-plus-blurb-per-entry format this write-up echoes.

  2. Letterboxd list pages — similarly present ranked film entries with a title, a quick descriptor, and consistent visual formatting per item.

  3. Perplexity AI (multi-item answer pages) — structures list-style AI answers with the same repeated title/stat/description pattern across several entries.
screens.whereToUse: This repeated-entry format fits any AI-synthesized ranked or curated list (movies, restaurants, products) where consistency across entries helps users compare items quickly without re-learning the layout each time.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for answers with only one or two items, where imposing a repeated multi-entry structure would feel like unnecessary overhead for content that could be presented more simply.

screens.name: Finding Keywords 01
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen shows the standard "Find on Page" tool activated from the earlier page-actions sheet, letting users search for specific text within the currently loaded page (here, the Google "best new movies 2025" results) rather than performing a new web search. The up/down chevrons anticipate multiple matches, letting users step through occurrences once a term is typed, and the dropdown caret next to the magnifying glass in the Find field likely offers additional search options (e.g., case sensitivity or match-whole-word) common to this type of control. Positioning "Done" prominently on the left as the clear exit point, paired with the keyboard's "search" action key to submit, follows conventional iOS in-page-search UI almost exactly, minimizing any need to learn new interaction patterns for this specific tool.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — purely functional labeling ("Find," "Done," "search") consistent with a standard utility tool, no persuasive or brand-voice copy present.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Consistency (Jakob's Law) — this Find-on-Page toolbar closely mirrors Safari's and other iOS apps' native in-page-search UI, requiring no new learning for users familiar with the platform convention.

  2. Efficient Match Navigation — up/down arrows let users step through multiple occurrences of a search term without retyping or re-searching.

  3. Clear Exit Point — a prominent "Done" button on the left ensures users can easily dismiss the tool once finished, a standard and expected placement.

  4. Contextual Tool Invocation — accessing this from the page-actions sheet (rather than requiring a separate menu hunt) keeps the feature discoverable alongside other page-level tools like Summarize and Share.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's "Find on Page" — uses a nearly identical toolbar layout (Find field, up/down arrows, Done button) for the same in-page text search function.

  2. Chrome's "Find in page" — offers comparable functionality with a similar input-plus-navigation-arrows structure.

  3. Firefox's page-search bar — follows the same established convention for locating text within a loaded page.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any browser or long-document viewer where users need to quickly locate specific text within currently displayed content, especially for long pages where scrolling to find a term manually would be inefficient.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for short pages or content where manually scanning would be just as fast as invoking a dedicated search tool — though this is a low-cost feature to offer regardless, since it doesn't interfere with normal browsing when unused.

screens.name: Finding Keywords 02
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen demonstrates the "Find on Page" tool working exactly as expected from standard browser conventions: typing "movies" instantly highlights all 37 occurrences across the visible page, with the currently active match distinguished by a yellow highlight (visible in the search bar's own text) while other matches receive a lighter white/boxed highlight (visible in "Shows and movies," "Movies" chip, "New 2025 movies"). This live-updating match count and highlighting gives immediate, precise feedback about how common the search term is on the page, letting users judge before even navigating whether the term is worth stepping through one by one. The clear (X) next to the match count offers a fast way to reset the search term without needing to manually delete each character, a small but meaningful efficiency touch for this kind of frequently-used utility.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — the only text present ("movies," "1 of 37") is either the user's own input or a functional count, with no app-authored persuasive or stylistic copy involved.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of System Status — the live "1 of 37" count and real-time highlighting confirm the search is actively working and show its overall scope immediately.

  2. Distinguishing Current vs. All Matches — using a stronger highlight color (yellow) for the active match versus a lighter treatment for other occurrences helps users track their current position among many results.

  3. Efficient Input Correction — the clear (X) button next to the match count allows quick term reset without manual deletion.

  4. Consistency (Jakob's Law) — this highlight-and-count behavior matches near-universal Find-on-Page conventions across Safari, Chrome, and desktop browsers, requiring no new learning.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's Find on Page (match count and highlighting) — uses the identical "X of Y" count format with yellow active-match highlighting, closely matching this implementation.

  2. Chrome's Find in Page — offers the same live count and highlight-all-matches behavior as text is typed.

  3. macOS/Windows browser Ctrl+F search — the desktop equivalent of this exact interaction pattern, reinforcing its status as a well-established, low-learning-curve convention.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any in-page text search tool where users benefit from immediate visual feedback (highlighted matches, running count) as they type, particularly on content-dense pages where scanning manually would be inefficient.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for extremely short pages with minimal text, where the overhead of a dedicated find tool with match counting would exceed the effort of simply scanning the page visually.

screens.name: Finding Keywords 03
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen shows the same Find-on-Page state as the previous screenshot, but with the keyboard collapsed (likely from tapping outside the input or scrolling), revealing more of the underlying page content — including a third match ("New 2025 horror movies") and the horror-movie poster carousel beneath it. This confirms the highlight-and-count system remains persistent and visible even without the keyboard actively present, letting users scroll and view highlighted matches in context without the keyboard obstructing the lower two-thirds of the screen. The floating Arc/Google toggle reappearing (previously hidden behind the keyboard) shows that the Find tool operates as an overlay on top of the existing page chrome rather than replacing it, consistent with the layered-overlay pattern used throughout the app's other tools (search sheets, voice assistant, incognito mode).
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — same as the previous screen, purely functional text with no app-authored copy.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Persistent State Across Keyboard Visibility — the Find tool's highlights and match count remain active and visible regardless of whether the keyboard is shown, letting users freely scroll to review matches in context.

  2. Non-Blocking Overlay Design — the Find toolbar sits as a thin bar at the bottom rather than consuming the full screen, preserving maximal page visibility for reviewing highlighted matches.

  3. Consistency of Layered UI — the reappearing Arc/Google toggle confirms Find-on-Page is implemented as a lightweight overlay atop existing page chrome, matching the app's broader pattern of stacking transient tools over persistent content.

  4. Efficient Context Review — collapsing the keyboard to see more matches in their natural page context (rather than requiring users to step through matches one at a time via the arrows) offers an alternative, scan-based way to review results.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's Find on Page (keyboard dismissal behavior) — similarly allows the keyboard to collapse while keeping the find toolbar and highlights active, letting users scroll through matches.

  2. Chrome's Find in Page toolbar — persists as a thin bottom or top bar independent of keyboard visibility, matching this behavior.

  3. Google Docs' in-document search — keeps its find toolbar and highlighted matches visible while allowing free scrolling through the document.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any in-page or in-document search tool where users benefit from freely scrolling to review multiple highlighted matches in their original context, rather than being forced to step through them one at a time.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit if the underlying content is extremely short, where collapsing the keyboard to scroll would add unnecessary steps compared to simply stepping through matches directly via the navigation arrows.

screens.name: Google Pay Searching & Finding 8
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen serves as a feature onboarding/explainer for a specific Google Pay capability ("Dine In") rather than a core transactional flow. It uses a vertical, numbered step-by-step layout to demystify a multi-stage physical-to-digital process (scan → order → pay).

The structure is a classic 3-step visual walkthrough, pairing a colorful, friendly illustration with a numbered badge (1, 2, 3) against a plain white background. This creates a strong visual anchor for each step, allowing users to scan the page quickly without reading dense paragraphs. The color-coded circles behind each icon (green, yellow, blue) subtly differentiate the steps while staying within Google's brand palette.

Below the educational content, a horizontally scrollable row of "Participating restaurants" logos grounds the abstract feature in concrete, recognizable real-world utility — answering the user's immediate question of "will this actually work at places I go?" before they even ask it.

The screen terminates in a single, unambiguous, full-width CTA ("Find a restaurant near you") that converts explanation into action, directly bridging discovery to a location-based search flow. The persistent back arrow and overflow menu in the top toolbar maintain standard iOS/Android navigational conventions, keeping this feature page feeling like a natural extension of the app rather than a walled-off tutorial.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is written in short, imperative, benefit-first phrases ("Scan QR code...", "Place your dine-in order", "Pay for your meal") that mirror real-world verbs a diner would use. This action-oriented microcopy reduces the perceived complexity of a task that spans a physical restaurant table and a digital wallet.

The header "experience in just three simple steps" (partially cut off in the scroll) explicitly signals ease and low friction — a critical trust signal for a new payment behavior. The tone is warm and approachable, reinforced by the human illustration eating a meal, rather than clinical or transactional.

The section title "Participating restaurants" is functional and transparent, setting correct expectations that this is not a universal feature but requires merchant participation, preempting user frustration.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Numbered step illustrations: Combining a bold number badge with a soft-colored circular illustration makes each step instantly scannable and memorable, reducing cognitive load for a multi-stage flow.

  • Social proof via restaurant logos: Showing real, recognizable brand logos (4Fingers, John's Pizzeria, etc.) instantly validates the feature's real-world usability and builds confidence before the user commits to trying it.

  • Single, action-oriented CTA: "Find a restaurant near you" is the only interactive commitment on the page, funneling all attention toward one next step and avoiding decision paralysis.

  • Consistent Google Material color system: Each step icon incorporates Google's four-color palette (via the QR icon and confetti details), reinforcing brand trust subliminally.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who are unfamiliar with QR-based dine-in payment flows — likely first-time feature adopters who encountered a "Dine in with Google Pay" prompt (perhaps via a restaurant table tent or in-app banner) and tapped through for more info. It's designed for both digitally cautious users needing reassurance and habitual scanners who just want quick confirmation of how it works.

Psychologically, it leverages the Zeigarnik effect and process transparency principle — by breaking an unfamiliar transaction into three discrete, visualized steps, uncertainty and hesitation around a new payment method are reduced. The restaurant logo row taps into social proof, reassuring users that established, trusted local brands already support this, which lowers the perceived risk of adopting new payment behavior.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this numbered step + illustration + CTA pattern when introducing any multi-stage feature that spans physical and digital touchpoints (e.g., QR ordering, in-store pickup, curbside checkout, loyalty scan-and-earn). It's ideal for feature discovery screens reached via a banner, settings menu, or promotional deep link, where the user needs quick conceptual onboarding before their first real-world attempt.

It's also effective for building trust in nascent behaviors (new payment rails, biometric setup, or scan-to-pay) where user hesitation is primarily due to lack of familiarity rather than lack of value.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for frequently repeated core flows (e.g., a returning user's daily QR payment) — inserting a 3-step tutorial every time creates unnecessary friction. It should be a one-time or opt-in explainer, not a persistent gate.

Also avoid if the feature has very few participating merchants, since the "Participating restaurants" social proof section would then highlight scarcity rather than adoption, undermining trust instead of building it.

screens.name: Google Pay Searching & Finding 9
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen functions as an educational, top-of-funnel explainer for a new feature ("Dine in with Google Pay") nested within a larger app. It uses a classic 3-step vertical process visualization to demystify a multi-stage utility (scan → order → pay) before the user commits to trying it.

The layout leans heavily on a numbered, icon-led list pattern: each step is paired with a soft-colored circular illustration (green, yellow, blue) that visually differentiates the stages while maintaining a cohesive Material/Google aesthetic. This reduces cognitive load by chunking a potentially unfamiliar workflow into three digestible, scannable units rather than a dense paragraph of instructions.

Below the steps, a horizontally scrollable row of restaurant logos acts as social proof and instills confidence that the feature is not vaporware — participating restaurants are named/branded, and an "...and more" tile implies breadth of availability without needing an exhaustive list, keeping the row compact.

The screen terminates in a single, high-contrast, full-width primary CTA ("Find a restaurant near you") pinned near the bottom, which converts the informational content directly into an actionable next step — a strong example of pairing education with immediate task initiation.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is concise, benefit-driven, and imperative ("Scan QR code...", "Place your dine-in order", "Pay for your meal"), mirroring real-world physical actions the user will take at a restaurant table. This mirrors the mental model of the user's actual journey, making the digital instructions feel like a direct translation of an offline ritual.

The header "...experience in just three simple steps" (truncated from a longer intro) explicitly frames the feature as effortless, using the number "three" to pre-set expectations of low friction. The CTA "Find a restaurant near you" is location-aware and action-oriented, nudging immediate exploration rather than passive reading.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Numbered Step Illustrations: Each step uses a distinct pastel color and custom icon, making the 3-part flow instantly scannable and memorable at a glance.

  • Social Proof via Restaurant Logos: Real restaurant branding builds credibility and answers the implicit user question "will this actually work at a real place?"

  • Single Dominant CTA: Only one actionable button is presented, eliminating decision paralysis and funneling all attention toward restaurant discovery.

  • Progressive Disclosure: Detailed feature information is tucked inside a drill-down screen (accessed via back arrow), keeping the main app surface clean while offering depth on demand.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets Google Pay users who are unfamiliar with the QR-based dine-in ordering flow — likely first-time feature discoverers who tapped into this explainer from a promotional banner, restaurant search result, or settings menu. The psychological trigger is uncertainty reduction: unfamiliar payment/ordering flows create friction and hesitation, so walking users through the exact sequence before they arrive at the restaurant lowers anxiety and increases the likelihood of adoption in a real-world, time-pressured dining context.

The restaurant logo strip additionally leverages social proof and authority — seeing recognizable or well-branded establishments participating reassures users the feature is legitimate and widely usable, not a beta gimmick.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when introducing a multi-step, real-world-linked digital process (e.g., contactless payments, curbside pickup, in-store scan-to-pay) where users need a mental model before attempting the flow live. It's ideal for feature announcement screens, help centers, or first-run explainers triggered contextually (e.g., after scanning a QR code for the first time).

Also valuable when you need to reassure users of real-world applicability — pairing an abstract feature explanation with tangible proof points (partner logos, locations) increases trust and conversion.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy explainer pattern for simple, self-evident features where a numbered walkthrough would feel patronizing or add unnecessary friction. If the feature is used frequently after the first explanation, don't force this screen repeatedly — gate it behind a "Learn more" link or show only once. Also avoid if the restaurant/partner list is very short, as an anemic logo row can undercut the social proof intent by highlighting limited availability rather than reassuring breadth.

screens.name: Google Pay Searching & Finding 7
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen functions as a feature onboarding/education layer nested inside the core payments app, rather than a standalone product. It uses a classic "How It Works" numbered-list pattern to introduce a new, potentially unfamiliar capability (QR-based dine-in ordering and payment) without requiring the user to leave their trusted Google Pay context.

The layout follows a strict top-to-bottom narrative flow: a clear title in the top nav bar sets scope, a bold headline reduces friction by promising simplicity ("just three simple steps"), a vertically stacked three-step illustrated guide builds a mental model, and a horizontally scrollable restaurant carousel provides immediate social proof/utility before a single, unmissable full-width CTA anchors the bottom of the screen. The page-control dash at the very bottom hints this is one panel in a larger swipeable/paged flow, likely part of a broader Explore or Discover section.

Numbering (1, 2, 3) combined with soft pastel circular illustrations (green, yellow, blue) creates a friendly, low-stakes visual rhythm that mirrors Google's Material illustration language used elsewhere in the app (e.g., success confetti in step 3 foreshadows the emotional payoff of payment completion).
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is warm, reassuring, and action-oriented, using words like "seamless" and "simple" to preemptively neutralize anxiety around a new payment flow in a public, social setting (a restaurant). Each step is written as a short imperative verb phrase ("Scan," "Place," "Pay"), which mirrors real-world action and lowers cognitive load by chunking the process into three digestible beats.

The header "Dine in with Google Pay" is functional and literal, prioritizing clarity over cleverness — consistent with Google's utilitarian brand voice. The CTA "Find a restaurant near you" is hyper-specific and localized, driving toward a concrete next action rather than a vague "Get Started."

  • Three-step mental model: Reducing a multi-stage restaurant transaction (ordering, table service, payment) into three numbered, illustrated steps dramatically lowers perceived complexity for a first-time user.

  • Color-coded step badges: Using Google's signature four-color palette (blue, red/yellow, green) across the numbered badges and illustrations reinforces brand recognition while visually differentiating each step at a glance.

  • Immediate social proof via restaurant carousel: Showing real, recognizable restaurant logos directly beneath the instructions builds credibility and answers the user's next unspoken question — "does this actually work near me?" — before they even tap the CTA.

  • Single, sticky, high-contrast CTA: The full-width blue "Find a restaurant near you" button is the only interactive commitment on the screen, removing decision paralysis and funneling all attention toward one measurable action.

  • Page control at footer: Signals this explainer is part of a swipeable series (likely Explore/Discover), letting curious users browse related features without a hard navigational commitment.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who are already comfortable with Google Pay for basic P2P or online payments but have not yet used its in-restaurant/dine-in capabilities — likely surfaced via an "Explore" tab, a promotional banner, or contextual discovery near a participating merchant. The psychological trigger at play is uncertainty reduction: dining out involves social visibility (paying in front of a server or companions), so users need confidence the process won't fail or embarrass them.

The numbered walkthrough leverages the Zeigarnik effect and chunking principles from cognitive psychology — breaking an unfamiliar task into three sequential, visually distinct steps makes it feel achievable and memorable. The restaurant carousel taps into social proof, reassuring users that real, known brands (pizzerias, cafes) already support this, which reduces the risk perception of trying something new.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this "numbered steps + illustration + proof + single CTA" pattern when introducing a discrete, self-contained feature inside a larger utility app — especially features involving a new interaction paradigm (like QR scanning) that users haven't encountered elsewhere in the product. It's ideal for:

  • In-app feature announcements or contextual "Learn More" deep links

  • Fintech/payments apps rolling out new merchant integrations

  • Any flow where trust and correct sequencing matter more than speed
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy explainer pattern for features that are already intuitive or that returning users will see repeatedly — it adds friction and feels condescending on repeat visits. It's also inappropriate for time-sensitive flows where the user just needs to complete a task quickly (e.g., an already-scanned QR code should jump straight to the menu/payment, not repeat the 3-step explainer). Additionally, this static, non-personalized version should be replaced with a dismissible or "don't show again" variant once the user has completed the flow once, to respect experienced users' time.

screens.name: Google Pay Searching & Finding 10
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen presents a curated "Maps List" (a Google Maps-powered feature surfaced inside Google Pay) that packages participating dine-in restaurants into a single, scrollable collection. The layout follows a classic hero-image-plus-detail-sheet pattern: a large, appetizing food photo occupies the top third of the viewport to create an immediate emotional/sensory hook, while a white content sheet slides up beneath it to hold metadata, actions, and the list itself. This is a well-established "peek and full-bleed" pattern borrowed from Google Maps' own list/collection UI, repurposed here for a payments app to drive habitual usage. The circular avatar badge ("G") anchors the list's identity, reinforcing that this is a branded, curated collection rather than a generic search result. Below the description, a horizontal progress bar with "Visited 0 of 44 places" gamifies the collection, subtly encouraging exploration and repeat engagement with GPay's dine-in payment flow. The card list at the bottom uses a horizontally-scrollable photo carousel per entry, rating, price/match percentage, category, and open/close status — dense but scannable information architecture typical of local discovery products. The back caret and overflow "..." menu in the top bar maintain consistency with native iOS navigation conventions, while the floating bookmark icon on each restaurant row offers a lightweight save action without leaving the list.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The copy is instructional and utilitarian, written in a friendly but functional voice ("Order your dine-in meal with Google Pay at these participating restaurants" / "Using your phone's camera, scan the QR code at your table and order food in Google Pay"). It reads like a mini tutorial embedded in a content list, prioritizing clarity over personality. The attribution line "By Google Pay Singapore · 44 places" borrows the social/editorial credibility convention of curated Maps lists, lending it an authoritative, editorial feel rather than an algorithmically generated one. The visited-progress counter ("Visited 0 of 44 places") adds a subtle motivational nudge without resorting to aggressive gamification language.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Cross-app feature surfacing: Google Maps' list/collection UI is elegantly repurposed inside Google Pay, letting the payments app borrow Maps' mature discovery UX instead of reinventing it.

  • Progress bar as engagement hook: "Visited 0 of 44 places" turns a static directory into a checklist-style goal, nudging users to return and "complete" the collection via repeat GPay dine-in payments.

  • Hero image immersion: Full-bleed, high-quality food photography at the top drives appetite appeal before any text is read, a proven pattern in food/dining discovery apps.

  • Dual entry actions (Follow / Share): Pill-shaped Follow and Share buttons let users subscribe to future updates or virally distribute the list, expanding organic reach at zero marginal cost.

  • Dense but scannable restaurant cards: Rating, review count, "% match," category, and open/closing hours are compactly arranged to support fast decision-making while browsing.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets Google Pay users in Singapore looking for dine-in restaurants that support QR-code ordering via the app — likely urban professionals or foodies who already use Google Pay for daily transactions and want convenience-driven discovery. The psychological triggers at play include curation bias (trusting an official "Google Pay Singapore" list over open search), gamified completion (the 0-of-44 progress bar taps into the human desire to close open loops, i.e., the Zeigarnik effect), and social proof via star ratings and review counts on each restaurant card, which reduce decision anxiety when choosing where to eat.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a platform wants to promote a specific behavior (e.g., using a payment method, visiting partner merchants) by wrapping it in a curated, list-based discovery experience. It's ideal for loyalty/partner programs, city guides, travel itineraries, or any collection-based content where progress tracking and social sharing can drive repeat engagement.
