The bottom tab bar keeps the core financial pillars (Spend, Budget, Chat, Save, Borrow, Habits) one tap away, reinforcing Cleo's hub-and-spoke information architecture where Chat is treated as an equal, first-class citizen alongside traditional finance dashboards.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The all-caps header "FEBRUARY'S BREAKDOWN" is bold and declarative, giving the screen a punchy, editorial tone rather than a sterile "Budget Summary" label typical of legacy banking apps.

The mascot's speech bubble—"Been 2 weeks of budgets. Thoughts?"—is written in first-person, casual, slightly cheeky phrasing, consistent with Cleo's "blunt friend" persona. It invites feedback rather than just displaying data, turning a passive dashboard into a two-way conversation starter.

Labels like "Limit," "Spent," "Due," and "Other" are compressed into colorful pill/chip tags rather than a legend, keeping the copy minimal and scannable. Numbers are given primary visual weight (large, bold), while contextual copy ("until $1,463", "per day") is smaller and secondary, respecting a clear typographic hierarchy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Metaphorical Data Visualization: Replacing bar/line charts with tactile, illustrated coin stacks makes abstract numbers feel physical and instantly comparable, reducing cognitive load for financially anxious or non-numerate users.

  • Dual-Tone Layout Hierarchy: The dark hero zone for macro visualization paired with a white card for granular numeric detail cleanly separates "feeling" from "fact" on a single screen.

  • Time-Elapsed Progress Bar: The "11 days left" segmented bar contextualizes spending against the calendar, nudging users to pace themselves rather than just showing a static total.

  • Conversational Check-in Banner: Embedding a mascot-voiced prompt directly in the dashboard blurs the line between "data screen" and "chat," reinforcing Cleo's chat-first identity even on a numbers-heavy page.

  • Inline Editable Goal: The small pencil icon next to "$1,463" lets users adjust their spending ceiling in-place without navigating to a settings screen, reducing friction for budget customization.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who are budgeting-averse or intimidated by traditional finance dashboards—typically younger, mobile-first users (Gen Z/millennials) who find spreadsheets and bank apps boring or shame-inducing. By using playful illustration (coin stacks, a thumbs-up mascot) and informal copy, Cleo lowers the emotional barrier to checking one's own spending, a task many people avoid due to anxiety or guilt.

The psychological triggers at play include loss aversion (visualizing how close "Out" is getting to the "Limit" stack height), social/conversational rapport (the mascot's casual check-in mimics a friend rather than an institution), and progress framing (the "11 days left" bar taps into planning and pacing behavior, similar to a fitness ring).
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when you need to present a comparative or ratio-based financial/health/usage metric (budget vs. actual, goal vs. progress) to a mainstream consumer audience who may be intimidated by traditional charts. It's especially effective in apps trying to differentiate on personality/tone (fintech, wellness, habit trackers) where injecting warmth and illustration can drive daily engagement and reduce avoidance behavior around sensitive data (money, weight, calories).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this approach for power users, accountants, or B2B/enterprise dashboards where precision, density, and comparability across many data points are required — illustrated metaphors don't scale well past 2-3 categories and can obscure exact values. Also avoid if the brand tone is meant to convey trust through seriousness (e.g., wealth management, insurance), where playful mascots and cartoon coins may undermine credibility.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 9
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen layers a modal Bottom Sheet ("Budget Settings") on top of a background dashboard ("February's Breakdown"), creating a clear visual hierarchy between the high-level summary and the granular controls needed to configure it. The background view abandons traditional bar/line charts in favor of a whimsical coin-stack illustration that visually encodes "In" vs "Out" cash flow as two towers of coins, with a ghost/outline coin stack representing the "Limit" ceiling still to be filled. This metaphor (money as literal stacked coins) is more intuitive and emotionally resonant for a non-finance-native audience than a sterile bar chart.

The date-range progress bar ("11 days left") gives a temporal anchor, letting users know how much of the month remains versus how much has been spent — critical for pacing behavior. Left/right chevron arrows suggest this breakdown card is swipeable across months (a carousel), keeping the interface uncluttered while still enabling historical browsing.

The bottom sheet uses a classic drag-handle affordance, large bold "Sledgehammer" style typography for the title, and a single stacked-list row (Linked Paycheck) as the first configurable item, with a live "last refreshed" timestamp reinforcing that this is real, synced data rather than a stale cache.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Cleo's signature irreverent-but-competent voice is dialed down here in favor of clarity, since this is a functional settings/data screen rather than a bantering chat moment. Headers are in bold, all-caps condensed type ("FEBRUARY'S BREAKDOWN", "BUDGET SETTINGS") which feels punchy and poster-like rather than corporate-fintech, staying true to the brand's rebellious personality even in utilitarian moments.

Microcopy like "Tweak your budget" is casual and low-pressure, framing budget editing as an easy, non-intimidating tweak rather than a serious financial task. "Last refreshed less than a minute ago" builds trust and reduces anxiety about data accuracy without requiring the user to manually pull-to-refresh.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Coin-stack data visualization: Replaces boring bars/donuts with a playful, on-brand metaphor (stacked coins) that still conveys quantitative comparison (In vs Out vs Limit) at a glance.

  • Layered Bottom Sheet pattern: Keeps the user's spatial context (the breakdown screen is still peeking out at the top) while surfacing deeper settings, reducing the feeling of a full context switch.

  • Time-remaining progress bar: Pairs a simple two-color bar with "11 days left" text to make budget pacing instantly scannable without requiring math.

  • Swipeable month navigation: Chevron arrows imply horizontal carousel navigation across months without needing a calendar picker or extra screen.

  • Freshness indicator: The "last refreshed" timestamp with a manual refresh icon builds transparency and trust in the linked financial data.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets everyday consumers — likely younger, budget-conscious users (Gen Z/Millennial) who find traditional banking apps and spreadsheets intimidating or boring. The illustrated, game-like coin visualization taps into a familiarity with mobile games and gamified finance apps, lowering the psychological barrier to engaging with what is normally an anxiety-inducing topic (spending limits, overspending).

The "11 days left" countdown leverages a mild urgency/scarcity trigger to nudge users toward checking in on their spending pace before month-end, while the settings sheet's simplicity (single paycheck row, clear $ amount) caters to users who want quick, low-effort control rather than deep customization.
screens.whereToUse: Use this layered bottom-sheet-over-dashboard pattern when you want users to adjust settings related to data they can still visually reference (e.g., editing a budget while seeing the budget chart). Use illustrated/metaphorical data visualizations (coin stacks, jars, plants) for younger or finance-anxious audiences where literal charts may feel cold or overly technical. The countdown progress bar is ideal for any cyclical/period-based tracking (billing cycles, challenges, subscriptions).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid whimsical illustrated charts for professional/enterprise financial tools, accountants, or power users who need precise, comparable data at scale (e.g., multi-category breakdowns, trend lines) — coin stacks don't scale well past 2-3 categories and lack precision for detailed analysis. Also avoid stacking a bottom sheet over a dashboard when the underlying context isn't needed for the task at hand, as it can feel like unnecessary visual clutter versus a clean full-screen settings page.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 11
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is Cleo's budgeting hub, notably a departure from the app's signature chat-first interaction model into a more traditional dashboard layout. It's structured in a clear vertical hierarchy: a top-line financial summary (safe-to-spend and daily budget), followed by a horizontally scrollable "Bills Due" module, and finally a "Spending" breakdown by category with progress bars.

The layout uses light, airy white space (a stark contrast to the app's dark, moody brand identity referenced in its overall look-and-feel) which suggests this screen prioritizes legibility and data clarity over the mascot-driven chat drama found elsewhere. Numbers are given massive visual weight (the $1,274.87 and $115.90 figures dominate the top of the fold), immediately answering the user's core anxiety question: "How much can I safely spend right now?"

The "Bills Due" section uses a horizontally scrollable card carousel pattern with a clear CTA to add more bills, reducing friction for expanding tracked recurring payments. Below, the "Other Spending" card is illustrated with a whimsical flying money bag (mascot-adjacent asset), softening what is typically an anxiety-inducing category (unaccounted discretionary spend) with playful visual language. Category progress bars (General, Transport) use simple horizontal fill bars with icon avatars, offering quick-glance status without requiring numeric literacy.

The bottom tab bar clearly signals Cleo's broadened surface area beyond chat: Spend, Budget, Chat, Save, Borrow, Habits — positioning "Budget" as a first-class citizen alongside conversational AI.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal, functional, and confident — favoring bold sans-serif numerals over lengthy explanation ("$1,274.87", "$115.90 per day"). Section headers are in bold, all-caps condensed type ("BILLS DUE", "SPENDING"), giving a punchy, headline-like energy consistent with Cleo's blunt personality even in a data-heavy context.

Playful, informal microcopy persists in small doses: "edit categories" sits inside a bright orange pill button accompanied by a comedic illustration of a winged money bag flying away — a visual pun implying spending is "flying away," reinforcing Cleo's signature irreverent humor even on a purely functional utility screen.

The empty state for "Other spending" ("0% of income") is rendered without judgment or a nagging tone, letting the illustration carry the emotional weight instead of preachy financial copy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Anxiety-first information hierarchy: The two most emotionally urgent numbers for a budget-conscious user — safe-to-spend total and daily allowance — are placed above the fold in the largest type on the screen, answering the user's core question within milliseconds of opening the app.

  • Editable target amount inline: The "until $1,463" with an adjacent pencil icon allows users to adjust their target/goal without navigating to a settings screen, reducing friction for personalization.

  • Mascot-adjacent illustration softens financial shame: The flying money-bag illustration on the "Other spending" card injects levity into what could otherwise feel like a scolding budget-tracking module.

  • Card-based bill carousel with inline add action: Bundling the "Add a bill" CTA directly into the horizontal scroll of existing bills (rather than a separate button elsewhere) keeps bill management contextual and low-friction.

  • Segmented navigation via bottom tab bar: Elevating "Budget" to a peer of "Chat" signals Cleo is not purely conversational but also a full financial-management surface, broadening its retention hooks beyond novelty chat interactions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who already trust Cleo enough to link financial accounts and want a fast, low-effort way to check "am I okay this month?" without parsing spreadsheets. The design leverages several psychological triggers:

  • Loss aversion & scarcity framing: Presenting a fixed "safe to spend" ceiling creates a soft guardrail that nudges restraint without explicit lecturing.

  • Chunking for cognitive ease: Breaking the month into a "per day" allowance transforms an abstract, intimidating monthly budget into a small, actionable daily number — a well-documented behavioral finance technique to improve adherence.

  • Playful illustration as shame-reduction: Money apps often trigger guilt; Cleo counters this with humor (the flying money bag) to keep users engaged rather than avoidant, which is core to Cleo's "blunt but funny coach" persona rather than a punitive tracker.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for personal finance, budgeting, or subscription-management apps where users need an at-a-glance status check without deep navigation. It's ideal for:

  • Home/dashboard screens for recurring financial check-ins (daily/weekly cadence).

  • Apps balancing serious financial data with a friendly, non-intimidating brand voice.

  • Products wanting to surface both fixed obligations (bills) and variable spending (categories) in a single scrollable view.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense dashboard approach for first-time users still in onboarding — the numeric density and multiple modules assume the user already has linked accounts and historical data, which would render this screen an empty, confusing shell for a fresh signup. Also avoid pairing playful illustrations with financial shortfall states (e.g., overdraft, missed bill) where levity could feel tone-deaf; humor should be reserved for neutral or positive framing only. Finally, this light/bright visual treatment breaks from Cleo's core dark, neon-moody identity, so it should be used sparingly and only where data clarity must outweigh brand consistency.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 10
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is the financial "home base" of Cleo, reframing a traditionally dry budgeting dashboard into a playful, illustrated experience. Instead of dense tables of transactions, the layout uses a hierarchy of large, bold numeric headlines ($1,274.87 remaining, $115.90/day) to instantly answer the user's most pressing question: "How much money do I have left?" This is a classic "glanceable" financial UX pattern, prioritizing a single hero metric over granular detail.

The page is organized into clear, card-based sections (Bills Due, Spending, Bank Charges) using a vertical scroll rather than tabs or nested menus, keeping cognitive load low. The horizontal carousel for "Bills Due" cleverly reuses a familiar pattern (like an app store carousel) to make an "Add a bill" CTA feel like a natural next step rather than an interruption.

The persistent bottom tab bar anchors navigation across Cleo's core financial pillars (Spend, Budget, Chat, Save, Borrow, Habits), with "Chat" sitting centrally—reinforcing that conversational AI is the connective tissue, not just one dashboard among many.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy leans into short, punchy declaratives rather than formal finance jargon: "Bills Due," "per day," "52% of income." There is no hand-holding explanatory text—the numbers are left to speak loudly via oversized typography, and the app trusts the user to interpret them quickly.

The illustrated hands (a purple thumbs-up and a pink rock-on/"I love you" gesture) inject Cleo's irreverent, meme-literate personality directly into a purely numerical context. This is a deliberate tonal choice: even when delivering potentially anxiety-inducing information (52% of income spent on essentials), the visual tone stays celebratory and low-stakes, softening judgment around spending habits.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Hero metric hierarchy: The remaining balance and daily spend allowance are rendered in massive, bold numerals, instantly answering the user's core anxiety ("Am I okay?") without requiring interpretation of charts or graphs.

  • Illustrated mascot hands as emotional punctuation: Rather than a full mascot character, isolated hand illustrations (thumbs-up, rock-on gesture) act as reaction emojis to financial data, injecting personality without cluttering the numeric content.

  • Bills-as-carousel with inline Add CTA: Embedding the "Add a bill" action as a card within the horizontal scroll (rather than a separate button) makes the empty/incomplete state feel like an invitation, not a nag.

  • Editable target inline: The "until $1,463" with a pencil icon allows quick inline editing of a payday/budget target directly within the hero stat, avoiding a separate settings screen.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially anxious or budgeting-averse users (often younger, gig-economy or paycheck-to-paycheck demographics) who are turned off by traditional finance apps' spreadsheet aesthetics. The playful illustrations and blunt, large-type numbers reduce the shame/anxiety typically associated with checking a bank balance, leveraging a psychological principle of "friendly authority"—Cleo delivers hard truths (like 52% of income going to essentials) but wraps them in humor and color to keep the user engaged rather than avoidant.

The daily spend allowance ("$115.90 per day") taps into the psychology of chunking a large abstract number into a manageable, actionable daily budget, which is proven to improve adherence to spending goals compared to a single monthly figure.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for financial, health, or habit-tracking apps targeting users who feel intimidated or bored by traditional data dashboards. It's ideal for surfacing a single "north star" metric (balance, calories, streak count) at the top of a home screen, paired with modular scrollable cards below for secondary info (bills, categories, charges). The inline-editable target and carousel-embedded CTA are great for reducing friction on recurring setup tasks like adding bills or budgets.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this style for enterprise, B2B, or professional finance tools (e.g., accounting, investment platforms) where users expect density, precision, and multi-metric comparison—oversized single-stat displays would feel unserious or hide critical detail. Also avoid heavy illustration/mascot elements in contexts where users need to process large volumes of transactional data quickly, as decorative graphics can compete for attention and slow scanning.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 12
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen translates a traditionally dry financial concept—the monthly budget summary—into a visually playful, low-cognitive-load dashboard. Cleo abandons ledger-style tables in favor of a split-canvas layout: the top half sits on a deep indigo "hero" background that houses the visual metaphor (stacked coin illustrations), while the bottom half snaps to a clean white card containing hard numeric data (balance remaining, daily allowance, and upcoming bills).

The coin-stack bar chart is the centerpiece. Rather than a standard bar or donut chart, Cleo uses skeuomorphic coin illustrations stacked to height, with a translucent "ghost stack" indicating the Limit versus solid colored stacks for actual Spent/Due/Other/In amounts. This reinforces the "money as tangible stuff" mental model, which is more intuitive for financially anxious or budgeting-novice users than abstract percentages.

Progress is dual-encoded: a horizontal pill progress bar ("11 days left") sits above the chart to show time elapsed in the cycle, while the coin stacks show money elapsed against the limit — letting users triangulate pace (are they spending too fast for how much time is left?) at a glance.

The screen also uses carousel arrows (left/right chevrons) hugging the edges, implying this Budget breakdown is one card in a swipeable series (likely by month or by category), reducing the need for a separate navigation drawer.

Below the fold, the white card re-grounds the user with exact figures and a "Bills Due" horizontal list with an inline "Add a bill" CTA, keeping the action of budgeting frictionless and integrated rather than buried in a settings menu.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is short, punchy, and all-caps for headers ("FEBRUARY'S BREAKDOWN", "BILLS DUE"), giving it a poster/headline energy rather than a bank statement feel. Labels like "In", "Out", "Spent", "Due", "Other" are single words — no jargon, no financial literacy required.

The thumbs-up illustration acts as a wordless emotional cue, implicitly telling the user "you're doing fine" before they've even parsed the numbers, softening what could otherwise be an anxiety-inducing check-in moment.

The mix of hard data ("$1,274.87 until $1,463") with casual framing ("per day") keeps the tone approachable, framing budgeting as a manageable daily target rather than an overwhelming monthly obligation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Skeuomorphic Coin-Stack Visualization: Replaces intimidating bar/donut charts with tangible, easy-to-read coin stacks that visually encode Limit vs. Spent/Due/In/Out.

  • Dual Progress Encoding: Time-based progress bar ("11 days left") paired with spend-based visual bars lets users instantly gauge if their pace is sustainable.

  • Emotional Micro-Affirmation: The thumbs-up mascot hand delivers instant, wordless emotional feedback on financial health before the user reads a single number.

  • Editable Target Inline: The pencil icon next to "$1,463" allows users to adjust their budget target without leaving the screen or entering a separate settings flow.

  • Integrated Bill Management: "Bills Due" list with an inline "+ Add a bill" tile merges tracking and action into a single horizontal scroll component.

  • Card Carousel Navigation: Left/right arrows imply swipeable breakdowns (e.g., by month), avoiding extra navigation chrome.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who are budgeting-averse or intimidated by traditional finance apps — likely younger users (Gen Z/Millennial) who find spreadsheets and dashboards alienating. The design leans on reduction of cognitive load (single-word labels, illustrative charts) and positive reinforcement (thumbs-up mascot) to counteract the shame or anxiety often associated with checking one's spending.

The pacing indicator ("11 days left") taps into loss aversion and time-pressure psychology, nudging users to self-regulate spending before month-end without an explicit warning or scolding tone, consistent with Cleo's "blunt but caring coach" persona.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when designing financial, health, or goal-tracking dashboards for audiences who are anxious about or unfamiliar with numeric/data-heavy interfaces. It's ideal for periodic (weekly/monthly) summary screens where you want to combine an at-a-glance visual metaphor with precise underlying data, and where emotional tone (encouragement/warning) needs to be conveyed as fast as the numbers themselves.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid illustrative/skeuomorphic charts like coin stacks for power users, accountants, or B2B financial tools that require precision, comparison across many data points, or exportable reporting — the playful metaphor sacrifices data density and comparability. Also avoid mascot-driven affirmations in contexts where the underlying financial situation is bad, as a cheerful thumbs-up could feel tone-deaf or minimize a real problem, potentially damaging trust.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 13
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is part of Cleo's automated bill-tracking setup flow, surfacing algorithmically-detected recurring transactions and asking the user to confirm which ones are actually "bills" (rent, subscriptions, transfers to a landlord, etc.). Rather than forcing the user to manually type out bill names and amounts, Cleo does the heavy lifting by scanning transaction history for repeating patterns (in this case, two E Transfer Sent transactions of the identical $169.50 amount, one month apart) and pre-surfaces them as a chronological, tappable stacked list.

The layout is intentionally sparse and single-purpose: a bold, oversized editorial headline anchors attention, a one-line grey subtext gives the exact interaction model ("Tap a transaction to add it as a bill"), and the list itself uses date-grouped section headers (February 12 / January 23) to help the user recall context. Merchant/institution avatars (colorful circular icons) add scannability and a touch of personality consistent with Cleo's playful visual identity, even on an otherwise transactional, utilitarian screen.

Navigation affordances are minimal but clear: a back arrow for step-based backward flow and a close (X) for exiting the whole task, which is standard for a modal/stepped setup flow. The disabled/greyed "Done" button at the bottom is a strong piece of state-driven feedback — it visually communicates that no selection has been made yet and will presumably activate once the user taps at least one transaction, reducing accidental empty submissions.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The headline "…ARE ANY OF THESE BILLS?" is written in Cleo's signature blunt, conversational voice — punctuated with a leading ellipsis that mimics natural speech, as if continuing a chat thread rather than presenting a sterile form. It reads like a text message from a sharp-tongued friend, not a bank statement. This casual phrasing softens what is otherwise a fairly mundane data-classification task (categorizing transactions), making it feel like part of an ongoing dialogue with the Cleo persona rather than a chore.

The supporting instruction, "Tap a transaction to add it as a bill," is refreshingly literal and functional — it removes any ambiguity about the interaction model in a single short sentence, which matters given there's no visible checkbox or explicit selection affordance on the row itself.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Editorial, oversized bold typography for the question injects brand personality and a chat-like informality into an otherwise dry financial categorization task.

  • Auto-surfaced candidate detection: Cleo does the pattern-matching work for the user by identifying recurring transactions of identical amounts, drastically reducing manual data entry.

  • Disabled "Done" CTA as a passive validation mechanism — prevents users from confirming zero bills and visually cues that an action is still required.

  • Date-grouped stacked list with colorful avatars aids fast visual recall and scanning of past transactions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users setting up Cleo's bill-tracking/budgeting feature, likely during onboarding or a "connect your bank" flow, who want automated financial organization without manually inputting every recurring payment. The psychological trigger at play is reduced cognitive load via smart defaults — by pre-filtering the transaction history down to only plausible bill candidates, Cleo lowers the activation energy needed to complete setup, increasing the likelihood the user finishes the task instead of abandoning a longer manual entry form. The conversational tone also builds parasocial trust with the Cleo mascot/persona, positioning it as a helpful, witty assistant rather than a cold utility.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a system can algorithmically infer structured data (bills, subscriptions, categories, tags) from a larger raw dataset and needs lightweight human confirmation rather than full manual entry. It's ideal for financial apps, subscription trackers, or any onboarding flow where reducing data-entry friction significantly boosts completion rates. Pair it with a disabled primary CTA to prevent empty/null submissions, and group results by clear, scannable metadata (like date) to aid recognition-based decision-making over recall.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when transaction/data volume is very high, as an unfiltered or noisy candidate list will overwhelm users and undermine the "we did the work for you" value proposition — pagination or smarter filtering would be needed. It's also unsuitable when the underlying detection algorithm has low confidence or high false-positive rates, since repeatedly asking users to correct wrong suggestions erodes trust in the AI's competence. Finally, this bare-bones list works only for simple binary confirmation tasks; more nuanced editing (adjusting amounts, frequency, due dates) would need a richer detail/edit screen.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 14
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a smart-detection confirmation form that appears when Cleo identifies a recurring transaction (an e-transfer to "Flora") and infers it may be a recurring bill. Rather than making the user manually create a bill from scratch, the app pre-fills all three critical fields — Amount ($169.50), Frequency (Monthly), and Next Payment Date (March 12, 2024) — based on transaction history pattern-matching.

The layout uses a classic single-column, vertically stacked form with generously sized tap targets and floating labels that stay visible even when a field is populated, reducing cognitive load. A light gray card container houses each field, providing clear visual separation without heavy borders or clutter. The mascot skull emoji at the top injects personality into what would otherwise be a mundane financial admin task, softening the seriousness of bill tracking.

The bottom sheet presentation (indicated by the drag handle at the very bottom) signals this is a modal, contextual action layered on top of a transaction detail or chat flow, not a full destination screen — keeping the user anchored to their original context (likely a chat conversation about this transaction).
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone stays functional but not sterile. The truncated header "E TRANSFER SENT FLORA..." preserves the raw, human transaction description rather than sanitizing it into generic banking language, reinforcing Cleo's "real talk" personality even in a mundane settings screen.

"BILL DETAILS" is set in Cleo's signature bold, condensed display typeface — treating a routine data-confirmation task with the same graphic weight as a big emotional moment, which keeps the brand voice consistent even in the "boring" parts of the app.

The question-style label "When is this next paid?" is conversational rather than the sterile "Due Date" a traditional bank app would use, mirroring how a friend would ask, not a form field.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Smart Pre-fill (Zero-Effort Data Entry): Cleo has already parsed the transaction and populated amount, frequency, and next date, turning a tedious manual entry task into a one-tap confirmation.

  • Mascot Injection: The purple skull emoji humanizes a purely administrative screen, keeping brand personality present even in utilitarian flows.

  • Bottom Sheet Modality: Presenting this as a sheet (not a full navigation push) keeps the task lightweight and reversible, implying "quick edit" rather than "big commitment."

  • Single Primary CTA: Only one clear action ("Add to bills") is presented, eliminating decision paralysis.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets users who are trying to get a handle on recurring expenses but are too disorganized or busy to manually track bills in a spreadsheet — Cleo's core demographic of financially anxious, spreadsheet-averse young adults. By automatically detecting the pattern (an e-transfer sent monthly to the same recipient), Cleo reduces the activation energy required to build a complete financial picture, leveraging the psychological principle of reduced friction increases task completion. Pre-filled fields also build trust and a sense of "the AI actually gets me," reinforcing Cleo's coach positioning rather than a passive ledger tool.
screens.whereToUse:
• Any flow where the system can infer structured data from unstructured input (e.g., transaction history, email parsing, calendar events) and wants to convert it into a trackable recurring item.

  • Bill trackers, subscription managers, budgeting apps, or expense categorization confirmation flows.

  • Whenever you want to reduce a "create new record" task down to a "confirm this record" task to boost completion rates.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern if your detection/inference accuracy is low — incorrect pre-filled data erodes trust faster than an empty form, since users may not carefully review pre-filled values before submitting.

  • Not suitable for highly sensitive financial commitments (e.g., loan agreements) where users should deliberately input data rather than passively confirm auto-detected values.

  • Avoid mascot/playful elements if the context is a serious compliance or legal disclosure screen.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 15
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen translates a traditionally dry financial statement into a visually rich, almost game-like "coin stack" visualization. Instead of a bar chart or pie chart, Cleo uses illustrated stacks of coins to represent In (income), Out (spending), and a translucent ghost-stack representing the Limit the user hasn't yet reached. This metaphor is instantly legible — taller stack = more money — without requiring any financial literacy to parse axes or legends.

The layout is split into two zones: a colorful, high-contrast "hero" header (indigo background) housing the visualization and period/progress indicator, and a clean white card below surfacing the hard numbers (remaining balance, daily spend allowance). This visual separation cleverly signals "the story" (top) vs. "the facts" (bottom), letting users skim the illustration for a gut-check and drop down for precision if needed.

A horizontal swipe/arrow affordance on both edges implies this breakdown is one page in a paginated carousel (likely swiping between months or between spending categories), keeping the single-screen real estate uncluttered while still offering depth via lateral navigation instead of vertical scrolling or drill-down taps.

The progress bar labelled "11 days left" doubles as a countdown/urgency mechanic tied to the budget cycle, reinforcing time-boxed financial accountability.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy is casual, terse, and personified — headers are shouted in bold caps ("FEBRUARY'S BREAKDOWN") giving a magazine/report-card feel rather than a sterile bank statement. Labels like "In," "Out," "Spent," "Due" are plain-English replacements for accounting jargon (credit/debit, expenditure/liability).

The floating chat bubble from Cleo's mascot — "Been 2 weeks of budgets. Thoughts?" — is classic Cleo voice: informal, second-person, prompting reflection rather than lecturing. It reframes a check-in as a casual text from a friend rather than a system notification, lowering the emotional friction of confronting spending habits.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Coin-stack metaphor: Converts abstract dashboard data into an intuitive, physical visual (height = money), removing the need to interpret charts or legends.

  • Ghost/ghosted "Limit" stack: Using a translucent overlay stack to show the untouched budget ceiling creates an implicit progress-bar effect layered directly into the illustration, rather than a separate UI element.

  • Dual-zone contrast layout: Bold color block for narrative/visual summary, clean white card for hard numeric truth — serving both emotional and analytical user needs on one screen.

  • Mascot-driven proactive check-in: The floating chat prompt turns a passive dashboard into a two-way conversation starter, staying true to Cleo's chat-first identity even on a data screen.

  • Editable target amount: The small pencil icon next to "$1,463" invites inline goal editing without leaving the dashboard, reducing friction for adjusting budget targets.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets financially anxious or budget-avoidant users — often younger adults who find traditional banking apps (tables, graphs, percentages) intimidating or boring. By gamifying the visualization (coin stacks, thumbs-up mascot reaction, progress bar countdown) Cleo taps into reward/loss framing psychology: a rising "Out" stack nearing the "Limit" ghost stack creates a visceral, almost game-over anxiety that's more motivating than a static number. The thumbs-up illustration provides immediate positive reinforcement/social-proof-like validation ("you're doing fine"), appealing to users who need encouragement rather than shame to stay engaged with money management.
screens.whereToUse: Use this coin-stack/illustrated comparison pattern when translating category comparisons (income vs. expense, actual vs. target, before vs. after) for audiences who may disengage from standard bar/line charts. It's ideal for consumer fintech, gamified habit trackers, or wellness apps where emotional engagement and quick comprehension outweigh the need for granular data precision. Pair with a secondary "facts" panel (as done here) for power users who still want exact figures.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in professional, B2B, or high-stakes financial contexts (e.g., accounting, tax, investment platforms) where users need precise multi-variable comparisons, historical trend lines, or exportable data — illustrations like coin stacks lack the precision and scannability of true charts at scale. Also avoid if the target demographic skews toward users who perceive playful visuals as undermining trust or seriousness around their finances.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 16
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a modal bottom sheet that transforms the traditionally dry task of "setting a budget" into a bold, tactile experience. The layout follows a clear top-down hierarchy: a huge, unmissable headline number ($1463) anchors the eye immediately, followed by a granular breakdown of category limits below.

The use of a stepper pattern (minus/plus circular buttons) instead of a raw numeric keyboard input is a deliberate friction-reduction choice — it lets users make quick, low-stakes adjustments to auto-calculated defaults rather than forcing them to do math or type. This shifts the cognitive load from "generation" to "editing," which is significantly easier for users who are anxious about budgeting.

The master toggle for "Category Limits" gives users an escape hatch to simplify the flow to a single overall number if they don't want granular control, respecting different user mental models (some want detail, some want simplicity). The scrollable list with clear iconography per category (mascot-style emoji icons in colored circles) keeps a playful tone even while displaying financial data.

The sticky CTA at the bottom ("Alright, I can do this") remains persistent regardless of scroll position, ensuring the user always has a clear path to completion without needing to scroll back up.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is deliberately colloquial and emotionally aware, diverging sharply from the clinical tone of typical banking apps. "SET YOUR LIMIT" in bold, condensed all-caps typography feels like a command from a coach or trainer, not a bank statement.

The CTA button text, "Alright, I can do this," is the standout copy choice — it's written in the user's internal voice, functioning as a self-affirmation rather than a generic "Confirm" or "Save" button. This subtly reframes budgeting from a restrictive chore into an achievable personal challenge, reducing the anxiety typically associated with spending caps.

Secondary text like "Based on your average spending" and "Including all bills" builds trust by signaling that the numbers aren't arbitrary guesses but are personalized and data-driven, reducing user resistance to the suggested limit.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Emotionally-coded CTA copy: "Alright, I can do this" replaces a generic confirm button, turning a financial commitment into a motivational, first-person affirmation.

  • Smart Defaults: The limit and category breakdowns are pre-filled based on historical average spending, drastically lowering the effort required to complete setup.

  • Granularity Toggle: A single switch lets users collapse complex category-level budgeting into one simple master number, catering to both power users and minimalists.

  • Tactile Steppers: Using +/- buttons instead of direct text input makes fine-tuning budget numbers feel like a game-like interaction rather than a spreadsheet task.

  • Playful Iconography: Custom illustrated icons (e.g., a flying dollar bill for 'Transfer Out') inject personality into standard financial categories.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially anxious users—often younger adults or those new to budgeting—who have historically been intimidated or bored by traditional finance apps (like Mint or bank dashboards). By using large, bold typography and a coaching tone, Cleo leverages the psychological principle of self-efficacy: telling the user "I can do this" reframes the budget limit as an achievable goal set by an ally, not a restrictive cage imposed by an institution.

The pre-filled "smart default" numbers exploit the anchoring effect and reduce decision fatigue; users are statistically more likely to accept a suggested default than to build a budget from a blank slate, satisfying the need for quick wins during onboarding or monthly resets.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for budget creation, goal setting, or any multi-variable numeric configuration screen where precision is less important than user buy-in. It is especially effective for:

  • Financial goal-setting flows (savings targets, spending caps).

  • Fitness or habit-tracking apps where users set daily/weekly targets.

  • Any "commitment" screen where you want the user to feel psychologically invested in a number they are about to see repeatedly.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, playful, stepper-based UI for professional or enterprise financial tools where users need to input large, precise figures quickly (e.g., business accounting or expense reporting), as tapping +/- buttons repeatedly for large deltas becomes inefficient and frustrating. Additionally, the informal, coach-like CTA copy ("Alright, I can do this") would feel inappropriate or condescending in a B2B or high-net-worth wealth management context where users expect neutral, authoritative language.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 21
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a smart-prefill confirmation form that appears after Cleo's AI has already detected a recurring transaction (Netflix) from the user's linked bank data. Rather than asking the user to manually input every detail of a bill, the app auto-populates the amount ($18.63), frequency (Monthly), and next payment date (February 21, 2024) based on transaction history pattern-matching.

The layout uses a bottom-sheet modal pattern (indicated by the drag handle at the bottom) layered over the main app, which keeps the user in flow without a full context switch to a new page. The visual hierarchy is clean and vertical: brand icon → bold title → three stacked editable fields → single primary CTA. This minimizes cognitive load since there are only three fields to review, and each uses a floating label style so the user always has context even while editing.

Field affordances are clearly differentiated: the amount uses a numeric input, frequency uses a dropdown/chevron for value selection, and date uses a calendar icon to signal a picker will launch. This consistent iconography reduces the need for explicit instructions.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone here is uncharacteristically neutral and utilitarian compared to Cleo's usual sarcastic personality — this is intentional. When money is on the line (confirming a real bill and payment date), the copy shifts to plain, functional language: "Amount," "Frequency," "When is this next paid?" This builds trust and reduces the risk of user error during a data-sensitive task.

The header "BILL DETAILS" is set in Cleo's signature bold, condensed display typeface, maintaining brand identity even in a purely functional screen. The CTA "Add to bills" is short, direct, and action-oriented, telling the user exactly what will happen next.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Smart Defaults / Prefill: Amount, frequency, and next due date are automatically populated from transaction history, drastically reducing manual data entry and the associated drop-off risk.

  • Brand Consistency in Utility Screens: Even a mundane form uses the Netflix brand icon and Cleo's distinct bold typography to keep the experience visually on-brand.

  • Progressive Disclosure via Bottom Sheet: Presenting this as a modal sheet (with a swipe-to-dismiss handle) rather than a full navigation push keeps the task feeling lightweight and reversible.

  • Icon-Assisted Field Affordance: The chevron and calendar icons clearly communicate interaction type (dropdown vs. date picker) without extra copy.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users setting up bill tracking/budgeting features — typically financially anxious or disorganized users who signed up for Cleo specifically because they don't want to manage spreadsheets. By pre-filling the data, Cleo removes the friction and effort that would normally cause this exact demographic to abandon a manual bill-tracking setup. The psychological trigger is reduced effort/cognitive load combined with automation-driven trust — the user feels the app "already knows" their finances, reinforcing Cleo's value proposition as an AI money coach rather than a passive tracker.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when confirming auto-detected recurring data (subscriptions, bills, income) where you have partial certainty from transactional/behavioral data. It's ideal for onboarding flows, bill/subscription managers, or budgeting apps where reducing manual entry directly correlates with activation and retention. Also effective anywhere a bottom sheet is preferable to a full-screen push for a lightweight, interruptible task.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the underlying data confidence is low — auto-filling incorrect values (wrong amount or date) can erode user trust faster than manual entry would build it. Also avoid for complex forms with many fields, where a bottom sheet's limited vertical space and lack of persistent navigation context could frustrate users. Not suitable for irreversible financial commitments without an explicit secondary confirmation step.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 17
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a full-screen modal (presented as a bottom sheet with a drag handle) that lets users manually set or adjust weekly/monthly spending budgets across a comprehensive list of pre-populated categories. Each row follows a highly scannable, repeatable pattern: an emoji-based icon in a colored circle, the category label, a stepper (minus/value/plus), allowing granular control without needing a keyboard or numeric input.

The use of a stepper control rather than a text field is a deliberate simplification — it lowers the cognitive and motor effort required to set a budget, especially on mobile, and it prevents invalid inputs (e.g., negative numbers, non-numeric characters) entirely by design. Categories with a $0 balance have their minus button greyed out/disabled, which is a subtle but important affordance that communicates state without needing extra copy.

The long vertical list (Bank Charges, Transport, Cash, Bills, Savings, Shopping, Holidays, Groceries, Entertainment, Eating Out, Loans, Expenses) is scroll-heavy, which could be a usability concern for one-handed thumb reachability, but it's mitigated by a sticky, high-contrast CTA button anchored at the bottom ("Alright, I can do this") that remains accessible regardless of scroll position. The close (X) icon top-right offers an easy escape hatch, reducing the feeling of being trapped in a mandatory flow.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The CTA copy "Alright, I can do this" is quintessential Cleo brand voice — informal, first-person, and emotionally encouraging rather than transactional (e.g., avoiding sterile copy like "Save" or "Confirm"). It reframes a potentially stressful task (budgeting) as an empowering personal commitment, putting words in the user's mouth that build self-efficacy and reduce anxiety around admitting/planning spending limits.

Category icons use playful, slightly irreverent emoji illustrations (a skull for "Bills" and "Loans", a diamond for "Shopping", cherries with eyes for "Groceries") rather than generic flat icons. This injects personality and humor into an inherently unglamorous financial task, aligning with Cleo's comedic, mascot-led identity and making the budgeting chore feel less clinical.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Stepper-over-keyboard input: Using large tappable +/- controls instead of a numeric text field removes friction and typing errors for a repetitive, tedious task.

  • Disabled state clarity: Greyed-out minus buttons on $0 categories visually communicate a floor limit without any explanatory copy needed.

  • Sticky bottom CTA: The persistent, high-contrast button ensures the primary action is always one thumb-tap away, regardless of scroll depth in a long list.

  • Playful iconography per category: Distinct, colorful emoji-in-circle icons make a long, otherwise monotonous list instantly scannable and add brand personality.

  • Emotionally-framed CTA copy: "Alright, I can do this" turns a mundane confirmation into an act of self-affirmation, reducing the psychological weight of budget-setting.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users who are actively engaging with Cleo's budgeting/coaching feature after being shown their spending breakdown — likely people who feel overwhelmed or anxious about tracking finances and need a low-friction way to set limits. The design leans on reducing perceived effort (steppers vs. forms) and self-determination psychology (framing the confirmation as a personal capability statement) to keep users engaged rather than abandoning the task out of frustration or shame, which is common in traditional budgeting apps.
screens.whereToUse: Use this stepper-list pattern when users need to configure multiple numeric values across many categories in one sitting (budgets, nutrition macros, inventory counts, notification frequency per channel). It's ideal when values are typically small, incremented in fixed steps, and precision to the cent/unit isn't critical. The sticky CTA + dismiss (X) combo works well for any long-form configuration modal where you want to reduce list-scroll anxiety while preserving an easy exit.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid steppers when users need to enter large, arbitrary, or highly precise numbers (e.g., entering an exact salary or large one-off transaction) — tapping + or - dozens of times becomes tedious and frustrating. In those cases, pair the stepper with a tappable numeric field or slider for direct entry. Also avoid this dense, single-column list approach if the category count is very high (30+), as it may still overwhelm users even with a sticky CTA; consider grouping, search/filter, or progressive disclosure instead.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 18
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen translates a dry financial statistic—monthly cash flow—into an emotionally resonant, illustrative story. Instead of a bar chart or line graph, Cleo uses two hand-illustrated coin stacks ("In" vs "Out") that visually communicate the imbalance at a glance: the "Out" stack towers over the "In" stack, making the overspend viscerally obvious before the user even reads a number.

The layout is vertically organized in a clear narrative sequence: header/date range → visual comparison → hero overspend number → conversational nudge → entry point to itemized spending. A horizontal carousel/pager (arrow controls) allows the user to swipe between months, reusing the same mental model for historical review without needing a separate navigation pattern.

The card transition from the purple "hero" zone into a white content sheet is a classic device to signal a change in information density—hero visualization on top, actionable/scrollable list content below. The bottom tab bar anchors the user within Cleo's broader hub-and-spoke navigation (Spend, Budget, Chat, Save, Borrow, Habits), reinforcing that budgeting is just one spoke of a larger financial coaching ecosystem.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is unapologetically blunt and comedic, consistent with Cleo's brand voice. "RIP budget" paired with a sparkly purple skull mascot turns a shameful financial event (overspending) into a shareable, meme-worthy moment rather than a guilt trip. This reframes financial failure as something to laugh about with a "friend" rather than be lectured about by an institution.

The label "overspent" under the large dollar figure is stated matter-of-factly, avoiding alarmist red banners or aggressive warning language typical of finance apps. The follow-up chat prompt, "Been 2 weeks of budgets. Thoughts?", is written in casual, texting-style shorthand—mimicking how a friend would check in, not how a bank would notify you of a bad month.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Anthropomorphized data visualization: Coin stacks and a mascot skull replace charts, making the abstract concept of overspending immediately legible and emotionally engaging.

  • Humor as a shame-reduction mechanic: "RIP budget" and the winking skull defuse the anxiety typically associated with overspending, keeping users from abandoning the app out of guilt.

  • Proactive conversational nudge: The dismissible chat bubble embedded directly in the data screen invites reflection and funnels users toward Cleo's core chat interface, blurring the line between passive dashboard and active coaching.

  • Consistent hub navigation: The bottom tab bar keeps budgeting contextually tied to Spend, Save, Borrow, and Habits, reinforcing a holistic money-coach narrative rather than siloed features.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially anxious, budget-averse young adults (likely Gen Z/Millennial) who have historically avoided traditional finance apps because of their clinical, judgmental tone. By using humor, illustration, and casual language, Cleo lowers the psychological barrier to confronting bad financial news.

The psychological trigger at play is shame mitigation via humor: users are more likely to return to and re-engage with an app that makes them laugh about failure rather than one that flags it in red alarming text. The chat prompt also leverages the social/parasocial trigger—being "checked in on" by a mascot creates a sense of accountability similar to a friend or coach, increasing retention and engagement with the chat feature.
screens.whereToUse:
• Financial or health apps targeting users prone to shame or avoidance around negative metrics (overspending, missed workouts, calorie overages).

  • Products aiming to differentiate from clinical/corporate competitors through mascot-driven personality and humor.

  • Summary/recap screens where a period-over-period comparison (month, week) needs to be understood instantly without requiring numeracy or chart literacy.

  • Apps that want to bridge passive reporting screens with an active conversational/support channel (e.g., embedding a chat CTA within a dashboard).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Enterprise, B2B, or professional finance tools where users expect precise, chart-based analytics (e.g., accounting software, investment platforms) — illustration-heavy metaphors can feel unserious or imprecise.

  • Contexts involving serious financial hardship or debt where humor could feel dismissive or insensitive rather than supportive.

  • Situations requiring exact data comparison across many categories, where illustrated coin stacks lack the precision of bar/line charts.

  • Older or more conservative user demographics who may perceive mascot humor as unprofessional or untrustworthy for money management.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 19
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen distills a traditionally complex financial report (income vs. expenses, daily burn rate, bills due) into a single-scroll, mascot-narrated summary. The layout uses a strong color-block split: a vivid purple 'hero' zone for the period header and countdown, and a white 'data' zone below for the numbers. This visual separation helps chunk information into 'when' (the date range/payday countdown) versus 'what' (the actual money breakdown) without needing tabs or accordions.

Notably, all monetary values are rendered as em-dashes ("-"), indicating either a zero-state before data syncs or a loading/placeholder condition. This is a critical empty-state pattern: rather than showing $0.00 (which implies no money) or a blank space (which implies broken UI), the dash communicates 'pending/unknown' in a friendly, non-alarming way.

The crystal ball emoji as a section divider is a delightful, on-brand touch that reframes a mundane 'left to spend / per day' stat block as a piece of fortune-telling, reinforcing Cleo's playful mascot-driven identity. The bottom-anchored Cleo prompt card ("Been 2 weeks of budgets. Thoughts?") acts as a persistent conversational hook, pulling users out of passive dashboard-viewing and back into the chat-first core loop. Navigation is handled by a simple 6-item tab bar, keeping the app's promise of 'no menu navigation' largely intact while still offering feature depth (Spend, Budget, Chat, Save, Borrow, Habits).
screens.tonalityAndContent: The copy is short, punchy, and casual — "MARCH'S BREAKDOWN" in bold condensed caps feels like a magazine headline rather than a bank statement. "11 days until payday" in mint green injects urgency and anticipation using color psychology (green = go/positive, countdown = anticipation). The Cleo prompt "Been 2 weeks of budgets. Thoughts?" is deliberately conversational and slightly cheeky, mimicking a friend checking in rather than a system notification, consistent with Cleo's 'blunt, comedic' persona. Labels like "left to spend" and "per day" are plain-language equivalents of what other finance apps would call 'remaining balance' or 'daily allowance,' lowering the cognitive load for non-finance-literate users.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dash placeholders instead of $0: Using "-" for empty monetary data avoids the false signal of zero balance, a subtle but important trust-preserving detail.

  • Crystal ball mascot moment: A whimsical illustration used as a functional divider between top-level totals and the spend/day breakdown, turning a boring stat block into a branded moment.

  • Persistent chat nudge card: The dismissible Cleo speech-bubble card at the bottom keeps the AI coach 'present' even on a non-chat screen, driving re-engagement into the core conversational loop.

  • Payday countdown progress bar: A minimal, wordless progress bar paired with "11 days until payday" gives an instant temporal anchor for budgeting decisions.

  • Bold color-blocking: The stark purple-to-white split visually segments 'period context' from 'financial data' without needing dividers or cards.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets financially anxious or budgeting-averse users (often younger, gig-economy or paycheck-to-paycheck demographics) who are put off by traditional finance-app spreadsheets and charts. By using mascot illustrations, playful copy, and a countdown to payday, Cleo taps into loss-aversion and anticipation triggers in a way that feels supportive rather than punitive. The dismissible chat prompt exploits the Zeigarnik effect and social reciprocity — having a 'friend' check in creates a mild obligation to respond, nudging users back into the retention-driving chat interface.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for financial, health, or habit-tracking dashboards where the goal is to reduce anxiety around numbers by softening zero/empty states, injecting mascot personality, and blending data display with conversational engagement hooks. Ideal for apps that want to minimize navigational complexity while still surfacing periodic (weekly/monthly) summaries.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this approach for power users, accountants, or B2B financial tools where dense, precise data (multi-account breakdowns, transaction-level granularity, exportable reports) is expected — the playful illustration and large whitespace would feel unserious and would waste valuable screen real estate. Also avoid dash-based placeholders in contexts where users need immediate confirmation that a value is genuinely zero versus not-yet-loaded, as ambiguity could cause confusion in high-stakes financial decisions.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 20
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen consolidates recurring and upcoming financial obligations into a single, digestible view, replacing the anxiety-inducing spreadsheet or bank statement scan with a simple hero-stat layout. The architecture uses a classic "header + list" pattern: a bold, oversized hero number ($18.63) anchors the top of the screen inside a light lavender card, immediately answering the user's most pressing question—"How much do I owe this cycle?"—before any scrolling is required.

Below the fold, the content is chunked into two clearly labeled sections, "Bills this budget" and "Future bills," using date-range subheadings (Feb 1 - Feb 29, March 12) to give temporal context without requiring the user to cross-reference a calendar. Each bill is rendered as a stacked list row with a recognizable brand icon (Netflix logo) or an illustrated emoji avatar (skull for a P2P transfer), paired with the merchant name, due date, and amount right-aligned for easy scanning—mirroring bank statement conventions users already trust.

The persistent bottom "Add a bill" CTA in Cleo's signature electric blue/purple ensures the primary action is always reachable, and the back arrow in the header maintains a lightweight drill-down navigation model consistent with a chat-first app that occasionally needs structured views.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is terse and label-driven rather than conversational here, a deliberate departure from Cleo's usual sassy chatbot voice. Words like "BILLS DUE" in bold condensed caps function like a tabloid headline, injecting urgency and weight into what is otherwise a mundane admin task. The lowercase "this budget" softens the stat, tying it back to Cleo's budgeting cycle language rather than generic finance jargon like "billing period."

Notably, the section for an unrelated peer-to-peer transfer ("E Transfer Sent Flora...") is tagged with a playful sparkly skull icon, injecting Cleo's irreverent personality into an otherwise sterile transactional list — a subtle wink that keeps the utility screen from feeling like a boring bank app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Hero Stat Pattern: Leading with a giant, oversized dollar figure immediately orients the user without requiring any cognitive parsing of a table or chart.

  • Illustrated Money Motifs: The floating 3D-style cash illustrations around the header reinforce the "money" theme emotionally, softening what could otherwise feel like a stressful debt reminder.

  • Temporal Grouping: Splitting bills into "this budget" vs "Future bills" helps users mentally separate immediate obligations from what's coming, reducing overwhelm.

  • Brand Recognition Icons: Using the actual Netflix logo instead of a generic icon speeds up scanning and builds trust that Cleo has accurately synced real transaction data.

  • Persistent Sticky CTA: "Add a bill" stays fixed at the bottom, ensuring the user can always take the next logical action regardless of scroll position.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially anxious users, particularly younger millennials/Gen Z who live paycheck-to-paycheck and often get blindsided by forgotten subscriptions or automated bill withdrawals. The psychological trigger at play is loss aversion reduction — by proactively surfacing the exact dollar amount due before it happens, Cleo removes the dread of surprise overdrafts, positioning itself as a protective "money coach" rather than just a tracker.

The visual softness (rounded cards, pastel lavender, playful cash illustrations) targets users who typically avoid traditional banking apps because they feel cold, judgmental, or overly clinical. The design reduces the shame often associated with looking at debts/bills by making the screen feel more like a friendly notification than a stern financial audit.
screens.whereToUse: Use this hero-stat + grouped list pattern for any screen summarizing recurring financial commitments, such as subscription trackers, upcoming invoices, loan repayment schedules, or utility bill dashboards. It's ideal when users need a fast "at-a-glance" total before drilling into line-item details, and when grouping by time horizon (current vs. future) adds clarity to planning.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the underlying data set is large or highly variable (e.g., dozens of daily micro-transactions), as the oversized hero number loses meaning and the flat list becomes unwieldy without search or filtering. It's also unsuitable for screens requiring bulk actions or edits, since there are no checkboxes, swipe actions, or batch controls present — a limitation for power users trying to manage many bills at once.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 22
screens.uxAnalysis: This section extends the budget overview into two actionable areas: upcoming bills and categorized spending. The "Bills Due" section pairs a real detected bill (Netflix, using its actual brand logo — a notable departure from Cleo's usual custom-illustrated iconography, since brand recognition matters more than personality here) with an equally-sized "Add a bill" card, treating bill management as an open, ongoing task rather than a fixed, closed list. The "Essential spending" category card surfaces both an absolute figure ($169.50) and a proportional one ("52% of income"), giving the user two different lenses on the same number — useful since a dollar figure alone doesn't convey whether that's a reasonable share of their income. "Edit categories" as a persistent, visible action (rather than buried in settings) reinforces that Cleo's categorization is user-correctable, not a black-box automatic classification the user must simply accept.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The section headers ("BILLS DUE," "SPENDING") stay in Cleo's bold condensed all-caps style, but the body copy here is almost entirely functional and numeric rather than narrative — a deliberate tonal restraint appropriate for a data-review screen where the priority is fast comprehension, not entertainment. The one illustrative flourish — a stylized pink hand making a "rock on"/horns gesture beside the Essential Spending figure — is a small personality touch that doesn't map to any literal meaning about the data, consistent with the app's established pattern of decorative-but-non-functional hand illustrations appearing throughout (thumbs up, pointing fingers) as a recurring visual signature rather than being tied to specific data meanings.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Real brand logo for bill recognition — using Netflix's actual icon (rather than a custom illustrated icon) prioritizes instant recognizability for a real, specific merchant, showing Cleo's icon system flexes between playful abstraction and literal branding depending on what best serves the user's need to quickly identify the item.

  • Dual-framing of spending figures — pairing an absolute dollar amount with a percentage-of-income figure gives users two ways to judge whether a spending category is reasonable, supporting better self-assessment than either number alone.

  • Equal-weight add action — sizing "Add a bill" identically to an actual existing bill (rather than as a small icon or link) treats bill-tracking as an ongoing, always-available task rather than a one-time setup step.

  • User-correctable categorization — the visible "edit categories" action signals that automatic spending classification is a starting point, not a fixed judgment, respecting that auto-categorization is often imperfect and users need an easy correction path.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Rocket Money, Truebill — use nearly identical "upcoming bill card + add bill" layouts within their own bill-tracking dashboards.

  • Mint (Intuit), historically — displayed spending-by-category cards with both dollar amount and percentage-of-budget/income framing, matching Cleo's dual-figure approach.

  • Copilot Money — offers a comparable "edit categories" action prominently placed near auto-categorized spending totals, respecting user correction of automatic classification.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (real-logo bill cards + equal-weight add action + dual-framed category spending figures + visible category-editing) fits any personal finance app's budget-detail view, where users need both to review upcoming obligations and understand spending proportionally, not just in absolute terms.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for extremely high-volume or highly granular category systems (e.g., dozens of narrow spending categories) where a card-based layout with large illustrative elements would become inefficient compared to a denser table or list view.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 23
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen is the destination of the "edit categories" action seen on the prior Budget screen, letting users redefine which spending categories Cleo treats as "essential" versus discretionary — directly affecting the "52% of income" essential-spending calculation shown on the dashboard. Presenting all categories as a visual grid of colorful circular icons (rather than a plain checklist) keeps interaction consistent with Cleo's illustrated icon system used throughout transactions and budget cards, while green checkmark badges provide clear, unambiguous selected-state feedback. Splitting categories into two color-coded zones (cool blue/green "Essential" vs. warm peach "Other") visually reinforces the conceptual grouping even before reading any labels, and the disabled "Save" button (matching the pattern established in earlier Plaid screens) suggests it activates only once a change has actually been made from the current saved state.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "SORT YOUR SPENDS" keeps the bold condensed header style, while "Tap to add or remove your categories" is a plain, clear instruction — appropriately minimal for a settings/configuration screen where clarity matters more than personality. This screen shows almost no distinctive Cleo voice in its copy, which is consistent with the pattern observed elsewhere: functional, configuration-heavy screens stay closer to neutral instructional language, reserving personality-forward copy for conversational or celebratory moments rather than utility screens.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual grouping reinforces conceptual categorization — using distinct background colors for "Essential" vs. "Other" sections lets users grasp the classification structure at a glance, before reading any category labels.

  • Consistent iconography aids fast recognition — reusing the same illustrated icons seen in the transaction list and budget category cards elsewhere in the app means users don't need to relearn visual language on this settings screen.

  • Clear selected-state feedback — green checkmark badges directly on each icon provide unambiguous confirmation of selection status, more visually direct than relying on border color or opacity changes alone.

  • Disabled Save until a change is made — following the same pattern as the Plaid phone-entry and credential screens, this prevents unnecessary save actions when nothing has actually changed.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Copilot Money — offers nearly identical category-classification screens letting users designate which spending categories count as "essential" or "fixed" versus "discretionary."

  • YNAB (You Need A Budget) — provides comparable category-grouping controls, though typically in a more text-list-driven format rather than Cleo's icon-grid approach.

  • Mint (Intuit), historically — allowed users to recategorize auto-detected spending types via a similar tap-to-toggle interface.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (icon-grid multi-select + color-coded grouping + clear selected-state badges) fits any personal finance app allowing users to customize how automatically-detected spending is classified, especially where the classification directly feeds into a headline metric (like "% of income on essentials") the user relies on.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for category systems too large to display as a manageable icon grid (e.g., 50+ granular categories) where a searchable list or nested structure would scale better than a flat grid of circular icons.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 25
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen extends the budget dashboard beyond simple spending tracking into a fuller financial picture: "Gaining" surfaces income and savings as their own first-class metrics (not just spending), while "Ignoring" transparently discloses that $250.00 in transactions have been excluded from budget calculations — an important trust signal, since silently dropping transactions from a budget total without disclosure could make the numbers feel inaccurate or untrustworthy. Pairing this disclosure with "Something not right? ?" gives the user a direct, low-friction path to flag or correct miscategorized/excluded data, rather than leaving them to wonder why their budget math doesn't match their expectations. The "Savings" card showing a placeholder "-" rather than "$0" is a subtle but meaningful distinction — it signals "no data configured" rather than "zero saved," avoiding a potentially discouraging false-zero reading.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The section headers "GAINING" and "IGNORING" (paired with the earlier-established "SPENDING") form a simple three-part vocabulary for organizing the budget dashboard, using plain, concrete verbs rather than more technical financial terms like "Income Sources" or "Excluded Transactions." "Something not right?" is a casual, approachable way to invite correction or feedback, avoiding more formal phrasing like "Report an issue" — consistent with Cleo's established conversational register even on a data-heavy utility screen.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Transparent disclosure of excluded data — explicitly showing an "Excluded" total (rather than silently omitting certain transactions from all calculations) builds trust in the budget math by accounting for every dollar somewhere.

  • Meaningful empty-state distinction — displaying "-" instead of "$0" for Savings avoids implying the user has literally saved nothing when the more accurate read is "no savings configured/tracked yet."

  • Progress bars at zero still convey structure — showing $0/$6 and $0/$924 with visible (if empty) progress bars establishes the budget framework even before any spending occurs in those categories, previewing what tracking will look like once activity begins.

  • Low-friction correction path — "Something not right?" placed directly near the data it might apply to reduces the distance between noticing a problem and reporting it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Mint (Intuit), historically — organized budget dashboards into comparable Income/Spending/Savings sections, with explicit handling of excluded or uncategorized transactions.

  • Copilot Money — displays similar "excluded" transaction totals transparently rather than silently omitting them from budget math.

  • YNAB — uses a comparable three-part conceptual structure (money in, money out, money set aside) to organize its own budget overview screens.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (transparent excluded-transaction disclosure + meaningful empty states + low-friction correction link) fits any personal finance app's budget summary where automatic transaction categorization inevitably produces edge cases, and where user trust in the underlying math depends on visible accountability for every dollar.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for extremely simple budget tools with no automatic categorization or exclusion logic — surfacing an "Ignoring" section would be unnecessary complexity if there's nothing being excluded in the first place.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 24
screens.uxAnalysis: This screenshot captures the direct result of the user reclassifying several categories (General, Shopping, Cash) from "Other" into "Essential" — a meaningful edit, since Shopping and Cash are more discretionary in nature than the original essential set (Bank Charges, Bills, Groceries, Loans, Expenses). The system correctly reflects this change by enabling "Save," following the same disabled-to-enabled feedback convention seen throughout this Plaid/Cleo flow (phone-entry, credential fields, etc.), reinforcing a consistent design-system-wide pattern for gated actions. This edit will directly affect the "52% of income" essential-spending metric shown on the Budget dashboard once saved, giving the user real, visible control over how their own financial narrative is framed by the app — rather than accepting Cleo's default categorization as fixed truth.
screens.tonalityAndContent: No copy changes from the previous screenshot — this is purely an interaction-state change, and the instructional copy correctly remains neutral and unchanged since the underlying task (tap to add/remove categories) hasn't shifted.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Consistent enabled/disabled feedback across the app — the Save button's activation upon change mirrors the exact same pattern used in the earlier Plaid credential and phone-entry screens, reinforcing a coherent, learnable interaction language throughout the entire product (not just within a single flow).

  • User agency over financial categorization — allowing the user to redefine what counts as "essential" acknowledges that automatic categorization is a starting hypothesis, not an authoritative judgment, and that "essential" is genuinely subjective (e.g., some users may consider limited shopping essential, others may not).

  • Direct traceability to a headline metric — because this screen's output feeds directly into the "% of income on essentials" figure seen elsewhere, giving users fine-grained control here has outsized influence on how they interpret their own financial health.

  • No confirmation friction for reversible changes — since spending-category classification is a low-risk, easily-reversible setting (not a destructive or financial-transaction action), the lack of any "are you sure?" step is appropriate.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Copilot Money — allows users to freely reclassify spending categories between essential/discretionary designations, directly affecting the app's own summary metrics, matching this pattern exactly.

  • YNAB — similarly lets users define which budget categories are treated as fixed/necessary versus flexible, with those classifications feeding into higher-level budget health indicators.
