screens.whereToUse: This pattern (user-adjustable category classification directly feeding a headline metric, with consistent save-button state feedback) fits any personal finance app where automatic categorization is used as a starting point but genuine spending priorities vary meaningfully across users.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit if the underlying metric needs to remain standardized or comparable across users (e.g., for aggregate benchmarking or a fixed regulatory definition of "essential" spending) — letting users freely redefine the category would undermine consistency needed for such comparisons.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 26
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen provides the detailed drill-down behind the summary "$326 Income" figure seen on the main Budget dashboard, letting the user verify exactly which transactions contributed to that total. Restating the figure at the top (here shown as $325.93, a minor variance from the $326 rounded figure on the dashboard) alongside "Received this budget" clarifies the timeframe scope before listing individual line items. The "Other Income" section header implies there could be additional income sub-categories beyond what's shown (though none are visible in this screenshot), suggesting Cleo's income categorization system has room to expand beyond a single flat list, similar to the Essential/Other spend structure seen in the category-editing screen.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven; visible text is limited to functional labels and figures ("INCOME," "Received this budget," "Other Income," transaction names and dates).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Drill-down preserves context — restating the total figure and timeframe scope ("Received this budget") at the top of the detail screen ensures the user doesn't lose sight of what they're reviewing details for.

  • Chronological transaction ordering aids verification — listing income sources by date (most recent first) makes it easy to cross-reference against what the user remembers receiving.

  • Transparent sourcing builds trust in the summary figure — showing the individual transactions that sum to the headline income total lets users verify accuracy rather than simply trusting an opaque aggregate number.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Mint (Intuit), historically — provided similar drill-down income-detail screens accessible by tapping a summary income figure on the main budget dashboard.

  • Copilot Money — offers comparable transaction-level detail views beneath aggregate income/spending totals shown on its dashboard.

  • YNAB — allows drilling into category totals to see the specific transactions contributing to any budget figure, matching this transparency pattern.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (drill-down detail screen restating context + chronological transaction list) fits any budget dashboard where summary figures need a transparent, verifiable breakdown accessible with minimal navigation friction.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for extremely high-volume income sources (e.g., a business account with hundreds of daily micro-transactions) where a flat chronological list without filtering, search, or additional categorization would become unwieldy.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 27
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen demonstrates proper empty-state handling for a drill-down detail view: rather than showing a blank white screen or an error when no savings transactions exist for the period, Cleo displays a purpose-built illustration and clear, specific copy ("No transactions for Savings this month") that confirms the screen loaded correctly and explains exactly why there's nothing to show. This directly explains the "-" placeholder seen on both this screen's header and the earlier main Budget dashboard's Savings card — confirming that dash represents "no data" rather than a loading error or zero-value calculation, an important distinction for user trust in the app's data accuracy. The empty-state illustration (a distinct top-hat-and-coin graphic, different from the piggy-bank imagery used in the header) is purpose-specific rather than reused generically, suggesting Cleo maintains a dedicated illustration for this particular no-data scenario.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "No transactions for Savings this month" is plain, specific, and non-judgmental — notably, it doesn't editorialize about the user having zero savings activity (e.g., no "You haven't saved anything yet!" guilt-inducing framing), which is a meaningful restraint given Cleo's typically more editorial, personality-forward voice elsewhere in the app. This measured tone is appropriate for what could otherwise feel like a mildly shameful admission (not saving money) — staying factual rather than commentary-driven avoids adding unnecessary emotional weight to an empty state.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Purpose-built empty states prevent confusion — a dedicated illustration and specific message confirm the screen loaded correctly with genuinely no data, rather than leaving the user to wonder if something is broken.

  • Consistent placeholder semantics — reusing "-" (rather than "$0") across both the summary dashboard and this detail screen maintains a consistent, learnable convention for "not yet tracked" versus "confirmed zero."

  • Restrained tone for a neutral-to-sensitive empty state — avoiding judgmental or overly cheerful commentary about a lack of savings activity respects that this could be a sensitive topic for some users, even within an otherwise playful app.

  • Empty state doesn't block the informative header — showing "0% of income" alongside the empty-state message provides some quantified context even without individual transactions to list.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Mint (Intuit), historically — used comparable illustrated empty states for budget categories with no activity in a given period, rather than blank screens.

  • YNAB — displays clear "no transactions" messaging for categories without activity, avoiding ambiguity about whether data failed to load.

  • Copilot Money — matches this restrained, non-judgmental tone for empty financial data states, particularly around savings or investment categories that may be legitimately inactive for some users.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (dedicated illustration + specific, non-judgmental copy + consistent placeholder semantics) fits any financial app's category detail screen where genuinely having no data is a normal, expected state (not every user saves every month) rather than an error condition.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for genuinely erroneous no-data states (e.g., a failed data sync) — using the same calm, expected-empty-state treatment for an actual system error would mislead users into thinking everything is fine when data may actually be missing due to a technical problem.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Logging & Tracking 1
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a classic asset detail view for a crypto wallet application, following the well-established "coin page" pattern popularized by Robinhood and Coinbase. The layout is hierarchically organized to guide the eye from macro (price) to micro (transaction actions):

  • Header identity block: The Bitcoin logo, asset name, and a secondary "Watch" CTA sit at the top, letting a non-holder bookmark the asset without commitment.

  • Price hero zone: A large, high-contrast price ($96,892.43) paired with a color-coded delta (green up-arrow, percentage change) gives an instant read on performance — leveraging pre-attentive processing so users don't need to do math.

  • Data visualization: A filled area/line chart with a gradient dot-fill pattern under the orange line adds visual richness without overwhelming the dark background. The line's organic curvature and the subtle dotted-fill texture make the chart feel "alive" and premium rather than a flat sparkline.

  • Time range segmented control: 1H/1D/1W/1M/1Y/All pills let users flexibly reframe the story the chart tells — critical for volatile assets where framing ("just look at 1H" vs "look at All") can shift perceived risk.

  • Balance + Action grid: Below the chart, the user's actual holding (0.00000 BTC) is shown, immediately followed by a two-row, four-column icon grid of transactional actions (Buy, Swap, Bridge, Cash out / Send, Receive, Text send, Share). This action grid is the conversion engine of the screen — it's placed directly below the balance so the empty state (0 BTC) becomes a call to action rather than a dead end.

The all-dark theme (true black background) reduces eye strain for extended market-watching sessions and makes the orange brand/chart color and green gain indicator pop with strong signal contrast — a deliberate choice mirroring financial terminal aesthetics (Bloomberg-esque) to convey seriousness and legitimacy.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal, numeric, and utilitarian — appropriate for a finance app where users want data density over narrative. Labels like "Buy," "Swap," "Bridge," "Cash out," "Send," "Receive," "Text send," and "Share" are single words, imperative, and icon-paired, minimizing cognitive load and translation friction.

The use of "Your balance" personalizes the otherwise market-wide data (Bitcoin price) and creates a clear delineation between "the market" and "my holdings." The green "↗" and percentage in parentheses follow standard financial notation, borrowing credibility from established trading platforms and stock ticker conventions users already trust.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dotted gradient chart fill: A distinctive stylistic choice — rather than a simple flat gradient, the area under the curve is filled with a dot-matrix texture that reduces visual heaviness while still communicating "volume/magnitude," giving the chart a unique, textured brand signature versus generic competitor charts.

  • Balance-adjacent action grid: Placing Buy/Swap/Bridge/Cash out directly beneath a zero balance turns an empty state into an implicit upsell — the user sees they own nothing and is immediately offered the exact remedy.

  • Segmented time-range control with pill highlight: Clear active-state (dark blue pill on "1D") gives immediate feedback on the selected timeframe without needing a page reload.

  • Secondary "Watch" CTA: Placed top-right in the header, it offers a low-commitment engagement path (watchlist) distinct from the high-commitment financial actions below, respecting different user intents on the same page.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets retail crypto investors and traders, ranging from curious newcomers checking Bitcoin's price to active holders managing their position. The design leverages several psychological triggers:

  • Loss/gain framing: Green color and upward arrow trigger dopamine-linked positive reinforcement, encouraging engagement and potential buying during upswings (a subtle urgency/FOMO driver).

  • Data legitimacy bias: The professional, dense chart and dark "trading terminal" aesthetic borrows visual cues from institutional trading tools, increasing perceived trustworthiness and reducing the "toy app" feeling that could deter serious investors.

  • Actionable proximity: Placing action buttons directly below the balance leverages the Zeigarnik effect / cognitive completion — a 0.00000 BTC balance feels like an "incomplete" state the user is nudged to resolve via Buy.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any single-asset detail or ticker page in fintech, crypto, or stock trading apps — anywhere a user needs to evaluate an asset's performance and then act on it (buy, sell, transfer). It's ideal when:

  • The product needs to balance passive market-watching with active transactional behavior on the same screen.

  • Users benefit from flexible time-range analysis of a metric (price, growth, engagement) via a segmented control.

  • You want to visually differentiate "browsing/watching" intent from "transacting" intent via distinct CTA tiers (secondary Watch vs. primary action grid).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this dense, action-grid-heavy layout for:

  • Novice-first onboarding contexts where 8 simultaneous action icons (Buy, Swap, Bridge, Cash out, Send, Receive, Text send, Share) could overwhelm a first-time user unfamiliar with crypto jargon like "Bridge."

  • Low-volatility or non-financial data where a large, dramatic price chart and percentage change would be unnecessary visual noise (e.g., static content pages).

  • Contexts where regulatory/compliance requirements demand more disclaimers or risk warnings near price data — this minimalist layout omits such framing, which may not be appropriate in strictly regulated markets.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Logging & Tracking 2
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen follows a classic Master-Detail pattern, drilling down from a portfolio list into a single asset (Bitcoin) to give the user a focused, data-rich view. The information hierarchy is deliberately vertical and scannable: identity (coin icon + name) sits at the top, followed by the large, high-contrast price figure, the delta/performance indicator, an interactive price chart, the user's personal holdings, and finally a dense grid of one-tap actions.

The use of a dark, near-black background with a single vibrant accent color (Bitcoin's signature orange for the chart, green for gains) creates a "trading terminal" aesthetic that signals seriousness and precision — important for a financial app trying to build trust. The segmented time-range control (1H/1D/1W/1M/1Y/All) is a well-worn but highly effective pattern that lets power users manipulate the chart without leaving the screen, minimizing cognitive load and navigation depth.

The two rows of circular icon+label action buttons (Buy, Swap, Bridge, Cash out / Send, Receive, Text send, Share) form a highly scannable, thumb-friendly toolbar. Placing these as a persistent grid rather than burying them in menus reflects the "Busy Urbans" target audience — users who want to execute an action in one or two taps without hunting through nested menus.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal, numeric, and utilitarian — "Bitcoin price," "Your balance," "0.00000 BTC" — prioritizing data clarity over marketing flourish. This is typical of financial/fintech UX where trust is built through precision and restraint rather than persuasive language.

The percentage change is color-coded (green with an up-arrow glyph) reinforcing the emotional signal of gains almost instantly, appealing to the dopamine-driven nature of price-watching behavior common among crypto users.

Action labels are single words ("Buy," "Swap," "Bridge," "Cash out," "Send," "Receive," "Text send," "Share") — terse, imperative, and instantly recognizable, reducing decision friction for time-pressed users.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented time-range selector integrated directly beneath the chart lets users instantly re-scope data (1H to All) without a modal or new screen.

  • Dual-row quick action grid exposes 8 core financial actions (Buy, Swap, Bridge, Cash out, Send, Receive, Text send, Share) as one-tap circular buttons, dramatically reducing time-to-action for a mobile, on-the-go user base.

  • "Watch" CTA in the top right offers a low-commitment engagement path for users who don't yet hold the asset, functioning as a soft conversion/retention hook.

  • Color-coded price delta (green, arrow icon, % and $ value) gives an at-a-glance emotional read on performance without requiring the user to parse numbers.

  • Dotted-fill area chart with a bold line adds visual texture and brand personality while keeping the data legible against the dark background.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for the app's "Busy Urbans" target audience: mobile-first, time-constrained users who check crypto prices in short bursts (commuting, waiting in line) and need to act quickly when an opportunity arises. The large, legible price and percentage change cater to quick glances, while the one-tap action buttons remove friction for users who don't have time to navigate multi-step menus.

Psychologically, the screen leverages loss/gain framing (green up-arrow with dollar and percentage gain) to trigger urgency and FOMO, nudging users toward the "Buy" or "Swap" actions immediately visible below. The "Watch" button taps into a lower-commitment psychological entry point, letting cautious or non-holding users passively track the asset — a common conversion funnel step in fintech apps before a first purchase.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any single-asset or single-item financial/data detail screen where users need to (1) quickly assess current status, (2) view historical trend, and (3) take immediate action. It's ideal for stocks, crypto, ETFs, fitness metrics, or any dashboard-to-detail drill-down where a time-series chart and quick actions are central to the user journey.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense action-grid layout for casual or low-frequency use cases where users are unfamiliar with the available actions — the terse one-word labels (e.g., "Bridge," "Text send") assume domain literacy and could confuse first-time crypto users. Also avoid an all-dark, data-heavy layout for audiences who value simplicity over granular control, such as first-time onboarding flows, where a more guided, less overwhelming interface would perform better.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Logging & Tracking 3
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a dedicated "coin detail" view for Bitcoin within a multi-chain crypto wallet app. The architecture follows a classic Master-Detail pattern where tapping an asset from a portfolio list drills into this dedicated view. The layout is vertically organized into three distinct zones: a balance header, a dense action grid, and an educational/resource footer.

The most functionally dense area is the 8-icon action grid (Buy, Swap, Bridge, Cash out, Send, Receive, Text send, Share). This is an aggressive information architecture choice — rather than hiding secondary actions behind a menu, the designers surface every possible transaction type as an equally-weighted circular icon button. This maximizes discoverability of features (especially newer ones like "Bridge" and "Text send") but sacrifices visual hierarchy; a novice user with a zero balance is shown "Cash out" and "Swap" with the same prominence as "Buy," which is the only logically available action at this state.

Below the fold, the "About Bitcoin" card and "Resources" list serve an educational function, transforming a transactional wallet screen into a mini content hub. This is important for a category (crypto) with high anxiety and knowledge gaps. The persistent bottom Tab Bar keeps global navigation (Home, Browser, Swap history, News, Wallets) accessible at all times, reinforcing the hub-and-spoke structure of the overall app.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is minimal, confident, and utilitarian — typical of institutional-grade fintech products. Labels are short, one or two words ("Buy," "Swap," "Bridge"), assuming a baseline of crypto literacy while still providing scaffolding for beginners via the "About Bitcoin" explainer.

The educational copy ("The world's first cryptocurrency, Bitcoin is stored and exchanged securely on the internet through a digital ledger known as a blockchain...") is written in plain, reassuring language rather than technical jargon, explicitly targeting newcomers who may be intimidated by blockchain terminology. The truncation with "View more" keeps the primary screen focused on transactions rather than pedagogy, while still making information available on demand.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Full action transparency: Instead of a hamburger/overflow menu, all eight transactional capabilities are exposed as first-class icon buttons, reducing navigation depth to zero for power users.

  • Embedded education layer: The "About [Asset]" and "Resources" (Whitepaper, Official website) sections turn a transactional screen into a trust-building content surface, critical for reducing anxiety in volatile/unfamiliar asset classes.

  • External link affordance: Explicit diagonal arrow icons on Whitepaper/Official website links clearly signal that the user will leave the app context, setting correct expectations.

  • Consistent iconography system: Uniform circular dark-grey buttons with monochrome line icons create a calm, unified visual rhythm across a functionally busy grid.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets both crypto-curious beginners and active traders simultaneously. The zero balance state ("0.00000 BTC") combined with an educational "About Bitcoin" module suggests this is likely a new user's first visit to an asset page before any deposit — the design anticipates onboarding-stage curiosity and provides just-in-time education to build confidence before a purchase decision.

Simultaneously, the exhaustive action grid (Bridge, Swap, Text send) caters to sophisticated DeFi users who expect granular control without extra taps. Psychologically, exposing all options at once leverages the availability heuristic — users feel the app is powerful and complete because every capability is visible, even if unused. The whitepaper/official site links serve as credibility signals, tapping into the trust deficit inherent to cryptocurrency products by pointing to primary-source, non-corporate documentation.
screens.whereToUse:
• Asset/instrument detail pages in fintech, trading, or crypto apps where users need both transactional controls and contextual education in one view.

  • Products serving a mixed audience of novices and experts, where progressive disclosure ("View more") lets each segment self-select their depth of engagement.

  • Any screen introducing a new or unfamiliar entity that benefits from paired "act now" and "learn more" affordances.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid an 8-icon flat action grid when only 2-3 actions are truly relevant to the current user state (e.g., a zero-balance user shown "Cash out" and "Send") — this creates decision paralysis and clutters the primary CTA. In such cases, prioritize the single most relevant action (e.g., "Buy") with greater visual weight and defer secondary actions to a "More" overflow. This pattern is also unsuitable for simple single-purpose apps where exhaustive action exposure would overwhelm a low-frequency or highly novice user base; a more guided, single-CTA flow would convert better.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Logging & Tracking 4
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen represents the empty state of a Notifications inbox within a cryptocurrency application. Rather than presenting a blank void when a user has no notifications, the design leverages a friendly illustration paired with a clear headline ("Welcome!") and a supportive subtext to explain why the space is empty and what action would populate it.

The layout is centered and minimal, placing the illustration as the primary visual anchor above two lines of text. The dark theme (near-black background) is consistent with typical crypto/fintech apps, reducing eye strain and giving a premium, "trading terminal" feel. The top navigation bar retains a back arrow and a settings/notification-preferences gear icon, allowing users to immediately configure their notification preferences even before any alerts exist — a smart placement that turns an empty state into an actionable moment rather than a dead end.

The bottom tab bar (Home, Explore/Markets, Swap/Transfer, News, Wallet) remains visible and persistent, reinforcing that this is a core section of the app and allowing quick navigation away from the empty state without feeling trapped.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is warm and welcoming ("Welcome!") despite being an error/empty condition, which reframes the lack of content as the beginning of a journey rather than a failure state. The supporting line — "Explore the world of crypto to start getting updates." — is instructional and motivational, nudging the user toward exploration (likely watchlists, price alerts, or portfolio actions) rather than leaving them confused about why the screen is blank.

The tone avoids technical or negative language (no "No notifications found" or "Empty"), instead using an inviting, almost onboarding-like voice that aligns with a beginner-friendly crypto platform trying to reduce intimidation around the complex subject matter.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Actionable Empty State: Instead of a static "nothing here" message, the screen tells the user exactly what to do (explore crypto) to start receiving value from this section.

  • Settings Access Preserved: The gear/preferences icon remains accessible in the top bar even with zero notifications, letting proactive users pre-configure alert types.

  • Custom Illustration: A bespoke phone-with-notification-bubble illustration adds personality and visually communicates the concept of "notifications" better than generic empty-state art.

  • Persistent Navigation: The tab bar stays fully functional, preventing the empty state from feeling like a navigational dead-end.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets new users of a crypto trading/portfolio app who have just signed up or freshly installed the application and have not yet added assets, watchlists, or price alerts. Psychologically, empty states are critical "first impression" moments — a poorly handled one can make an app feel broken or abandoned. By using a positive, guiding tone ("Welcome!"), the design reduces the anxiety/confusion new users feel and instead frames the empty inbox as an opportunity, leveraging the curiosity gap and a subtle call-to-action to drive users toward core engagement actions (adding coins to watchlist, enabling price alerts) that will eventually populate this screen with content, increasing long-term retention and notification opt-in rates.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any inbox, feed, or list screen that can legitimately be empty for new users — notification centers, activity feeds, order histories, chat lists, or saved/favorites screens. It's especially effective in fintech/crypto apps where user trust and guidance are paramount. Pair the empty state with a direct link or button to the action that generates content (e.g., "Browse Markets" or "Set a Price Alert") to shorten the path from empty state to first value.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this soft, welcoming approach for empty states caused by errors, failed loads, or connectivity issues — those require distinct error messaging and recovery actions (e.g., "Retry") rather than an onboarding-style welcome. Also avoid this pattern if the notification screen is a low-frequency, secondary feature; over-designing minor empty states can be unnecessary engineering/design effort. Additionally, ensure this state doesn't appear for returning users who previously had notifications, as it could confuse them into thinking their history was wiped.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Logging & Tracking 5
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen represents the "zero state" of a crypto wallet's Transactions tab, reached when a user has not yet performed any send, receive, swap, or NFT activity. Rather than showing a blank void or a generic "no data" message, the designers invested in a custom, brand-appropriate illustration composed of two overlapping "pill" shapes with directional arrows and token icons, visually explaining the concept of transactions (money moving in and out) before the user has any real data to look at.

The layout follows a strict vertical hierarchy: a large, bold page title anchors the top, the illustration occupies the visual center as the focal point, followed by a two-line explanatory headline/subhead pairing, and finally a single, clear call-to-action pinned near the bottom. This funnel-shaped structure guides the eye downward in a single, uninterrupted path, minimizing cognitive load.

The bottom tab bar remains persistent, reinforcing that this is one of several core sections of the app (Home, Explore/Browser, Swap, Activity, Wallet), and the active "Activity/Transactions" icon is clearly highlighted in a filled blue circle, giving unambiguous location feedback within the IA.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is short, reassuring, and forward-looking. "No transactions yet" avoids negative or technical framing (e.g., "Error: no data found") and instead uses "yet," which implicitly promises that this state is temporary and activity is expected. The supporting line, "Your crypto and NFT activity will appear here once you start using your wallet," educates the user on what will populate this space and mentions NFTs alongside crypto to signal the breadth of supported asset types.

The CTA "Add crypto to your wallet" is action-oriented and directly tied to resolving the empty state, converting a passive dead-end into a guided next step.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Custom illustrative empty state: Instead of a generic icon, a bespoke graphic depicting bidirectional arrows and token badges visually teaches the mental model of "transactions" before any real data exists.

  • Single, unambiguous CTA: "Add crypto to your wallet" gives the user exactly one obvious next action, removing decision paralysis in a moment that could otherwise feel like a dead end.

  • Reassuring temporal framing: The word "yet" and future-tense copy frame the empty state as a beginning rather than a failure or missing feature.

  • Consistent navigational context: The persistent bottom tab bar with a highlighted active icon keeps users oriented within the broader wallet app even on a content-less screen.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets new or first-time crypto wallet users (likely post-onboarding, pre-funding) who have just created or imported a wallet but have not yet transacted. The psychological goal is to prevent early-stage churn: a blank or broken-looking screen at this critical "first impression" moment could make users doubt the app is functioning correctly or worth continuing with. By pairing an inviting illustration with clear guidance and a direct CTA, the design reduces anxiety, builds trust in the product's polish, and nudges the user toward the activation moment (adding/funding crypto) that drives long-term engagement and retention.
screens.whereToUse:
• Any list, feed, or history screen (transactions, orders, messages, notifications) that a new user will encounter before generating data.

  • Situations where converting an empty state into an activation opportunity is valuable, e.g., prompting a first deposit, first post, or first connection.

  • Fintech, crypto, and banking apps where trust and clarity are paramount during onboarding.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Screens where the user has already completed the primary action but simply has no results due to filtering — here the CTA should be "Clear filters" rather than an unrelated onboarding action.

  • High-frequency or power-user contexts where a large illustration would feel like unnecessary friction slowing down repeated access to a data screen.

  • Error or connectivity-failure states, where illustrating "emptiness" as normal could mask an actual bug that needs a distinct error message and recovery action.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Logging & Tracking 6
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is a dedicated transaction ledger screen for a Bitcoin-only wallet, prioritizing radical clarity over density. The design uses a strict black background (true OLED black, not dark grey) to reduce visual noise and make the two accent colors—orange (Bitcoin brand) and green/red (value polarity)—pop immediately.

Content is organized using a chronological, date-grouped stacked list pattern. Section headers ("TODAY", "MAY 07, 2025") act as temporal anchors, letting users quickly scan for recent activity without needing to parse full timestamps on every row. Each row follows a strict 4-column grid: icon, label/counterparty, value in fiat, and value in crypto. This dual-currency display (fiat first, crypto second) is a deliberate hierarchy choice—it prioritizes the number users understand instinctively (USD) while keeping the technically accurate BTC amount available for power users.

The screen is sparse below the two entries, resulting in a large amount of unused negative space. While this preserves visual calm, it also signals a very new wallet/account with low activity, which could be an opportunity for an empty-state nudge or educational content in that dead zone.

Navigation is handled by a 5-icon tab bar at the bottom, with the current "Transactions" tab (paper/list icon) highlighted in a soft blue circular indicator, providing unambiguous location feedback within the app's IA.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal, functional, and confidence-inspiring rather than playful. Labels like "Sent" and "Received" are blunt and universally understood, avoiding crypto jargon for the core action. Supporting metadata ("To bc1qfw...yec7", "From 3K5vYn...fSpZ") is truncated to keep the row scannable while still offering on-demand verifiability for security-conscious users—a critical trust signal in financial/crypto contexts where full addresses matter but shouldn't clutter the primary view.

Color-coding text is used semantically instead of decoratively: negative amounts in white/red-adjacent neutral, positive amounts in green, positive being clearly the "good news" color psychologically wired into users from banking apps and stock tickers.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-value display: Showing fiat and crypto amount together removes the mental math burden of converting BTC to real-world value, which is a huge UX unlock for mainstream crypto users.

  • Semantic color-coding: Green/positive and neutral/negative signage lets users triage transaction direction in a half-second glance, without reading text.

  • Date-grouped chronological list: Mimics familiar bank statement/SMS patterns, reducing the learning curve for non-crypto-native users.

  • Truncated addresses: Balances security/verifiability with visual cleanliness—full trust info is present but doesn't overwhelm.

  • High-contrast dark theme: Pure black background reduces eye strain during frequent glance-checks (a common crypto user behavior) and conserves battery on OLED displays.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday cryptocurrency holders—likely retail Bitcoin investors or spenders using the wallet for peer-to-peer payments—rather than institutional traders. The emphasis on fiat conversion, plain-language verbs ("Sent"/"Received"), and simplified single-asset focus (Bitcoin only) suggests the audience skews toward mainstream/beginner-to-intermediate crypto users rather than developers or exchanges.

Psychologically, the design leverages loss aversion and reassurance: negative transactions are rendered in neutral tones (not alarming red) while positive transactions get an affirming green, subtly reducing anxiety about spending money and rewarding the dopamine hit of receiving funds. The date-stamped ledger format also taps into the same trust-building mental models users already have from traditional banking apps, lowering the psychological barrier to trusting a decentralized financial tool.
screens.whereToUse:
• Financial/fintech apps requiring a clear, auditable log of money movement (banking, crypto, expense trackers).

  • Any product needing to translate a technical unit (BTC, points, tokens) into a familiar currency for user comprehension.

  • Apps targeting non-expert users where trust and clarity outweigh information density.

  • Contexts where date-based grouping meaningfully aids recall (recent activity feeds, order histories).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• High-frequency trading platforms where users need dense, tabular data (open/close price, fees, timestamps to the second) rather than simplified rows.

  • Multi-asset portfolios where a single-currency-per-row layout would force excessive scrolling; a table/master-detail view would scale better.

  • Contexts where address/counterparty verification is legally or operationally critical—full, non-truncated identifiers may be required instead.

  • Light-mode-first brand systems where a forced black theme would clash with broader design language.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Logging & Tracking 7
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen is a transaction receipt/detail view surfaced after tapping a Bitcoin transaction from history. It follows a strict vertical information hierarchy: token identity (icon + status word) at top, timestamp beneath, a bordered card detailing the From/To flow with a directional arrow, then granular blockchain metadata (hash, network fee, total), and finally a persistent row of quick actions anchored to the bottom. The From/To card is the visual centerpiece, using color coding (white for outgoing minus amount, green for incoming/net amount) to instantly communicate the money movement direction without requiring the user to parse wallet addresses. Truncated addresses (bc1ql4...h4wz) reduce cognitive load while remaining verifiable. The separation between 'human-readable' financial summary (top card) and 'technical/audit' data (hash, fee, total) respects the mental model of two different user needs: 'What happened to my money?' and 'Can I verify/prove this on-chain?'. The bottom action row (Send again, View asset in wallet, View on block explorer) turns a passive receipt into an actionable hub, reducing the number of taps needed for common follow-up tasks.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The tone is neutral, technical, and factual — appropriate for a financial/legal record. Labels like "Sent," "From," "To," "Transaction hash," and "Network fee" are plain-language terms rather than crypto jargon, making the screen accessible to less experienced holders while still surfacing the raw hash and fee for power users who want on-chain verification. The info icon next to "Network fee" signals that further explanation is available on demand, avoiding upfront clutter while supporting novices. Numeric precision (0.000014 BTC, $0.45) builds trust through transparency of exact costs.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Color-coded amount deltas: Minus figure in white/red-neutral vs. plus figure in green instantly clarifies the direction and net value of the transfer at a glance.

  • Dual-layer information architecture: Separates the emotional/financial summary (top card) from the technical/audit trail (hash, fee) so each user type finds what they need without scrolling friction.

  • Persistent action bar: Send again, View asset in wallet, and View on block explorer transform a static receipt into a functional next-step launcher, reducing navigation depth.

  • Truncated but tappable addresses: Balances readability with the ability to drill into full address details, a classic crypto UX compromise.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Designed for busy, mobile-first crypto users who need to quickly confirm 'did my transaction go through, how much did it cost, and who got the money' without parsing raw blockchain data. The block explorer link and hash serve power users/auditors who need cryptographic proof, while the plain-English framing and color psychology (green = received, white/neutral = sent) serve mainstream, less technical users. This dual accommodation reflects Coinbase's broad worldwide audience spanning first-time wallet owners to experienced DeFi users.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any financial or record-keeping detail screen where users need both a quick emotional summary (what happened) and detailed audit data (proof/verification) — e.g., bank transfer receipts, invoice details, order confirmations, or blockchain transaction views. Ideal when follow-up actions (repeat, share, verify) are common next steps.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense receipt-style layout for simple, low-stakes confirmations where users don't need line-item breakdowns (e.g., a simple 'Message sent' toast). Also avoid exposing raw technical fields like transaction hashes to audiences who would find them confusing without an option to hide/collapse them behind progressive disclosure.

screens.name: Home Screen 11
screens.uxAnalysis: This is the most familiar screen in the flow, relying on established music player conventions rather than introducing new patterns. Playback controls, the scrubber, and artwork all appear where users expect them, minimizing the learning curve. Shazam's distinctive touch is how the timeline communicates the preview limit: displaying a total duration of 1:25 makes the listening gate explicit without needing a "preview" label or interrupting playback. The animated CTA subtly draws attention through peripheral motion while users focus on the transport controls above. The only ambiguity comes from the skip buttons, which imply a playback queue even though the interface never reveals what that queue contains.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven. The only strings are the track title, artist, timestamps, and the CTA carried unchanged from earlier screens. Worth noting that the trial incentive line present on the result screen is absent here, so this variant shows the gate without the offer — the same inconsistency observed between the video card and the artist card in the carousel.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Consistency with external convention — Jakob's law in its purest form: a media player that behaves like every other media player requires no learning, and this screen spends none of the user's attention on novelty.

  2. Disclosure through the interface itself — The 1:25 total communicates the limit of free playback more precisely than any label, and it does so before the user invests in listening rather than after.

  3. Determinate over indeterminate — Unlike the recognition phases earlier in this flow, playback has a knowable duration, and the design correctly switches to an exact progress representation.

  4. Peripheral motion for the commercial ask — Animating the CTA rather than enlarging or recolouring it lets the conversion prompt register without competing with the controls the user came to use.

  5. Persistent escape route — Close remains top-left, unchanged across every screen from listening through purchase, so the exit never has to be found.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (now playing screen) — Artwork, scrubber, three-button transport, overflow top-right. Shazam is reusing the parent product's player layout almost exactly, which makes the eventual handoff feel like continuation rather than transfer.

  2. Spotify (free tier previews and 30-second clips) — A shortened playable segment with the upgrade prompt adjacent, letting duration itself communicate the limit. Same gating logic, same placement.

  3. SoundCloud (Go+ preview playback) — Full transport controls over a truncated stream with an upgrade CTA in view, a fair comparison for offering real playback control over content the user does not fully have access to.
screens.whereToUse: This fits freemium media where a genuine, controllable sample precedes a purchase decision, and where a visible duration can carry the gating message without a label — music, audiobook, and podcast previews.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the free segment is too short for transport controls to be meaningful, where skip controls imply a queue the product cannot actually provide, and in any context where the preview's truncation is not visible in advance, since a clip that stops without warning reads as a fault rather than a limit.

screens.name: Home Screen 12
screens.uxAnalysis: This menu reflects what Shazam expects users to do after identifying a song, and its ordering makes that priority clear. Streaming appears first, followed by purchasing, saving, viewing the artist, and finally sharing—a sequence that aligns both with commercial value and likely user frequency, making it feel practical rather than overly promotional. The "Listen On:" header technically applies only to the first two options, yet the visual treatment presents all actions as a single list. Notably, playback pauses when the menu opens, suggesting this is intended as a decision point rather than a quick overlay, though it means dismissing the menu requires users to resume playback manually. The changing preview duration also reveals that Shazam's audio clips vary by source instead of using a fixed preview length.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Borderline — the menu is five labels, and the labels are the whole interface.

Every row is verb-first or destination-named, and each one tells the user exactly what will happen: "Buy on iTunes" names the store and the transaction, "Add to Library" names the outcome rather than the mechanism, "Go to Artist" names the destination. Nothing is euphemistic and nothing hides a cost — "Buy" is not softened to "Get", which matters on a screen where a neighbouring row leads to a free trial.

"Listen On:" is the weak string. The trailing colon is unusual in iOS menu headers and reads as a form label rather than a section title, and the scope problem is real: it accurately introduces Apple Music and iTunes but sits above five rows, three of which are not listening destinations. A user parsing the menu top-down gets a promise the list stops keeping after two items. Either a second header for the remaining group or a heavier divider would resolve it.

The register is consistent with the rest of the app — plain, short, sentence case, no marketing language inside the menu itself. The commercial pressure lives in the ordering, not the wording, which is the more durable way to do it.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Progressive disclosure — Five secondary actions kept out of the player's primary surface until asked for, protecting a screen whose main job is playback.

  2. Ordering as recommendation — Menu sequence is the design's opinion about what users want next; here the commercial and behavioural orderings align, which keeps it from reading as manipulation.

  3. Labels that predict outcomes — Each row states its consequence plainly, so no action requires a tap to understand — particularly important where one row initiates a purchase.

  4. Context preservation — Artwork, title, scrubber position, and CTA all remain visible around the menu, so the user never loses the object the actions apply to.

  5. Grouping without grouping cues — A scoped header over an unscoped list is the screen's one structural flaw; uniform dividers make two logical groups read as one.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (track overflow menus) — Same anchored popover with icon-and-label rows covering play, add, artist, and share; Shazam is reusing the parent product's menu component and conventions.

  2. Spotify (track context menus) — Comparable set — save, artist, share — collected behind an ellipsis on the now-playing screen, showing the pattern is category-standard for music players.

  3. SoundHound — The direct competitor offers the same post-identification action set including multiple streaming destinations, which makes Shazam's single-service list a visible contrast rather than a category norm.
screens.whereToUse: This fits media players and result screens where several secondary actions apply to one clearly identified object, and where surfacing them all inline would crowd a surface whose primary job is playback or content display.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit when one action dominates the others, where a single visible button beats a hidden menu, and when the actions are destructive or irreversible, since a compact list with uniform styling gives a purchase or a delete the same visual weight as a share.

screens.name: Browser
screens.uxAnalysis: The screen serves as a hero/cover panel for a content-discovery flow: before the user scrolls into the actual list of 65 artists, Shazam frames the collection with a branded illustration and an editorial pitch explaining what "Fast Forward" is and why it matters. This front-loads context and emotional framing (discovery, momentum, "artists to watch") so the subsequent list of names reads as curated and credible rather than an arbitrary index. The minimal top bar (close + overflow) keeps the focus entirely on the hero content, and the downward chevron does the wayfinding work a button normally would, cueing the user to scroll rather than tap.
screens.tonalityAndContent: This is a copy-driven screen — machinery is minimal (a close icon, an overflow icon, an illustration, and a chevron), so the headline and subtext carry the entire user proposition. The tone is aspirational and confident ("most exciting talent," "set to make waves"), positioning Shazam as a tastemaker discovering talent early rather than just an ID tool. The copy is benefit-framed toward status/discovery ("get ahead of what's next") rather than feature-framed, which suits the Browsing/Discovery flow well: it primes the user to view the list below as curated expertise, increasing perceived value of the artists they're about to scroll through. There's no explicit CTA label — the chevron implies "keep scrolling" — which works here since the desired action is exploration, not conversion.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Progressive disclosure: the hero panel withholds the actual artist list until the user scrolls, controlling pacing and building anticipation before the payload.

  2. Von Restorff effect (framing): the glowing, high-contrast illustration and bold "2026" numerals make this feel like a flagship editorial moment rather than a routine list screen.

  3. Recognition over recall: minimal chrome (X, •••, chevron) relies on universally recognized icons instead of labeled buttons, reducing cognitive load.

  4. Aesthetic-usability effect: the polished gradient/illustration increases perceived credibility of the curation, even before any artist data is shown.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Spotify (Wrapped / Radar editorial covers) — uses the same hero-illustration-plus-headline pattern before revealing a curated artist or track list, for the same reason: framing curation as an editorial event.

  2. Apple Music (New Music Daily / playlist cover pages) — similar full-bleed cover art and short descriptive copy precede a track/artist list, establishing tone before content.

  3. YouTube Music (charts/moments covers) — comparable hero banners introduce algorithmic or editorial collections with a short mission statement before the list.
screens.whereToUse: This Featured/Hero Merchandising pattern fits best as the entry point to editorial or curated collections (year-end lists, trending charts, seasonal roundups) where framing and credibility matter more than immediate task completion.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for utilitarian or frequently-revisited lists (e.g., a user's own saved Shazams or search results), where the extra scroll-past hero content only adds friction without adding discovery value.

screens.name: Home Screen 13
screens.uxAnalysis: This is the deepest content view in the flow, dedicated entirely to reading. Nearly every control is removed, while the blurred album artwork becomes atmosphere instead of the focal point, allowing the lyrics to dominate the screen. The blur preserves the album's color palette without competing with the text, and the centered layout with generous line spacing reflects how lyrics are consumed—in short, rhythmic phrases rather than as continuous prose. Notably, the screen contains no subscription prompts or playback upsells, showing the same restraint seen in the expanded artwork view. The one unanswered question is whether the lyrics sync with playback, as that single behavior determines whether this is simply a reading interface or a true companion to the listening experience.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Not applicable in the product sense — the text filling this screen is the song's lyrics, a third-party creative work rather than interface copy, and it is not Shazam's voice to analyse. I won't reproduce any of it here.

What is worth noting is the app's typographic treatment of that content: no attribution line, no songwriter credit, and no licensing mark is visible in the frame, and the only product strings present are the inherited track title and artist in the header. The interface says nothing at all on this screen, which is the correct editorial choice when the content is someone else's writing.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Content-first minimalism — Chrome reduced to a header and one action, matching the earlier expanded-artwork view; the app consistently gets out of the way at the deepest level of a drill-down.

  2. Legibility through defocus — Blurring the artwork preserves colour identity while removing high-frequency detail, which is what makes light text over a busy illustration readable at all.

  3. Typographic setting matched to content type — Centred, widely leaded lines suit sung phrasing; the same text set as left-aligned paragraphs would read as poetry criticism rather than a song.

  4. Restraint at the point of attention — No conversion element on a screen the user chose deliberately, preserving the credibility of the asks made elsewhere in the flow.

  5. Contrast risk carried by the background — Light text over a sampled image has no guaranteed contrast ratio; here the mid-tones are dark enough, but a pale album would put this pattern under real strain.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (lyrics view) — Identical treatment of full-bleed colour-sampled background with centred lyric text and minimal chrome; Shazam is inheriting the parent product's component and its licensing pipeline.

  2. Spotify (lyrics panel) — Colour-extracted background behind large centred lines, comparable in using the release's own palette to make a shared template feel track-specific.

  3. Genius — Lyrics as a destination in their own right rather than a playback overlay, a fair comparison for how a lyrics surface is structured when reading, not syncing, is the primary use.
screens.whereToUse: This fits deep content views where text the user explicitly requested should dominate — lyrics, transcripts, poems, long-form quotes — and where a source image can supply visual identity once defocused enough to stop competing.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the user needs to act while reading, since stripping controls forces a return trip for any next step, and wherever background images cannot be constrained for contrast — a light or high-contrast source image would make the same layout unreadable.

screens.name: Home Screen 18
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen clarifies the playback model by revealing the active queue and its source. The bottom strip identifies the collection being played—Kate Bush Top Tracks—making the skip controls meaningful by showing exactly what users are navigating through. It also highlights an inconsistency in the preview experience: this track lasts 47 seconds, compared with earlier previews of 1:25 and 0:58, suggesting preview lengths vary without explanation. The most noticeable visual change is the orange progress indicator, replacing the teal used on previous player screens. Unless intentionally artwork-driven, this shift weakens the consistency of the playback interface by giving the progress state a different visual identity from one track to the next.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven. The strings are track metadata, timestamps, and two labels on the source strip.

Worth noting: "PLAYING" as an all-caps eyebrow above the playlist name is the second all-caps label in the flow after "READ MORE", again breaking the sentence-case convention the app otherwise holds. It is also slightly redundant — the transport already shows pause, which means playing — though it does usefully distinguish "this is the source of what you hear" from "this is a playlist you might open. The track title truncates mid-parenthetical, cutting the remaster year that distinguishes this version from the original, on the one screen where knowing which version is playing matters most.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Naming the context — Identifying the queue turns skip controls from unexplained affordances into scoped navigation; the user knows where they are and what comes next.

  2. Consistency with external convention — Transport layout, scrubber, and source strip follow the universal player model, so nothing here needs learning.

  3. Determinate progress where duration is known — Exact position and total are shown, correctly distinct from the indeterminate patterns used during recognition.

  4. Gating made visible but not explained — The short total discloses the limit numerically, but variable preview lengths across tracks give the user no stable expectation.

  5. Accent instability — A progress colour that changes per track weakens a signal the rest of the flow had used consistently; system colours generally should not be content-derived.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (now playing with queue source) — Artwork, transport, and a bottom strip naming the playing source; Shazam is reusing the parent product's player structure almost exactly.

  2. Spotify (now playing from a named playlist) — Same convention of surfacing the queue's name beneath the controls so skip has visible scope.

  3. SoundCloud (Go+ preview playback in a set) — Truncated streams played consecutively within a named collection, a fair comparison for stepping through gated previews.
screens.whereToUse: This fits playback within a defined collection where the user benefits from knowing the source and being able to move through it — playlists, albums, and queued previews.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit for one-off playback with no queue, where skip controls and a source strip imply structure that does not exist, and where preview durations vary so widely that transport controls promise more continuity than the content delivers.

screens.name: Home Screen 19
screens.uxAnalysis: Expanding the queue preserves playback in a compact header, keeping transport controls, progress, and artwork visible while users browse the track list. This is an effective trade-off, as it allows users to jump between songs without losing control of playback. The currently playing track is indicated with a subtle animated equalizer, clearly showing position without distracting from the list itself. The most significant change is the full-width Apple Music banner placed above the queue, making the subscription offer the most prominent commercial element in the flow. While this placement is logical for users encountering repeated preview limits, it noticeably increases the emphasis on conversion. The queue also clarifies its scope by including featured appearances alongside the artist's own songs, showing that Top Tracks extends beyond a strictly personal catalog.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven in the banner — this is the first time the conversion ask gets more than a single line, and the extra room changes what it can argue.

"Listen to full tracks, albums and more on Apple Music. Up to 2 months free." does something the earlier "Play Full Song" could not: it names the scope of what a subscription unlocks. The user has just been stepping through 45-second previews, so "full tracks" answers the specific frustration in front of them, and "albums and more" widens it without listing features. Leading with the benefit and putting the offer second is the correct order — the trial is the mechanism, not the pitch. It is also the first time the two-month offer appears as a complete sentence rather than a hedged fragment, though "up to" survives intact.

"Listen on Apple Music" as the CTA is a destination label rather than an action label, which reads as less committal than "Try it free" or "Subscribe" — arguably too soft, since tapping leads to a purchase sheet rather than to listening. A user could reasonably expect this button to start playback.

The section heading reuses the playlist name exactly as it appeared in the collapsed source strip, so the user knows without checking that this is the same queue expanded rather than a different list.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Context preserved during navigation — Collapsing rather than replacing the player keeps transport and position available while the user scans, which is what makes jumping within a queue a one-step action.

  2. Low-weight current-item marking — An animated equalizer identifies the playing row without competing with the list's scanability, and its motion doubles as a playback status signal.

  3. Argument sized to the objection — The banner's extra space is spent naming what the subscription removes ("full tracks"), which is precisely the limit the user has been hitting.

  4. Escalating commercial prominence — Conversion moves from a subordinate line to a full banner above the content; effective, but this is the loudest ask in the flow and it now uses a fifth accent colour.

  5. Honest scope, unlabelled — The queue includes a guest appearance under another artist's name, which is accurate to "top tracks" but may read as an error without a clarifying label.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (queue view with now-playing indicator) — Collapsed player over a scrollable queue with an equalizer marking the current row; Shazam is reusing the parent product's component directly.

  2. Spotify (free tier queue with upgrade banner) — An upgrade block placed above or within a list of gated tracks, framed around removing the specific limitation the user is hitting.

  3. YouTube Music (playlist view with Premium prompt) — Comparable in surfacing a subscription banner at the head of a list whose items are partially restricted.
screens.whereToUse: This fits queue and playlist views in freemium media where the user is stepping through limited previews, and where a banner can name the specific restriction being lifted rather than pitching a subscription abstractly.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the list is short enough that a banner crowds out the content, and where the user has no recurring friction to relieve — a prominent upgrade block above a list the user can fully access reads as an advertisement rather than an answer.

screens.name: Home Screen 20
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen closes the deepest path in the flow by ending the queue with a second subscription prompt. Unlike the banner at the top of the list, this one appears only after users reach the end, making it feel like a natural conclusion rather than an interruption. The messaging also shifts in scope, moving from unlocking a specific track to accessing the entire music catalog—a fitting transition after users have explored the limits of preview playback. While the pitch becomes more generic, its placement is less intrusive because it appears only after the content has been exhausted. Throughout the experience, the pinned player remains visible, ensuring playback controls stay accessible even while scrolling through a long queue.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven — the closing block is three lines and they carry the whole ask.

"Want more?" is well-judged as a terminal headline. It is a question rather than a command, it arrives exactly when the answer is likely yes, and it presumes nothing — a user who has reached the end of a list has demonstrated interest, so the question is genuinely responsive rather than rhetorical. It also mirrors the "Wrong song?" construction used in the error path, so the app has a consistent habit of opening with the user's own likely thought.

"Listen to 100 million songs" is the flow's first use of scale as an argument, and it is a considered escalation. Earlier asks named the immediate benefit — full tracks, this album, this artist — because the user's desire was specific. At the end of a finite list, the specific desire is exhausted, so switching to catalogue breadth is the correct next argument. The number does work that adjectives cannot: "millions of songs" would be forgettable, a concrete figure is not.

"Up to 2 months free" appears for the fourth time in the flow, unchanged and still hedged. Consistency across every surface is genuinely valuable here — the offer never varies, so the user is never given cause to suspect different terms in different places — but "up to" continues to defer the real number to conditions never shown.

"Listen on Apple Music" remains a destination label rather than an action label, so it still under-promises the commitment: tapping leads toward a purchase sheet, not toward listening.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Terminal placement — An offer at the natural end of a finite list obstructs nothing and arrives when the user's immediate goal is complete, which is the least costly position a commercial ask can occupy.

  2. Argument scaled to context — Shifting from track-specific benefit to catalogue breadth matches what the user has just learned about the product's limits.

  3. Persistent playback controls — Pinning the collapsed player means a long scroll never costs the user transport access or position awareness.

  4. Consistent offer terms — The same two-month framing on every surface removes any suspicion that terms vary by entry point.

  5. Bracketed asks — Opening and closing the same list with the same offer is defensible individually but doubles the commercial density of a single view.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Spotify (free tier playlist end-of-list upgrade prompts) — Terminal upgrade blocks closing a list of partially gated tracks, framed around catalogue access; the closest structural match.

  2. YouTube Music (Premium prompt at the end of a queue) — Comparable placement of a subscription pitch after the content runs out rather than interleaved with it.

  3. Apple Music (in-app upsell blocks for non-subscribers) — The component styling, red pill, and offer phrasing are the parent product's, which is why the ask looks native rather than bolted on.
screens.whereToUse: This fits the end of finite lists in freemium products where the user has just exhausted the free experience, and where a catalogue-scale argument is the natural next thing to say once track-specific desire is satisfied.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit for infinite or paginated lists where a terminus never arrives, and where the same offer already appeared at the top of the same view — repeating an identical ask within one scroll adds pressure without adding information.

screens.name: Find Concerts 3
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen clarifies that the play control on each concert row previews the artist's music rather than the event itself. That is an effective choice, allowing users to confirm their interest in the artist without leaving the tour list or interrupting the process of comparing dates and saving events. The floating now-playing pill also behaves consistently with the result screen, acting as a persistent playback control that follows users across different parts of the app. This continuity strengthens the overall experience by making audio management predictable regardless of context. The main drawback is its placement: with only a single result on screen, the floating pill sits directly above the search field, creating two stacked floating elements in the same corner and making the interface feel less balanced.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven. No strings have changed from the previous capture; the only difference is control state and the addition of an unlabelled indicator.

Worth noting that the now-playing pill carries no text at all — no track name, no artist — so a user who has scrolled away from the source has an equalizer icon and no indication of what is playing. On the result screen that was acceptable because the track was named directly above it; here, on a concert list, nothing on screen identifies the audio.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Preview before commitment — Letting a user hear the artist from a ticketing list addresses the actual uncertainty at that moment: whether they like them enough to attend.

  2. Global playback handle — The same pill, position, and behaviour across unrelated surfaces means audio control is learned once and works everywhere.

  3. Playback without navigation — Previewing in place preserves list position and the triage flow the per-row save supports.

  4. State toggle in the thumbnail — Play becoming pause in the same target means stopping requires no visual search.

  5. Unlabelled and unanchored indicator — The pill names nothing and floats above empty space, stacked with the search field in one corner.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Spotify and Apple Music — Persistent mini-players following the user across browse, search, and library surfaces; the convention this pill abbreviates.

  2. Bandsintown — Comparable in offering artist previews from tour listings so users can evaluate before buying.

  3. SoundCloud — Inline row-level playback with a global transport handle, matching the play-in-place-then-control-anywhere model.
screens.whereToUse: This fits list surfaces where audio helps a decision the list is asking the user to make, and where a persistent global handle already exists to control playback started anywhere.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where audio is incidental to the task, since a floating indicator adds chrome without aiding the decision, and where the indicator cannot identify what is playing — an unlabelled handle on a screen with no visible source leaves the user unable to tell what they are hearing.

screens.name: Browser Mini Player
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen extends the Fast Forward 2026 discovery flow into a Master–Detail pattern: selecting an artist from the curated list opens a dedicated profile with identity context — name, genre, country — and a ranked "Top Songs" list. The floating mini-player acts as a lightweight preview, letting users sample audio without leaving the profile. Each song row pairs a Shazam popularity count with a direct Apple Music action, connecting discovery — how often a track is Shazamed — with conversion to streaming.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Progressive disclosure (Master–Detail): the list-to-detail drill-down keeps the initial Fast Forward list uncluttered while letting interested users go deeper on one artist.

  2. Recognition over recall: album art thumbnails and consistent Shazam-count badges let users scan popularity at a glance rather than reading numbers in context each time.

  3. Consistency & standards: every song row repeats the same layout (art, title, artist, Shazam count, Apple Music button), reducing learning cost as the user scrolls.

  4. Minimal viable interruption: the mini-player overlays rather than replaces the screen, and includes its own dismiss "X", so preview listening doesn't derail browsing.

  5. Recognition via social proof: the Shazam-count badge functions as a lightweight social-proof signal reinforcing why this artist made a curated "rising talent" list.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Spotify (Artist page) — same Master–Detail pattern: tapping an artist from a chart/playlist opens a profile with Popular/Top Songs list and inline play controls.

  2. Apple Music (Artist page) — comparable header (name, genre) plus a ranked track list with play affordances per row.

  3. SoundCloud (Artist profile from a curated chart) — similar drill-down from a discovery list into an artist page with play counts and a persistent mini-player.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any music-discovery product where users move from a curated/ranked list into individual artist exploration and want to preview tracks without losing their place in the broader list.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for simple, flat catalogs with few tracks per artist, where a full drill-down page and persistent mini-player would add more navigation overhead than the content justifies.

screens.name: Browser Events
screens.uxAnalysis: This continuation of the artist Master–Detail page adds more context beneath Top Songs: a horizontally browsable album card and an Events module for upcoming tour dates. Alongside the persistent mini-player, the screen turns a simple artist lookup into a fuller artist hub — letting users preview music, explore the album, and discover shows without leaving the page. The "More About" control adds progressive disclosure, keeping the main view scannable while offering deeper biographical context on demand.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Progressive disclosure: the collapsed "More About Belly Gang Kushington" button hides biography detail until explicitly requested, keeping the page lean.

  2. Recognition over recall: the page-control dots under the album carousel give a lightweight positional cue without requiring numeric labels.

  3. Chunking (Gestalt: proximity): songs, album, and events are grouped into clearly separated sections/cards, helping users parse different content types at a glance.

  4. Minimal viable interruption: the mini-player persists across scroll positions so a preview can continue uninterrupted while the user explores album and event info.

  5. Actionable content over passive info: the Events card pairs a date with a direct "See All" link, converting discovery into a concrete next action (checking tour dates) rather than static text.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Spotify (Artist page — Discography + Concerts sections) — same combination of album carousel and upcoming shows/events module beneath the top tracks list.

  2. Apple Music (Artist page) — comparable "Albums" horizontal carousel and expandable "About" section pattern.

  3. Bandsintown / Songkick embedded in artist profiles — same event-card format (date block + short description + "See All") used to surface concerts tied to an artist.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern suits rich artist/creator profile pages where users benefit from consolidated access to discography, live events, and biography in one scrollable hub, especially in music discovery or fan-engagement apps.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for lightweight or transactional artist references (e.g., a simple track-attribution tooltip or search-result snippet), where surfacing albums, events, and expandable bios would add unnecessary depth to a quick lookup.

screens.name: Concert Date Result
screens.uxAnalysis: This is the strongest empty state in the flow because it explains both the problem and the path forward. Unlike the earlier location search, which simply reported no results, this screen attributes the outcome to the active filters, keeps the artist visible through the avatar, and offers a single, meaningful recovery action. The highlighted filter chips reinforce the explanation by showing exactly which constraints produced the empty result, while View All Dates focuses on the user's goal rather than the underlying mechanism, maintaining consistent terminology across the concert experience. The only limitation is that recovery is all-or-nothing: users can remove every constraint at once, but there is no quick way to relax just the date or location while preserving the other filter.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven — and this is the flow's most competent empty-state writing.

"No Concerts Here" is well chosen. "Here" locates the failure in the filtered region rather than in the artist's schedule, so it does not imply the artist has stopped touring. It is also short enough to read as a headline rather than a message.

"Looks like this artist has no concerts with your preferred options" does the thing the Location sheet failed to do: it names the cause. "Your preferred options" attributes the empty result to the filters rather than to the data or the user's error, which is both accurate and non-accusatory. "Looks like" softens it into an observation rather than a verdict — slightly casual against the app's usual register, but appropriate for a low-stakes miss.

The one imprecision is "preferred options", which is vaguer than it needs to be when the two chips above name the constraints exactly. "…in Los Angeles tomorrow" would have been more concrete and no longer.

"View All Dates" remains the flow's best-named escape, consistent across three surfaces now.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Cause named, not just outcome — Attributing the empty result to the applied filters turns a dead end into a diagnosable state.

  2. Subject kept present — The artist avatar keeps the search's object visible, so the message reads as specific rather than as generic system failure.

  3. Diagnosis and remedy co-located — Lit chips show which constraints caused the miss while the button removes them, both within one glance.

  4. Outcome-named recovery — "View All Dates" describes what the user will get rather than what the control does, and means the same thing on every surface it appears.

  5. All-or-nothing escape — No option to relax one facet while keeping the other, so a user who wants Los Angeles on any date must start over.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Airbnb — Over-filtered searches return an explanation naming the filters plus a broadened-search action; the closest structural match.

  2. Bandsintown / Songkick — Category equivalents that surface all tour dates when a location or date filter returns nothing.

  3. Eventbrite — Comparable empty states that keep the applied filters visible while offering a single widening action.
screens.whereToUse: This fits over-constrained filtered searches where the cause is knowable and a single widening action resolves it, particularly where keeping the search subject visible reassures the user nothing was lost.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where multiple facets could each be relaxed independently, since a single all-or-nothing escape discards constraints the user wanted to keep, and where the empty result reflects genuinely absent data rather than filter tightness.

screens.name: Set Location 3
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen resolves the uncertainty from the previous state by confirming that the search completed and found no matching location. Retaining the query in the search field, alongside a clear button, makes refinement easier than starting over, while the persistent Near Me shortcut provides an immediate fallback throughout the failed search. The weakest element is the recovery guidance: "Try searching again" offers little practical help beyond restating the outcome. More useful suggestions—such as entering a city or postcode, showing recent searches, or offering nearby locations—would better support recovery. The full-height sheet also feels oversized for such a minimal empty state, leaving a large amount of unused space that makes the experience feel less considered.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven — two lines are the entire state, and they are the difference between silence and communication.

"No results" is the correct headline. It is plain, it names the outcome rather than blaming the input ("Invalid location" would imply user error), and it is scoped to the search rather than to the app. Two words carry the fact.

"Try searching again." is the weaker line, and it is the same species of filler observed earlier in this flow with "Please wait". It occupies the slot where guidance belongs and spends it restating the only action available.
