screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing & Updating 8
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen presents a binary privacy decision (Public vs. Private profile visibility) using large, tappable card-style radio selections rather than a simple toggle or dropdown. This is a deliberate elevation of an important, consequence-bearing decision to a full-attention UI pattern. Each option is paired with a clear, plain-language explanation of what happens to the user's data, removing ambiguity around technical privacy terminology.

Below the primary choice, a secondary, lower-stakes setting ("Personalized content") is presented as a simple switch, correctly signaling a difference in decision weight and reversibility between the two settings. The visual hierarchy—large radio cards up top, smaller toggle below—mirrors the cognitive load hierarchy of the decisions themselves.

The layout uses generous vertical spacing, a single-column flow, and a dark theme with a bright blue accent to draw the eye directly to the selected/recommended state. A back arrow at the top-left preserves the user's ability to exit without completing the step, which is appropriate since this is likely part of an onboarding or account setup flow (as suggested by the page control dots at the bottom).
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is short, direct, and reassuring. The subheading "You can change this anytime" pre-emptively reduces decision anxiety by lowering the perceived stakes of the choice — a classic friction-reduction technique for privacy-sensitive decisions.

Each option's description avoids jargon: "Anyone can search for your username and see your profile details" and "Your username and profile details will be hidden from public view" are symmetrical, parallel sentence structures that make comparison effortless. The "Personalized content" description ("Use your data to suggest assets, apps, and more that you might like") frames data usage as a user benefit rather than a data-collection admission, softening what is otherwise a data-tracking consent request.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Recommended badge: The inline "Recommended" label next to Public nudges users toward the platform's preferred (likely growth-oriented) default without being coercive or blocking the Private choice.

  • Card-based radio selection: Using full-width, bordered cards instead of small radio buttons increases tap target size and makes the selected state (blue border/glow) immediately legible at a glance.

  • Risk-reducing microcopy: "You can change this anytime" directly targets loss-aversion anxiety, making users more comfortable choosing quickly instead of stalling on a "permanent" feeling decision.

  • Decoupled granular toggle: Separating "Personalized content" (data usage/ads) from profile visibility (social exposure) avoids conflating two distinct privacy concerns into one confusing control.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users during onboarding/account setup for a social, finance, or crypto-style app (the "assets" reference in the personalization copy suggests fintech/crypto). The design assumes users are privacy-conscious but time-pressed, so it minimizes reading effort while still surfacing legally/ethically necessary consent (personalization/data usage).

Psychologically, the screen leverages the default effect (pre-selecting/recommending Public) and reversibility framing to overcome the natural hesitation users feel around irreversible-seeming privacy choices, increasing completion/conversion rates through this onboarding step while still respecting compliance requirements around explicit consent for personalization.
screens.whereToUse:
• Account creation or onboarding flows requiring an explicit profile visibility choice (social apps, marketplaces, fintech/crypto apps with public profiles).

  • Any screen where a binary but high-impact decision must be made clearly, paired with a lower-stakes, adjustable data preference.

  • Situations where regulatory or trust requirements mandate visible, explicit consent for personalized data use (GDPR/CCPA-adjacent flows).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy card-based pattern for trivial, low-consequence settings — it adds unnecessary visual weight and slows down flows where a simple switch would suffice.

  • Don't use a "Recommended" nudge if the recommended option primarily benefits the business at the clear expense of user privacy; this erodes trust once users realize the framing.

  • Not ideal for screens with more than 2-3 options, as large cards would force excessive scrolling — use a list or dropdown instead for many choices.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing & Updating 12
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a dedicated Security settings hub within what appears to be a multi-wallet crypto application. The layout follows a classic grouped-list settings pattern, segmented into three clear zones: Backups (per-wallet seed phrase/backup management), Security lock (authentication method selection), and Biometrics (partially visible at the bottom, likely for Face ID/Touch ID toggles).

The information hierarchy is strong: bold section headers separate unrelated concerns, while secondary gray helper text ("At least one option must be selected," "Only affects standard wallet") proactively answers questions before the user has to ask them, reducing support burden and confusion. Each wallet (Wallet 1, Wallet 2) is presented as its own drill-down row, acknowledging that this app supports multiple wallets with potentially independent backup states — an important scalability decision for power users managing several accounts.

The toggles for "Opening the app" and "Making a transaction" let users granularly control friction vs. security trade-offs, which is critical in a financial app where too much friction causes drop-off, but too little erodes trust. The system enforces a safety rail (at least one option must stay on) to prevent users from accidentally disabling all protection.

Dark theme with high-contrast white text and a single blue accent color for interactive toggles keeps the eye anchored to actionable elements while the rest recedes, appropriate for a security-critical, low-frequency-visit screen.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is terse, functional, and reassuring rather than alarmist — typical of fintech/crypto security UX where trust is paramount. Labels like "Lock method," "Require unlock when…" and "At least one option must be selected" are written in plain, unambiguous language avoiding technical jargon (e.g., no mention of "biometric APIs" or "keychain").

Micro-copy such as "Only affects standard wallet" is a subtle but important trust-building disclosure, clarifying scope of the toggle so users aren't left guessing whether hardware/cold wallets are also affected. This kind of contextual disambiguation is essential in crypto products where misunderstanding a security setting can lead to real financial loss.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Forced minimum security floor: The system explicitly requires at least one unlock trigger to remain active, preventing users from accidentally leaving their wallet completely unprotected.

  • Scoped disclosure text: "Only affects standard wallet" removes ambiguity about which assets a toggle governs, critical in multi-wallet architectures.

  • Per-wallet drill-down for backups: Treating each wallet's backup as its own navigable row scales cleanly to N wallets without cluttering the top level.

  • Granular unlock triggers: Separating "Opening the app" from "Making a transaction" gives users fine control over the security/convenience trade-off at different risk levels.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets crypto-savvy users managing multiple wallets who hold real financial value on-device and are highly sensitive to both security and usability. The design leans on the psychological principle of loss aversion — by making backup and lock settings prominent and impossible to fully disable, the app reduces the anxiety of "what if I lose access to my funds." It also respects user autonomy by allowing biometric convenience for routine actions (opening app) while optionally hardening the more consequential action (transactions), aligning security friction with actual risk level.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any app handling sensitive financial, health, or identity data where users need transparent, granular control over authentication behavior. Ideal for multi-account or multi-wallet products where different sub-entities may need independent backup/security states. Also effective whenever you need to prevent a user from disabling all protection accidentally — enforce a "cannot go below one" rule.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this level of granularity in low-stakes consumer apps where excessive security toggles create decision fatigue without real benefit. If an app only has a single account/wallet, per-item drill-down backup rows are unnecessary overhead — a single backup section suffices. Also avoid burying critical security actions (like backup) below the fold or without visual differentiation, as this reduces the likelihood users complete essential setup steps.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing & Updating 11
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a dedicated Security preference center for a crypto wallet application, structured into clear, digestible sections: Backups, Security Lock, Require Unlock When..., and Biometrics. The dark theme (near-black background) is a deliberate choice common in fintech/crypto apps, signaling seriousness, reducing eye strain during frequent checking, and subtly evoking a "vault" or "bank-grade" aesthetic.

The information architecture uses grouped list sections separated by hairline dividers, each with a bold section header. This chunking reduces cognitive load, allowing users to scan for the exact security lever they want to adjust without parsing a monolithic list. Navigational drill-down rows (Wallet 1, Wallet 2, Lock method) use the standard chevron affordance to indicate deeper configuration screens, following a classic Master-Detail settings pattern.

Critically, the "Require unlock when..." section pairs binary switches with contextual helper text directly beneath the toggle label (e.g., "Only affects standard wallet"), preventing ambiguity about scope — an important detail in high-stakes financial software where miscomprehension could lead to a false sense of security or accidental fund exposure. The inclusion of a constraint note ("At least one option must be selected") proactively communicates a validation rule before the user tries to disable both switches, reducing frustrating trial-and-error.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is terse, functional, and highly literal — typical of security/settings surfaces where clarity trumps personality. Labels like "Lock method," "Backups," and "Biometrics" are single- or two-word nouns that map directly to system concepts, minimizing translation effort for the user.

Helper microcopy is used surgically rather than decoratively: "Only affects standard wallet" and "At least one option must be selected" exist purely to prevent errors and set accurate expectations, not to entertain. This restraint is appropriate for a security context — playful or verbose copy here would undercut the perceived seriousness of protecting financial assets.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Scoped toggle disclaimers: Inline sublabels (e.g., "Only affects standard wallet") sitting directly under a switch eliminate misunderstanding about what exactly a security control governs, which is essential when multiple wallets have different protection needs.

  • Proactive validation messaging: Stating "At least one option must be selected" before the user attempts an invalid state avoids a jarring error later and builds trust that the app has sane security defaults.

  • Segmented settings grouping: Dividing Backups, Lock, Unlock Triggers, and Biometrics into visually separated blocks with bold headers turns a long settings list into an easily scannable set of mental categories.

  • Drill-down chevrons for complex sub-flows: Wallet-specific backup and lock-method configuration are pushed to secondary screens, keeping this main security hub lightweight and focused on high-level toggles.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users — an audience that is inherently anxious about asset loss/theft and typically more security-literate than average mobile users. The psychological driver here is control and reassurance: by exposing granular toggles (unlock on app open vs. unlock only on transaction) and biometric options, the app signals that the user — not a custodian — is fully in charge of their security posture, reinforcing the self-custody value proposition.

The dark, low-stimulation UI and unambiguous labeling cater to users making high-stakes decisions (protecting real monetary value), where any confusion or dark-pattern-like ambiguity could cause severe loss of trust or actual financial harm.
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any settings surface governing access control, authentication, or protection of sensitive data/assets — banking apps, password managers, health record apps, and enterprise admin consoles. It's especially effective when:

  • Multiple independent security mechanisms need to coexist (lock method + trigger conditions + biometrics).

  • Users manage multiple protected entities (e.g., multiple wallets/accounts) requiring per-item configuration via drill-down.

  • You need to prevent invalid states (e.g., zero security enabled) and want to communicate that constraint before it's hit.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, text-heavy grouped-list approach for casual consumer apps where security is a background concern rather than a primary use case — it would feel overly clinical. Also avoid burying critical scope disclaimers (like "only affects standard wallet") in small gray subtext if the consequence of misunderstanding is severe; in extremely high-risk flows, consider an explicit confirmation dialog or tooltip instead of relying on passive helper text that can be skimmed past.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing & Updating 10
screens.uxAnalysis:

The layout uses a single-column stacked list with clear section grouping (Wallets, Networks, Security, Display, Connect to Coinbase). Each row uses a two-line pattern — a bold label plus a muted descriptor — which lets users scan intent without opening the page. This "label + subtitle" convention reduces cognitive load significantly compared to icon-only or label-only rows, since crypto settings (Networks, Security, Passcode/backup/Face ID) are unfamiliar to many mainstream users.

The active wallet is rendered as an elevated, tinted Card rather than a plain list row, visually distinguishing "your identity" from generic settings and reinforcing that this is the object all subsequent settings act upon. A search bar sits at the top for direct access, acknowledging that a power-user settings menu can grow long as more chains/features are added.

The bottom tab bar persists, keeping global navigation (home, browser, swap, activity, wallet) accessible even while deep in a settings screen, which is a strong choice for a non-modal settings experience.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy is terse, functional, and utilitarian — typical of an infrastructure/finance tool rather than a lifestyle app. Row subtitles ("Recovery phrase, profile, connections, and more", "Passcode, backup, Face ID", "Dark mode, currency, balances, language") act as inline previews, compressing multiple sub-settings into one scannable line instead of forcing a tap-to-discover approach.

The use of the human-readable identity alexsmithmobbin.cb.id instead of a raw 0x hex address is a deliberate tone choice: it humanizes an otherwise intimidating blockchain address and reduces the "cold, technical" feel typically associated with crypto wallets.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Identity-first architecture: The wallet name/ENS card is visually promoted above generic settings, anchoring the whole screen around "who you are" before "what you configure."

  • Compound subtitles: Grouping related sub-settings into one descriptive line (e.g., "Passcode, backup, Face ID") lets users predict content before navigating, reducing exploratory taps.

  • Persistent bottom tab bar: Settings remains part of the primary navigation shell rather than a full-screen takeover, letting users jump to swap/browse without back-tracking.

  • Search-first affordance: A prominent search bar at the top acknowledges the long-tail complexity of wallet settings and gives power users a fast escape from scrolling.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users, ranging from onboarding newcomers to experienced multi-chain traders. The psychological anchor is trust and control: because losing a recovery phrase means permanent loss of funds, the design elevates Security and the wallet identity card to the top of the hierarchy to reduce anxiety and reinforce that the user is in command of their asset custody.

The ENS-style human-readable name (vs. a hex address) leverages the recognition-over-recall principle, making the wallet feel personal and less error-prone when sharing/verifying identity. The "Connect to Coinbase" row taps into familiarity bias for users migrating from custodial exchanges, bridging Web2 comfort with Web3 self-custody.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this compound stacked-list settings pattern when:

  • Your app has many distinct configuration categories that benefit from grouping (finance, security, or multi-account apps).

  • Users need to understand what's inside a section without tapping in — critical for high-stakes/finance UX.

  • You want to spotlight a primary object (account/wallet/profile) distinctly from secondary settings via card treatment.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The settings list is short (under ~6 items) — the extra visual weight of subtitles and cards becomes unnecessary overhead.

  • Users are unfamiliar with the vocabulary used in subtitles (e.g., "recovery phrase") without any onboarding context, which can increase confusion instead of reducing it.

  • The product is casual/low-stakes, where such heavy security emphasis (Face ID, backup, passcode) at the top may feel excessive or intimidating.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing & Updating 13
screens.uxAnalysis:

Toggles are used for binary security requirements (app opening, transaction signing, change protection), each paired with contextual helper text directly beneath it when nuance is needed (e.g., "Only affects standard wallet"). screens.tonalityAndContent:

Helper text such as "Only affects standard wallet" and "Require entering your recovery phrase if your biometrics change" is written in plain, jargon-light language despite the technical subject matter, helping non-expert crypto users understand consequences before they toggle a switch.

screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline value preview on drill-down rows: "Lock method" shows "Face ID" directly in the list row, letting users confirm current configuration without an extra tap.

  • Enforced minimum security constraint: The explicit note "At least one option must be selected" prevents users from disabling all unlock requirements, protecting them from an insecure default.

  • Contextual safeguard messaging: Explaining that changing biometrics without "Change protection" enabled could bypass recovery-phrase verification builds user trust and educates on security trade-offs at the point of decision.

  • Scoped setting clarification: "Only affects standard wallet" clarifies toggle scope for multi-wallet setups, preventing false assumptions about hardware/other wallet types.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

The psychological drivers at play include loss aversion (users fear losing access or funds, so the screen reassures via explicit constraints and explanations) and need for control/transparency (crypto-native users expect granular, explicit toggles rather than opaque automatic security, reflecting Web3 values of self-custody and user sovereignty).

The inclusion of biometric and recovery-phrase safeguards also speaks to more advanced/security-conscious users who understand device compromise risks (e.g., someone else's fingerprint being added to a phone), while helper copy accommodates less technical users by explaining consequences in plain language.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this grouped-toggle-with-inline-preview pattern for any settings screen governing sensitive, irreversible, or security-critical actions — financial apps, password managers, health data apps, or enterprise admin consoles. It's ideal when:

  • Multiple related boolean settings need logical grouping under clear section headers.

  • Users need to see current configuration state without extra navigation (inline value labels).

  • Certain combinations of settings are invalid and must be prevented via inline constraint messaging rather than after-the-fact error dialogs.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense settings-list approach for onboarding or first-run experiences, where users are unfamiliar with terminology like "Lock method" or "Change protection" — a wizard or guided setup would be more appropriate there. It's also unsuitable for low-stakes preference settings where verbose helper text would feel like unnecessary friction. Additionally, if the toggles have complex interdependencies beyond a simple "at least one required" rule, a plain list of switches may not sufficiently communicate the logic, requiring a more visual or wizard-based configuration flow instead.

screens.name: Dark Mode Library Edit
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen supports the Deleting & Removing flow by letting users select multiple library entries at once, a significant efficiency gain for a library that could grow to dozens or hundreds of tracks. The persistent "2 selected" status pill keeps the selection count visible alongside the trash action, reducing the risk of deleting the wrong number of items. Placing the delete icon directly beside the counter also ties the destructive action to its scope, making it clear what will be affected before the user commits.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Content → Deleting & Removing (multi-selecting library items for bulk deletion)
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Bulk action efficiency: multi-select with a single delete action for all chosen items avoids the friction of repeated single-item deletion flows.

  2. Visibility of system status: the "2 selected" pill and filled blue checkmarks on selected rows continuously confirm exactly what will be affected by the pending delete action.

  3. Clear selected vs. unselected states: the visual contrast between empty circle outlines and filled blue checkmarks makes scanning which items are selected fast and unambiguous.

  4. Contained mode entry/exit: the "Done" button provides an obvious, low-friction way to exit selection mode without needing to complete a delete action.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Photos (multi-select mode for batch deleting photos) — same pattern of circular selection controls, a selected-count indicator, and a bulk delete action.

screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any list or library view where users are likely to want to remove multiple items at once, letting them avoid the friction of repeated single-item delete confirmations.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for short lists where users rarely need to delete more than one item at a time, where introducing a full multi-select mode would add unnecessary UI complexity compared to a simple per-row delete action (e.g., a swipe-to-delete gesture).

screens.name: Pro Benefits Menu
screens.uxAnalysis: The pairing is odd: an overflow menu with just two items puts the app's least reversible action directly under its sales pitch, separated by a hairline. The destructive treatment itself follows iOS convention correctly (red, last position), though whether it confirms before deleting isn't visible here. Worth correcting from the last frame: the toolbar greying isn't a defect — it tracks which menu is open, dimming the active chip while its menu is presented, which retroactively explains the earlier "Live Activity" greying. The Pro entry point here is the fifth distinct monetisation surface across this set (onboarding, comparison table, loading caption, feature card, now this), and none is aggressive alone, but the cumulative effect is a funnel that's never far away.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Two labels, and the contrast between them is stark.

"View Pro Benefits" — "View" rather than "Upgrade" or "Get Pro" is a deliberate softening. It promises information, not a transaction, which lowers the cost of tapping and matches the comparison sheet seen earlier (which showed features and no prices). The whole Pro funnel in this app follows the same pattern: show, don't ask. "Benefits" rather than "Features" is framed from the user's side, though it's the one word here doing marketing rather than description.

"PRO" badge — a bordered monochrome pill rather than the orange used for "FLIGHTY EXCLUSIVE" in the comparison table. Restrained, and it doubles as a state indicator: its presence implies the user doesn't have Pro, which is information the row's label alone doesn't carry.

"Delete" — bare, unqualified, and slightly under-specified. Delete what? The flight from My Flights, presumably, but "Delete" alone could plausibly read as deleting data, history, or the sharing link. "Remove Flight" or "Stop Tracking" would name the object and, importantly, convey that the flight itself is unaffected — the user is removing it from their list, not cancelling anything. On a screen about air travel, an unqualified "Delete" in red is a fractionally more alarming word than the action warrants.

The two labels also differ in structure: one is verb-plus-object, the other bare verb. Consistency would help.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Group by category, not by leftover — an overflow holding one commercial link and one destructive action mixes unrelated intents in a two-item list.

  2. Destructive styling is correct — red label, red glyph, last position, matching platform convention.

  3. Name the object in destructive labels — "Delete" alone doesn't say what's removed, and "Remove Flight" would reassure that nothing real is affected.

  4. Chip dimming tracks the open menu — the active chip greys while its menu is presented, a consistent signal across both toolbar frames.

  5. Low-friction monetisation — "View" rather than "Upgrade" keeps the fifth Pro surface informational rather than transactional.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Mail / Notes (overflow menus) — destructive action last, red, with the object named ("Delete Message").

  2. Spotify / YouTube (in-context upgrade rows) — a Pro entry inside a menu with a tier badge, informational rather than transactional in label.

  3. Apple Calendar (event actions) — management actions grouped away from account or subscription concerns.
screens.whereToUse: Best where an overflow genuinely collects secondary actions on the object at hand, with destructive items styled and positioned per platform convention. A badged upgrade row works when the label promises information rather than a purchase.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit when the menu holds only two items of unrelated kinds — the upgrade belongs with account or settings, not beside a delete. Also wrong when a destructive label doesn't name its object, since the user must infer the blast radius.

screens.name: Delete Archive 01
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen shows the search field replaced by a prominent "Clear All" option, styled in red to signal its destructive nature, likely surfaced by tapping into the search bar (a common pattern where an empty search state offers a quick bulk action) or via a swipe/reveal gesture. Notably, "Edit" in the top-left now appears dimmed/inactive, suggesting the interface has shifted into a distinct mode where bulk-clear is the primary available action rather than the individual per-item edit/delete flow "Edit" would normally provide — though the exact trigger and full interaction model can't be confirmed from this single frame. The red color and trash icon clearly signal irreversible consequence, appropriately using visual weight to differentiate this from the app's typical blue/neutral action styling.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "Clear All" is short, direct, and unambiguous — appropriately blunt for a destructive, irreversible bulk action where any softening language could create false expectations about reversibility.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Color-Coded Destructive Actions — using red specifically for "Clear All" (versus the app's standard blue for other actions) immediately signals higher-consequence, harder-to-reverse behavior.

  2. Efficient Bulk Management — offering a single "Clear All" action avoids requiring users to individually select and delete many archived tabs one at a time.

  3. State-Dependent Controls — "Edit" appearing dimmed while "Clear All" is active suggests the interface intentionally limits available actions to avoid conflicting or redundant controls in this particular state.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Mail app's "Trash All" in a folder view — uses an identical red, icon-paired "Clear All"-style action for bulk-deleting items in a list.

  2. Safari's "Clear History and Website Data" — offers a comparable prominent, red-styled bulk-clear action for browsing history.

  3. Photos app's "Delete All" in Recently Deleted — follows the same visual convention (red text, trash icon) for irreversible bulk removal.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any list-management interface (history, archive, cache) where users may accumulate many entries over time and benefit from a fast, clearly-marked bulk-clear option distinct from selective, one-by-one deletion.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit if invoked too easily or without a confirmation step, since an irreversible bulk-delete action needs sufficient friction (like a confirmation dialog) to prevent accidental data loss — whether this screen leads to such a confirmation isn't visible here.

screens.name: Delete Archive 02
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen confirms the "Clear All" action from the previous screenshot successfully executed, removing both archived entries and replacing the list with a proper empty state rather than a blank or broken-looking screen. Beyond simply stating there's nothing here, the body copy does double duty as onboarding-style guidance: it explains what content types populate this space ("Manually closed and auto-archived tabs") and proactively points to a related setting ("adjust the auto-archive frequency in Settings"), which is a thoughtful detail — a user landing on an empty Archive might reasonably wonder why nothing appears here yet, and this copy answers that implicit question without requiring them to search elsewhere. Notably, the search bar and "Edit"/"Clear All" controls seen in prior screens are entirely absent here, since there's nothing to search or manage once the archive is empty — the UI correctly reduces to only what's relevant for a genuinely empty state.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "Nothing here yet!" uses light, approachable phrasing with an exclamation point, avoiding a cold or clinical tone for what is otherwise a mundane empty-list message — consistent with the app's broader playful voice established in onboarding. The follow-up sentence shifts to a more instructive register, explaining both what populates this space and where to adjust a related behavior, striking a good balance between friendly tone and genuinely useful information rather than being empty style over substance.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Actionable Empty States — going beyond "there's nothing here" to explain what would appear and where to adjust settings turns a dead-end screen into a small moment of orientation.

  2. Contextual Cross-Reference — pointing directly to "Settings" for adjusting auto-archive frequency saves the user from having to independently discover that this behavior is configurable.

  3. Minimal UI for Empty States — removing the search bar and edit controls (present when content exists) avoids offering functionally meaningless options once there's nothing to search or manage.

  4. Confirmation Through Absence — the transition from a populated list to this empty state is itself implicit confirmation that the "Clear All" action succeeded, without needing an additional toast or message.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Gmail's empty inbox/trash state — uses similarly friendly copy paired with brief explanatory text about what would populate the list.

  2. Dropbox's empty folder state — offers comparable guidance-style empty-state copy explaining what content type belongs there.

  3. Notion's empty database view — pairs a light, approachable headline with practical guidance on populating or configuring the view.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any list or archive view that can be legitimately empty (either from having nothing yet or after a bulk-clear action), where brief, friendly guidance about what belongs there and how to adjust related settings adds real value over a bare "no results" message.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for lists that are conceptually never expected to be empty in normal use (e.g., a required configuration list), where a prominent empty-state explanation might cause more confusion than reassurance about whether something has gone wrong.

screens.name: Clear Browser Data 01
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen gives users granular control over browsing-data deletion rather than an all-or-nothing "Clear Everything" action — three independently toggleable categories (History, Cache, Cookies/Site Data) let a user, for example, clear cookies to fix a broken login without also losing their browsing history. All three toggles default to "on," meaning the "Clear" button as currently configured would wipe all three categories at once, but the user retains the option to selectively disable any category before confirming. Compared to the earlier "Clear All" archive action (which had no visible granular options), this data-clearing flow is more thoughtfully scoped, reflecting the higher stakes and more varied use cases around clearing history/cache/cookies versus simply clearing a list of already-archived tab references.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Labels are plain and specific (Clear History, Clear Cache, Clear Cookies and Site Data), each unambiguous about exactly what data category it controls — appropriate precision for a destructive action where vague terminology could lead to unintended data loss.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Granular Control Over Destructive Actions — separating history, cache, and cookies/site-data into independent toggles respects that users often want to clear only some categories, not all of their browsing data at once.

  2. Sensible All-On Default — defaulting all three toggles to "on" matches the likely most common intent (a full data clear) while still allowing customization for the minority who want a partial clear.

  3. Explicit Confirmation Gate — requiring a deliberate "Clear" tap (rather than the toggles alone taking immediate effect) ensures the user actively confirms before this irreversible action executes.

  4. Category-Level Transparency — clearly naming each data type being cleared helps users understand the real-world consequences (e.g., "Clear Cookies" will log them out of sites) before proceeding.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's "Clear History and Website Data" settings — offers comparable granular toggles for different data categories before a final confirmation step.

  2. Chrome's "Clear browsing data" screen — uses nearly identical category-based toggles (History, Cookies, Cache) with an explicit confirm button.

  3. Firefox's "Delete Browsing Data" settings — provides the same pattern of independently toggleable data categories before an irreversible clear action.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any privacy/data-clearing feature where users have genuinely different reasons for clearing data (fixing a login issue vs. general privacy cleanup vs. freeing storage), and where granular control reduces the risk of clearing more than intended.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for simpler, single-purpose clear actions (like the earlier Archive "Clear All") where the data being cleared is homogeneous and doesn't benefit from category-level separation — adding unnecessary toggles there would overcomplicate a straightforward action.

screens.name: Clear Browser Data 02
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen closes the loop on the "Clear Data" flow analyzed in the previous screen: after tapping "Clear" with all three toggles (History, Cache, Cookies/Site Data) enabled, a simple toast confirms "Cleared browsing data" without requiring the user to manually verify the action took effect. Using a lightweight, auto-dismissing toast (rather than a full-screen success state or another modal) is appropriately proportionate for this confirmation — the action was already explicitly confirmed via the "Clear" button tap in the prior modal, so this final toast serves as a brief acknowledgment rather than requiring another user decision. This closes out a well-structured three-step destructive-action pattern seen consistently across this app (options/toggles → explicit confirm button → brief completion toast), matching the same structure used for the earlier "Clear All" archive action, reinforcing a consistent design language for irreversible operations throughout Settings.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "Cleared browsing data" uses past-tense, factual phrasing that plainly states what happened, appropriately brief and unembellished for a confirmation toast — no persuasive or celebratory language is needed here since this is simply closing the loop on an action the user already deliberately initiated.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Lightweight Post-Action Confirmation — a brief toast (rather than a full modal or screen) matches the low informational need at this stage, since the user already explicitly confirmed the action via the "Clear" button.

  2. Consistent Destructive-Action Pattern — this three-step sequence (granular toggles → explicit confirm → completion toast) mirrors the structure used elsewhere in the app (e.g., the Archive's "Clear All"), giving irreversible actions a predictable, learnable interaction model throughout.

  3. Non-Blocking Feedback — the toast overlays but doesn't obstruct the underlying Settings screen, letting the user continue browsing settings immediately without needing to dismiss anything.

  4. Past-Tense Factual Copy — stating what happened ("Cleared") rather than what will happen avoids any ambiguity about whether the action is complete.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's "Cleared History and Data" confirmation — uses a comparable brief system confirmation after a destructive browsing-data clear action.

  2. Chrome's "Browsing data cleared" toast — provides an identical lightweight, auto-dismissing confirmation following the same type of action.

  3. Standard iOS toast/snackbar conventions — this pattern follows established platform norms for confirming completed background actions without requiring further user interaction.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits confirming the completion of any destructive or significant action that was already explicitly confirmed via a prior button tap, where a brief, non-blocking toast is sufficient acknowledgment without needing to interrupt the user's flow further.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for actions where the user needs to review specific details of what was cleared/changed (e.g., which exact accounts were affected) — a bare "Cleared browsing data" toast wouldn't be sufficient feedback if more detailed confirmation were actually necessary for user trust or troubleshooting.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Deleting & Removing 2
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen represents the empty state of a browser's "History" section, likely from a travel or exploration-themed browser app (given the illustration style and copy). The layout follows a minimalist, dark-mode-first design philosophy that places a single, centered illustration and message in the vertical and horizontal center of an otherwise empty viewport.

The top navigation bar is stripped down to essentials: a back arrow for immediate escape and a contextual overflow menu (three-dot icon) for secondary actions like "Clear history" settings, even though there is nothing to clear yet. This is a smart forward-looking decision, keeping the UI chrome consistent whether or not content exists.

The bottom tab bar remains fully visible and interactive, reinforcing that this empty state is not a dead end but simply one view within a larger navigational ecosystem (Home, Browser/Globe, Sort/Compare, List, Wallet). The active tab (globe icon) is highlighted with a soft blue halo, giving clear orientation feedback.

The illustration itself is a stylized browser window with a clock icon overlay, immediately communicating the semantic meaning of "history" without needing to read the headline text — a strong example of icon/illustration reinforcing textual content for faster comprehension.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is short, friendly, and action-oriented rather than clinical. Instead of a sterile "No data available" message, the app uses "No history yet" paired with the encouraging subtext "Get out there and start exploring."

This phrasing does double duty: it explains the absence of data while subtly nudging the user toward the desired behavior (browsing/navigating), and it hints at the app's brand voice — energetic, adventurous, and casual, likely aligned with a travel, maps, or discovery-focused product rather than a purely utilitarian one.

The word "yet" is a deliberate micro-copy choice that implies inevitability and positivity — the user *will* have history soon, framing the empty state as a beginning rather than a lack.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Purposeful, on-brand illustration: The browser-window-with-clock icon visually reinforces the concept of "history" instantly, reducing cognitive load.

  • Encouraging micro-copy: "No history yet" + "Get out there and start exploring" reframes an empty/negative state into a motivational, action-inviting moment.

  • Consistent chrome: Top bar and bottom tab bar remain fully functional and visible, preventing the empty state from feeling like a broken or dead-end screen.

  • Dark theme with high-contrast accent illustration: The light-blue illustration pops against the black background, drawing the eye directly to the focal point without visual clutter.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets first-time users or users who have recently cleared their browsing history, most commonly within browser, maps, or travel-discovery apps. The design leverages the psychological principle of reframing absence as opportunity — rather than making the user feel like something is "missing" or "broken," the copy and illustration together trigger a sense of anticipation and invitation to engage with the core product (browsing/exploring).

The use of a friendly, informal tone ("Get out there") suggests the target demographic is casual consumers rather than enterprise/professional users, who typically respond well to encouraging, low-friction language that reduces the intimidation of an empty interface.
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern for any list-based screen (history, favorites, cart, notifications) that can legitimately be empty for new users.

  • Ideal when you want to convert a potentially discouraging "nothing here" moment into a motivational nudge toward a core action.

  • Effective in consumer-facing apps with a friendly or adventurous brand voice (travel, lifestyle, social, discovery apps).

  • Pair with a custom illustration that visually explains the screen's purpose to reduce reliance on text alone.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid overly casual copy ("Get out there and start exploring") in enterprise, financial, or medical contexts where users expect precise, neutral language.

  • Do not use a generic empty state illustration if the underlying feature is complex — consider adding a direct CTA button (e.g., "Start Browsing") rather than relying solely on passive suggestion.

  • Not suitable if the history list can be pre-populated with system-generated or synced data, where an empty state would rarely be seen and investment in custom illustration isn't justified.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Deleting & Removing 1
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen represents the browsing history log for Coinbase Wallet's built-in decentralized application (dapp) browser. It follows a familiar, low-friction pattern borrowed directly from mobile web browsers (like Safari or Chrome), reducing cognitive load for users who need to find a dApp they visited previously but forgot to bookmark.

The layout uses a simple chronological grouping ("TODAY") to organize entries, keeping the list scannable. The information hierarchy prioritizes the Site Title (bold, high contrast) over the URL and timestamp (dimmed, secondary), which helps users identify the "PancakeSwap" brand instantly rather than parsing the raw URL string.

The screenshot notably shows the destructive "swipe-to-delete" interaction mid-action, revealing a red action pane with a trash icon. This is a standard iOS/Android pattern for list management that keeps the default UI clean of clutter (no visible delete buttons) while making deletion just one swipe away for privacy-conscious users.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone here is purely utilitarian and functional, mirroring standard OS browser controls rather than branded "crypto" language. There is no persuasive copy; the content is purely factual metadata (Site Name, Domain, Time).

By using generic browser terminology ("History") rather than crypto jargon, Coinbase Wallet lowers the barrier to entry for users transitioning from standard web browsing to Web3 interactions, reinforcing that interacting with dApps should feel as normal as browsing any website.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Familiar Mental Model: Adopting the standard mobile browser "History" list UI removes the learning curve for users navigating decentralized applications.

  • Non-Destructive Default View: Hiding delete controls behind a swipe gesture keeps the primary list clean and scannable, only exposing high-risk actions (deletion) upon deliberate user intent.

  • Metadata Hierarchy: Clear visual separation between the human-readable Site Title and the machine-readable URL/Timestamp aids quick scanning.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves the "Busy Urban" persona who uses the wallet's dApp browser for frequent DeFi activities (like swapping tokens on PancakeSwap). Since crypto users often visit dozens of specific dApp URLs that are hard to remember or type manually, this history feature acts as a safety net for quick re-access.

Psychologically, the swipe-to-delete pattern taps into privacy concerns specific to crypto users; since financial dApp interactions can be sensitive, users are given an easy, discoverable way to clear specific traces of their activity without needing to dig through settings menus.
screens.whereToUse: Utilize this pattern for any list-based content that requires chronological logging and individual item management, such as browser history, search history, or transaction logs. It is ideal when users need to revisit previous states quickly without bookmarking every item, and when list decluttering (deletion) is a common secondary action.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for critical, irreversible actions where a single swipe might be triggered accidentally (e.g., deleting a wallet seed phrase or confirming a crypto transaction). Additionally, if the target audience is less tech-savvy or unfamiliar with swipe gestures, relying solely on hidden actions without a visible "Edit" mode alternative could hide functionality and hurt discoverability.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 03
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen provides clean before/after confirmation across two separate settings interactions traced through this analysis set: the Default Search Engine changed from Google to "Browse for Me" (as selected several screens earlier), and Archive Inactive Tabs changed from "1 day" to "3 days" (as selected in the immediately preceding popover). Both changes persist correctly and display accurately in their parent Settings list, confirming the app's settings architecture reliably propagates sub-screen selections back to the main Settings view without requiring an explicit save action. This also demonstrates, in aggregate across this whole app-icon/language/search-engine/archive-timing sequence, a consistent and reliable settings-interaction pattern throughout the app: navigate to a row → make a selection (via popover or dedicated screen) → return to see the updated value reflected immediately.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Reliable State Propagation — both changed settings correctly display their new values upon returning to the parent Settings screen, without requiring a manual refresh or save confirmation.

  2. Consistent Interaction Model Across Settings — the same select-then-confirm pattern (whether via popover or dedicated sub-screen) applies uniformly across different setting types (search engine, archive timing, language), giving the whole Settings experience a cohesive, predictable feel.

  3. Immediate Effect Without Explicit Save — no "Save" or "Apply" button was needed at any point in this sequence; each selection takes effect and displays immediately upon choice.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. iOS Settings app (immediate value persistence) — uses an identical pattern where sub-screen selections instantly update and display in the parent settings list without requiring a save step.

  2. Any well-designed settings architecture (Safari, Chrome, etc.) — follows this same immediate-persistence convention as a baseline usability expectation for modern mobile settings.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (immediate persistence without explicit save) fits virtually all mobile settings interfaces, where requiring a separate save action for individual preference changes would add unnecessary friction and risk of lost changes if a user navigates away.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit only for settings with significant, hard-to-reverse consequences (e.g., account deletion, irreversible data actions), where an explicit confirm/save step is appropriate specifically to prevent accidental changes — a distinction correctly reflected in this app's separate use of confirmation dialogs (like the earlier "Clear All" archive action) for higher-stakes actions.

screens.name: Archive
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen makes tangible the "Auto-archives old tabs" feature promoted back in onboarding ("no more virtual dust bunnies") and the "Archive Inactive Tabs: After 1 day" setting seen in the Settings screen — confirming these auto-archived tabs land in a dedicated, searchable, chronologically-grouped Archive rather than simply disappearing. Both entries shown are genuinely related (coffee recipe searches), demonstrating this as a real session history rather than placeholder content, and grouping by "TODAY" (with presumably other date headers for older entries) mirrors standard browser history conventions. The presence of both "Edit" (for bulk actions like deletion) and a search field suggests this Archive is designed to scale to potentially many entries over time, requiring both search and management tools once the list grows beyond a single day's worth of tabs.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — plain, functional list content (tab titles inherited from the browsed pages, URLs, and a date-group label), with no persuasive or brand-voice copy present on this screen.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Feature Follow-Through — this screen delivers on the "auto-archive" promise made during onboarding and confirmed in Settings, showing archived tabs land somewhere retrievable rather than being silently lost.

  2. Chronological Grouping — organizing entries under date headers like "TODAY" follows familiar browser-history conventions, aiding quick temporal orientation.

  3. Scalable Management Tools — providing both Edit (bulk actions) and Search upfront anticipates the Archive growing significantly over time as tabs continue to auto-archive daily.

  4. Consistent Favicon Usage — using site favicons (the Google "G") alongside titles and URLs gives quick visual source recognition, consistent with standard browser history/bookmark list conventions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's Tab History / Recently Closed Tabs — organizes closed or archived tabs chronologically with title, URL, and favicon, closely matching this screen's structure.

  2. Chrome's History page — groups browsing history by date with search functionality, mirroring this Archive's date-grouped, searchable list.

  3. Arc Browser desktop's own Archive feature — the mobile app's Archive directly parallels the desktop Arc browser's auto-archiving tab-management system, maintaining feature consistency across platforms.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any browser or tab-management feature where content is automatically moved out of active view after a period of inactivity, requiring a dedicated, searchable, chronologically-organized location for users to retrieve or manage that archived content later.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit if archived content should be permanently and irretrievably removed rather than stored for later retrieval — in cases requiring true deletion rather than archiving, a distinct "delete" flow (rather than an archive-and-search model) would be more appropriate.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 01
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen serves the Setting Up flow by consolidating browser-wide configuration into a single scrollable Preference Center. Grouping related rows into visually divided Stacked Lists (identity/defaults, search/language, behavioral toggles) reduces cognitive load versus one long flat list, while Switches give immediate binary control and chevron rows use Drill-Down navigation to defer complexity (e.g., full language list, search engine picker) to dedicated sub-screens. The two Tile shortcuts at the top (Downloads, Archive) act as quick-access exceptions to the otherwise list-based hierarchy, prioritizing frequent destinations above the settings proper.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Chunking (Miller's Law): Dividers break ~14 settings into 5 digestible clusters instead of one long list.

  2. Recognition over recall: Trailing value text (e.g., "Google", "After 1 day", "Native App") shows current state inline, so users don't need to open each row to check it.

  3. Progressive disclosure: Chevron rows (Global Site Settings, Languages, Search Engine) push secondary complexity to nested screens, keeping this page scannable.

  4. Fitts's Law: Full-row tap targets (not just the switch/chevron) make toggles and navigation rows easier to hit on mobile.

  5. Consistency: Icon-label-value-chevron row pattern repeats identically throughout, lowering the learning curve as users scan down.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari (iOS Settings) — same grouped Stacked List + chevron drill-down pattern for browser preferences, a near-identical information architecture.

  2. Chrome (iOS Settings) — uses the same colored-icon-plus-label row convention and trailing value text for settings like default search engine.

  3. Notion (iOS Settings) — groups toggles and drill-down rows into dividered sections in a comparable Preference Center layout.
screens.whereToUse: This grouped Stacked List + Preference Center pattern fits any settings surface with a moderate-to-large number of independent preferences that benefit from being scanned at a glance, especially where some options are binary (toggle) and others need a dedicated picker screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when there are only a handful of settings (a flat list would suffice) or when settings are highly interdependent and better presented as a guided wizard rather than an unordered menu.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 02
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen resolves the earlier ambiguity around the "Archive Inactive Tabs: After 1 day" value-display row seen in multiple prior Settings screenshots — confirming it's a genuine five-option selector (12 hours, 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 30 days) rather than a fixed setting, using the same compact popover-with-checkmark pattern established by the earlier "Swipe to Navigate" setting. Offering a spread from as short as 12 hours to as long as 30 days accommodates very different browsing habits: users who open many disposable tabs might prefer aggressive 12-hour archiving to keep their tab list tidy, while users who reference tabs over longer periods might prefer 30 days to avoid losing something they were still planning to revisit. This directly ties back to the "auto-archive old tabs" feature promoted during onboarding ("no more virtual dust bunnies") — this popover is where that promised convenience becomes a precisely tunable setting rather than a fixed, non-configurable behavior.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — plain numeric duration options (12 hours, 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 30 days) with no persuasive framing, appropriate for a straightforward duration-selection control.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Resolving Prior Ambiguity — this screen retroactively confirms the "After 1 day" value seen in earlier Settings screenshots was genuinely configurable, not a fixed label.

  2. Range Accommodates Diverse Habits — offering both very short (12 hours) and long (30 days) options serves meaningfully different tab-management styles without forcing a one-size-fits-all default.

  3. Consistent Selector Pattern — reusing the same compact popover-with-checkmark format as the earlier "Swipe to Navigate" setting maintains a predictable interaction model for similar types of choices throughout Settings.

  4. Feature Follow-Through — this control makes the onboarding-promised "auto-archive" feature concretely adjustable, giving users direct control over how aggressively that promise is enforced.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's "Close Tabs Automatically" duration picker — offers a nearly identical range of duration options (1 day, 1 week, 1 month) for automatically closing inactive tabs.

  2. Chrome's "Auto Tab Groups" or memory-saver duration settings — provides comparable configurable timeframes for tab-management automation.

  3. Firefox's tab-unloading/archiving thresholds — similarly lets users choose how long inactive tabs remain before being archived or unloaded.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any automated content-management feature (archiving, auto-deletion, auto-logout) where users benefit from choosing a personally appropriate threshold, especially when a single fixed default wouldn't suit meaningfully different usage patterns across the user base.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for settings where offering multiple duration options would create confusing inconsistency (e.g., security-critical timeouts where a single, carefully chosen default is safer than user-configurable flexibility).

screens.name: Booking Details Page
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen reveals what the Booking Code and Seat tiles actually collect — PNR, seat number, seat position, and cabin class, all optional and user-supplied. The input types are well matched to the data: free text for PNR and seat (paste affordance on the former), chips and radio rows for the enumerable position and class. The seat position chips are a subtle hedge though — a user typing "14A" is arguably already declaring "Window," so asking separately either reflects the app's distrust of inferring position from letter, or a deliberate choice not to depend on it, but either way it costs an extra tap. What's missing across this screen and the tiles that led here is the payoff: four optional fields with no stated benefit, when other screens show the data does resurface (boarding-pass sticker, Live Activity mockup) — a single line naming that would turn this from chore into unlock.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Sparse and functional, with one placeholder worth noting and one label doing quiet work.

"Booking Details" — a title naming the record type rather than the action, correct for a form that edits an existing object.

"FLI123" as placeholder — models format rather than restating the label, the same good pattern as "AA101" in the report form. It's also a joke: FLI is Flighty's own initials in PNR shape. Small, and it means the example can't be mistaken for a real airline's format.

"Booking Code" rather than "PNR" or "Record Locator" — the plainest available term, with the expert term appearing in the icon glyph for those who recognise it. Same layered approach as the airport picker's ICAO codes.

"Seat Number" as the section label but "Seat" as the placeholder — a small inconsistency, and the placeholder is the weaker of the two since it restates rather than models. "14A" would have followed the pattern set one field above.

"Aisle / Middle / Window" — the universal vocabulary, no explanation needed. The clipped fourth chip suggests further options (Exit Row, Bulkhead, or similar).

"Economy / Premium Economy / Business" — standard cabin nomenclature, presumably with First below the fold. Note these are the industry's terms, not simplified ones, consistent with the app's willingness to use ICAO codes and "REMARKS".

"Done" — unambiguous, singular, and blue. Notably better than the profile flow's "Complete", and it appears here without a Cancel counterpart, implying changes commit as made rather than on confirmation.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Match the control to the data — free text for unbounded values, chips and radios for enumerable ones, so nothing is typed that could be tapped.

  2. Placeholders that model format — "FLI123" teaches the shape of a PNR without a label or hint.

  3. Layered vocabulary — plain labels on screen, expert terms in glyphs and options, serving both audiences without a mode switch.

  4. No stated payoff — four optional fields with no explanation of what they unlock, despite the app having clear answers elsewhere.

  5. Redundant input — seat position is largely inferable from the seat letter, so asking for both costs a tap.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Wallet / airline apps (booking entry) — PNR with paste affordance and seat details, though usually populated from a pass rather than typed.

  2. TripIt (manual trip details) — optional booking metadata entered by the user with a stated benefit for each field.

  3. App in the Air (seat and class entry) — the same enumerable-versus-free-text split for seat data.
screens.whereToUse: Best where a product holds most of a record from its own data and only a few fields require the user, and where those fields split cleanly into typed and tappable. Paste affordances suit any field whose value typically arrives via copy from an email.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit when optional fields have no stated benefit, since users skip what they can't see the point of. Also wrong to request data the app can derive from something the user has already supplied.

screens.name: Filled Booking Details Page
screens.uxAnalysis: The notable behaviour here is the keyboard switch: the seat field shows the numeric-symbol layout, even though "D23" needs a letter that layout can't produce — so the user toggled ABC/123 mid-entry for a three-character value, when an alphanumeric-plane keyboard type exists precisely for cases like this. Everything else holds up: PASTE persists on the filled PNR field, and the position chips stay unselected despite "D23" being entered, reinforcing the earlier-noted redundancy of asking for position separately from a seat letter that already implies it. Minor but real: the keyboard covers the cabin class list from "Business" down, so completing this four-field form top-to-bottom requires a dismissal step nothing signals.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Unchanged from the previous frame; the filled state changes little.

"FLI578" — the entered value, and note it follows the placeholder's own format ("FLI123"). The mock is using Flighty's self-referential PNR shape as real data, which is internally consistent if slightly unrealistic — a genuine Qantas PNR wouldn't begin FLI.

"D23" — an unusual seat designation. Standard commercial layouts run row-then-letter ("23D"), not letter-then-row. Either the mock has them inverted, or the field genuinely accepts any string without validation. Given the app declines to validate airport codes elsewhere in this set, the latter is plausible — and it matters more here, since seat data feeds the boarding-pass share artifact where an inverted value would be visible to recipients.

"Done" in the navigation bar and "done" on the keyboard — two commit affordances, differently cased, doing different things: one dismisses the keyboard, one closes the sheet. On a form where the keyboard obscures remaining options, having two similarly-labelled commits adjacent is a small ambiguity.

Still absent, three screens into this feature: any statement of what these fields unlock.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Keyboard type should match the data — an alphanumeric seat number on a numbers-only layout forces a mid-value toggle that a combined keyboard would eliminate.

  2. Paste stays useful after fill — retaining the affordance on a populated field serves correction as well as entry.

  3. No defaults on genuinely unknown fields — empty radios correctly avoid guessing a cabin class.

  4. Unvalidated free text — "D23" inverts the standard seat convention and the field accepts it, on data that will appear in a shared artifact.

  5. Keyboard occludes remaining options — the class list is cut from "Business" down, so completion requires an unsignalled dismissal.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Wallet (pass details) — seat and class populated from the pass itself rather than typed, avoiding the format question entirely.

  2. App in the Air (seat entry) — alphanumeric seat field with a combined keyboard layout.

  3. TripIt (manual booking entry) — free-text booking fields with light format validation on save.
screens.whereToUse: Best for short optional forms where each field's input type can be matched to a keyboard and enumerable values are tapped rather than typed. Persistent paste affordances suit any field whose value is typically copied.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit when field values feed shared or exported artifacts without validation, since malformed input becomes visible to third parties. Also wrong when the keyboard covers controls the user must still reach to finish.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Adding & Creating 1
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen follows a well-established "Master-Detail" pattern common in fintech and trading apps, where tapping an asset from a list drills down into a dedicated detail view. The layout prioritizes information hierarchy in a classic F-pattern: identity (icon + name) at top, the hero metric (current price) as the dominant typographic element, and supporting delta/performance data directly beneath it in color-coded green to reinforce positive momentum at a glance.

The dotted-area sparkline chart is the visual centerpiece, using a gradient/dot-fill technique under the line to create depth without overwhelming the dark background — a technique that keeps focus on the line trajectory while still communicating volume/magnitude visually. The segmented time-range control (1H/1D/1W/1M/1Y/All) sits immediately below, letting users manipulate the exact same data model without navigating away, which reduces context-switching cost.

Below the fold, the screen cleanly separates "your balance" (personal state) from a two-row grid of transactional actions (Buy, Swap, Bridge, Cash out, Send, Receive, Text send, Share). This 4x2 icon grid uses consistent circular buttons with clear iconography and labels, lowering cognitive load by chunking 8 possible actions into recognizable, tappable targets rather than a cluttered toolbar. The persistent bottom tab bar keeps global navigation always accessible, reducing the risk of the user feeling "lost" in a deep-linked asset screen.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is extremely minimal and numeric-led, letting the data (price, percentage change) do the storytelling rather than marketing language. Labels like "Buy," "Swap," "Bridge," "Cash out," "Send," "Receive," "Text send," and "Share" are single-word imperatives — direct, utilitarian, and action-oriented, typical of financial tooling where clarity and speed trump personality or warmth.

The use of "Your balance" personalizes the otherwise market-wide data (Bitcoin price is global; balance is personal), subtly reminding the user of their own stake even when it's zero, which doubles as a soft upsell nudge toward the "Buy" button directly below it.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Hero metric typography: The price is rendered in oversized, bold white text, immediately establishing visual hierarchy and making the number scannable within milliseconds.

  • Color-coded performance indicator: Green up-arrow and percentage change leverage instant, culturally-ingrained color psychology (green = gain) without requiring the user to read text.

  • Dotted gradient-fill chart: A stylistic differentiation from typical solid-fill area charts, adding brand personality while retaining data legibility.

  • Segmented time range control: Enables instant re-scoping of the chart on the same screen, avoiding a page reload or navigation, which keeps the interaction lightweight and fast.

  • Dual-row action grid: Groups 8 core financial actions into a scannable icon+label grid, balancing information density with touch-target usability.

  • "Watch" pill button: A low-commitment CTA placed prominently in the top-right, letting users follow an asset without depositing funds — a classic engagement-before-monetization funnel step.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets retail crypto investors and traders, ranging from curious newcomers checking prices to active users managing holdings. The zero balance shown ("0.00000 BTC") suggests this view is also shown to prospective holders who don't yet own the asset, and the design leans on this to nudge conversion.

Psychologically, the screen uses social proof via price momentum (a rising green chart implies FOMO — "everyone is winning, don't miss out"), and friction reduction (Buy is the first and most visually prominent action button) to convert passive lookers into active buyers. The "Watch" button caters to loss-averse or hesitant users who aren't ready to transact, offering a lower-commitment engagement path that keeps them retained in the app ecosystem via price alerts/notifications instead of losing them entirely.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any asset-centric or ticker-based application — stocks, crypto, ETFs, commodities, or even NFT floor prices — where users need to view a time-series metric alongside immediate transactional actions. It's ideal when the product needs to support both passive monitoring (watchlists) and active transacting (buy/sell/swap) from a single, focused screen. It also works well for account/wallet detail pages where balance display and quick actions need equal prominence.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense action-grid approach for novice-only or simplified consumer apps where 8 simultaneous actions may overwhelm first-time users — consider progressive disclosure or a simplified 2-3 action set instead. This pattern is also unsuitable for non-financial content where a real-time trend chart isn't relevant, or in contexts where balance is always zero/non-applicable (e.g., editorial or informational crypto news apps), since the "Your balance" and multiple wallet actions would create clutter and irrelevant affordances.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Adding & Creating 2
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a classic crypto asset detail view, structured around a "master" price chart with "spoke" action shortcuts beneath it. The information hierarchy is deliberate: the coin icon and "Watching" status pill sit at the top, followed by the largest visual weight given to the current price ($96,892.43) and its delta (+2.65%), reinforcing that price movement is the single most important data point for a trader.

Below this, a dotted area chart with a gradient fill communicates trend at a glance without requiring the user to parse granular numbers — the dot-matrix texture is a distinctive visual signature that differentiates this from a generic line chart. A horizontal timeframe segmented control (1H/1D/1W/1M/1Y/All) lets users rescope the trend instantly, a pattern borrowed from institutional trading terminals but simplified for consumer use.

The "Your balance: 0.00000 BTC" line is a subtle but important commerce cue — it signals to a non-holder that they currently own none of this asset, priming the two rows of circular action buttons below (Buy, Swap, Bridge, Cash out / Send, Receive, Text send, Share) as an implicit call-to-action funnel toward acquisition. Notice Buy is visually first and uses a "+" icon, nudging first-time purchase.

A toast notification, "Added to watchlist," overlays the Receive/Text send buttons at the bottom, confirming the result of tapping "Watching" up top. This is a lightweight, non-blocking confirmation that doesn't interrupt the user's flow.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal, functional, and numeric-first — typical of finance apps where users want data density over narrative. Labels like "Buy," "Swap," "Bridge," "Cash out," "Send," "Receive," "Text send," and "Share" are single-word imperative verbs, keeping the action grid scannable and reducing cognitive load.

The toast message "Added to watchlist" uses plain, past-tense confirmation language — reassuring without being celebratory, appropriate for a low-stakes, reversible action. The green up-arrow and percentage figure leverage color coding (green = gain) that is near-universal in financial UI, requiring no explanation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dot-matrix area chart: A distinctive stylistic treatment of the price trend line that stands out from typical solid-fill charts, reinforcing brand identity while still being instantly readable.

  • Non-blocking toast confirmation: "Added to watchlist" appears as an overlay without a modal or page transition, letting the user continue browsing immediately — reducing friction for a low-commitment action.

  • Dual-row action grid: Splitting 8 actions into two rows of 4 circular icon buttons maintains a clean, uncluttered layout while surfacing the full range of transactional options (buy, swap, bridge, cash out, send, receive, text send, share) without needing menus.

  • Zero-balance transparency: Explicitly showing "0.00000 BTC" rather than hiding the balance row builds trust and subtly nudges the user toward the Buy CTA.

  • Segmented time range control: A familiar, thumb-friendly horizontal selector for chart granularity that avoids dropdown menus.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets retail crypto investors and casual traders ranging from curious first-timers to more frequent active users, evidenced by the mix of both passive (Watching, chart, price) and highly active (Swap, Bridge, Cash out) actions on one screen. The presence of "Bridge" and "Swap" — advanced DeFi-adjacent actions — suggests the app serves a self-custody wallet audience comfortable with cross-chain transactions, not just simple buy/sell brokerage users.

Psychologically, the screen leverages loss/gain framing (green up-arrow, bold percentage) to trigger FOMO and encourage action while price is rising. The "Watching" toggle and confirmation toast tap into a completionist/tracking instinct — users like to feel they're monitoring an asset even before committing capital, which increases app engagement (return visits to check price) and primes eventual conversion to a Buy action.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any single-asset or single-item detail screen where price/value fluctuates over time — cryptocurrency, stocks, ETFs, commodities, or even fantasy sports odds. It's ideal when you need to combine a monitoring experience (chart + watchlist) with an immediate transactional funnel (buy/sell/transfer) on one uninterrupted screen. The toast-over-action-grid technique is broadly reusable anywhere you want to confirm a background-state change (favorited, saved, subscribed) without halting the user's task.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid cramming 8 action buttons into two dense rows on screens targeting less sophisticated or first-time users — the sheer number of options (Buy, Swap, Bridge, Cash out, Send, Receive, Text send, Share) can overwhelm someone unfamiliar with crypto terminology like "Bridge" or "Text send." For simpler consumer finance products, consider progressive disclosure (e.g., a single "More actions" sheet) instead of exposing everything at once. Additionally, positioning a toast directly on top of interactive buttons (as seen here, covering Receive/Text send) risks accidental mis-taps or hidden affordances if the toast lingers too long — use short auto-dismiss timers and ensure toasts don't block critical CTAs like "Buy."

screens.name: Cleo Adding & Creating 2
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen represents a transitional loading state, likely triggered when Cleo hands off from its native chat interface to a web-view (e.g., for a bank-linking flow, a payment provider, or a legal document). The layout is intentionally sparse: a determinate progress bar at the top signals that the system knows how long the process will take, while a large, pulsing brand-colored circle occupies the center of the screen as the primary loading indicator.

The use of a modal-style top bar with an explicit "Loading..." label and a close (X) affordance is a deliberate UX choice that gives the user a clear escape hatch, reducing anxiety during an indeterminate wait. Placing the close button top-right respects platform conventions (iOS modal dismissal) and ensures the user never feels trapped in a stalled flow, which is critical for a finance app where trust is paramount.

The stark whitespace below the loader is a temporary void that will be populated once content resolves — this is a placeholder/skeleton state rather than a final design, but its cleanliness ensures no jank or layout shift once real content streams in.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The copy is minimal and functional — just "Loading..." — which is appropriate for a system status message rather than a conversational Cleo moment. This is a deliberate tonal shift: Cleo's personality-driven, sassy voice is reserved for chat bubbles and financial roasts, not for utilitarian system states like network waits. Here, clarity and speed of communication trump personality, which is the correct prioritization for a transient screen the user should barely notice.
