  • Transparent fee breakdown with contextual help: The info icon next to "Network fee" offers progressive disclosure — power users can ignore it, novices can tap for clarity, without cluttering the primary UI.

  • Recipient avatar generation: Auto-generated colorful icon for the unnamed wallet address helps users visually distinguish/recognize addresses at a glance, mitigating the risk of sending to the wrong address.

  • Asymmetric CTA weighting: The muted Cancel button vs. the vibrant gradient Confirm button guides the eye to the primary action while never hiding or disabling the escape path.

  • Explicit Total Cost line: Separating "amount sent" from "network fee" and summing them into a "Total cost" prevents the common crypto UX pitfall of surprise fees.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets cryptocurrency holders — ranging from casual retail users making small transfers (note the tiny $1.00 test-sized amount, suggesting either a micro-payment use case or a first-time trial send) to more experienced holders comfortable reading BTC-denominated values and wallet addresses.

Psychologically, the design leverages the endowment effect and loss aversion inherent to irreversible blockchain transactions: because Bitcoin sends cannot be undone, the interface compensates with maximum transparency (exact fees, exact amounts, wallet identifiers) to reduce anxiety and give users full confidence before committing. The deliberate friction of a dedicated confirmation screen (rather than an inline swipe-to-send) exploits the peak-end rule for high-stakes actions — ensuring the last thing a user sees before an irreversible action is a calm, complete summary, not a rushed gesture.
screens.whereToUse: Use this confirmation pattern for any high-stakes, irreversible, or costly action: cryptocurrency/financial transfers, bank wire transfers, permanent account deletions, or any operation involving real money where a fee is deducted. It's especially valuable when the transaction involves multiple data points (amount, fee, recipient, total) that the user must verify before committing.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, full-screen confirmation pattern for low-stakes, easily reversible actions (e.g., toggling a setting, liking a post) — it would introduce unnecessary friction and feel patronizing. Also avoid dense financial jargon and unexplained fee breakdowns for a mainstream/non-crypto-native audience without additional onboarding or simplified fee toggles (e.g., "fast" vs "slow" fee tiers), as raw BTC values and network fee terminology can alienate less technical users.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Transferring Money 8
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a dedicated transaction success confirmation for a crypto wallet "send" flow. It uses a full-screen, high-contrast dark modal to interrupt the user's flow and unambiguously signal that a financial action has completed. The layout follows a strict vertical hierarchy: a large affirmative icon at the top, a human-readable confirmation message, the primary fiat amount as the hero element, the secondary crypto-denominated amount beneath it, and a single, unmissable call-to-action at the bottom.

The use of negative space is deliberate — by isolating the confirmation content in the middle of an otherwise empty black canvas, the design eliminates distraction and forces the user's attention onto the outcome. The dimmed tab bar visible behind/beneath the sheet indicates this is likely presented as a modal overlay on top of the wallet's main navigation, reinforcing that this is a transient, task-completion state rather than a permanent screen.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal, declarative, and reassuring: "Successfully sent" is short, past-tense, and unambiguous — there is no room for the user to wonder whether the transaction is pending or failed. Displaying the fiat value ($1.00) in large bold type before the native BTC amount (0.00000971 BTC) is a deliberate content strategy choice: it caters to users who think in dollars first and crypto second, lowering the cognitive barrier typically associated with cryptocurrency's small decimal denominations.

The single-word button label "Done" is intentionally low-friction — it signals finality and closure rather than prompting further action, which is appropriate for a terminal state in a task flow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Fiat-first hierarchy: Leading with the USD equivalent before the raw BTC value respects the mental model of mainstream users unfamiliar with crypto decimals.

  • Singular focus: Removing all navigation and secondary actions except "Done" prevents decision paralysis at a moment when the user just wants closure.

  • Iconography as instant feedback: The oversized checkmark in a solid color circle communicates success in under a second, before the user even reads the text — critical for reducing anxiety in financial transactions.

  • Gradient CTA: The blue-to-teal gradient "Done" button visually differentiates itself as the primary and only actionable element, reinforcing a clear exit path.

  • Ambient context preservation: The dimmed tab bar behind the modal subtly reminds the user which app section they'll return to, maintaining spatial orientation.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday crypto wallet users — including newcomers who are anxious about irreversible blockchain transactions — by immediately resolving the core fear point: "Did my money actually send?" Financial transactions, especially crypto ones with no customer-service safety net, trigger heightened stress; a large, unambiguous success state exploits the psychological principle of closure, giving the user a clean mental checkpoint and reducing the urge to double-check or panic-refresh.

Showing both fiat and crypto values serves dual audiences: casual users who value USD context, and power users who want to verify the exact satoshi/BTC amount moved.
screens.whereToUse:
• Terminal confirmation screens for irreversible or high-stakes actions (payments, transfers, submissions, bookings).

  • Any flow where user anxiety about "did it work?" is high, such as banking, crypto, or e-commerce checkouts.

  • Multi-step wizards or flows that benefit from a clear, singular exit point back to the main app.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy, full-screen interruption for low-stakes or frequent actions (e.g., liking a post) — use a lightweight toast/snackbar instead to avoid flow disruption.

  • Don't use if users may need to immediately take a follow-up action (e.g., share receipt, add note) — a single "Done" button with no secondary options can be too restrictive in flows that benefit from next-step guidance.

  • Not ideal when transaction status is uncertain (e.g., blockchain pending confirmations) — this pattern implies finality, which could mislead users if the transaction can still fail or be reversed.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 11
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is Venmo's final payment confirmation screen, structured as a modal/full-screen takeover with clear exit points (back chevron and close 'X') to reduce anxiety about being "trapped" in a transaction flow. The layout follows a classic vertical hierarchy: recipient identity (avatar + name) at top, the dominant focal point being the large, oversized dollar amount ($2), followed by a note/memo field ("Ticket") that provides transaction context.

The screen cleverly uses whitespace to create breathing room between the "what" (amount/memo) and the "how" (payment method and privacy settings), preventing cognitive overload despite packing multiple decision points into one screen.

Below the fold, the design shifts to functional/utilitarian mode: a Privacy toggle (defaulting to 'Public', a notable social-first design choice for Venmo), a funding source selector showing the Venmo balance card with available funds, and an opt-in purchase protection toggle. The sticky, full-width teal "Pay" button anchors the bottom of the screen, ensuring the primary CTA is always visible without scrolling — critical for reducing drop-off at the final conversion step.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal and transactional, letting numbers and icons do the talking. The oversized "$2" typography treats the amount as the hero content, reinforcing that this is a lightweight, casual money transfer rather than a formal banking transaction.

The purchase protection copy ("Get a full refund if an eligible purchase isn't what you paid for. Seller pays a small fee.") is written in reassuring, plain-English terms rather than legal jargon, with the benefit (full refund) bolded and highlighted in blue to draw the eye. The "Terms apply" disclaimer is intentionally de-emphasized in small blue text, satisfying legal requirements without disrupting the flow.

The CTA "Pay" is short, direct, and unambiguous — no filler words, reinforcing decisiveness at the point of commitment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Oversized Amount Typography: Making the dollar figure the largest element on screen ensures the user has zero ambiguity about what they're confirming before committing.

  • Sticky Bottom CTA: The "Pay" button remains fixed at the bottom, always accessible regardless of scroll position, minimizing friction at the moment of conversion.

  • Default Public Privacy Toggle: Surfacing the privacy setting inline (rather than hiding it in settings) is a transparent, if socially-motivated, design decision central to Venmo's feed-based social identity.

  • Opt-in Purchase Protection Upsell: The protection toggle is presented as a value-add with a plain-language benefit statement rather than a scary insurance disclaimer, increasing opt-in likelihood.

  • Dual Exit Affordances: Both a back arrow and a close 'X' give users flexible ways to abandon or edit the transaction, respecting user control at a high-stakes financial screen.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers making informal peer-to-peer or small merchant payments (e.g., splitting event tickets, paying a friend). The psychological design leverages commitment and clarity — by isolating the amount and recipient with generous whitespace, it reduces the chance of costly payment errors, which is critical for irreversible financial transactions.

The default 'Public' privacy setting taps into Venmo's unique social proof/network effect model, where visible transactions (without amounts) implicitly advertise the app to the recipient's and payer's social graph, driving viral growth.

The purchase protection toggle uses loss aversion framing (protecting against a bad purchase) to nudge adoption of what is likely a monetized feature or fee-generating service for Venmo, transferring the small fee cost to the seller to keep the buyer's decision frictionless.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for final-step confirmation screens in payment, checkout, or any high-stakes transactional flow where the user must review key facts (amount, recipient, method) before an irreversible action. It's ideal for P2P payment apps, ticketing checkouts, or invoice settlement flows where trust and clarity are paramount.

The sticky CTA + toggleable add-on pattern (protection/insurance) is also reusable for any checkout flow needing to upsell optional protections without derailing the primary conversion path.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimalist, single-focus layout for complex B2B or multi-line-item transactions where users need to review itemized breakdowns, taxes, or multiple recipients — the lack of detail here would create distrust in more complex scenarios.

Defaulting privacy/visibility to 'Public' should be avoided in contexts involving sensitive personal or financial data (e.g., medical payments, salary transfers) where users expect privacy-by-default rather than opt-out exposure.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Transferring Money 9
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen represents the "day zero" state of the Coinbase Wallet home/portfolio dashboard, encountered immediately after a user creates or imports a new self-custody wallet. The layout follows a classic Hub & Spoke model, anchoring the user's total balance ($0.00) at the top as the hero metric, followed by primary transactional actions (Buy, Swap, Cash out) as pill-shaped buttons, and a segmented control below to toggle between asset categories (Crypto, NFTs, DeFi).

The core UX challenge here is turning a potentially discouraging "empty" moment into an actionable onboarding step. Instead of a blank or sparse screen, Coinbase uses a rich Empty State illustration combining the Coinbase logo, a link/chain icon, and a generic wallet icon to visually communicate the concept of "connecting" an external source of funds to the wallet. This reduces cognitive load by pairing an abstract instruction ("add crypto") with a concrete visual metaphor.

Navigation is handled by a persistent bottom Tab Bar (Home, Browser/dapp, Swap/transfer, Activity, Wallet switcher), ensuring the empty state doesn't trap the user — they can immediately jump to the dapp browser or other sections despite having no funds yet. The top bar cleverly surfaces account switching (Address 1 dropdown), search, a QR/scan-like icon for receiving funds, and settings with a notification dot, keeping power-user affordances present even in a zero-state.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is short, encouraging, and instructional rather than apologetic. "Add crypto to get started" uses an active, forward-looking verb ("get started") that reframes an empty wallet as the beginning of a journey rather than a failure state or error.

The subtext, "You can add funds with your Coinbase account or another wallet," proactively answers the user's likely first question ("how do I get money in here?") and offers two clear paths — leveraging the Coinbase ecosystem (frictionless for existing customers) or interoperability with other wallets (appealing to crypto-native users). This dual messaging is tailored to Coinbase Wallet's mixed audience of newcomers and self-custody veterans.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual Empty-State Illustration: Rather than a generic "no data" graphic, the illustration visually depicts linking the Coinbase exchange to an external wallet, directly foreshadowing the CTA's function.

  • Persistent Primary Actions: Buy/Swap/Cash out remain visible even at $0 balance, subtly nudging the user toward the Buy action (highlighted with a vibrant blue-to-teal gradient) as the fastest path to value.

  • Dual CTA Redundancy: The same "Add crypto" action is reinforced twice — once implicitly via the "Buy" quick action and again via the explicit sticky "Add crypto" button — maximizing conversion opportunity without being repetitive in placement.

  • Full Navigation Available: The tab bar and top icons remain fully functional, so a first-time user isn't dead-ended; they can explore dapps or settings before funding the wallet.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets the "Busy Urbans" segment identified for Coinbase Wallet — time-constrained users who need to immediately understand what action to take without reading lengthy explanations. The design leverages the Zeigarnik effect and goal-gradient psychology: showing $0.00 alongside a clear single next step ("Add crypto") creates a mild tension that motivates task completion, similar to an unfinished progress bar.

The choice to offer two funding paths (via Coinbase exchange or an external wallet) evidences a dual-persona strategy: converting existing Coinbase.com/App customers (low-friction, trusted rails) while not alienating self-custody-first crypto natives who prefer transferring from cold storage or other wallets.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any financial, wallet, or portfolio-tracking app's zero-balance or zero-data first-run state — especially where the empty state is not a bug but an expected, common condition (e.g., new bank accounts, investment apps, loyalty point balances). It is ideal whenever the next action is singular and unambiguous, allowing for one dominant CTA to be repeated in multiple visual forms (quick action pill + sticky button).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy illustrative empty-state approach in data-dense B2B or enterprise dashboards where users expect immediate access to tools/filters rather than motivational graphics. Also avoid over-using redundant CTAs (Buy button + Add Crypto button) in contexts where multiple next-steps are equally valid, as it may bias users toward one path and hide equally important alternatives (e.g., importing an existing wallet address).

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 10
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen represents a peer-to-peer payment composer, likely embedded within a messaging app's iMessage app-drawer experience (similar to Apple Cash). The layout follows a strict vertical hierarchy that mirrors a checkbook or calculator mental model: recipient identity at top, a massive numeric amount in the center as the undisputed focal point, an optional memo field, and dual primary actions at the bottom.

The design leverages a single-purpose, distraction-free canvas — there is no navigation chrome, tab bar, or extraneous content competing with the numeric input. The large, bold "$2" typography (using a native-feeling numeric display font) immediately communicates that amount entry is the primary and only task on this screen, reducing cognitive load to a single decision point.

Placing 'Request' and 'Pay' as two equally-weighted, full-width pill buttons side-by-side is a critical UX decision: it collapses two distinct financial intents (asking for money vs. sending money) into one screen without forcing a mode-switch or additional navigation step, at the cost of requiring extra care to prevent mis-taps given real money is at stake.

The presence of the system keyboard with a contextual sticker/emoji tray (concert ticket, ticket stub, bandage emoji stickers) reveals this is a native OS-level payment sheet layered on top of a messaging thread, blending playful, social communication affordances (stickers) with a serious financial transaction — a hybrid pattern unique to consumer P2P payments.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is minimal, numeric, and utilitarian — almost entirely free of persuasive copy. The interface trusts the user to already understand the mental model of sending/requesting money, so no onboarding or explanatory text is needed.

The memo/description field defaults to placeholder text "Ticket," giving a contextual, human touch that ties the transaction to a real-world reason, which increases trust and reduces ambiguity for the recipient who will see this note.

The "Gift" pill with a wrapped-gift emoji injects a light, celebratory tone into an otherwise transactional flow, subtly nudging users toward a more social, generous framing of sending money rather than a cold financial transfer.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-focus numeric input: The oversized dollar amount dominates the visual hierarchy, ensuring zero ambiguity about the primary task.

  • Dual-intent action buttons: 'Request' and 'Pay' are presented together, letting the user decide direction of money flow at the last possible moment rather than pre-selecting a mode earlier in the flow.

  • Contextual memo field with smart default: Pre-filling "Ticket" reduces typing friction and anchors the transaction to a real-life context.

  • Inline clear (X) affordance next to the amount allows instant correction without needing a backspace-heavy re-entry.

  • Native keyboard + sticker tray integration: Blending social stickers with a financial input field shows deep integration into a messaging OS layer, keeping the user in-context rather than switching apps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers performing casual, social financial exchanges — splitting bills, paying back friends for concert tickets, or gifting small amounts within a chat conversation. The design assumes familiarity with mobile messaging and light financial literacy, targeting a mass-market, non-power-user audience.

Psychologically, the design exploits the reduction of friction principle: by keeping the amount entry and action buttons on a single uncluttered screen, it minimizes the "activation energy" required to complete a micro-transaction, which is critical for casual payments where users might abandon the flow if it feels like a "banking app" experience. The playful gift/sticker elements also leverage social reciprocity and warmth cues to make sending money feel like a friendly gesture rather than a formal transaction.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for consumer P2P payment or money-request flows embedded in social/messaging contexts, especially where speed and low cognitive friction are paramount (splitting bills, casual reimbursements, gifting). It's ideal when the recipient context (identity, thread) is already established, allowing the UI to focus purely on amount and intent.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this stripped-down pattern for high-value, formal, or business financial transactions where additional verification, itemization, tax details, or explicit confirmation steps are legally or contextually necessary. The dual Pay/Request buttons side-by-side could also be risky in contexts where accidental mis-taps might trigger irreversible large payments — a confirmation step or clearer visual differentiation should be added for high-stakes amounts.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 12
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen represents the final confirmation step of a peer-to-peer payment flow within Venmo, structured to minimize friction while strategically inserting a monetization upsell before the final commit action. The layout follows a strict vertical hierarchy: recipient identity (avatar + name) at the top, the transaction amount as the dominant visual element (large, bold typography), a note/memo field ("Ticket"), followed by metadata (Privacy setting, funding source, and an optional protection add-on) before the terminal CTA.

The amount ($2) is rendered in an oversized, high-contrast serif-adjacent numeral treatment that dwarfs every other text element on the screen — a deliberate choice to make the user pause and visually confirm the sum before authorizing payment. This acts as a final checkpoint against fat-finger errors.

The funding source card (Venmo balance with visible dollar figure) is placed directly above the fold near the CTA, reducing cognitive load by pre-answering "what am I paying with?" without requiring a tap-through, while still affording a chevron for users who want to change it.

The 'Turn on for purchases' protection toggle is visually contained in its own bordered card, separated from the core payment metadata, which frames it as an optional, dismissible enhancement rather than a mandatory step — reducing perceived friction while still surfacing incremental revenue opportunity (seller-funded fee) at the point of highest intent.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal, transactional, and confident, consistent with a financial utility app where trust and clarity outweigh personality. Numbers and labels ("Ticket", "Public", "Balance: $150.11") are stated factually without embellishment, reinforcing a sense of precision and control appropriate for money movement.

The upsell copy for Purchase Protection uses reassuring, benefit-first language: "Get a full refund if an eligible purchase isn't what you paid for." The word "full" and "refund" are bolded to draw the eye and reduce loss-aversion anxiety, while "Seller pays a small fee" cleverly reframes the cost away from the payer, making the toggle feel risk-free to enable.

"Terms apply" is included as a compliance/legal safety net in small blue text — visible but unobtrusive, satisfying regulatory disclosure needs without disrupting the primary flow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Oversized amount typography: Using a giant numeral for the dollar amount creates an unmissable final-check moment, reducing costly user error in irreversible money transfers.

  • Contextual upsell at peak intent: The Purchase Protection toggle is inserted at the exact moment the user is primed to pay, when willingness to accept small trade-offs for security is highest.

  • Zero-cost framing: Explicitly stating "Seller pays a small fee" removes the primary objection (cost) a payer would have to opting in, driving toggle adoption.

  • Visible funding source with balance: Surfacing "Balance: $150.11" inline lets users self-verify sufficient funds without an extra tap, preventing failed transaction friction.

  • Privacy control surfaced, not buried: The "Public" privacy setting for the transaction feed is shown prominently, respecting Venmo's social feed model while giving users an easy escape hatch to change visibility.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers using Venmo for casual, often social payments (splitting event tickets, group purchases, informal goods/services) rather than professional invoicing. The presence of "Ticket" as the memo and "Public" privacy suggests a casual peer transaction rather than a formal purchase, aligning with Venmo's core demographic of younger, socially-networked users who view payments partly as a social feed activity.

The Purchase Protection toggle specifically targets users engaging in semi-commercial P2P transactions (buying goods/tickets from strangers or acquaintances) where trust is lower than with friends — leveraging loss-aversion psychology and a "free-to-you" framing to convert protection into a low-friction default upgrade, which indirectly monetizes the seller side of the transaction for Venmo/PayPal.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this large-numeral confirmation + optional protection toggle pattern whenever:

  • Designing final-step payment/checkout confirmation screens where transaction irreversibility demands a clear visual double-check moment.

  • You need to introduce an optional paid or value-added service (insurance, protection, warranty) without creating a hard blocker or extra step in the flow.

  • The paying party isn't the one bearing the cost of the add-on, making an opt-in toggle an easy, guilt-free "yes."

  • Displaying account balance or funding source inline can prevent failed payment attempts and additional taps.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The transaction flow is high-volume/repetitive (e.g., recurring bill splits among trusted contacts), where an extra toggle each time creates unnecessary friction and decision fatigue.

  • The protection/upsell fee is charged to the payer rather than a third party — bundling a hidden cost toggle at the final step can feel manipulative or dark-pattern-like if not fully transparent.

  • Users are in a professional/B2B payment context where oversized playful typography and social privacy settings (Public/Private) feel out of place or unprofessional.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 13
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is a payment confirmation/checkout screen within Venmo, structured as a modal (indicated by the bottom sheet drag handle and close "X" button) that overlays the host app's flow. The layout follows a clear visual hierarchy: recipient identity at the top (currently loading/blurred), a massive, unmissable dollar amount ($2) as the focal point, a short payment memo ("Ticket"), followed by privacy status, funding source, and a protection upsell toggle before the final CTA.

The large, oversized typography for the amount immediately anchors the user's attention and confirms exactly what they are about to pay — a critical moment for trust and error-prevention in a P2P payment flow. The funding source card (Venmo balance with visible balance amount) gives the user confidence they have sufficient funds without needing to navigate elsewhere.

The CTA button is in a loading state (spinner), indicating the screen is captured mid-transaction, which also reveals an important pattern: the button becomes actionable/disabled feedback loop is tightly coupled to toggle interaction above it, likely re-validating price/fee changes when Purchase Protection is toggled on.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal, confident, and transactional, consistent with a financial utility app. "Turn on for purchases" is action-oriented and low-friction, while the supporting line ("Get a full refund if an eligible purchase isn't what you paid for. Seller pays a small fee.") uses reassuring, benefit-first language that pre-empts objections by clarifying the buyer bears no cost.

The word "full refund" is bolded and in the same blue as links, subtly implying more information is available and drawing the eye to the strongest benefit phrase. "Terms apply" is deliberately small and low-contrast, fulfilling legal/compliance requirements without competing with the primary conversion message — a classic pattern of transparent-but-unobtrusive disclosure.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Oversized amount display: The $2 figure dominates the screen, reducing cognitive load and preventing costly payment errors by making the transaction amount impossible to miss.

  • Contextual upsell placement: The Purchase Protection toggle is inserted at the exact decision point before the pay action, when the user is most primed to consider risk mitigation.

  • Shield icon reinforcement: Pairing the toggle with a checkmark-shield icon visually reinforces the "protection/safety" concept without needing extra copy.

  • Transparent fee framing: Explicitly stating "Seller pays a small fee" removes buyer hesitation, framing the upsell as risk-free for the person making the decision.

  • Privacy status surfaced early: Showing "Private" with a lock icon builds trust that the transaction won't be publicly visible, addressing a known Venmo user concern.

  • Funding source transparency: Displaying the live Venmo balance next to the payment method removes the need to check balance elsewhere, reducing friction and failed payment attempts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers making small peer-to-peer or purchase payments (e.g., splitting costs, buying tickets from an individual seller) who value speed and simplicity but may be wary of scams in informal marketplace transactions. The psychological trigger at play is loss aversion combined with low-cost risk reduction: by toggling on protection, the buyer feels shielded from the small but real risk of being scammed by a private seller, especially relevant for ticket resale — a category historically prone to fraud.

The design also leverages the endowment of trust in existing balance ("Venmo Balance: $150.11") to reduce anxiety about payment failure, appealing to users who prefer using existing funds over linking a card.
screens.whereToUse:
• Peer-to-peer payment or marketplace checkout flows where buyer protection or insurance can be offered as an optional add-on.

  • Any transaction confirmation screen where displaying the amount prominently is critical to prevent user error.

  • Flows where you want to introduce a low-friction monetizable upsell (protection, insurance, warranty) exactly at the point of commitment, without requiring a separate screen or interrupting momentum.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for high-trust, verified-business transactions where buyer protection is redundant or already implied, as it can create unnecessary doubt about the seller's legitimacy.

  • Do not use for recurring or trusted-contact payments (e.g., paying a roommate you frequently transact with) — the added upsell step introduces friction that feels irrelevant and can annoy repeat users.

  • Avoid stacking multiple upsells or toggles on a payment confirmation screen, as it dilutes focus from the core action and can raise perceived risk/complexity.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 14
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is Venmo's core "hub" experience, combining a transactional success confirmation with an always-on social feed. Architecturally, it's a single vertically-scrolling stream anchored by a persistent bottom Tab Bar, with the "Pay/Request" icon and floating cobalt-blue "V" action button doubling down as the app's primary conversion point.

The top of the stack surfaces a transient success banner ("You sent a payment to...") that behaves like a toast/confirmation card rather than a full-screen interstitial — this keeps the user in flow rather than forcing them through a dead-end confirmation screen. Immediately below it, a merchandising card for the Venmo Debit Card is injected natively into the feed, mimicking the visual weight of a social post so it doesn't feel like a disruptive ad unit.

The remainder of the screen is a reverse-chronological Stacked List of transactions from the user and their network, each row following an identical template: avatar, actor/action/recipient line, relative timestamp, privacy icon, a memo line (often emoji-laden), and social engagement affordances (like/comment/overflow). This consistent card structure lets users scan dozens of transactions at speed, which suits the "Busy Urban" target audience who want quick confirmation and light social browsing in the same breath.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is deliberately terse and human — "You paid," "Ticket," "Water," "Happy pup! 🐕" — favoring emoji and one-word memos over formal transaction descriptions. This casualness reframes a financial ledger as a diary of everyday social moments, lowering the psychological weight typically associated with money movement.

The success banner uses an affirming green checkmark and active voice ("You sent a payment to...") for immediate positive reinforcement. The debit card promo uses upbeat, low-friction language ("Set up in seconds!") paired with an urgency-free but action-oriented CTA ("Apply now") to cross-sell without feeling pushy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Confirmation-as-feed-item: Rather than a modal blocking the UI after payment, the success state is woven directly into the scrollable feed, preserving momentum and letting users immediately see social context around their action.

  • Native ad merchandising: The Venmo Debit Card promo is styled identically to a feed card (rounded corners, illustration, single CTA), reducing banner blindness and increasing perceived relevance.

  • Privacy iconography inline: Small lock/shield/people icons next to each timestamp communicate the visibility setting (private, friends, public) without cluttering copy — a subtle but critical trust signal for a payments app that defaults to public sharing.

  • Emoji as content, not decoration: Memo fields like "Happy pup! 🐕" turn a receipt into a shareable social artifact, which is core to Venmo's differentiation from purely utilitarian payment apps.

  • Persistent floating brand mark: The circular "V" logo overlapping the tab bar reinforces brand identity at the exact spot users tap most, subtly anchoring trust during the highest-frequency interaction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Designed for busy urban users who split bills, pay rent, or reimburse friends on the go, this screen leverages social proof and habit-loop reinforcement: seeing friends' transactions normalizes frequent app usage and subtly nudges the viewer to reciprocate (request/pay) when they see activity. The immediate, unobstructed success confirmation caters to users who need fast validation without extra taps, respecting their limited time. The playful emoji/memo culture also appeals to a demographic that treats Venmo as a lightweight social network, not just a wallet, driving daily engagement rather than purely transactional, need-based visits.
screens.whereToUse:
• Any app where a transactional or utility action (payment, booking, submission) benefits from being paired with ongoing social or activity context to encourage return visits.

  • Products wanting to normalize a new behavior (e.g., splitting costs, tipping) by publicly displaying peer activity as implicit social proof.

  • Feeds needing to inject native promotional content without breaking visual rhythm — mimicking the card style of surrounding content.

  • Situations where instant, low-friction success confirmation (banner/inline) is preferable to a blocking modal, keeping users in their task flow.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Highly sensitive financial contexts (e.g., banking, investing, healthcare payments) where public/social visibility of transactions could violate user expectations of privacy or regulatory compliance.

  • Enterprise or B2B tools where users need dense, unambiguous confirmation screens rather than socially-styled feed entries — ambiguity here could undermine trust in accuracy.

  • Apps with a predominantly older or privacy-conscious demographic who may be uncomfortable with default-public activity streams and casual tone.

  • Contexts where merchandising cards embedded in transactional feeds could be perceived as manipulative or distract from critical account/security information.

screens.name: Subscription Screen 04
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is the first screen in the entire twenty-plus-screen sequence to show what using the product actually looks like. That is a remarkable fact: the flow has asked eight questions, made an efficacy claim, collected registration details, and presented three tiers of social proof before depicting a single lesson. The depiction, when it finally arrives, is well chosen — a scatter plot with a fitted curve and two draggable parameter sliders, with a hand mid-drag. It demonstrates the "learn by doing" premise from the welcome screen concretely: you move a control, the curve responds, understanding follows. Someone who has never used Brilliant now knows what a session involves.

It also, notably, matches the user's answers. The exercise is regression-fitting — squarely within Data Analysis & Probability, the subject selected during onboarding. If this asset is segment-specific rather than fixed, it is the first commercially-positioned screen to act on the personalization the flow collected, which would be a meaningful use of that data.

The placement is the problem. This is the strongest argument the paywall has, and it sits below three tiers of social proof, well past the fold. A user who scrolls only to the reviews never sees the product at all.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven in part, though the illustration carries most of the argument.

The heading "Learn efficiently" is weaker than what it introduces. It names an abstract quality where the visual directly above shows a specific mechanism. Something naming the mechanism — manipulating a model to see how it behaves — would connect the two. As written, the heading and the illustration are making different arguments.

"Level up with Premium" as the section title is the flow's first use of gaming vocabulary. It sits oddly against a product that has otherwise spoken in the register of a patient tutor, and against an audience of curious adults rather than gamified learners.

The course count has changed. This section states "100+ interactive courses" while the timeline section, two scroll positions above, states "70+ interactive courses." Both figures appear in the same scrollable screen describing the same Premium tier. One of them is wrong, and a user who notices will reasonably wonder which other numbers are unreliable — particularly given the flow has already made an unattributed "6x" claim and a 365-lessons projection.

"Real-time feedback" is accurate and well-matched to the illustration, since the visible exercise is exactly that: adjust, observe, adjust again.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Show the product — a single depiction of real use does more persuasive work than three tiers of testimony, and it arrives too late in the scroll to do that work for most users.

  2. Heading-to-visual alignment — an abstract benefit label above a concrete demonstration wastes the specificity the illustration provides.

  3. Internal consistency of claims — two different course counts on one screen undermines every other figure the paywall states.

  4. Personalization finally applied — a subject-matched demo would be the first commercial use of the onboarding answers, if it is indeed segment-specific.

  5. Persistent disclosure — price and trial terms remain pinned through every scroll position, which is consistently well handled.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo — shows an actual exercise screenshot on its Super paywall, positioned above testimonials rather than below.

  2. Headspace — depicts a real session interface as the hero of its subscription screen.

  3. Notion — leads its upgrade screens with product screenshots on the same logic: demonstration outperforms description.
screens.whereToUse: Best near the top of a paywall, where a depiction of real use answers "what am I actually buying" before any social proof is offered.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit buried below multiple proof tiers, and poor fit where the depicted feature isn't representative of typical use — a flattering edge case sets an expectation the product won't meet.

screens.name: Subscription Screen 08
screens.uxAnalysis:
This scroll position shows the catalog module doing its most useful work: naming actual courses. Five titles plus a count of fifteen more gives a concrete sense of depth in a single category — twenty courses in Foundational Math alone — which is far more persuasive than any aggregate figure, and it lets the user verify coverage rather than trust it. The progressive-disclosure expander is the right call: showing five and offering the rest keeps the section scannable while making the full inventory available on demand.

The institutional strip beneath is a fourth distinct proof type on this paywall, after platform awards, press quotes, and user reviews. It answers a different question from all of them — not is this popular or do users like it but who made this content. For a STEM product asking €105.99, creator credentials are arguably the most relevant credibility signal of the four, and it is placed last, closest to the button.

The overall paywall architecture is now fully visible: timeline → institutional awards → press → user reviews → feature carousel → catalog browser → creator credentials → CTA. That is seven distinct persuasion modules in one scrollable screen. Comprehensive, but long enough that most users will decide before reaching the strongest evidence.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven in the credibility line, which is carefully worded.

"All of our 100+ courses are crafted by award-winning teachers, researchers, and professionals from:" — the construction is precise about what it claims. It says the courses are made by people from these institutions, not that the institutions endorse Brilliant. That distinction matters legally and ethically, and the sentence gets it right. A sloppier version ("courses from MIT and Caltech") would imply institutional partnership that almost certainly does not exist.

"Crafted" and "award-winning" are the softer parts. "Crafted" is a marketing verb where "written" or "built" would do, and "award-winning" is unspecified — which awards, won by whom, is left open. Both are mild against the general standard of paywall copy, but they are the kind of unbacked qualifier this flow has used repeatedly.

Course titles are plainly descriptive — Solving Equations, Understanding Graphs, Geometry Fundamentals, Vectors, Systems of Equations. No cleverness, no branded names. Right for a catalog where the user is scanning for recognition.

"15 additional courses" states an exact number rather than "more," which is the stronger construction — the user learns the category holds twenty courses without expanding anything.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Named inventory beats counted inventory — five real titles plus an exact remainder tells the user more about value than "100+ courses" does.

  2. Progressive disclosure — showing five and offering fifteen keeps the section scannable while making full depth one tap away.

  3. Credential proof placed last — creator affiliations are the most relevant credibility signal for a technical education product, and they sit closest to the CTA.

  4. Careful claim construction — "professionals from" rather than "courses from" avoids implying institutional endorsement.

  5. Proof stack length — seven persuasion modules in one scroll means the strongest evidence sits where the fewest users will reach it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Coursera — leads with university affiliation as its primary credibility signal, though with actual institutional partnerships rather than staff provenance.

  2. MasterClass — names instructor credentials prominently on conversion screens, the same creator-provenance argument.

  3. Duolingo — surfaces named unit listings with an expander on its paywall catalog view.
screens.whereToUse: Best deep in a catalog-driven paywall, where naming real courses answers the value question and creator credentials close the credibility gap for technical subject matter.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit where the named inventory is thin or the titles are generic, and poor fit where institutional names would imply a partnership that does not exist — the phrasing has to carry that distinction as carefully as it does here.

screens.name: Subscription Screen 05
screens.uxAnalysis:
The page dots resolve something the previous frame left ambiguous: the regression exercise wasn't a standalone section but slide two of a four-slide carousel, and this is slide three. That changes the earlier reading. The paywall isn't a single long scroll of proof with one product shot buried in it — it has a dedicated, swipeable product-demonstration module. The weakness is that the carousel's presence was invisible until this slide, since the previous capture showed no dots at that scroll position. A user who scrolls past without noticing the affordance sees one slide of four.

The demo itself is well chosen. A pixel grid with a hand drawing on it, feeding into a network diagram with weighted connections, communicates a neural network far better than any description would — and it shows the user doing something rather than reading. It also pairs with the regression demo to suggest a range from statistics to machine learning.

Notably, this slide is not matched to the user's stated subject. The regression exercise mapped cleanly onto Data Analysis & Probability; this one is squarely Computer Science. So the carousel appears to be a fixed catalog tour rather than segment-personalized, which retracts my provisional reading of the previous frame.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven, and this slide contains the flow's most questionable phrase.

"Apply your learnings" is the weakest heading yet. "Learnings" as a plural noun is corporate jargon that sits badly against a product otherwise written in plain, warm English. "Put it to work" or "Build something real" would say the same thing in the flow's established register.

"Hacking a password" is a genuine problem. It appears in a list of what the user will get hands-on with, alongside building a neural network. The intent is transparent — Brilliant almost certainly has a cryptography or password-security course teaching how hashing and brute-force attacks work, which is standard, legitimate CS education. But the phrasing describes an offensive action rather than a subject. "How password cracking works" or "cryptography and password security" would convey the same appeal without framing the product as teaching users to hack. On a paywall shown to a general audience including minors — an app that markets to educators and complies with COPPA and FERPA — this is a phrasing choice worth revisiting. It is the only copy in twenty-plus screens that would give a parent or school administrator pause.

"Cutting-edge applications" is filler of the same family as "supercharge" from the earlier interstitial. The examples that follow are concrete and do the work; the adjective adds nothing.

What works: naming two specific, recognizable projects is far stronger than promising abstract capability. A user can picture building a neural network. That specificity is exactly what the "Learn efficiently" heading on the previous slide lacked.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Carousel affordance appears late — page dots visible only on some slides means the swipeable module may go unnoticed, costing three-quarters of its content.

  2. Concrete examples outperform abstract benefit language — naming actual projects gives the user something to picture, unlike the previous slide's heading.

  3. Register consistency — "learnings" and "cutting-edge" break a voice the flow otherwise maintained carefully across twenty screens.

  4. Framing matters for sensitive subject matter — describing an offensive action rather than the underlying subject creates avoidable exposure for an app serving educational and minor audiences.

  5. Demonstration over description — the drawn-digit-into-network visual explains the exercise faster than any sentence could.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo — uses a swipeable feature carousel on its Super paywall with page dots and per-slide product shots.

  2. Headspace — presents subscription benefits as a carousel of illustrated capability slides above a persistent CTA.

  3. Sololearn — showcases specific buildable projects rather than abstract skills on its conversion screen.
screens.whereToUse: Best as a compact feature tour on a paywall, where several distinct capabilities each merit their own visual and the carousel affordance is clearly signposted from the first slide.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit where the dots aren't consistently visible, since undiscovered slides are wasted production cost, and poor fit for describing sensitive technical subjects in action-verb form on a general-audience commercial screen.

screens.name: Subscription Screen 01
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is the flow's commercial destination, and it is built on the most user-respecting paywall pattern available: the trial timeline. Rather than presenting a price and hoping, it lays out exactly what will happen and when — access today, a reminder on day 5, a charge on day 7 with a named date. That structure directly addresses the specific anxiety that suppresses trial conversion, which is not the price but the fear of forgetting to cancel. Promising a reminder two days before the charge is the strongest trust signal on the screen, and it is the reason this pattern converts better than a bare pricing table.

The first timeline stage is doing quiet strategic work: "Set your learning goals" is shown struck through and checked, retroactively converting eleven screens of onboarding into step one of a purchase funnel. The user arrives feeling they are two-thirds through a process rather than at the start of a sales pitch. That is elegant, and slightly manipulative — the onboarding was never framed as part of a purchase.

Two structural changes mark the shift out of onboarding: the back chevron is replaced by a close X, and the progress bar is gone entirely. The user can now dismiss rather than retreat, which correctly signals a different kind of screen.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven, and the most consequential writing in the entire flow.

Disclosure quality is genuinely good. The screen states the trial length, the exact charge date, the annual price, the monthly equivalent, and the ability to cancel. That combination exceeds what many subscription apps disclose, and the pinned placement above the CTA means it cannot be missed. This is the transparency that App Store guidelines require and that many apps meet only technically.

The price framing does real work. "105,99 € per year (8,83 € per month)" leads with the amount actually charged, then supplies the smaller number for comparison. Leading with the annual figure is the honest ordering — the reverse, showing €8.83 prominently with the annual total in fine print, is the standard dark pattern. This screen does not do that.

"Start your 7-day free trial" as the CTA names exactly what the tap does. Not "Continue," not "Get Premium" — the word trial is in the label, so nobody taps it believing they are buying outright.

The day-5 reminder is the trust anchor. Committing in writing to warn the user before charging them is the single most reassuring sentence available on a trial paywall, and it is given equal weight to the access and charge stages rather than buried.

Where it is less clean: the day-7 stage is cut off mid-sentence by the pinned footer — "Cancel anytime before" is truncated at the exact clause explaining how to avoid the charge. The most consequential sentence on the screen is the one the layout hides. Whether it scrolls into view is likely, but the cutoff falls in the worst possible place.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Anxiety reduction over persuasion — the timeline converts an unknown future obligation into a dated sequence, which addresses the actual barrier to trial signup.

  2. Honest price ordering — annual first, monthly in parentheses, is the transparent construction; the inverse is the pattern regulators scrutinize.

  3. Commitment escalation — marking onboarding as a completed step reframes a sales screen as continuation, leveraging investment the user made under a different premise.

  4. Match between label and consequence — the CTA names the trial explicitly rather than obscuring what the tap initiates.

  5. Truncation at the worst clause — the cancellation instruction being the cut-off text undermines an otherwise exemplary disclosure.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Blinkist — pioneered the trial-timeline paywall with the same three-beat structure and reminder promise.

  2. Duolingo — uses an equivalent timeline for Super trials, positioned at the same point after onboarding.

  3. Calm — presents access-today, reminder-before-charge, charge-date stages in an identical vertical sequence.
screens.whereToUse: Best as the conversion screen following a substantial onboarding, where a trial is genuinely offered and the app will honestly send the pre-charge reminder it promises.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit where the reminder isn't actually sent — the timeline's entire credibility rests on that promise being kept — and poor fit before any value has been demonstrated, since the timeline explains mechanics rather than making a case for the product.

screens.name: Subscription Screen 11
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is the paywall's final module and the one that satisfies its regulatory obligations. Everything Apple's guidelines require for an auto-renewing subscription is present and legible: the price, the billing period, what the price buys, that renewal is automatic, when renewal occurs, how to cancel, and links to both terms and privacy policy. That is a complete disclosure, and it is placed above the CTA rather than buried in a settings screen.

The timeline is repeated here in full — the same four stages shown at the top of the paywall. Bookending a long screen with the same mechanics is defensible: a user who has scrolled through nine modules gets the terms restated at the point of decision rather than having to recall them. It also means the two most important pieces of information on the paywall, what happens when and what it costs, are the first and last things seen.

The whole paywall's architecture is now visible end to end: timeline → awards → press → reviews → feature carousel → catalog browser → creator credentials → tier comparison → timeline again with legal terms. Nine modules. Thorough to the point that most users will decide long before reaching this one — which matters, because this is where the auto-renewal terms live.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven, and this is the flow's most consequential text after the price itself.

"You won't be charged until after your free trial ends." A plain-language reassurance sitting above the legal block, addressing the specific fear that stops trial signups. Placing it before the dense terms means the anxious user gets their answer without parsing legalese.

The subscription terms are unusually complete. They name the charging entity (iTunes account), the exact amount, the period, that renewal is automatic, the renewal window (within 24 hours before period end), and where to cancel (App Store settings). Many apps disclose less. The construction is standard boilerplate, which is appropriate — this is not the place for voice.

"Cancel anytime in your App Store settings" is the sentence that matters most, and it names the actual location rather than saying "cancel anytime" without a path. That distinction separates honest disclosure from technical compliance.

The presentation undercuts the content. All of this is rendered in light gray, centered, at small size — the lowest-contrast text on the entire paywall. The information is legally sufficient and practically hard to read. There is no requirement that terms be styled to disappear, and a darker gray would cost nothing.

"Upon subscribing" is a small tonal oddity against the flow's plain English, though it is standard in this class of copy.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Complete disclosure before purchase — price, period, auto-renewal, renewal timing, cancellation path, and both policy links are all present above the CTA.

  2. Plain-language reassurance precedes legalese — the "you won't be charged until" line answers the real question before the dense block that formalizes it.

  3. Naming the cancellation path — telling users where to cancel, not just that they can, is the difference between honest and technically compliant.

  4. Contrast undermines legibility — the most consequential text on the screen is styled as the least readable.

  5. Bookending the mechanics — repeating the timeline at the decision point means users who scrolled far don't have to recall terms from nine modules ago.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo — places full App Store subscription terms with policy links directly above its Super CTA.

  2. Calm — discloses auto-renewal mechanics in a small-type block at the base of its trial screen.

  3. Headspace — pairs a plain-language "you won't be charged" line with formal terms in the same position.
screens.whereToUse: Required on any auto-renewing subscription screen; best placed above the CTA with a plain-language summary preceding the formal terms.
screens.whereNotToUse: No context permits omitting it. The pattern to avoid is styling it below usable contrast or placing it behind a "details" link, both of which meet the letter of the requirement while defeating its purpose.

screens.name: Subscription Screen 13
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen belongs to Apple, not Brilliant, and that is precisely its value. Every prior disclosure came from the party selling the subscription; this one comes from the platform processing the payment, and it independently restates the same terms. A user who skimmed the paywall's gray legal block gets the material facts again — trial length, price, renewal date, cancellation path — in high-contrast black on white, from a source with no incentive to obscure them.

The confirmation mechanism is the other notable element. Requiring a physical double-click of the side button rather than a tappable button makes accidental purchase essentially impossible: it is a deliberate hardware gesture that cannot be triggered by a mis-tap or by an overlay directing attention. Comparing this to the notification permission screen earlier in the flow is instructive — there, an app-drawn arrow survived the system dim and pointed at "Allow." Here there is nothing to point at, because the confirmation is not on screen.

For the app, this screen is the transaction's honest checkpoint. Everything Brilliant could control has been used persuasively; this is the moment the platform interposes a neutral summary.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Not the app's copy — this is Apple's standard StoreKit sheet, and its construction is worth noting as the benchmark the app's own disclosure is measured against.

"1-week free trial / Starting today" and "105,99 € per year / Starting on 24 Feb 2025" present the two financial facts as a labelled pair with dates attached. Compare the app's own version: the same information, but rendered in light gray centered small type. Apple's is black, left-aligned, and hierarchically ordered. The contrast in legibility between the two disclosures of identical facts is the most instructive thing on this screen.

"No commitment. Cancel at any time in Settings › Apple Account at least one day before each renewal date. Plan automatically renews until cancelled." This names the exact settings path, the deadline relative to renewal, and the automatic nature of renewal. The app's version said "cancel anytime in your App Store settings" — accurate but vaguer, and it omitted the one-day-before deadline, which is the operationally important detail.

"Account: account@refero.design" confirms which Apple Account will be charged, a detail the app could not supply and one that matters on shared or family devices.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Platform-mediated disclosure — an independent restatement of terms by the payment processor is structurally more trustworthy than the seller's own version.

  2. Hardware confirmation prevents accidental purchase — a physical double-click cannot be triggered by a mis-tap, an overlay, or a directional graphic.

  3. Legibility as a disclosure quality — identical facts rendered in high-contrast black here versus light gray in the app shows how much presentation affects whether terms are actually read.

  4. Precision in the cancellation path — naming the exact settings location and the one-day deadline is more actionable than "cancel anytime."

  5. Account transparency — showing which account is charged addresses a real failure mode on shared devices.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Every iOS subscription app — this sheet is mandatory and identical across Duolingo, Calm, Headspace, and Spotify; it is the platform's uniform checkpoint.

  2. Google Play Billing — Android's equivalent sheet serves the same independent-restatement function.

  3. The comparison worth drawing is not to other apps but to Brilliant's own preceding disclosure, which covered the same ground less legibly.
screens.whereToUse: Mandatory for all iOS in-app subscriptions; not a design choice available to the app.
screens.whereNotToUse: Not applicable — the pattern to avoid is treating this sheet as sufficient and under-disclosing in the app's own UI on the assumption that Apple will cover it.

screens.name: Subscription Screen 06
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is the most substantive section of the paywall and the first genuinely interactive one — every prior module was scroll-only. It answers the question a purchase decision actually turns on: what do I get for the money. Six subject filters expose the catalog's breadth, and selecting one swaps both a representative exercise and a course list, so the user can verify content exists in the area they care about rather than trusting a headline number.

The personalization finally shows up here too. "Data" is preselected — matching the subject the user chose during onboarding — which is the first time in the commercial section that an earlier answer visibly changes what's displayed. That is a meaningful and well-placed use of the collected data: it puts the most relevant evidence in front of the user by default while leaving the other five categories one tap away.

The preview exercise is also the strongest product depiction so far. An area model with overlapping colored regions, a legend summing to 45%, and a real multiple-choice question with a Submit button shows an entire interaction loop rather than a decorative fragment. Someone can look at this and understand exactly what a lesson involves.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven in part, though the interactive module carries most of the argument.

The headline — "Build quantitative & technical problem solving skills" — is the most credential-oriented framing in the entire flow. Every prior headline spoke to curiosity, habit, or method: learn by doing, smarter every day, you'll fit right in. This one speaks to capability acquisition, and it arrives at the point of sale. That shift is deliberate: curiosity gets people through onboarding, but skills justify €105.99. It is also the least warm sentence Brilliant has written here, using an ampersand and a four-word noun phrase where the flow's voice has otherwise been conversational.

The category labels are well chosen. "Foundational Math" and "Advanced Math" as separate entries signal the catalog serves both the Beginner and the Advanced tiers offered during calibration — a user who self-identified at either end can see they're accommodated. "Electives" is a sensible catch-all that avoids listing everything.

"Courses in Data" is plain and functional, and the visible course title — "Exploring Data Visually" — is descriptive rather than clever, which is right for a catalog listing.

The preview question ("What proportion of moviegoers saw both movies?") is a small but real piece of voice: it frames a probability problem around something ordinary rather than abstract set notation. That is consistent with the app's stated pedagogy and does more to convey teaching style than any adjective on the previous slides.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Show the catalog, not a count — browsable categories with real course names answer the value question far better than "70+" or "100+" claims, and sidestep the contradiction between them.

  2. Personalization applied where it matters — preselecting the user's chosen subject is the first commercial use of onboarding answers and puts relevant evidence first.

  3. Interactivity signals confidence — letting users poke at the catalog before paying implies the content will hold up to inspection.

  4. Complete interaction loop shown — question, options, and Submit together convey the lesson format in a way partial visuals cannot.

  5. Register shift at the point of sale — moving from curiosity language to skills language is strategically sound but noticeably colder than the rest of the flow.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo — surfaces course and unit previews on its paywall so users can confirm their language is well covered.

  2. Coursera — leads subscription screens with browsable catalog categories rather than aggregate course counts.

  3. Sololearn — shows filterable track listings with sample exercises at the conversion point.
screens.whereToUse: Best on a subscription paywall for a broad-catalog product, where users need to verify coverage in their specific area before committing, and where an earlier answer can preselect the most relevant category.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for single-purpose products with nothing to browse, and poor fit if the visible course list is thin — exposing the catalog invites scrutiny and only helps when the inventory rewards it.

screens.name: Subscription Screen 07
screens.uxAnalysis:
Comparing this against the previous frame confirms the catalog module works as designed: changing the chip swaps the preview exercise, the window title, and the course list header together. Nothing is stale, and the response is immediate enough that the module rewards exploration — which is the point of exposing a catalog before purchase.

The preview content is again well selected, and arguably better than the Data one. A parabola with a single large rectangle over-estimating the area at 15.3 against a true value of 10, plus a slider currently at one partition, communicates the entire concept of Riemann integration in one static frame: drag the slider, add rectangles, watch the estimate converge. The accompanying panel says exactly that. For a user weighing whether the app can teach genuinely hard material, this is a stronger argument than any testimonial on the screen — it shows a difficult concept made manipulable.

One structural note: the chip layout reflows when selection changes. In the previous frame "Data" sat on the top row and the selected chip's raised card appeared there; here "Advanced Math" occupies the second row and the rows have redistributed. The arrangement is not a fixed grid, so the filter positions move as the user browses.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven only in the preview panel, and that copy is the most instructive text in the flow.

"With more and more rectangles, we get better estimates for the area under the curve." This is the clearest single demonstration of Brilliant's teaching voice anywhere in the twenty-plus screens. It explains integration without the words limit, infinitesimal, or sum notation — plain English describing what the user will watch happen. Someone intimidated by calculus reads this and sees an approach they could follow.

That matters because the flow has spent enormous effort claiming effective teaching — the 6x statistic, "learn by doing," "interactive problem solving that's effective and fun" — and this is the first place it actually demonstrates it. The demonstration is buried inside a mockup, in small type, on the sixth scroll position of a paywall.

"Continue" in the mockup echoes the button label used across all of onboarding, a small continuity touch suggesting the real lesson UI uses the same vocabulary.

The headline is unchanged from the previous frame and still carries the flow's coldest, most credential-oriented framing.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Filter feedback is complete — preview, title, and list header all update together, so no part of the view contradicts the selected state.

  2. Teaching demonstrated, not claimed — one sentence and one visual do more to prove pedagogical quality than every efficacy claim earlier in the flow.

  3. Difficulty range made visible — offering an integrals preview alongside foundational categories shows the catalog spans the calibration tiers the onboarding asked about.

  4. Exploration is cheap — one tap per category with instant content swap encourages the browsing that builds purchase confidence.

  5. Layout instability on state change — chips reflowing between rows as selection moves makes the filter set feel less like a stable control surface.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo — swaps unit previews on filter selection within its paywall catalog view.

  2. Coursera — category chips drive both a featured preview and a course listing on subscription screens.

  3. Khan Academy — surfaces subject-specific sample exercises to demonstrate teaching approach before commitment.
screens.whereToUse: Best on a broad-catalog subscription paywall where users need to confirm depth in their area, and where sample content can demonstrate teaching quality rather than assert it.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit where categories have uneven depth — letting users browse into a thin category does more harm than a headline count would — and poor fit if the preview exercises aren't representative of typical lesson quality.

screens.name: Subscription Screen 03
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is the paywall's third proof tier, and the structure of the whole screen is now clear: mechanics (timeline), then institutional authority (awards and press), then peer voice (reviews), then the ask. Three distinct kinds of evidence stacked in descending formality, each answering a different objection — what will happen to me, is this legitimate, do people like me benefit.

The testimonials here are considerably better chosen than the single-word press quotes above them. Both describe outcomes rather than impressions, and the first one in particular maps directly onto the segmentation the onboarding performed: it mentions technical job interviews and real-world problem solving, which speaks straight to the "Professional growth" and "Learning specific skills" answers offered on questions one and two. Whether these rotate by segment can't be determined from one capture, but if they do, it would be the first time the flow has used its collected answers on a screen that matters commercially.

The aggregate number does the heavier lifting though. Fifty thousand five-star reviews is a scale claim that is both specific and, unusually for this flow, verifiable — App Store ratings are public.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy-driven, and the strongest social proof in the entire sequence.

The aggregate headline: "Over 50,000 5-star reviews" is precise where earlier claims were vague. Compare it to the first interstitial's "millions of people use Brilliant" — same intent, far better execution. It specifies the rating tier, gives a countable figure, and points at something a skeptical user can check independently. Worth noting it counts only five-star reviews rather than stating an overall average, which is selective but not misleading, since the claim is explicitly scoped.

Jacob S.'s testimonial is the best-written proof on the screen. It follows the classic before/after structure — previously struggled to understand, now feels confident — and names two concrete applications. It is long enough to be credible as something a real person wrote, and it answers the efficacy question the "6x" claim asserted without evidence.

R.T.'s testimonial is weaker and does something the first avoids: it explicitly endorses the paid tier ("The premium subscription is absolutely worth it"). Placing a price-justification quote directly above a price is transparently instrumental. Real reviews rarely open by validating a subscription's value; the phrasing reads as selected-for-purpose, and its three exclamation marks push it toward advertising register. Its placement immediately above the CTA is the least subtle moment on the screen.

Attribution remains thin. "Jacob S." and "R.T." follow the same first-name-and-initial pattern as "Bob V." during onboarding, with no platform, date, or verification link — despite the headline citing App Store reviews that are publicly attributable.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Layered proof — three tiers of evidence in descending formality lets each answer a different objection rather than repeating the same reassurance.

  2. Specificity converts — a countable review figure outperforms the "millions of people" framing used earlier, and is independently checkable.

  3. Outcome over impression — testimonials describing what changed for the reviewer carry more weight than the single-word press pulls above them.

  4. Instrumental placement is visible — a quote endorsing the subscription's value, sited directly above the price, invites the suspicion it was chosen for that job.

  5. Persistent disclosure — the price and trial terms remain pinned through every scroll position, so the commercial terms are never out of view.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Blinkist — stacks aggregate review counts with individual testimonials above its trial CTA in the same descending-formality order.

  2. Calm — cites App Store review volume alongside selected user quotes on its subscription screen.

  3. Duolingo — uses review-count aggregates and short user testimonials at the Super conversion point.
screens.whereToUse: Best as the final proof tier on a trial paywall, after mechanics and institutional credibility, where peer testimonials in the user's own segment can close the remaining doubt.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit where testimonials cannot be attributed to a verifiable source, and poor fit when a quote's job is visibly to justify the price — that placement invites scrutiny of the whole proof stack rather than closing the sale.

screens.name: Subscription Screen 09
screens.uxAnalysis:
This confirms the expander works and reveals what it was hiding: twenty courses in a single category, spanning Solving Equations at the entry end to Number Theory and Contest Math at the other. That range is the section's real argument. A user who self-identified as a Beginner sees Mathematical Fundamentals and Everyday Math; one who called themselves Advanced sees Contest Math and Number Theory. The calibration question asked five screens into onboarding is answered here, implicitly, by inventory rather than by claim.

The layout is where it falters. Courses flow in a variable-column arrangement — two per row, then one, then two, then three — driven by title length rather than a fixed grid. The result is a ragged wall of twenty items with no alphabetical order, no difficulty grouping, and no visual hierarchy. "Logic II" appears eight rows above "Logic," which is the clearest symptom: the list has no ordering logic a user can perceive, so scanning for a specific topic means reading every entry. For a section whose job is to let users verify coverage, that friction is avoidable.

The expanded state also pushes the institutional credibility strip and everything below it further down, which on a paywall this long is a meaningful cost.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Not applicable in the conventional sense — this screen is a list of proper nouns with no prose beyond the section header and the persistent price line.

The course titles themselves are worth a brief note, since they are the only voice present. Most are plainly descriptive (Solving Equations, Systems of Equations, Number Bases), but a handful carry the app's personality: "Calculus in a Nutshell" promises approachability on the subject users most fear, "Beautiful Geometry" frames math aesthetically rather than instrumentally, and "Knowledge and Uncertainty" and "Infinity" read as conceptual rather than procedural. Those four do real positioning work — they signal a product interested in mathematical ideas, not just exam preparation, which matches the "Following my curiosity" option offered during onboarding.

"Logic" and "Logic II" are the exception and a small problem. Numbered sequels imply an order the list does not display, and separating them by eight entries means a user cannot tell which to start with or that a sequence exists at all.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Inventory answers the calibration question — a range from Everyday Math to Contest Math demonstrates the catalog serves every tier the onboarding asked users to self-select.

  2. Unordered lists resist scanning — no alphabetical, difficulty, or sequence ordering means finding a specific course requires reading all twenty entries.

  3. Layout driven by content width — a flow arrangement rather than a grid produces a ragged edge that makes the list feel unstructured.

  4. Sequenced courses need adjacency — "Logic" and "Logic II" separated by eight items breaks the only ordering relationship visible in the set.

  5. Expansion cost on a long screen — revealing fifteen more items pushes remaining proof modules further from reach on a paywall already running seven modules deep.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Coursera — presents catalog listings with explicit sorting and difficulty filters rather than a flat unordered set.

  2. Duolingo — orders unit listings by progression, so position communicates difficulty without labels.

  3. Khan Academy — groups subject content by level, which is the structure this list would benefit from.
screens.whereToUse: Best where a category's full inventory is genuinely impressive and the user needs to verify a specific topic exists — with ordering or grouping applied so that verification is fast.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit as an unordered flat list past roughly a dozen items, where scanning cost outweighs the reassurance of seeing everything; a grouped or filterable view serves the same purpose better.
