  2. Notion's share extension setup prompt — offers comparable framing around extending the app's reach into other apps via the native Share Sheet.

  3. Instapaper's share-extension onboarding — follows a similar "Set up" / "No thanks" structure for this exact type of iOS integration feature.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits promoting an iOS Share Sheet extension where the setup process can be initiated with a single tap (rather than requiring cross-app manual steps), and where framing the feature's benefit concretely (saving links from anywhere) helps users immediately grasp its value.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit if the underlying setup genuinely requires manual steps outside the app's control (like the earlier desktop-sync and widget flows) — in that case, omitting numbered instructions here (as this screen does) could leave users confused about what "Set up" actually does if it turns out to require additional manual configuration.

screens.name: Google Pay Login 1
screens.uxAnalysis: This is the initial launch screen displayed while the Google Pay app initializes, authenticates cached sessions, and establishes network connectivity. The layout is radically minimal: a single branded glyph (the abstract "G Pay" ribbon icon composed of Google's four brand colors) sits centered in a sea of white space, with the "Google" wordmark anchored near the bottom to reinforce parent-brand trust. There are no navigation elements, no loading spinners, and no copy—just a static, confident brand moment. This restraint is intentional; it buys the engineering team time to perform background tasks (token refresh, balance sync, biometric checks) without making the user feel like they are waiting, since a static logo feels faster than a visible progress bar for sub-second loads.
screens.tonalityAndContent: There is zero copywriting on this screen—no taglines, no "Welcome back," no loading text. The absence of language is itself a message: Google Pay is positioning money movement as being as frictionless and unremarkable as opening any other Google utility. The only "content" is the logo mark and the Google wordmark, which together transfer the trust equity of the broader Google ecosystem onto the financial product.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Brand-as-Loader: Using the static logo itself as the loading state avoids the need for a spinner, making initialization feel instantaneous and premium rather than technical.

  • Trust Transference: Pairing the Pay-specific icon with the full "Google" wordmark borrows the credibility of Google's core brand to de-risk a sensitive financial app.

  • Radical Whitespace: The generous negative space around the mark signals calm, safety, and precision—critical emotional cues for a product that handles the user's money.

  • No Distraction: Zero UI chrome (no back button, no menu) ensures the user's attention is fully captured by the brand moment before any functional decisions are required.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets the entire mainstream user base of Google Pay, from first-time downloaders to daily active users tapping the app icon to make a quick payment. Psychologically, it leverages the "Peak-End Rule" and mere brand exposure: a clean, recognizable, colorful mark reassures the user this is the trusted Google product they intended to open, reducing any anxiety about misdirected taps or fraudulent clone apps. For a payments app specifically, this instant, unambiguous brand confirmation is a critical anti-fraud and trust-building UX moment before any sensitive data (balances, transaction history) is displayed.
screens.whereToUse: Use a static branded splash for apps where cold-start or session-resume times are extremely short (under ~1 second) and where brand trust is a primary conversion lever (fintech, banking, identity/auth apps). It works best as a placeholder while lightweight background tasks (auth token check, cache read) complete, not for screens with heavy network dependency.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if actual load times are unpredictable or exceed 1-2 seconds, since the lack of a progress indicator can make the app feel frozen or unresponsive. Also avoid it when the splash needs to communicate essential information (e.g., mandatory app updates, maintenance notices) — in those cases a determinate progress bar or explanatory text is required to manage user expectations.

screens.name: Google Pay Login 2
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is the very first branching decision point in the Google Pay onboarding funnel, appearing immediately after splash/launch. The layout is deliberately austere: a logo, a two-line welcome header, a short vertical list of three country options represented as flag + text rows, and a single disabled primary CTA ("Continue") pinned to the bottom.

The use of a radio-list style selection (rendered here as simple tappable rows rather than explicit radio buttons) reduces cognitive load — the user scans flags visually rather than reading text, which is faster for international recognition. The button is greyed out/disabled by default, enforcing a deterministic linear flow: the user cannot proceed until a valid selection is made, which prevents downstream errors in regulatory/regional configuration (critical for a financial app where payment rails, KYC, and currency differ drastically by country).

The transparency at the bottom ("If your country doesn't appear here, stay tuned...") is a subtle but important piece of expectation-setting copy that gracefully handles the empty/edge case of unsupported geographies without making the user feel blocked or confused.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is warm and inviting ("Welcome to Google Pay") paired with a functional, plain-language instruction ("Please select the country where you live"). There's no jargon, no legal density — consistent with Google's broader design ethos of frictionless simplicity.

The closing disclaimer is written with a reassuring, almost conversational tone ("stay tuned until we launch"), softening what could otherwise feel like a rejection or limitation message for users in unsupported regions.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Disabled-until-valid CTA: The greyed-out "Continue" button visually enforces that a selection must be made, preventing empty submissions and setting a clear affordance pattern used throughout the app.

  • Flag-first recognition: Using flag icons as the primary visual identifier lets users scan and identify their country almost instantly, faster than reading text alone — a smart use of pre-attentive visual processing.

  • Graceful unsupported-region messaging: Rather than a hard error or blank state, the app proactively informs users their country may not be listed yet, managing expectations without frustration.

  • Single decision per screen: True to Google's minimalist onboarding philosophy, this screen asks for exactly one input, eliminating any distraction or decision fatigue.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets brand-new users installing Google Pay for the first time, across multiple regulatory markets (India, Singapore, US shown as examples — implying a global rollout). The psychological driver here is trust through familiarity: seeing your home country's flag immediately at the top of a financial app builds a sense of localization and safety before any money-related data is requested.

Because Google Pay's feature set, currency, and compliance requirements vary dramatically by country (UPI in India vs. card-linked wallet in the US), this gate exists to correctly route the user into the appropriate feature/legal flow. Placing it as the very first step — before any account creation — avoids wasted onboarding effort and possible legal exposure from serving the wrong flow to the wrong user.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when your app's core functionality, compliance obligations, or supported feature set differs materially by region and must be locked in before any further onboarding steps. It's ideal for:

  • Fintech/payments apps with country-specific regulatory flows (KYC, banking rails, currency).

  • Apps rolling out in phases to a limited set of markets.

  • Any onboarding flow where a single early input meaningfully changes the downstream user journey.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, dedicated full-screen selector when:

  • The app's country/locale can be reliably auto-detected from device/carrier/IP settings with high confidence — forcing manual selection here adds unnecessary friction.

  • The list of supported countries is very long (50+), where a flag-list without search becomes tedious to scroll; a searchable country picker or bottom sheet would be more appropriate.

  • Region doesn't materially affect the product experience — in that case, this decision could be deferred to settings rather than gating the entire onboarding flow.

screens.name: Google Pay Login 3
screens.uxAnalysis: This is the very first substantive step in the Google Pay onboarding flow, appearing immediately after the splash/logo screen. The layout is radically simple: a large, friendly headline ("Welcome to Google Pay"), a single clear instruction, and a vertical list of three country options rendered as a stacked list with flag icons, country names, and a checkmark indicating the pre-selected/detected option (Singapore). The screen deliberately limits choice to a small, geo-relevant set of countries rather than showing an exhaustive global list, reducing cognitive load and decision fatigue at the very first interaction point. A single, high-contrast, full-width primary CTA ("Continue") anchors the bottom of the screen, following Google's convention of one primary action per screen. A small transparency note at the bottom ("If your country doesn't appear here, stay tuned...") preemptively handles the edge case of unsupported regions, turning a potential dead-end/frustration point into a soft, expectation-managed message rather than an error. The overall visual language is stripped of any card borders, shadows, or ornamentation—pure white canvas with functional typography—which reinforces trust and seriousness appropriate for a money app, and matches Google's minimalist utility aesthetic described in the app's design ethos.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The copy is warm and welcoming ("Welcome to Google Pay") but instantly transitions to a purely functional instruction ("Please select the country where you live"), setting the tone that this is a utility, not a lifestyle app. The disclaimer text at the bottom is written in a reassuring, almost apologetic tone ("stay tuned until we launch...") which manages expectations for users outside the supported markets without making them feel excluded or blocked. There's no marketing fluff, no exclamation points, no urgency language—consistent with Google's restrained, trustworthy brand voice for a financial product.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Smart Default Pre-selection: Singapore is already checked, implying the app used device locale/SIM/IP data to pre-select the most likely country, minimizing the need for the user to search or scroll.

  • Deliberately Short List: Only 3 countries are shown instead of a full scrollable list of 190+ countries, reducing choice overload for a decision that 95%+ of users will answer the same way as their device already indicates.

  • Graceful Edge-Case Messaging: The "if your country doesn't appear" note transforms a potential frustration/blocker into a soft, non-committal promise, preserving goodwill even for users who can't proceed.

  • Single, Unmissable CTA: The full-width blue "Continue" button is the only actionable element besides the list, keeping the decision path linear and unambiguous.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets brand-new users installing Google Pay for the first time, often in emerging or mixed-currency markets (India, Singapore, US are shown as examples, reflecting Google Pay's actual multi-region product split). The psychological trigger at play is reduction of friction via smart defaults: by pre-checking the most probable country, Google removes an unnecessary decision for the majority of users while still giving control to the minority who travel or have ambiguous locale settings. The trust-first design (flags, familiar Google logo, muted colors) is aimed at users who are inherently cautious about handing a company access to their financial identity, so the screen intentionally avoids any salesy or gamified elements that might feel dissonant with a banking-adjacent context.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for early-onboarding steps where a single, high-stakes configuration choice (country, region, currency, language) determines downstream legal, regulatory, or catalog behavior. It's ideal when you can pre-detect a likely default via device signals and want to confirm rather than force manual selection. Also effective whenever you need to set correct expectations for feature availability by region without hard-blocking the user experience.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this exact minimal-list pattern when your app must support all/most countries in the world (e.g., a global messaging or travel app) — in that case a searchable full list or typeahead is more appropriate than a static short list. Also avoid pre-checking a default silently if the choice carries legal/compliance weight (e.g., tax residency) without an explicit confirmation step, since users may not notice the pre-selection and select the wrong country unintentionally.

screens.name: Google Pay Login 4
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is the first meaningful data-entry step after launching Google Pay, and it is engineered to be as frictionless as a native phone dialer. The system keyboard is a custom numeric telephone pad that occupies nearly 40% of the viewport, signaling to the user that this is a quick, single-field task rather than a lengthy form. The country selector (SG flag + calling code) is pre-detected and pre-filled, removing a decision point for the vast majority of users while still remaining editable via a tappable pill in the top-right.

The input itself uses a two-part masked layout: a locked country-code chip on the left and an active, blue-outlined text field on the right pre-populated with a placeholder pattern (0000 0000) that communicates the expected format without the user needing to guess digit grouping. Focus state is unambiguous — the active field has a saturated blue border against an otherwise monochrome page, drawing the eye immediately to where input is required.

The primary CTA ("Next") sits in a persistently disabled/greyed state, a classic guardrail against premature submission, and will presumably activate only once a validly formatted number is entered. An info icon adjacent to the disclosure text offers progressive disclosure for privacy-curious users without cluttering the primary flow with a paragraph of legal text.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is warm but efficient — "Welcome to Google Pay" is a friendly greeting, immediately followed by task-oriented, plain-language instruction: "Use your PayNow number. Don't have one? You can register later." This sentence does double duty: it explains a market-specific integration (PayNow is Singapore's real-time payment addressing system) and proactively removes anxiety for users who lack one, eliminating a potential drop-off point.

The disclosure copy below the field ("People with your number will see your name and photo to connect with you across Google services.") is refreshingly transparent and written in second person, framing data sharing as a benefit ("connect with you") rather than a risk, which is a deliberate softening of what is otherwise a sensitive privacy trade-off.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Auto-detected country/calling code: Pre-fills SG +65 based on locale/SIM, removing an entire decision and typing step for most users.

  • Format-hinting placeholder: "0000 0000" shows exact digit grouping expected, functioning as inline guidance without a separate label or tooltip.

  • Disabled-until-valid CTA: The greyed "Next" button prevents premature/error-prone submissions and gives a clear visual reward the moment valid input is detected.

  • Native numeric keypad: Forces the correct input method automatically, avoiding user error of switching keyboards manually.

  • Contextual escape hatch: "Don't have one? You can register later" pre-empts a likely blocker and keeps the funnel moving instead of losing users without a PayNow ID.

  • Transparent data-use disclosure with info affordance: Builds trust proactively rather than burying consent in a settings page.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets a first-time Google Pay user in Singapore (or a locale-specific market with a real-time payment ID system like PayNow), most likely someone migrating from a bank app or another wallet who expects minimal friction. The psychological driver is reducing entry-cost anxiety: financial onboarding is inherently trust-sensitive, so every micro-decision (country code, format, whether a PayNow ID is mandatory) is resolved for the user before they even ask the question, lowering cognitive load and abandonment risk during a step that determines whether the user proceeds into the app at all.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any mobile onboarding flow requiring phone-number capture, especially in fintech, messaging, or identity-linking contexts where the number doubles as an account identifier (e.g., payment apps, OTP-based auth, contact-matching social apps). It's ideal when regional payment ID schemes (PayNow, UPI, PIX) need to be integrated without confusing users unfamiliar with the underlying rails.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy phone-first approach for global apps where phone-based identity is not a strong regional norm, or where users may be privacy-averse about phone-number-based social discovery (in which case an email-first or anonymous flow may convert better). Also avoid disabled-CTA-without-feedback patterns if there's no real-time inline validation messaging explaining why the button remains inactive, as this can frustrate users who don't intuit the correct format.

screens.name: Google Pay Login 7
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a critical juncture in the Google Pay setup flow, combining account selection with legal consent aggregation. The layout is intentionally sparse, using a single-focus design pattern to eliminate distraction during a high-stakes decision point (agreeing to financial data sharing).

The account card (Avatar + Name + Email + Expandable Chevron) sits isolated at the top, immediately followed by a large amount of negative space before the legal text and CTA. This vertical separation psychologically distances the "simple" identity choice from the "heavy" legal commitment, making the screen feel less intimidating despite the dense disclosure text.

The disclosure text is split into two distinct paragraphs: one governing standard ToS/Privacy (with blue hyperlinks for progressive disclosure), and a second, bolder paragraph specifically calling out sensitive data collection (phone number, device, location). Separating these acknowledges that financial/location data requires a more explicit, isolated warning than standard boilerplate.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is direct, transparent, and slightly formal, befitting a financial services legal disclosure. The heading "Choose an account" is simple, but the subtext "This is how people on Google Pay will see you" reframes a technical settings choice into a social/identity context, helping the user understand the real-world implication of the selection.

The legal copy avoids dense "legalese" walls by using bolded keywords (implied via structure) and short sentences. Crucially, it uses active, specific language: "Google Pay collects your phone number, device, and location" rather than vague terms, adhering to modern privacy-transparency standards (like GDPR/CCPA) while building trust through radical honesty.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Identity Reframing: Using "This is how people on Google Pay will see you" transforms a mundane account picker into a personal branding decision, increasing user attention to detail.

  • Layered Consent: Separating standard ToS/Privacy Policy links from the specific "what we collect" data statement ensures the sensitive information isn't buried in a wall of legal text.

  • Expandable Account Selector: The chevron indicates that even in a linear onboarding flow, the user retains agency to switch Google accounts, respecting multi-account usage patterns.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new Google Pay users, specifically those already logged into the Google ecosystem (Gmail) but new to the payments product. The design leverages the "Path of Least Resistance" psychological trigger by pre-filling the account information (Smart Defaults), reducing the cognitive load required to proceed.

The strategy relies on "Transparency as Trust-Building"—by explicitly stating what data is collected (location, phone number) before asking for a single tap of "Accept," Google preempts anxiety and regulatory friction, betting that clarity increases conversion rates for the "Accept and continue" CTA more than obscurity would.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when onboarding requires binding a user's identity/profile data to a financial or sensitive service. It is ideal for:

  • Payment app setup flows where an OAuth/SSO account must be confirmed.

  • Any "point of no return" step requiring explicit consent for data sharing with third parties.

  • Flows where multiple accounts might exist and switching context is necessary before finalizing.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for low-stakes app registrations where dense legal disclosure would cause unnecessary drop-off (e.g., a simple to-do list app). Additionally, avoid presenting this much legal text without a "read more" option on smaller screen form factors, as it can overwhelm the visual hierarchy if the account selector card was more complex or contained multiple entries.

screens.name: Google Pay Login 10
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen represents the critical security checkpoint in Google Pay's onboarding flow: phone number verification via a one-time passcode (OTP). The design is stripped down to its bare essentials—no illustrations, no marketing copy, just the task at hand. This minimalism is intentional; verification screens are transactional friction points, and every additional visual element increases cognitive load and abandonment risk.

The layout follows a strict vertical hierarchy: a large, legible headline ("Verify your number"), a supporting instruction line that references the masked destination number, and a six-digit OTP input row rendered as individually boxed digits with underline separators. The system has auto-detected and auto-filled the code from an SMS (visible as the six digits already populated), and the seventh "slot" position shows a spinning loading indicator rather than an empty box—signaling that verification is actively processing rather than waiting for user input.

Below the input row, a plain-text status message "Verifying OTP…" reinforces the system state in words, not just iconography, ensuring accessibility and reducing ambiguity about what's happening. The back chevron and overflow menu (three-dot icon) in the top toolbar provide escape hatches without cluttering the primary task, and the bottom home indicator confirms this is a native-feeling full-screen modal step within a larger multi-step flow.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The copy is clipped and instructional—"Verify your number," "Enter the OTP sent to [number]"—typical of Google's terse, utilitarian voice. There's no attempt at reassurance or personality injection; the tone trusts the user to understand a standard OTP flow without hand-holding. The status line "Verifying OTP…" uses an ellipsis to communicate an in-progress, non-blocking state, which is a small but important microcopy choice that prevents users from feeling stuck or wondering if the app has frozen.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Autofill + Auto-Verify: The OTP is automatically read from SMS and submitted without requiring the user to tap "Continue," collapsing two steps into one and removing manual entry friction entirely.

  • Segmented digit boxes: Each digit occupies its own cell, making the code highly scannable and reducing perceived complexity versus a single long text field.

  • Inline loading state within the input row: Rather than a separate spinner or full-screen loader, the seventh box repurposes itself into a circular progress indicator, keeping the loading feedback spatially tied to the action.

  • Masked phone number blur: The destination number is obscured (blurred) in this instance, a subtle privacy-conscious detail useful for screenshots/demos while preserving realistic layout proportions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets every new or returning Google Pay user attempting to link/verify a phone number—an near-universal audience given phone-number verification is often the very first mandatory step in a payments app, essential for both identity assurance and regulatory compliance (KYC). The psychological driver here is reducing perceived effort and anxiety around security steps: financial onboarding is inherently trust-sensitive, and users are primed to abandon flows that feel slow or overly manual. By auto-filling and auto-submitting the OTP, Google Pay leverages the "path of least resistance" principle, keeping momentum in the funnel and minimizing drop-off at a step known for high abandonment rates industry-wide.
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for any identity or account-security verification step (phone, email, 2FA) in flows where speed and trust are paramount—financial apps, fintech onboarding, or any registration gate requiring SMS-based verification. It's especially valuable when the OTP can be programmatically read (via SMS Retriever API / Autofill APIs) to eliminate manual copy-paste friction. Use the segmented-box UI whenever the code has a fixed, short length (4–8 digits) to aid scanning and error detection.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid auto-submission when the OTP length or format is unpredictable, or when users might need to review/edit the code before submitting (e.g., in regions with unreliable SMS parsing, where false-positive autofill could trigger premature, incorrect submissions). This pattern should be avoided if the platform doesn't reliably support SMS autofill (e.g., certain Android OEM restrictions or web contexts without the WebOTP API), since users would then face empty boxes but expect the app to "know" the code, increasing confusion. Also avoid over-blurring or hiding the phone number entirely without an option to reveal/edit it, since users need to confirm they're verifying the correct number.

screens.name: Google Pay Login 5
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is the entry point of the Google Pay onboarding flow, localized for the Singapore market. The layout follows a strict single-column, single-task hierarchy: logo for brand trust, a large friendly headline, a short instructional subtext, and a single input group (country code + phone number). There is no visible primary CTA button in the viewport, implying the keyboard will surface a "Next" affordance once digits are entered, or the system relies on the phone's native return key—reducing visual clutter until the user commits to input.

The screen uses generous negative space above and below the input fields, which lowers cognitive load and signals that this is a quick, low-friction step rather than a dense form. The bottom of the screen is anchored by a warm, human illustration of three friends transacting/socializing with a checkmark badge, reinforcing the emotional payoff (successful, easy payments among friends) before the user has done anything at all.

The pre-filled placeholder "0000 0000" and country flag chip (SG, +65) act as smart, localized defaults, minimizing the user's decision-making burden. The top-right "..." overflow menu and region selector give escape hatches for switching country/region or accessing more options without cluttering the primary path.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is warm and conversational ("Welcome to Google Pay") paired with a functional, almost technical instruction ("Use your PayNow number"). The parenthetical reassurance—"Don't have one? You can register later."—is a critical anxiety-reducing microcopy choice: it removes a potential blocker (not having a PayNow ID) at the exact moment a user might abandon the flow, telling them implicitly that failure to comply now is not fatal.

Overall tone is helpful and non-alarmist, consistent with Google's utilitarian, low-jargon design language. It treats a financial onboarding step with the same ease as a search query, per the brand's philosophy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Anxiety-Deflecting Microcopy: Proactively answers the "what if I don't have this?" objection inline, rather than waiting for an error state.

  • Localized Smart Defaults: Auto-detected country code (+65) and region (SG) tag remove a data-entry step for the vast majority of users in that geography.

  • Emotional Payoff Priming: The bottom illustration of friends with a checkmark badge visually foreshadows a successful, social, and effortless outcome before any task is completed, building motivation to proceed.

  • Minimal Field Count: Only one true input (phone number) is required to advance, embodying a "search-bar simplicity" ethos for a financial app.

  • Progress Bar Sliver: The thin dark bar at the very bottom acts as a subtle system-level progress/gesture indicator without competing with content.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users in Singapore who are likely already familiar with PayNow (Singapore's national real-time payment system) via their banking apps. By anchoring identity/verification to an existing trusted rail (PayNow number) instead of asking users to create a new username/password, Google Pay piggybacks on pre-existing trust and mental models, lowering the activation barrier for a financial product.

The psychological trigger at play is reduction of perceived effort and risk: financial onboarding is historically fraught with friction (KYC forms, document uploads), so presenting it as a single phone-number field mimics the simplicity of messaging-app sign-up, defusing the intimidation typically associated with fintech registration.
screens.whereToUse:
• First-touch onboarding screens for fintech or payment apps where minimizing initial friction is critical to conversion.

  • Any flow leveraging a pre-existing national/regional identifier (e.g., national payment IDs, national IDs) to bootstrap trust and skip account creation.

  • Contexts where an optional/deferred step (like registration) can be clearly communicated to prevent early drop-off.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern in regions/markets without a widely-adopted equivalent identifier — the phone-number-first pattern would need a fallback (e.g., email) to avoid excluding users.

  • Not suitable for high-risk financial actions requiring stronger upfront verification (e.g., large money transfers, credit applications), where a lightweight single-field entry could create false expectations of a "light" process.

  • Avoid if the target audience is unfamiliar with the referenced system (PayNow), as the terminology would confuse rather than reassure.

screens.name: Google Pay Login 8
screens.uxAnalysis: Google Pay uses a single-purpose, distraction-free full-screen native keyboard flow to verify a phone number via a 6-digit One-Time Password. The layout follows a strict top-to-bottom hierarchy: a minimal back/overflow toolbar, a bold headline, a masked destination phone number, six empty underline slots representing the OTP digits, and a native numeric keypad pinned to the bottom half of the screen. This mirrors an iOS system-style OTP input rather than a custom boxed input, reducing cognitive load because the pattern is instantly recognizable from countless other apps and OS-level SMS verification flows. The lack of any other content (no illustrations, no marketing copy) reinforces the utilitarian, 'get-it-done' brand ethos of Google Pay. A visible countdown timer ('Request a new OTP in 00:27') manages user expectation and prevents premature retry taps, while doubling as a subtle urgency mechanic that keeps the user engaged and waiting rather than abandoning the flow.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The copy is terse, direct, and instructional — 'Verify your number' and 'Enter the OTP sent to [number]' — with zero fluff or brand personality injected into a security-critical moment. This is intentional: financial/identity verification screens benefit from clinical, unambiguous language that builds trust through seriousness rather than charm. The secondary line 'Having trouble? Request a new OTP in 00:27' anticipates user friction (not receiving the code) and preemptively offers a recovery path, gated by a timer to prevent spam-triggered re-sends.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native keyboard reuse: Leverages the OS-level numeric keypad instead of a custom in-app one, reducing engineering overhead and matching user muscle memory instantly.

  • Masked phone number confirmation: Shows (a blurred/obscured) destination number so the user has confidence the OTP is going to the right place without fully exposing PII on screen.

  • Segmented underline OTP field: Six discrete slots visually communicate exactly how many digits are expected, reducing input anxiety and errors.

  • Timed resend gating: The 00:27 countdown next to 'Request a new OTP' prevents accidental spam-tapping while still communicating that recovery is possible.

  • Radical minimalism: Removing all non-essential UI (illustrations, tips, branding) keeps focus entirely on the single task of digit entry.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets every Google Pay user at account setup or re-authentication — a universal, non-segmented audience since phone verification is mandatory for all. The psychological trigger at play is trust-through-friction: users psychologically associate a short, slightly annoying verification step with heightened security, which increases confidence in a financial app. The countdown timer also taps into loss-aversion/patience conditioning, subtly discouraging premature exits by giving a concrete, finite wait time rather than an ambiguous 'please wait.'
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any identity or security verification step (phone, email, 2FA) in fintech, banking, or any app handling sensitive personal/financial data. It's ideal when you need to confirm real-world contact ownership before granting access to money-movement features, and when you want to minimize distraction so users complete the step quickly without confusion.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this bare-bones approach in contexts where users need more reassurance or guidance, such as first-time onboarding for less tech-savvy audiences who may not understand OTP conventions — here, additional micro-copy or an illustration explaining 'why we verify' would help. Also avoid indefinite or overly long resend timers, which frustrate users who legitimately did not receive the code; and don't use this stripped-down layout if the product needs to reinforce brand personality or emotional connection at this touchpoint.

screens.name: Google Pay Login 6
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is the first substantive step of the Google Pay onboarding flow, immediately following the splash/logo moment. The layout is a textbook single-screen form reduced to its absolute minimum viable input: a country code selector (pre-filled to the detected locale, "SG +65") and a single phone number field. The native numeric keypad is already summoned and docked at the bottom of the screen, removing an extra tap and signaling to the user exactly what type of input is expected before they even read the label.

Visual hierarchy is deliberately sparse: white canvas, a single focused input outlined in Google Blue, and one primary action (a full-width pill "Next" button) sitting in a fixed, thumb-friendly position directly above the keyboard. There is no back-and-forth scanning required — the eye moves top-to-bottom in a straight line from logo → headline → helper copy → input → disclosure → CTA.

An info "i" icon next to the privacy disclosure offers progressive disclosure for users who want more detail on data usage, without cluttering the primary flow with a wall of legal text. The overflow menu (•••) in the top right hints at secondary options (e.g., sign-in help, language) without competing with the primary task.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is short, plain, and reassuring — consistent with Google's utilitarian voice. "Welcome to Google Pay" is a warm but brief greeting, immediately followed by a functional instruction ("Use your PayNow number") that ties the product to a locally trusted payment rail (Singapore's PayNow), building instant credibility and relevance for the target market.

Critically, the microcopy pre-empts a likely objection — "Don't have one? You can register later." — reducing friction and abandonment risk for users who don't have PayNow set up. The privacy disclosure ("People with your number will see your name and photo...") is transparent and proactively surfaced rather than buried in terms & conditions, which builds trust at the exact moment personal data is being requested.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Auto-detected country code: Pre-filling "SG +65" based on locale/SIM removes a decision and a tap, accelerating time-to-value.

  • Keyboard pre-summoned: The numeric keypad is already visible on screen load, telegraphing input type instantly and saving a tap.

  • Objection handling in microcopy: "Don't have one? You can register later" defuses the #1 drop-off reason (not having a PayNow number) directly inline.

  • Just-in-time privacy disclosure: Explaining visibility of name/photo right beside the input, with an expandable info icon, builds trust exactly when the sensitive data is requested rather than hiding it in legal fine print.

  • Single focused CTA: One full-width, high-contrast "Next" button with no secondary competing actions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new users onboarding onto Google Pay in a market with real-time bank transfer infrastructure (Singapore's PayNow), a mainstream, non-technical audience who values speed and low cognitive load over customization. The psychological trigger at play is friction reduction combined with trust priming: by minimizing the number of fields and pre-answering the most common user hesitation ("I don't have a PayNow number"), Google removes early-funnel abandonment. The transparent, proactive privacy statement leverages the trust-through-transparency principle — users are more likely to comply with a personal data request when the consequence is stated plainly and immediately, rather than discovered later.
screens.whereToUse:
• Financial, fintech, or identity-linked onboarding flows where phone number is the primary account identifier.

  • Any flow tied to a real-time payment rail or bank-linked identifier (e.g., UPI, PayNow, Zelle) where explaining the "why" of the field builds necessary trust.

  • Situations where you want to reduce early funnel drop-off by pre-answering a common "I don't have this" objection inline rather than via FAQ or support.

  • Locale-aware forms where auto-detecting country/region context saves the user a decision.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this ultra-minimal single-field pattern when multiple pieces of identity information are required upfront — it works because it isolates one decision; stacking several fields breaks the flow's simplicity.

  • Not suitable when the phone number's visibility/privacy implications are more complex than can be summarized in one sentence — that requires a dedicated consent screen instead of an inline note.

  • Avoid auto-focusing the keyboard immediately if the country code itself is frequently wrong for the user base, as it may bury an important correction step.

screens.name: Google Pay Login 9
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen tackles a critical trust checkpoint in the money-movement flow: confirming that the person holding the device actually owns the phone number tied to the account. The layout is deliberately spartan — a back arrow, an overflow menu, a two-line headline/subhead pairing, a segmented six-digit OTP input, a countdown-gated resend link, and the native numeric keypad occupying the bottom half of the viewport.

The segmented digit boxes (each with its own underline) are a critical micro-interaction choice over a single text field. As each digit is typed, the corresponding underline turns from grey to blue, giving continuous, granular feedback on progress toward the 6-digit target without requiring the user to count characters themselves. The blinking cursor in the sixth slot signals exactly where input will land next, eliminating any ambiguity.

Vertical space below the resend line is left intentionally blank — this is not a design gap but a concession to the OS-level numeric keypad, which dominates roughly 45% of the screen. By pushing the keypad up against the input immediately, Google Pay minimizes eye and thumb travel distance, reducing the time-to-complete for a task users want to get through as fast as possible.

The disabled/countdown state on 'Request a new OTP' is a subtle but important guardrail against spamming the SMS gateway, while still reassuring the user that a recovery path exists if the code never arrives.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is terse and instructional, typical of Google's product voice: "Verify your number" as a direct command/title, followed by "Enter the OTP sent to [number]" which confirms *where* the code went — reducing anxiety that it was sent to the wrong destination or lost entirely.

"Having trouble? Request a new OTP in 00:01" is a masterclass in empathetic microcopy: it pre-empts frustration by acknowledging that the code might not arrive ("Having trouble?"), while the ticking timer manages expectations and prevents the "why isn't this working" outrage that comes from an unresponsive resend button. There is no jargon, no explanation of what OTP even stands for — it assumes basic user familiarity, consistent with a mainstream utility rather than a security-obsessed enterprise tool.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented digit boxes with progressive underline fill: Turns an abstract 6-digit code into a visual progress bar, giving the user constant positive feedback as they type.

  • Auto-advancing cursor: The blinking caret automatically jumps to the next empty slot, so the user never has to manually tap between fields.

  • Countdown-gated resend CTA: Prevents abuse/spam while transparently telling the user exactly when they'll regain control, avoiding dead-end frustration.

  • Full-bleed native keypad: Uses the system numeric keyboard instead of a custom one, ensuring familiarity, correct key hit-targets, and haptic consistency with the OS.

  • Masked destination display: Shows a redacted/blurred phone number to confirm the OTP's destination without fully exposing PII on screen.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves virtually every Google Pay user at a critical trust-and-safety gate — during initial account setup, adding a new payment method, or re-authenticating after a suspicious login. Because Google Pay moves real money, verifying phone ownership is a foundational anti-fraud control that protects both the user and Google from account takeover and unauthorized transactions.

Psychologically, the design leans on reduction of friction under urgency: users entering an OTP are almost always mid-task (trying to complete a payment or finish setup) and want zero cognitive overhead. The progressive visual feedback (underline fill) taps into the same completion-bias psychology as a progress bar — each digit typed feels like a small win, keeping momentum high and abandonment low.
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this segmented-OTP-with-native-keypad pattern whenever:

  • You need to verify phone number or email ownership as part of onboarding, login, or a sensitive account change.

  • The code has a fixed, known length (4-8 digits) that can be visually chunked.

  • Speed and low cognitive load are priorities — e.g., financial, delivery, or ride-hailing apps where users are often in a hurry.

  • You want to discourage abuse of resend functionality without blocking the user from recovering permanently.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this exact pattern when:

  • The verification code has variable length or is alphanumeric — segmented boxes lose their visual clarity advantage and can feel constraining.

  • You're on a form with many other fields on the same screen; dedicating a full screen to just OTP entry would feel disproportionately heavy for a secondary or optional verification step.

  • Users may need to paste a code copied from an email/SMS app — ensure paste support is included, as purely segmented inputs sometimes block clipboard paste, causing frustration.

  • Accessibility is a major concern for very low-vision users — six discrete tap targets can be harder to navigate with screen readers than a single labeled field.

screens.name: Google Pay Login 11
screens.uxAnalysis:
This is the primary landing screen of Google Pay, architected as a Hub & Spoke model that funnels every possible money-movement action through a single, decluttered surface. The top third is dedicated to a decorative, localized illustration (Singapore skyline with the Merlion, dragon boat, HDB flats) that sits behind the "G Pay" wordmark — a branding move that reduces the cold, transactional feel typically associated with finance apps.

Below the "fold" (indicated by a pull-tab affordance), the layout shifts into strict utility mode: a promotional banner, then horizontally-scannable avatar rows for "People" and "Businesses", capped by a floating primary action button ("New payment"). The visual hierarchy prioritizes who you pay over how much or what for — reinforcing Google Pay's contact-first payment philosophy rather than a ledger-first or balance-first philosophy common in banking apps.

The scan icon (top-left) and profile avatar (top-right) bookend the header, giving one-tap access to the two most frequent entry points (camera-based QR pay, and account/profile) without needing a settings menu.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy is warm, casual, and emoji-forward ("🏖️ Travel deals with Google Pay!"), which is atypical for financial software but consistent with Google's broader consumer-friendly tone of voice. The promotional card uses excitement-driven language ("Win vouchers") paired with a low-friction CTA ("View offer") rather than aggressive sales copy.

Section labels ("People", "Businesses", "Explore") are simple one-word taxonomy headers — no explanatory subtext is needed because the iconography (avatars, logos) does the communicative heavy lifting. The fallback avatar for an unsaved contact ("+65 8802…") shows the system gracefully handling incomplete data without breaking the visual rhythm of the row.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dismissible, non-blocking promo banner: The travel deals card is contained and closable (X icon), respecting user attention without gating core functionality behind it.

  • Contact-first spoke navigation: Surfacing recent People and Businesses as tappable avatars turns "who do I pay" into a one-tap decision, mirroring the recall-over-recognition mental model used in messaging apps.

  • Persistent floating action button: "New payment" stays anchored regardless of scroll position, guaranteeing the core task is always one thumb-reach away.

  • Localized illustration as brand warmth layer: Region-specific art (Merlion, dragon boat) softens the utilitarian nature of a payments app and builds local relevance/trust.

  • Dual quick-entry icons in header: Scan (left) and Avatar/Profile (right) bookend the screen, covering the two most frequent non-list actions without extra taps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves a mass-market, mobile-first consumer who already has an established social/payment graph (friends, group chats like "Foodies", local merchants) and wants near-instant repeat transactions. The design leans on familiarity and habit-formation psychology: by front-loading known contacts and businesses, it reduces the cognitive load of remembering names or numbers, exploiting the recognition heuristic.

The promotional banner exploits reward/lottery-style triggers (win vouchers) to nudge transaction frequency, targeting price-sensitive users in Southeast Asian markets where voucher/cashback culture drives app engagement. The gentle, illustrated splash panel signals Google's brand trust transplanted onto a financial use case, easing anxiety for users who may be new to digital payments.
screens.whereToUse:
• Consumer fintech apps where repeat transactions to a known set of people/merchants dominate usage (P2P payments, food delivery wallets, super-apps).

  • Apps needing to soften a utilitarian task (money transfer) with brand personality via a hero illustration.

  • Home screens that must balance promotional real estate with core task shortcuts without letting marketing overwhelm utility.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Enterprise or B2B finance tools where balance/ledger data is more critical than a "who to pay" contact list — burying account balance below the fold would frustrate power users.

  • Apps serving a high volume of one-off/unknown-payee transactions, where a contact-first UI adds friction instead of removing it.

  • Compliance-heavy contexts where a playful, emoji-driven promo tone could undermine perceived trust or seriousness (e.g., wealth management, insurance).

screens.name: About
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen combines legal and informational content — Terms, Privacy, Attributions, and version info — with the higher-stakes Account Management flow of account deletion. "Delete Account" is visually separated in red from the neutral links, following destructive-action conventions that signal severity and irreversibility. The supporting copy is especially useful, clarifying exactly what will and will not be deleted — including the associated Apple Account — before the user takes action, reducing ambiguity without needing a lengthy confirmation flow.
screens.tonalityAndContent: This screen is largely interaction-driven (rows and a button), but the "Delete Account" action includes copy-driven support: the explanatory paragraph below it is deliberately precise and reassuring in a narrow sense — it draws a clear boundary ("It will not delete your associated Apple Account") to prevent the user from over-estimating the action's scope, which matters for trust on a destructive, hard-to-reverse action. The tone is plain and factual rather than alarming, appropriate for pre-empting anxiety about data loss while still being honest that songs and associated data will be deleted from iCloud.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Destructive-action distinction: red color-coding and isolation of "Delete Account" from other rows follows established convention for high-consequence actions, reducing accidental taps.

  2. Preemptive clarity over post-hoc confirmation: consequence text is shown directly under the button rather than solely in a follow-up dialog, letting users make an informed decision before committing.

  3. Scope transparency: explicitly stating what is and isn't deleted (Shazam data and iCloud songs vs. the Apple Account) prevents a common source of user distrust — vague deletion language.

  4. Recognition over recall: standard chevron affordance on Terms/Privacy/Attributions rows signals drill-down navigation consistent with the rest of the app's settings.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Instagram (Settings → Account → Delete Account) — same pattern of a red delete action paired with explanatory scope text distinguishing app data from linked accounts.

  2. Spotify (Account settings → Close Account) — comparable placement of a destructive account action within a legal/about-adjacent settings section, with clarifying copy.

  3. Apple ID (Sign Out / Delete Account flows in iOS Settings) — similar convention of red destructive text plus a plain-language consequence statement before any confirmation dialog appears.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any settings screen offering account deletion, where the priority is making an irreversible action clearly visible and its consequences unambiguous before the user commits.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for lower-stakes preference changes or reversible settings, where this level of red-flagging and explanatory framing would feel disproportionate and add unnecessary friction or alarm.

screens.name: Delete Account
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen enforces identity verification before the destructive Account Deletion flow can proceed, requiring re-authentication through Apple, Google, or email on Shazam's own web domain. Routing the step to shazam.com suggests the deletion and authentication backend is shared across Shazam's app and web properties, allowing one identity flow to serve both. Surfacing data-use disclosure and the privacy-policy link directly on the sign-in screen also reinforces transparency at the moment sensitive identity and account data are being handled.
screens.tonalityAndContent: This is a partially copy-driven screen: alongside functional sign-in controls, a short paragraph explains why Shazam retains history data ("to let you access it at a later time and to recommend music you may like") and discloses that eligibility for other Apple product offers may be checked. The tone is plain and disclosure-oriented rather than persuasive — it reads as a compliance-driven transparency statement rather than marketing copy, appropriate given this page sits inside a sensitive Account Management/deletion context where the lever that matters is trust, not conversion.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Step-up authentication for destructive actions: requiring re-sign-in before deletion can proceed reduces the risk of accidental or unauthorized account destruction.

  2. Multiple auth pathways: offering Apple, Google, and email sign-in reduces friction for users regardless of which method they originally used to create their account.

  3. Just-in-time disclosure: placing the data-use explanation and privacy link directly on the re-authentication screen puts relevant information exactly where a privacy-conscious user would want it, right before deletion.

  4. Consistency across app/web boundary: retaining Shazam's own branding (logo, wordmark) within the browser-hosted page maintains continuity despite the context switch from native app to web.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Spotify (web-based account deletion requiring re-login) — same pattern of routing a destructive account action through a web sign-in gate with multiple auth provider options.

  2. Netflix (Cancel/Delete account flow requiring password re-entry) — comparable re-authentication step before finalizing account removal.

  3. Google (Delete Account flow requiring re-sign-in) — same principle of confirming identity via sign-in immediately before a destructive, irreversible account action.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any account-deletion or other high-consequence account action where confirming the requester's identity via re-authentication is necessary to prevent accidental or malicious account destruction.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for low-stakes or easily reversible settings changes, where forcing a full re-sign-in flow (especially one that exits to an external browser) would introduce unnecessary friction disproportionate to the action's risk.

screens.name: Delete Account 5
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen represents the highest-stakes step of the Account Management → Deleting & Deactivating Account flow: after selecting "Permanently delete," the interface escalates from a simple radio choice to a Verification step requiring the Current password Text field, directly supporting Destructive-Action Confirmation by ensuring the person taking the action is genuinely the account owner. Anticipating the likely failure mode of a forgotten password, the screen also offers an Account Recovery path via the "request a password reset email here" link, so users aren't blocked or forced to abandon the flow, while the repeated Premium-subscription banner reinforces the financial consequence before the final red "Delete" button is pressed.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Error prevention (step-up authentication): Requiring the current password specifically for the irreversible "Delete" path (not the reversible "Deactivate" path) matches verification friction to the severity of the action.

  2. Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors: The forgotten-password link is placed exactly where a user would get stuck, preventing dead-end frustration.

  3. Visibility of system status: Restating the Premium-subscription cancellation warning at the point of highest commitment reinforces consequence awareness right before the final tap.

  4. Consistency and standards: Reusing the same red destructive-button styling and Premium banner from the deactivation screen keeps the visual language consistent between the two paths.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. GitHub (delete repository/account) — requires re-entering a password or the resource name as step-up verification before an irreversible delete action.

  2. Facebook (permanent account deletion) — asks users to confirm their password before finalizing permanent deletion, with a similar recovery-focused help link.

  3. Amazon (close account) — combines an irreversibility warning, password confirmation, and subscription-cancellation notice in a comparable sequence.
screens.whereToUse: This combination is well suited to any irreversible, high-consequence action — account deletion, payment removal, data wipe — where confirming true user identity and warning of side effects (like losing a paid subscription) meaningfully reduces regret and accidental loss.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's excessive for reversible or low-risk actions, such as toggling a setting or temporary deactivation, where a password re-entry step would add friction without a proportional safety benefit.

screens.name: Delete Account 1
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen resolves several concerns raised during registration. "Deactivate or delete account" is present and reachable in two taps from the tab bar — the sort of thing apps frequently bury. "Export your data" is also present, which is a GDPR data-portability right made available in the interface rather than requiring a support request.

The grouping is well judged: profile facts, then credentials, then irreversible or data-rights actions. Placing export and deletion in their own section separates consequence from routine editing.

The values shown confirm what registration collected. Name and age appear as editable profile fields, which retroactively answers a question raised at the sign-up form — age is stored and adjustable rather than being a one-time compliance gate. That said, an editable self-reported age is a weak instrument if it drives any under-13 branch, since a user can simply change it.

One notable absence: no delete-account warning or destructive styling. The row reads in the same weight and colour as "Export your data," so nothing visually distinguishes an irreversible action from a benign one. The confirmation presumably lives behind the chevron, but the entry point gives no signal.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Plain and functional, consistent with the parent Settings screen.

"Export your data" uses second person and an action verb, framing it as a right the user exercises rather than a feature the app provides. Better than "Data export."

"Deactivate or delete account" names both options in one row, which is honest — they are different outcomes with different reversibility, and collapsing them into "Delete account" would misrepresent the choice. Slightly long for a row label, but the precision is worth it.

Field values are right-aligned in grey with the email truncated by ellipsis. Truncation is unavoidable at this width and the full value sits one tap away.

No explanatory text anywhere — no note about what export includes, no warning about deletion. Appropriate for a list screen where each row leads to its own context.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Data rights surfaced in the interface — export and deletion are two taps from the tab bar rather than buried or support-gated.

  2. Grouping separates consequence from routine — profile, credentials, then irreversible actions.

  3. Age is editable — confirming it is a stored profile field, which also weakens it as a compliance instrument.

  4. No destructive styling on deletion — the entry point gives no visual signal that the action is irreversible.

  5. Precise labelling — "Deactivate or delete" names two distinct outcomes rather than collapsing them.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo — comparable account screen with profile fields, credentials, and a delete option.

  2. Headspace — separates data export and deletion into their own group below account details.

  3. GDPR-compliant consumer apps generally — surfacing portability in-product rather than by request is the stronger implementation.
screens.whereToUse: Standard construction for account management where profile editing, credentials, and data rights all need to be reachable.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit if destructive actions carry no visual distinction at the entry point — the pattern relies on the sub-screen to supply all the caution.

screens.name: Delete Account 4
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen closes out the Account Management → Deleting & Deactivating Account flow by pairing a binary Radio Button choice with two Inline Help / FAQ banners that front-load consequences before the user commits: one clarifies exactly what's needed to reverse a temporary deactivation, the other warns that an active Premium subscription will be auto-cancelled. Surfacing this information above the action button, rather than after tapping "Deactivate," supports the Destructive-Action Confirmation pattern by giving the user everything needed for informed consent in one glance, reducing the chance of a surprised or frustrated user later.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of system status: The Premium-subscription banner tells the user a side effect (auto-cancellation) that isn't obvious from the radio choice alone, preventing an unpleasant surprise.

  2. Error prevention: Spelling out the exact credentials needed to reactivate reduces the odds of an unrecoverable mistake, a core heuristic for destructive or hard-to-reverse actions.

  3. Recognition over recall: The reactivation instructions are hyperlinked ("here") rather than requiring the user to remember or search for them later.

  4. Match between system and real world: Plain, non-technical language ("nobody, not even Brilliant staff members, will be able to help you") sets a realistic, unambiguous expectation of consequence.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Spotify (account/subscription cancellation) — similarly surfaces an active-subscription warning banner before finalizing an account-ending action.

  2. Dropbox (account deletion) — pairs a reversible vs. irreversible choice with explicit credential/recovery information before the final destructive button.

  3. Slack (deactivate workspace account) — uses the same layered-warning-then-CTA structure, explaining reactivation requirements ahead of a colored confirmation button.
screens.whereToUse: This combination fits subscription products where deactivation has real financial or data-recovery consequences the user must understand before committing, especially where an active paid plan is affected.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's overkill for reversible, low-consequence settings toggles or free-tier account changes where no subscription or unrecoverable data loss is at stake.

screens.name: Delete Account 2
screens.uxAnalysis: This is the entry point of the Account Management → Deleting & Deactivating Account flow, presenting a Multi-Select checkbox list as a Single-Screen Form before the user can proceed to the deactivate/delete decision seen in later steps. With no reason yet checked, the screen is in its default, unanswered state — the survey step exists to collect churn-reason data for the product team without blocking or delaying the user's ability to eventually deactivate, since (per earlier screens in this flow) selection here is not a hard gate to continuing.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Not applicable — this screen is interaction-driven, not copy-driven.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Recognition over recall: Pre-written checkbox reasons let the user recognize their situation rather than compose free-text explanations, lowering the effort to respond.

  2. Non-blocking data collection: Presenting the reason survey as unselected and optional (based on the flow continuing regardless of selection) avoids forcing users through unnecessary friction just to leave.

  3. Consistency and standards: Reuses the same checkbox-list layout and copy seen in the flow's later, partially-completed states, maintaining a predictable pattern throughout.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Netflix (cancel subscription flow) — opens with a similar unselected "why are you leaving" checklist before the final cancellation step.

  2. Duolingo (account deletion) — begins its exit flow with an equivalent blank reason-selection screen.

  3. Slack (deactivate workspace) — uses a comparable initial feedback-collection step before presenting the deactivate/delete choice.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any account or subscription cancellation flow where the product team wants structured, low-friction feedback on why users are leaving, collected before the user reaches the final destructive-action step.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's unnecessary for non-account-ending actions, or for flows the product wants to keep as short as possible, where an extra feedback step would only add friction without functional benefit.

screens.name: Delete Account 3

Combining the exit survey with the deactivate/delete decision on a Single-Screen Form reduces friction for the retention team's data collection while still surfacing the higher-risk permanent-delete path with explicit, unambiguous consequence language, which is standard practice for account-closure flows that need both product feedback and informed user consent.
