screens.keyHighlights:
1. Recognition over recall: Pre-written reason checkboxes let the user recognize their situation rather than compose free text, lowering effort.

  2. Reversibility as a safety net: The temporary-deactivation option is placed and worded to nudge risk-averse users away from permanent loss, consistent with error-prevention heuristics.

  3. Clarity of consequence: The permanent-delete option spells out "can't be recovered, even by staff," directly supporting informed consent for a destructive action.

  4. Visibility of system status: Persistent tab bar keeps the user oriented within the app even mid-flow, reducing disorientation during a sensitive task.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo (account deletion flow) — also pairs an exit-reason checklist with a distinct, separately confirmed permanent-delete step.

  2. Netflix (cancel subscription flow) — uses a similar "why are you leaving" reason list before finalizing a subscription-ending action.

  3. Slack (workspace/account deactivation) — separates temporary deactivation from permanent deletion with explicit irreversibility warnings, matching this screen's structure.
screens.whereToUse: This Flow/pattern combination fits any subscription or account-based product that wants structured churn feedback while still giving users a safer, reversible off-ramp before committing to permanent deletion.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for low-stakes settings changes or non-destructive actions, where forcing a reason-selection step before proceeding would add unnecessary friction.

screens.name: Edit Profile 2
screens.uxAnalysis:
This frame clarifies that the name is required, while the photo is optional. The disabled “Complete” button communicates the requirement, but only through colour, giving users no explanation when tapped.

The keyboard also exposes a layout issue: the explanatory copy truncates just when the user needs it, while the illustration remains prioritised.

The strongest detail is the iOS autofill suggestion. Using the correct text-field content type lets users fill the required name with one tap, making the only mandatory input nearly frictionless.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Mostly carried over and analysed previously; this state changes two things.

"Your Name" as placeholder — restates the field's identity rather than modelling valid input. Minor here, since name fields are self-evident, but it's the same pattern as "Your Email Address" in the Copilots banner. A product this careful with copy elsewhere is defaulting on placeholders.

"Complete" in its disabled state — now demonstrably the wrong word. Greyed out, with an empty name and an empty avatar above it, it reads as you haven't finished without saying which part. "Save" or "Continue" would be clearer at full strength, and would at least narrow the ambiguity when dimmed. What the screen actually needs is a required-field indicator, or helper text appearing on an attempted tap.

The truncated subheading is a layout failure rather than a writing one, but it has a copy consequence: the persuasive sentence is now a fragment ending in "share flights a…", which reads as broken rather than abbreviated. If the sheet must compress, the copy should shorten to a complete short sentence rather than clip a long one.

The exclamation mark survives the compression, so the one flourish remains while the justification disappears — the personality outlasts the reasoning.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Gate on what you actually need — requiring the name and leaving the photo optional is the right call, and it corrects the impression the previous frame gave.

  2. Free friction reduction via platform — a correctly typed text field means autofill offers the answer in one tap, without the app building anything.

  3. Disabled buttons don't explain themselves — the only control that could tell the user what's missing is the one that's inert; a required marker or on-tap helper text would fix it.

  4. Keyboard avoidance is truncating the motivation — the sentence justifying the task is clipped exactly when the user is deciding whether to do it.

  5. Priority under compression — the clipped illustration keeps its space while the explanatory copy loses its ending; the ranking should invert when the keyboard is up.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. WhatsApp (profile setup) — name required, photo optional, with the CTA gated on the name alone. Same requirement structure, more explicit about it.

  2. Apple (Contact Photo & Poster setup) — name field with autofill and a genuinely skippable image step, labelled as such.

  3. Signal (registration profile) — mandatory display name, optional avatar, with helper text stating which is which rather than relying on button state.
screens.whereToUse: Best for short forms where a single field is genuinely required and the platform can prefill it, so the ask collapses to one tap. Gating the CTA is appropriate when the requirement is obvious from context and the field count is small.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit whenever the reason for the disabled state isn't self-evident, or when more than one field is required — users then face a dead button with no diagnosis. Also wrong where keyboard compression clips content the form depends on to motivate completion.

screens.name: Edit Profile
screens.uxAnalysis:
The timing is the strongest decision. Flighty delays profile creation until it has a clear purpose: someone is about to see the user. After tracking, sharing, and inviting without an account, the profile request feels contextual rather than extractive.

The illustration helps by showing exactly where the profile will appear, making the request for a name and photo more understandable.

The weaknesses are the four-layer modal stack and unclear optionality. “Complete” suggests the avatar may be required, while the X provides no clear explanation. There’s also no indication of who can see the profile, despite the screen collecting personal information.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Short, playful, and the tonal outlier of this entire set.

"Edit Your Profile" — mislabelled for the moment. This is a first profile setup, not an edit; nothing exists yet, as the empty avatar shows. "Edit" implies returning to change something, which sets the wrong expectation and makes the screen read as a settings detour rather than a step in the invite flow. "Set up your profile" or "Add your photo" would name the actual task.

"Don't be a mystery flyer!" — the most personality-forward line anywhere in the product, and it's doing real work despite the exclamation mark. It reframes an empty avatar from incomplete form field to how you'll appear to people who know you, which is a social motivation rather than a compliance one. "Mystery flyer" is domain-native wordplay that lands. The risk is register: this is the only exclamation mark in a product otherwise written like an instrument panel, and it sits three taps from a permissions sheet. Charming, slightly incongruous.

"This is what friends see when you share flights and how you'll appear in your flight log." — two justifications, and the second is the interesting one. The first is social (friends see you); the second is personal (your own log). Naming a self-facing benefit gives a user with no strong social motivation a reason to bother, which is a thoughtful hedge. It also quietly previews a feature — a flight log with identity attached — that hasn't appeared anywhere else in this flow.

"Complete" — the weakest string on the screen. It's an adjective-as-verb with no object, and it doesn't say what completes. Worse, on a screen where the avatar is unfilled, "Complete" reads as finish the thing you haven't finished, implying the photo is mandatory. "Save," "Done," or "Continue" would each be clearer, and "Continue" would additionally signal that the invite flow resumes after this.

What's missing: no skip label, no statement of who can see the profile, and no indication that the name is editable.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Just-in-time identity — asking for a profile at the first moment it has a function, rather than at launch, is why this ask is likely to convert.

  2. Showing the destination — the header illustration makes the consequence of the upload concrete, turning an abstract request into an obvious one.

  3. Prefill reduces the ask to one field — the name arriving populated means the real request is a single photo, which is the minimum viable version of this screen.

  4. Ambiguous requirement — "Complete" beside an empty avatar with no visible skip implies the photo is mandatory when it very likely isn't.

  5. Scope unstated — a face and a name are introduced with no visibility statement, immediately after a screen that made a precise one.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. WhatsApp (profile setup) — name prefilled, photo optional, requested once the social context exists rather than at install.

  2. Apple (Contact Photo & Poster) — shows a live preview of how you'll appear to others before asking for the image, same "show the destination" logic.

  3. Strava / Untappd (post-first-share profile prompts) — identity requested at the point of first social exposure in an otherwise solo product.
screens.whereToUse: Best where a product delivers full value anonymously and identity only becomes meaningful at a specific social moment. Deferring the ask to that moment maximises willingness, and prefilling from the device reduces it to a single optional action.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit when it lands mid-flow on top of several open modals, as here — an identity request should interrupt as little as possible, and four layers deep the user has lost the thread of what they were doing. Also wrong when the profile carries visibility implications the screen doesn't state.

screens.name: Edit Profile 3
screens.uxAnalysis:
This frame confirms the gating logic: name required, photo optional. The enabled button communicates this only through colour, without explicitly explaining the requirement.

Keeping the keyboard open with the CTA visible is effective, and the earlier text truncation appears to be temporary rather than a structural issue.

The remaining weakness is the “Complete” label. With an empty avatar still visible, it suggests the profile is finished when it isn’t. “Save” or “Continue” would better match the action.

The visible carousel dots underneath are also distracting, revealing navigation from a layer the user can’t currently access.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Unchanged from the prior frames and analysed there. Two observations specific to this state:

"Complete" as an enabled button — the ambiguity sharpens rather than resolves. Disabled, it read as "you haven't finished." Enabled, beside an empty avatar, it reads as "you're finished" — two opposite meanings from one word depending on state, with the visual evidence contradicting the second. This is the clearest argument in the set for a plainer verb.

The subheading now renders in full — "This is what friends see when you share flights and how you'll appear in your flight log." At full length the sentence's structure is visible: social justification first, personal second. Given that the personal benefit ("your flight log") is the one that motivates a user with no social intent, and given it's the clause that vanishes first under compression, it might deserve the leading position.

The screen still never says the photo is optional, never says the name is required, and never states who can see the profile.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. State change as the only feedback — enabling the CTA is the sole signal that the requirement is met; nothing in text ever confirms what was needed.

  2. Layout at rest versus in transition — the copy truncation seen mid-keyboard-animation doesn't persist, so the earlier concern is a transitional artifact rather than a fixed flaw.

  3. Label contradicts the visual — "Complete" beside an empty avatar sends opposing signals about whether the task is finished.

  4. Commit without dismissing — keeping the CTA above the keyboard means typing and confirming are one continuous action.

  5. Orphaned navigation — the carousel's page dots remain visible for a layer the user can't currently interact with, four modals deep.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. WhatsApp (profile setup) — identical requirement shape, name-gated CTA, optional photo, but with the optionality stated rather than inferred.

  2. Signal (registration) — mandatory display name with helper text naming it as required, avoiding the disabled-button-with-no-diagnosis problem.

  3. Apple (Contact Photo & Poster) — an explicitly skippable image step with a labelled skip, where this flow relies on the button's colour to convey the same thing.
screens.whereToUse: Best for one-field forms where the requirement is self-evident and platform autofill can supply the answer, so state-based validation carries no real cost. Keeping the CTA above the keyboard is right whenever the form is short enough to commit without scrolling.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit once more than one field is required or the requirement isn't obvious, since colour-only validation leaves users without a diagnosis. Also wrong where an optional field looks conspicuously unfinished beside a CTA labelled as completion.

screens.name: Edit Menu
screens.uxAnalysis:
The ordering is thoughtful: Contacts → Photos → Camera, moving from least effort to most. Leading with Contacts is especially smart because users may already have a curated profile photo there.

“Recommended” is also an interesting choice. Rather than presenting equal options, Flighty actively guides users toward the fastest, lowest-friction path.

Combined with name autofill, the entire profile can be completed in just a few taps. The trade-off is the increasingly deep modal stack: five layers, multiple dismiss controls, and a menu partially covering the underlying copy.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Terse, functional, and one word doing outsized work.

"Fill From Contacts" — "Fill" rather than "Import" or "Use" frames this as populating a field rather than transferring data, which is a softer, more accurate description of what happens. It also avoids the word "Contacts" reading as a permission ask; the phrasing suggests the app is reaching for your own card, not your address book. Whether that's the technical reality can't be told from here, but the copy is careful not to imply broad access.

"Recommended" — the steer, and it's honest. It doesn't say "fastest" or "easiest," which would be claims about the user's experience; it says the app recommends it, which is a claim about the app's opinion. Small distinction, but it's the difference between guidance and pressure.

"Open Photos" / "Take Photo" — verb-first, platform-standard, no embellishment. Correct register for a menu; anything more personable here would be noise.

What's absent is any statement of what happens to the image. This is the fourth screen in the flow to introduce personal data — after the name, after the invite, after the flight itself — and none of them has said where it goes or who sees it. "Fill From Contacts" in particular touches data the user considers private by default, and a single line about local versus uploaded handling would cost one row.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Order by effort, not by convention — leading with the zero-friction source rather than the technically obvious one reflects how users actually complete optional fields.

  2. Opinionated defaults inside neutral chrome — "Recommended" spends a little of the system menu's impartiality to save the user a decision, in the user's favour.

  3. Cumulative friction removal — autofill plus contact-card photo means the whole profile is completable in a few taps with no typing, which is what makes an optional field actually get filled.

  4. Honest hedging in the label — "Recommended" is a statement of the app's view rather than an unfalsifiable claim about ease.

  5. Five layers deep — the menu overlaps the copy it interrupts, three dismiss controls are visible at once, and the exit path is now genuinely opaque.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple (Contact Photo & Poster setup) — offers Memoji, Photos and Camera in a ranked list with a suggested option surfaced first. Direct platform lineage for both the menu and the steer.

  2. WhatsApp (profile photo) — same three-source menu, but without a recommendation, so the user makes a decision they didn't need to make.

  3. Signal (avatar picker) — Photos-first ordering, which is the convention this screen deliberately breaks.
screens.whereToUse: Best when an optional field has one source that's dramatically cheaper than the others and the app can say so without misleading. Ranked menus fit anywhere the options aren't genuinely equivalent — presenting them as equal when they aren't just transfers work to the user.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit when the recommended option carries a privacy cost the label doesn't disclose, since "Recommended" then reads as steering rather than helping. Also wrong when it lands this deep in a modal stack, where any new layer compounds an already-opaque exit path.

screens.name: Profile Complete
screens.uxAnalysis:
The plus-to-pencil swap is a strong micro-interaction. The same control changes meaning with the state: the photo confirms success, while the pencil signals that it can be changed—without needing a toast or message.

More importantly, the flow stays remarkably lightweight. No account, password, email verification, or OAuth—just a name and photo sourced from existing device data.

The remaining issues are mostly copy and privacy. “Complete” still sounds like a state rather than an action, while the screen never explains who can see the profile photo, despite it being tied to shared travel information.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Unchanged from prior frames; the completed state changes how two strings land.

"Edit Your Profile" — finally correct. The irony is that the title was accurate for none of the states it was shown in except this one, which is the state immediately before the sheet dismisses. A title that only becomes true at the moment it disappears is a title chosen for the wrong screen.

"Don't be a mystery flyer!" — now redundant. The user has supplied a face; the copy is still telling them not to be anonymous. A completed form usually shifts its framing to confirmation ("This is how friends will see you"), and holding the recruitment line means the screen never acknowledges the user did the thing it asked. Small missed moment.

"Complete" — the label's problem inverts here. With an empty avatar it implied incompleteness; with a filled one it reads as a description of the current state rather than an action to take. A user could plausibly read the blue pill as a status badge rather than a button. "Save" or "Continue" would remain unambiguous across all three states, which is exactly why they'd be better.

Still unstated across the entire flow: who sees this profile, and whether friend access can be revoked. Both questions have now survived five screens of a feature explicitly about granting people access to your travel.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. State-appropriate affordances — swapping plus for pencil confirms success and offers revision in the same control, with no extra UI.

  2. The artifact is the confirmation — showing the uploaded photo is more convincing than any success message would be.

  3. Identity without accounts — a name and a face captured in two taps, no signup, delivers on the product's stated no-account posture.

  4. Labels should hold across states — "Complete" means something different empty, filled, and disabled; a verb like "Save" would not.

  5. Visibility still unstated — a photograph is now attached to a movement-sharing feature with no scope or revocation statement anywhere in the flow.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple (Contact Photo & Poster) — same add-to-edit badge transition on the avatar, same no-account identity model.

  2. WhatsApp (profile photo) — pencil-on-avatar convention for a populated image, with the same in-place edit affordance.

  3. Signal (profile setup) — comparable two-field, no-account identity capture, but with an explicit note on who the profile is visible to.
screens.whereToUse: Best where identity is genuinely optional to the core product and can be sourced from device data, so the whole capture collapses into a couple of taps. The add-to-edit badge transition suits any single-slot media field where the filled state should also be revisable.
screens.whereNotToUse: A poor fit where the profile carries visibility consequences the flow doesn't state — a face attached to location-adjacent sharing needs a scope line before commit, not after. Also wrong where the CTA label can't hold a consistent meaning across empty, filled and disabled states.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing Profile 4
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a settings/profile hub for a self-custodial crypto wallet (Coinbase Wallet, based on the .cb.id ENS-style domain). It follows a classic "Hub & Spoke" pattern: a profile header sits atop a vertically stacked list of drill-in rows, each of which pushes to a dedicated detail screen (recovery phrase, connected dapps, public addresses, privacy, private key, token allowances, color). The layout prioritizes scannability with a single-column list, generous vertical spacing, and consistent chevron affordances signaling further navigation depth.

The most critical design decision is the surfacing of wallet security status directly in the list via a colored status chip ("Not backed up" in alert-red) rather than burying it in a sub-page. This turns a passive settings list into an active risk-communication surface. The dark theme (near-black background, high-contrast white text) reduces eye strain and reinforces a premium, "vault-like" feel appropriate for a financial/security-sensitive product.

Notably, the screen appears to be a stitched/scrolled composite (two status bars and a duplicated back arrow are visible), suggesting this is actually two screens captured together — likely "Wallet Settings" transitioning into a secondary "Security/Privacy" sub-list. This reveals a long, single scrolling settings page rather than nested categories, trading a flatter IA for more scrolling.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
Copy is terse, functional, and unembellished — typical of Web3 tooling aimed at users who already understand blockchain jargon ("Recovery phrase," "Token allowances," "Export public addresses," "Private key"). There's no hand-holding or explanatory subtext under any row, which assumes technical literacy.

The one moment of tonal deviation is the "Not backed up" chip — its red color and directive language function almost as a warning label, injecting urgency into an otherwise neutral, utilitarian list. This is a deliberate psychological nudge: everything else is calm gray/white, so the red pulls the eye immediately toward the highest-risk unresolved task.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline risk signaling: The "Not backed up" badge embedded directly in the list row eliminates the need to open a sub-page to discover a critical security gap, reducing time-to-awareness for self-custody risk.

  • Editable identity avatar: The pencil-badge overlay on the profile picture is a well-established affordance that communicates editability without needing a separate "Edit" label near the avatar itself.

  • Human-readable identity (ENS-style name): Displaying "alexsmithmobbin.cb.id" instead of a raw hex address (0x...) dramatically improves memorability and trust, translating blockchain complexity into a familiar username paradigm.

  • Flat, chevron-driven list architecture: Every row uses the same visual grammar (label left, value/status right, chevron far right), making the entire settings area predictable and easy to scan despite covering highly disparate topics (security, social, customization).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets crypto-native users — likely intermediate-to-advanced Web3 participants who hold their own private keys and interact with decentralized apps (dapps), given the presence of "Token allowances," "Connected dapps," and "Export public addresses." The design assumes prior familiarity with self-custody risks (seed phrases, private keys), so it forgoes educational tooltips in favor of information density.

Psychologically, the red "Not backed up" chip exploits loss-aversion: users are reminded, every time they visit settings, that their funds are one device-loss away from permanent inaccessibility. This persistent, mildly anxiety-inducing cue is a deliberate retention/completion driver, nudging users toward the "Recovery phrase" backup flow without an intrusive modal.
screens.whereToUse:
• Financial, crypto, or security-sensitive apps where a small number of settings carry outsized risk (e.g., 2FA not enabled, backup missing, unverified email).

  • Account/profile hub screens that aggregate identity, security, and customization controls under one scrollable list.

  • Any settings IA where you want to surface status-at-a-glance (via chips/badges) instead of forcing users to drill into every row to discover state.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for mainstream/non-technical audiences without adding contextual explanations — terms like "Token allowances" or "Private key" will alienate novice users without inline help or tooltips.

  • Don't rely on color-only status indicators (red chip) without an icon or accessible label, as this fails colorblind and accessibility guidelines if not paired with sufficient contrast/text.

  • Avoid flat single-list architecture once the number of settings grows large; beyond ~15-20 rows, group into categorized sub-sections or a sectioned/grouped table to prevent excessive scrolling.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing Profile 5
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a critical step in the Coinbase Wallet onboarding flow where users claim a human-readable identity (a .cb.id subdomain built on ENS) to replace their long, unmemorable public wallet address. The layout follows a classic single-screen form pattern: a clear title, a cautionary subtitle, a single input field with a fixed suffix (.cb.id), a legal/consent checkbox, and a single primary CTA at the bottom.

The information architecture is deliberately linear and single-focused — there is only one input to fill, which reduces cognitive load and decision fatigue at a stage where users are still building trust with the product. The back arrow in the top-left preserves a sense of control, letting users retreat without feeling trapped in the flow.

Below the main input, the screen smartly introduces an escape hatch/alternative path ("Use your own ENS") for power users who already own an ENS domain, using an icon, short description, and a "Learn how" link. This prevents advanced crypto-native users from feeling forced into adopting a new, potentially redundant identity, while not distracting first-time users who will likely ignore it.

The primary CTA "Claim my username" is styled as a large, full-width pill button, but it appears in a muted/disabled-looking blue tone, likely indicating it is inactive until the checkbox is ticked and a valid username is entered. This is a subtle but effective way to guide the user's eye to the two remaining required actions before progressing.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is casual, encouraging, and slightly playful ("Pick your username," "Choose wisely!") which softens what is otherwise a fairly permanent and technical decision (claiming a blockchain-based namespace). The exclamation point injects energy and urgency without being alarming.

Microcopy is used efficiently to set expectations and reduce future frustration — explicitly stating "You can only change this once a year" preempts support tickets and manages expectations around a constraint that is unusual in most consumer apps (most usernames are either permanent or freely changeable).

The "Powered by ENS" label and the "Use your own ENS" module inject technical credibility and transparency, reassuring crypto-savvy users that this isn't a walled-garden proprietary system but is built on an open, portable standard (Ethereum Name Service).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Constraint transparency upfront: Clearly stating the one-year change limitation before the user commits, rather than burying it in fine print, builds trust and reduces buyer's remorse.

  • Escape hatch for power users: The "Use your own ENS" card intelligently segments the audience, offering an alternate path for existing ENS holders without cluttering the primary flow.

  • Fixed domain suffix in input field: Displaying ".cb.id" as a static suffix inside the text field removes ambiguity about the format and prevents user error/typos.

  • Disabled-state CTA: The muted button color visually signals that required steps (checkbox, input) remain incomplete, guiding the user's next action without explicit error messaging.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new-to-wallet or new-to-Coinbase-Wallet users, ranging from crypto beginners intimidated by hex addresses to crypto-native users who already have an ENS name. The psychological trigger here is identity ownership and personalization — giving users a memorable, personal handle transforms an abstract wallet address into something that feels like "theirs," increasing emotional investment in the product early in the funnel.

The "choose wisely" framing also leverages a mild commitment/loss-aversion trigger, making the decision feel meaningful and encouraging users to invest more time and thought into onboarding, which correlates with higher long-term retention.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when onboarding requires a unique, user-owned identifier (e.g., username, handle, subdomain) that will be referenced elsewhere in the product. It's ideal when:

  • The identifier has real technical/legal constraints (rarity of change, uniqueness validation) that must be communicated early.

  • There's an alternative technical path for advanced users (e.g., BYO domain/ID) that shouldn't block the primary simple flow.

  • You want to convert an intimidating technical detail (blockchain address) into something ownable and human-friendly.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, single-purpose full-screen treatment when:

  • The username/identifier is trivial to change later — in that case, a lighter-weight inline prompt is less friction-inducing.

  • The user base is highly non-technical and unfamiliar with concepts like ENS; introducing "Powered by ENS" jargon without simplification may cause confusion or drop-off.

  • Onboarding flows are already lengthy — adding another mandatory step with legal checkbox agreement can increase abandonment if not clearly essential.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing Profile 1
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen presents a dedicated avatar/profile picture customization flow, structured as a classic preview-then-select pattern. A large, live preview of the currently selected avatar sits prominently at the top-center, immediately confirming the user's choice before they commit. Below it, a dense grid of pre-designed, whimsical character icons is arranged in a scrollable 5-column layout, allowing users to browse many options without overwhelming a single viewport (the grid is intentionally cut off at the bottom to signal more content via scroll).

A horizontal color swatch selector sits just above the primary actions, letting users tint the background of their chosen icon — a lightweight secondary customization layer that multiplies the effective number of unique avatar combinations without multiplying asset count. The selected icon and color are both marked with a clear blue ring/border, giving unambiguous selection state feedback.

The layout terminates in two clearly hierarchized CTAs: a high-emphasis gradient "Save" button for the primary path (pick a preset), and a secondary "Choose your own" button beneath it for users who want to upload a custom photo instead. This progressive disclosure keeps the primary flow simple while still surfacing power-user/personalization options.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is playful and low-stakes, reinforced by whimsical, cartoonish monster/character iconography (aliens, vampires, cacti, pizza slices, kings) rather than realistic human avatars. This immediately lowers the psychological barrier to picking an identity image — there's no "right" choice, only fun ones.

Copy is minimal and purely functional ("Customize", "Save", "Choose your own"), letting the visual grid do all the communicative work. The lack of instructional copy assumes user familiarity with avatar-picker conventions (tap to select, color strip to tint, save to confirm), which is appropriate given how ubiquitous this pattern is across chat and gaming apps.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live large preview: Immediate, prominent visual feedback of the exact avatar+color combination before saving reduces uncertainty and buyer's remorse.

  • Decoupled color layer: Separating icon choice from background color turns a finite icon set into a much larger combinatorial space of unique-feeling avatars with minimal design effort.

  • Dual-path CTA hierarchy: Presenting "Save" (fast, preset path) above "Choose your own" (custom upload path) nudges most users toward the frictionless default while still respecting power users who want a personal photo.

  • Clear selection affordances: The blue ring around both the selected avatar and selected color provides unmistakable, consistent state indication across two different selector types.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users in early onboarding or profile-setup moments, particularly in social, gaming, or community apps where identity expression matters but photo uploads may feel too exposing or slow. Playful monster/character illustrations appeal broadly across age groups and reduce the social pressure of "picking a good photo," which is a common onboarding drop-off point.

Psychologically, offering many small, distinct, colorful options triggers a sense of self-expression and ownership ("this one feels like me") while the color-tint layer taps into a desire for uniqueness/differentiation without added decision fatigue, since color choice is a much simpler decision than icon choice.
screens.whereToUse:
• Onboarding flows for social, messaging, or gaming apps needing quick identity/avatar setup without requiring camera/photo permissions.

  • Anonymous or pseudonymous platforms where playful avatars reduce identity friction (e.g., forums, gaming lobbies, kids' apps).

  • Any settings screen where users may want to periodically refresh or customize their profile appearance.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Professional or B2B platforms (e.g., enterprise SaaS, banking) where a cartoonish avatar set would undermine trust or brand seriousness — real photo or initials-based avatars are more appropriate.

  • Contexts where verified real identity is critical (e.g., ID verification, video calling with strangers) and a whimsical avatar could enable impersonation or reduce accountability.

  • Screens with very limited space where a full-screen dedicated picker is disproportionate to the value of the customization.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing Profile 2
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen represents a dedicated identity customization module, likely used during onboarding or in account settings to let users personalize their profile avatar. The layout follows a clear top-to-bottom hierarchy: a large preview of the selected avatar sits prominently at the top, acting as a live-updating focal point, followed by a scrollable grid of selectable icon options, a horizontal color swatch selector, and finally two clearly weighted CTAs at the bottom.

The selected state uses a strong blue ring/halo around the chosen icon (the joystick), providing unambiguous visual feedback that reinforces the connection between the grid selection and the large preview above — a classic 'select and preview' interaction pattern. The grid itself uses circular masks with a dark, muted background for unselected items, which keeps focus on the colorful illustrated icons themselves and prevents visual clutter despite the density of options (25+ icons visible).

The color swatch row beneath the grid follows the same selection paradigm (ring indicator) and lets users theme the background of their chosen icon, adding a second layer of personalization without needing a full custom upload. The dual-button footer — a gradient 'Save' primary CTA and a distinct 'Choose your own' secondary action — smartly separates the 'quick personalization' path from the 'power user' path (likely camera roll upload), catering to both casual and highly invested users in a single screen.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The screen uses extremely minimal, functional copy ("Customize", "Save", "Choose your own") rather than playful or narrative text. This restrained tonality is intentional: it lets the vibrant, quirky, illustrated icon set (aliens, monsters, skulls, sneakers) do the emotional and personality-driven communication instead of words. The interface trusts visual language over textual explanation, appropriate for a gaming, social, or crypto-native audience already familiar with avatar/PFP culture.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live Preview Binding: The large avatar circle at the top instantly reflects grid and color selections, giving users immediate, low-friction visual confirmation.

  • Dual Selection Rings: Both the icon grid and color palette use the same halo/ring selection affordance, creating a consistent, learnable interaction pattern across two different control types.

  • Progressive Disclosure of Power Options: "Choose your own" is placed as a secondary, lower-emphasis action beneath the primary Save button, letting default users move fast while still surfacing custom upload for those who want it.

  • Dark Canvas for Color Pop: The near-black background makes the saturated, quirky icon illustrations and color swatches highly legible and vibrant, reducing visual competition.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users in gaming, Web3/crypto, or social-first apps where avatars/PFPs are a core part of identity and self-expression (e.g., Discord, Reddit, crypto wallets, gaming platforms). The offbeat, illustrated character set (monsters, skulls, aliens) suggests a younger, internet-native demographic that values individuality and humor over corporate polish.

Psychologically, this leans on the IKEA effect and self-expression bias — letting users invest a small amount of effort in choosing/combining an icon and color makes them feel more ownership over their profile, increasing attachment to the app. The joystick icon as default/selected state also subtly reinforces a gaming-adjacent brand identity.
screens.whereToUse:
• Onboarding flows where personalization increases emotional investment and completion rates.

  • Profile/avatar settings for social, gaming, or community apps.

  • Any feature requiring a quick 'pick from curated set' experience before offering a more effortful custom upload path.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Enterprise, B2B, or highly formal applications where playful illustrated avatars would undermine professional credibility.

  • Contexts where brand consistency requires uniform, non-customizable profile imagery (e.g., verified professional directories).

  • Low-bandwidth or accessibility-critical contexts where color-only selection differentiation could be problematic without additional labeling for colorblind users.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing Profile 8
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a milestone celebration confirming that a user has successfully claimed a human-readable crypto username (e.g. a Coinbase ID / ENS-style handle). The layout follows a classic "success state" template: a large, vibrant custom illustration dominates the vertical center, a bold headline reinforces the accomplishment, a supporting line of body copy explains the practical benefit, and a single full-width primary CTA ("Done") closes the loop.

The illustration itself is a clever piece of visual storytelling — a stylized wallet/card shape combined with a large green checkmark badge communicates "identity verified & secured" without needing extra text. Sparkle/star accents surrounding the illustration inject a sense of delight and reward, mimicking the visual language of gamified apps and premium unlockables.

Information hierarchy is extremely simple and linear: Icon → Headline → Subtext → CTA. There is no competing navigation, no secondary actions, and no distractions, which is appropriate because this is a terminal/confirmation step in an onboarding or account-setup flow (evidenced by the page indicator dots at the bottom suggesting this is the final step of a multi-step flow).

The dark, near-black background combined with saturated blue/yellow/cyan gradients creates a premium, "crypto-native" aesthetic that aligns with Web3/fintech branding conventions, while maintaining high contrast and legibility for the white text.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is short, celebratory, and personal. "You claimed your username!" uses second-person voice and an exclamation mark to create an emotional payoff, treating the mundane act of registering a handle as an achievement worth celebrating — similar to unlocking a badge in a game.

The subtext, "alexsmithmobbin.cb.id is ready to send and receive crypto," immediately grounds the celebration in tangible utility: the user now understands exactly what this username unlocks (a functional payment identity), reducing any ambiguity about why this step mattered.

The CTA label "Done" is minimal and neutral — it signals closure of the flow rather than pushing the user toward a new action, respecting the fact that this is a wrap-up screen, not a conversion moment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Custom celebratory illustration: A bespoke wallet+checkmark graphic communicates security and success instantly, more memorable than a generic checkmark icon.

  • Emotional reframing of a utilitarian task: Registering a username is elevated to a "claim" and celebrated like a reward, increasing perceived value of the product feature.

  • Dynamic personalization: The user's actual chosen username is echoed back in the confirmation copy, reinforcing ownership and correctness.

  • Single, unambiguous exit path: Only one button (Done) prevents decision fatigue and clearly signals flow completion.

  • Sparkle motif & gradient palette: Subtle decorative elements amplify the "premium unlock" feeling without cluttering the layout.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new or returning crypto wallet users (likely Coinbase Wallet, given the ".cb.id" domain) who are going through account/identity setup. The target demographic is comfortable with crypto terminology but still benefits from reassurance that the technical action (claiming an ENS-like username) succeeded.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Peak-End Rule — users disproportionately remember the end of an experience, so ending onboarding on a visually delightful, celebratory high point increases overall satisfaction and perceived product quality. The checkmark and gradient "unlock" imagery also tap into reward/achievement psychology common in gamification, making an administrative task feel like a win, which increases the likelihood of continued engagement with the app.
screens.whereToUse:
• End of any multi-step onboarding, registration, or setup wizard where a meaningful account attribute (username, ID, address) has just been created.

  • Confirming irreversible or identity-defining actions (claiming a handle, verifying an account, minting an asset) where reassurance and delight both matter.

  • Any flow where you want to convert a technical/administrative success into a moment of positive brand emotion before returning the user to the main app.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy celebratory treatment for frequent, low-stakes confirmations (e.g., saving a form field) — it would feel disproportionate and slow down repeat interactions.

  • Don't use if the user needs to take an immediate follow-up action; a single "Done" button with no secondary CTA can strand users who need next steps (e.g., "fund your wallet now").

  • Not suitable for enterprise/B2B tools where a more restrained, efficiency-first tone is expected.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing Profile 10
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen presents a single-screen form for editing a user's public-facing profile in what appears to be a crypto wallet or Web3 identity app (evidenced by the ".cb.id" domain, indicative of Coinbase's ENS-like naming system). The layout follows a clear, vertically stacked information hierarchy: identity (avatar + username) at the top, followed by progressively less critical optional fields (Bio, Website, Twitter, Reddit).

The dark mode UI with high-contrast white text on near-black background reduces eye strain and aligns with the aesthetic expectations of crypto-native users. Each input field uses a consistent bordered, transparent-fill style with light gray placeholder text, which keeps the interface calm and unintimidating despite requesting personal data.

A large tappable avatar with an overlaid camera icon badge clearly signals editability without needing an explicit label, leveraging established mobile design conventions. The persistent, full-width "Save" CTA is anchored at the bottom, though it appears in a disabled/dimmed state until the user makes a change — a subtle but effective way to prevent premature or empty submissions.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is written in a friendly, reassuring, and low-pressure tone. The subtitle "Your profile is public. You can make it private in Manage privacy. All fields are optional." does double duty: it transparently discloses the default privacy state (public) and immediately offers an escape hatch (link to privacy settings), while explicitly removing pressure by stating "All fields are optional."

Field labels ("Bio", "Your website", "Twitter username", "Reddit username") are short, literal, and free of jargon. Placeholder copy like "Describe yourself" and "Add your website address" uses conversational, second-person phrasing rather than terse technical labels, making the form feel more like a personal profile than an account settings form.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Transparent privacy disclosure with inline escape hatch: Immediately informing users their profile is public, paired with a linked "Manage privacy" shortcut, builds trust and reduces anxiety before they even start filling out fields.

  • Explicit "optional" framing: Stating "All fields are optional" upfront lowers the perceived commitment and cognitive load, increasing completion likelihood for at least partial data.

  • Disabled-state Save button as a state indicator: The dimmed "Save" button visually communicates that no changes have been made yet, preventing wasted taps and reinforcing that the form tracks dirty state.

  • Avatar edit affordance via camera badge: The small circular camera icon overlapping the avatar is a widely recognized pattern requiring no additional instructional text.

  • Social handle fields without @ symbols or URLs: Asking only for "username" rather than full profile URLs reduces friction and input errors.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users of a decentralized identity or crypto wallet platform (likely Coinbase Wallet, given the ".cb.id" naming) who are setting up a public-facing on-chain identity/profile, similar to an ENS domain profile. This audience is typically privacy-conscious, given the crypto space's cultural emphasis on pseudonymity and self-custody, which explains why privacy status and controls are surfaced so prominently and early.

The psychological trigger at play is reduction of form anxiety — by front-loading reassurance ("optional", "public but you can change it"), the design reduces the natural hesitation crypto users have about exposing personal identifiers (social handles, websites) tied to a wallet address. The social fields (Twitter, Reddit) also tap into social proof and identity verification motivations common in Web3 communities, where linking social accounts increases perceived legitimacy and trust of a wallet/ENS profile.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for optional profile completion flows, especially in contexts where users may be wary of sharing personal information (crypto, finance, health, or any platform with public-facing profiles). It's ideal when:

  • You want to encourage — not mandate — profile enrichment.

  • Privacy status varies by user and needs to be surfaced contextually.

  • The form has a mix of identity, bio, and social-linking fields that benefit from a calm, low-pressure layout.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when profile completion is critical to core functionality (e.g., KYC, onboarding steps required for compliance) — the "optional" framing and passive tone would undermine urgency and completion rates. It's also less suitable for dense enterprise or B2B tools where users expect efficient bulk-editing rather than a single long vertical scroll of individual fields. Additionally, a disabled-until-dirty Save button can be problematic if users don't realize a field change is required to activate it — consider adding a tooltip or subtle animation cue.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing Profile 3
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a dedicated Customize flow that lets a user personalize their profile avatar by combining two independent variables: a quirky illustrated icon and an accent background color. The architecture follows a classic "large preview + grid selector" pattern: a big circular preview sits pinned at the top, immediately reflecting any change made below it, giving the user a constant, unambiguous visual anchor of what will be saved.

Below the preview, a dense 5-column grid of icon tiles is presented in a scrollable list. The currently selected icon is clearly distinguished with a glowing pink ring/halo treatment that visually pops against the pure black background, making state recognition instantaneous even in a busy grid. The grid appears to cut off content above the fold (partial icons visible at the very top), signaling to the user that this list is scrollable — a subtle affordance for continued exploration.

Beneath the icon grid, a horizontally scrollable color rail (pill-shaped container) allows independent color selection, decoupling "what shape" from "what color," which multiplies the number of unique avatar permutations without multiplying UI complexity. The selected color similarly uses a ring indicator for consistency with the icon selection pattern.

The screen closes with a strong dual-CTA footer: a primary gradient "Save" button for users happy with a preset combination, and a secondary "Choose your own" button that likely escalates to a full custom upload flow (camera roll/photo). Stacking these vertically with equal visual weight (both using the same warm gradient) nudges users toward action while still offering an escape hatch to full personalization.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is playful, expressive, and identity-driven rather than corporate. The icon set — skulls, monsters, aliens, crowns, dinosaurs, floppy disks — leans into an edgy, Gen-Z/gamer aesthetic rather than generic corporate avatars, suggesting this app targets a younger, community- or gaming-oriented audience (possibly Discord-like chat, gaming, or social app).

Microcopy is minimal and functional: "Customize," "Save," "Choose your own." There's no explanatory text or tooltips needed because the interaction model (tap icon, tap color, tap save) is self-evident from visual affordances alone — a sign of a mature, confident design system that trusts users to understand direct manipulation without hand-holding.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live merged preview: The top avatar circle updates instantly to reflect combined icon + color selections, reducing cognitive load and eliminating guesswork before committing.

  • Decoupled customization axes: Separating "icon" and "color" into two independent selectors multiplies personalization variety with minimal added UI surface area.

  • Consistent selection affordance: Both the icon grid and color rail use the same glowing ring/halo pattern to indicate "currently selected," creating a learnable, consistent visual language across different control types.

  • Dual-path footer CTA: Offering both a fast preset "Save" path and an escape-hatch "Choose your own" (custom upload) path caters to both low-effort and high-effort personalization users.

  • Dark canvas for color pop: The pure black background makes each vividly colored icon and the gradient buttons visually vibrant, reinforcing a premium, expressive brand identity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users — likely teens to young adults in gaming, chat, or social communities — who place high value on self-expression and identity signaling within a digital space. Avatars function as a proxy for personality in text-based or low-photo-sharing environments, so offering a rich, characterful icon library (rather than realistic human avatars) taps into the psychological drive for individuality and in-group belonging (owning a "rare" or "cool" icon/color combo).

The instant visual feedback loop (live preview) leverages the psychological principle of immediate reward and reduces the anxiety of "will this look right" before committing, encouraging more exploration and ultimately higher engagement with the customization feature — which correlates with increased app attachment and retention.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this live-preview + grid-selector pattern when:

  • Building profile/avatar customization in social, gaming, or community apps where identity expression drives engagement.

  • You have two or more independent visual attributes (shape, color, pattern, accessory) that can be combined for a large personalization matrix without a large asset library.

  • You want to offer a "quick pick" preset path alongside a more effortful custom upload path, serving both casual and power users.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this approach when:

  • The brand requires realistic/professional avatars (e.g., B2B, enterprise, healthcare apps) where playful illustrated icons would undermine trust or seriousness.

  • The customization options are very limited (1-2 choices) — a full-screen grid would be overkill; a simple dropdown or few thumbnails would suffice.

  • Screen real estate is extremely constrained (e.g., a small widget or embedded flow) — the large preview plus scrollable grid plus color rail requires considerable vertical space to work well.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing Profile 6
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a single-field form focused on claiming a human-readable blockchain username (a Coinbase-hosted ENS subdomain, .cb.id). The layout is intentionally minimal: a back arrow, a single labeled text field, real-time availability feedback, an informational card about ENS interoperability, a required legal checkbox, and a single primary CTA.

The core UX strength is the real-time inline validation pattern — as the user types, the input border turns green and a confirmation microcopy ("Good one! That's available.") appears instantly below the field. This removes the traditional "submit and wait" anxiety associated with username selection (a notoriously frustrating flow on most platforms where desired names are taken).

The suffix ".cb.id" is anchored to the right of the input, visually locked as non-editable, which reduces cognitive load — users only need to think about the customizable portion of their identity, not the domain structure.

Below the form, an illustration + copy block cross-sells the idea that this action is part of the broader Ethereum Name Service (ENS) ecosystem, reassuring crypto-native users that this isn't a walled-garden identity but is portable/interoperable — an important trust signal for Web3 audiences who value decentralization.

The primary button ("Claim my username") remains present but is deliberately gated behind the unchecked "I agree to subdomain terms" checkbox, following standard legal-consent-gating for irreversible on-chain actions (username registration is typically permanent/immutable).
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is casual, warm, and encouraging rather than technical or transactional — "Good one! That's available." reads like a friendly nudge from a peer rather than a system message, which softens the intimidating, technical nature of blockchain identity registration for newcomers.

The secondary content block ("Use your own ENS... You can import your ENS name into Coinbase Wallet. Learn how →") is written for the more advanced crypto user, offering an escape hatch without derailing the primary happy path — a smart layered communication strategy addressing both novice and expert personas on the same screen.

Legal/consent language is kept short and blue-linked ("subdomain terms") to stay unobtrusive while still satisfying compliance requirements.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Instant availability feedback: Green border + affirming microcopy eliminates the classic "username taken" submit-and-retry loop.

  • Fixed domain suffix: ".cb.id" displayed as a static, non-editable label inside the field, clarifying scope of input without extra explanation.

  • Dual-audience content: Serves onboarding beginners (simple claim flow) and sophisticated ENS-savvy users (import your own ENS) on the same screen without clutter.

  • Consent gate before irreversible action: Checkbox required before the CTA can be meaningfully activated, appropriate for a blockchain-permanent action.

  • Minimalist single-focus layout: No competing information; the eye is drawn directly to the input and validation state.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new and existing Coinbase Wallet users setting up a human-readable crypto identity to replace long hexadecimal wallet addresses. The primary psychological trigger is anxiety reduction — claiming a username/handle is often stressful due to fear of unavailability or, in crypto, fear of an irreversible/costly mistake. Instant positive validation ("Good one! That's available") triggers a small dopamine hit and momentum toward task completion.

The ENS cross-reference targets more sophisticated Web3 users who already hold identities elsewhere, building trust through interoperability rather than lock-in, which is a key value proposition in decentralized identity products.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a user must select a unique identifier (username, handle, subdomain, workspace slug, email alias) where availability is uncertain and real-time backend lookups are feasible. It's especially valuable for:

  • Sign-up flows requiring unique handles (social apps, SaaS workspace URLs, crypto wallets/ENS)

  • Situations where users psychologically need reassurance before committing to a permanent or hard-to-change identifier

  • Flows targeting both novice and power users, where a secondary "advanced option" can be surfaced non-intrusively
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid real-time availability checks on high-latency or expensive backend systems (e.g., actual on-chain lookups) without debouncing/loading indicators, as it can feel broken if validation lags behind typing. Also avoid this pattern if the identifier isn't unique/permanent — instant validation theater adds unnecessary complexity for fields with no real availability constraints. Do not gate consent checkboxes behind vague legal language; ensure "subdomain terms" links are actually accessible and understandable, especially for irreversible blockchain registrations.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing Profile 7
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a critical identity-creation step in Coinbase Wallet's onboarding flow, where a new user selects a human-readable username (a subdomain of .cb.id) to replace their cryptographically opaque wallet address. The layout follows a classic single-field form pattern optimized for focus: a large, bold headline, a short instructional subhead, a single prominent text input, and one primary CTA at the bottom.

The inline validation state ("Good one! That's available.") rendered in green directly beneath the input field is the standout interaction detail — it gives the user immediate, low-friction confirmation without requiring a submit action, reducing anxiety around whether their desired name is already taken (a common pain point in username-based systems). The input field itself uses a green border to reinforce the "valid/available" state visually, creating a tight feedback loop between color, icon-free text, and copy.

Below the input, a secondary informational card introduces ENS (Ethereum Name Service) import as an alternative path, using an icon, short description, and a "Learn how" link with a directional arrow — a classic non-blocking upsell/education pattern that doesn't interrupt the primary flow but offers power users an escape hatch. Finally, a mandatory checkbox for subdomain terms sits just above the CTA, gating the action legally without adding much friction since it's pre-checked or easily tappable.

The dark theme with a vivid blue-to-teal gradient CTA button creates strong visual hierarchy, drawing the eye immediately to the single actionable next step once validation passes.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is warm, conversational, and slightly playful ("Choose wisely!", "Good one!"), which softens what is otherwise a fairly permanent and technical decision (usernames tied to blockchain identity can only be changed once a year). This tone choice is deliberate: crypto/web3 products often feel intimidating or overly technical, so injecting casual, encouraging language humanizes the experience.

The warning about annual change frequency is transparently stated upfront rather than hidden in fine print, which builds trust and sets correct expectations before commitment. The validation microcopy "Good one! That's available." rewards the user's choice with positive affirmation rather than a neutral "Available" label, reinforcing a sense of accomplishment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Real-time inline availability validation with celebratory, human microcopy instead of a sterile system message.

  • Color-coded field state (green border + green text) that visually confirms success without needing extra iconography.

  • Non-intrusive power-user escape hatch (ENS import card) that educates advanced users without cluttering the primary flow for novices.

  • Upfront expectation-setting about the one-year change limitation, reducing regret and support tickets later.

  • Single clear CTA with strong gradient contrast against the dark background, eliminating decision paralysis.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new-to-web3 or newly onboarded Coinbase Wallet users who need a memorable, shareable identity (like a Venmo handle or Twitter handle) instead of a 42-character hex wallet address. The psychological trigger at play is identity ownership and personalization — letting users "claim" a name taps into the same territorial/ownership instinct seen in domain registration or social handle selection, increasing emotional investment early in onboarding (a form of the IKEA effect/sunk-cost commitment).

The scarcity-adjacent messaging ("Choose wisely," limited annual changes) also nudges users toward careful, deliberate action, increasing perceived value of the username itself. Meanwhile, the ENS card specifically targets more crypto-native users who already own a decentralized identity, ensuring the product feels flexible to both segments simultaneously.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any onboarding flow requiring a unique, permanent, or semi-permanent identifier (usernames, handles, subdomains, workspace slugs). It's especially effective when:

  • Real-time availability checking is possible via backend/API.

  • The choice carries some weight or permanence that benefits from upfront disclosure.

  • You want to offer an alternate/advanced path (like ENS import) without disrupting the primary happy path for mainstream users.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy single-field emphasis pattern when:

  • Usernames are trivial to change later — the "choose wisely" framing would create unnecessary anxiety for a low-stakes decision.

  • Availability checks are slow or unreliable, which would make the instant-feedback microcopy misleading or laggy, breaking trust.

  • The audience is highly non-technical and unfamiliar with concepts like ENS — introducing it could cause confusion rather than serve as a helpful escape hatch.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing Profile 12
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen represents a classic Single-Screen Form pattern used for editing a user's decentralized identity profile (a Coinbase/cb.id wallet identity). The layout follows a strict vertical rhythm: an identity header (avatar + editable camera icon + username/ENS-style domain) sits above a series of clearly labeled, boxed text inputs for Bio, Website, and social handles (Twitter, Reddit, GitHub).

The use of large touch targets, generous vertical spacing, and consistent input field styling (rounded rectangles with subtle borders on a near-black background) creates a calm, low-friction editing experience appropriate for a financial/crypto app where trust and clarity are paramount. Placeholder text ("Add your website address", "Twitter username") clearly communicates expected input without requiring separate helper text, reducing cognitive load.

Critically, the screen closes the loop with a Toast/Snackbar confirmation ("Profile updated") that overlays the primary save button at the bottom, giving the user immediate, low-intrusion feedback that their edits persisted without forcing a modal interruption or full-page navigation.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal and utilitarian, typical of Web3/crypto identity products: field labels are short, sentence-case, and functional ("Bio", "Your website", "Twitter username"). There is no marketing fluff — the tone is neutral and task-focused, reinforcing that this is a settings/utility screen rather than a persuasive or onboarding moment.

The pre-filled bio ("crypto enthusiast") and the .cb.id domain suffix subtly reinforce the product's crypto-native identity, signaling to users that this profile doubles as an on-chain/Web3 identity rather than a generic social profile.

The confirmation toast "Profile updated" uses plain, past-tense confirmation language — simple, reassuring, and non-intrusive.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Layered avatar edit affordance: A small camera badge icon overlaid on the avatar communicates editability without needing a separate "Change photo" button.

  • Consistent field architecture: Every input uses identical visual treatment (label above, bordered box below, greyed placeholder), making the form scannable and predictable.

  • Non-blocking save confirmation: The "Profile updated" toast appears directly above/over the save button, confirming success exactly where the user's attention already is, avoiding a jarring modal or page redirect.

  • Identity as domain: Displaying the human-readable username alongside its ".cb.id" address bridges Web2 familiarity (usernames) with Web3 concepts (wallet-linked domains).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets crypto-native users and early Web3 adopters who are setting up a public-facing decentralized identity (ENS-like ".cb.id" domain) tied to their wallet. The inclusion of GitHub and Reddit alongside Twitter as social links signals a target audience of developers, traders, and community participants active in crypto-adjacent social spaces.

Psychologically, the form leverages completion motivation (empty fields with placeholders subtly invite the user to fill them in, similar to a profile-completeness nudge) and identity expression — allowing users to link social proof (Twitter/GitHub/Reddit handles) that builds credibility and reputation within crypto communities where pseudonymous trust matters greatly.
screens.whereToUse:
• Profile/account settings screens where users manage personal or public identity information.

  • Web3/crypto apps needing to link an on-chain identity to off-chain social proof.

  • Any form requiring multiple optional fields where low pressure, clear labeling, and immediate save feedback improve completion rates.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for complex, multi-section profiles with 10+ fields — consider grouping into an accordion or multi-step form to prevent excessive scrolling.

  • Not ideal when fields require heavy validation (e.g., verifying social handles); this flat single-screen form lacks visible inline validation states.

  • Avoid overlaying toast confirmations directly on top of primary action buttons if the button may need to be tapped again quickly — it can obscure or delay interaction.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing Profile 9
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is the central settings hub for a self-custody crypto wallet account, organized as a vertical Stacked List of navigational rows beneath a profile header. The hierarchy is deliberate: identity (avatar, ENS-style name) sits at the top, followed by a prominent "Edit profile" pill button, then a divider that visually separates "who you are" from "how your wallet is secured and configured."

The information architecture groups security-critical actions (Recovery phrase, Show private key, Token allowances) alongside lower-stakes preferences (Manage privacy, Color, Connected dapps). This mixing is a minor UX risk — critical, irreversible-consequence actions like exporting a private key sit at the same visual weight as cosmetic settings like "Color." A more mature pattern would visually demarcate a "Security" section from "Preferences."

Each row uses a consistent right-chevron affordance signaling drill-down navigation, giving users a predictable mental model: tap row → go deeper → back arrow returns. Status is communicated inline and contextually (e.g., "0" dapps connected, colored swatch preview) rather than forcing the user to enter each sub-screen to find out — a strong scan-ability decision that respects user time.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is terse, label-only, and utilitarian — typical of Web3 tooling aimed at users who already understand blockchain terminology (recovery phrase, public addresses, token allowances, private key). There is no hand-holding or explanatory subtext, which assumes technical literacy.

The one piece of emotionally-charged copy is the "Not backed up" badge, rendered in alarming red against a dark red pill. This is a deliberate tonal shift from the otherwise neutral list — it functions as a warning label, using color psychology to trigger loss-aversion anxiety ("you could lose everything") without being an intrusive modal.
screens.keyHighlights:
Contextual risk badge inline in a list row. Rather than a separate banner or modal nagging the user to back up their seed phrase, the app embeds the "Not backed up" status as a colored chip directly next to the relevant setting. This is elegant because it surfaces critical security debt exactly where the user would act on it, at zero extra cognitive cost, and without being disruptive to the primary task flow.

Inline metadata previews. "Connected dapps" shows a live count (0) and "Color" shows a live swatch before the user drills in — reducing unnecessary navigation and giving at-a-glance state awareness.

Editable identity affordance. The small pencil badge overlaid on the avatar is a universally recognized "tap to edit" icon, reinforcing discoverability of profile customization without adding a separate button.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users (e.g., Coinbase Wallet, given the ".cb.id" ENS-style naming) who are expected to already understand concepts like seed phrases, private keys, and token allowances. The audience is likely intermediate-to-advanced crypto natives rather than total beginners, evidenced by the absence of educational tooltips.

Psychologically, the design leverages loss aversion via the red "Not backed up" badge — non-custodial wallets place 100% of recovery responsibility on the user, so the product must proactively remind them of catastrophic risk (permanent loss of funds) without being so aggressive it triggers dismissal fatigue. Placing this warning passively in a list (versus a blocking modal) respects user autonomy while still nudging responsible behavior.
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for account/settings hubs in security-sensitive apps (crypto wallets, password managers, banking apps) where you need to surface multiple configuration and security actions in a scannable list. It's ideal when:

  • You have a mix of identity, security, and preference settings that benefit from a single entry point.

  • You need to communicate live status (counts, backup state, color) without forcing drill-down.

  • You want to nudge users toward a critical action (like backing up a recovery phrase) subtly rather than via a disruptive modal.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat-list approach when the number of settings grows large or spans very different risk tiers — burying a "delete wallet" or "export private key" action in the same visual weight as "Color" can lead to costly user errors. In those cases, group settings into labeled sections (e.g., "Security," "Preferences," "Advanced") with stronger visual separation, or add secondary confirmation friction for destructive/high-risk rows.

Also avoid this pattern for non-technical or mainstream consumer audiences without adding inline explanations — jargon like "token allowances" or "public addresses" will confuse novice users and should be paired with tooltips or plain-language subtitles.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing Profile 11

The layout follows a strict vertical rhythm: a contextual privacy disclaimer at top, an identity block (avatar + ENS-style username), followed by a series of labeled text inputs for optional metadata (Bio, Website, Twitter, Reddit), and a sticky, high-contrast gradient CTA pinned to the bottom of the viewport.

The visual hierarchy is strong — bold oversized H1 ("Edit profile details") immediately communicates the screen's purpose, while the smaller supporting text de-risks the interaction by clarifying visibility settings and optionality of fields. Dark mode is used effectively here, giving the crypto-native audience a "pro tool" aesthetic rather than a consumer social app feel.

The avatar edit affordance (camera badge overlaying the profile picture) is a well-established convention that requires no additional label, saving vertical space. Each input field uses outlined borders with generous padding, ensuring large tap targets and clear separation of concerns despite the monochrome dark palette.

The persistent 'Save' button uses a vibrant blue-to-teal gradient that stands in stark contrast to the black background, functioning as the single unambiguous next action regardless of how far the user scrolls down the form.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The copy is minimal, functional, and reassuring. "All fields are optional" combined with the explicit privacy disclosure ("Your profile is public. You can make it private in Manage privacy") reduces friction and anxiety for a crypto-savvy audience that is often hyper-sensitive about on-chain identity exposure and doxxing risk.

Field labels are terse utility labels (Bio, Your website, Twitter username, Reddit username) rather than playful copy, matching the expectations of a financial/utility app rather than a social entertainment app. The inline link "Manage privacy" is embedded directly in the descriptive sentence, allowing contextual navigation without cluttering the UI with an extra button.
screens.keyHighlights:

  • Explicit "All fields are optional" framing: This single line drastically lowers commitment anxiety, encouraging completion of at least some fields since there is no penalty for skipping.

  • Persistent gradient CTA: The Save button remains fixed at the bottom, decoupled from scroll position, so users are never confused about how to commit their changes.

  • Identity block merges avatar editing and username display: Combining the editable avatar with the read-only username and human-readable ENS-style domain (alexsmithmobbin.cb.id) reinforces Web3 identity conventions in one compact component.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets crypto-native users of a Web3 wallet (Coinbase Wallet), a demographic that is generally privacy-conscious, technically literate, and wary of unsolicited data collection. The design leverages autonomy and control as a psychological trigger: by foregrounding privacy status and marking every field optional, the product signals respect for user agency, which builds trust — a critical currency in crypto products where users self-custody assets and are naturally guarded.

The inclusion of social handles (Twitter, Reddit) rather than more mainstream ones (Instagram, Facebook) is a deliberate targeting signal, acknowledging that the crypto/DeFi community congregates primarily on Twitter/X and Reddit, reinforcing platform-community fit.
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern for optional profile-completion forms where reducing friction and anxiety is more important than mandating data collection (e.g., Web3 identity, professional networking, niche community apps).

  • Ideal when the app has a linked separate privacy control panel and you want to surface a summary/link rather than duplicating controls.

  • Effective for dark-mode-first products targeting technical or privacy-sensitive audiences (crypto, security tools, developer platforms).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this sparse, all-optional structure for onboarding flows where certain profile data is critical for personalization or matching (e.g., dating apps, marketplaces) — mandatory fields should be visually distinguished from optional ones.

  • Not suitable when the number of profile fields is very large; a flat scrolling list would become unwieldy and should be split into grouped sections or an accordion.

  • Avoid embedding a privacy policy summary inline if the privacy implications are complex — this shorthand works only for simple public/private toggles, not granular permission systems.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing Profile 13

  • One-tap copy affordance: Placing a copy icon in the top nav bar acknowledges a core crypto user need — quickly copying an address/ID to share or paste elsewhere — without cluttering the primary content area.

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets crypto-native and crypto-curious users on platforms like Coinbase Wallet who need a simple way to represent and share their on-chain identity. The design specifically serves users who value quick shareability (via the copy button) and want their blockchain address abstracted into a friendly, memorable handle rather than a cryptic hex string.

  • Not suitable when the product needs to emphasize security warnings or verification status prominently (e.g., KYC/AML flows), since the playful, social tone may undercut trust/compliance messaging.
