screens.name: Cleo Pre-Onboarding 8
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a single-question step within a multi-step form (wizard) pattern, isolating the request for an email address as its own discrete micro-task. By dedicating an entire screen to one input field, the designer minimizes cognitive load and maximizes completion likelihood — a classic "one thing per screen" strategy that reduces perceived effort even though the overall onboarding sequence may be lengthy.

The segmented progress bar at the top (5 segments, second one partially filled) gives the user a clear mental model of how much is left, curbing abandonment anxiety. The bold, oversized "EMAIL" label acts as a visual anchor and title, while the smaller supporting sentence clarifies why the data is needed ("to receive the code"), preemptively answering the user's "why do you need this?" objection.

Navigation affordances are dual: a back arrow (top-left) for step regression and a close/X (top-right) to exit the flow entirely — both standard, expected placements for modals/wizards. The primary CTA ("Next 👉") is docked at the bottom in a thumb-friendly zone, currently rendered in a disabled/greyed state, which visually communicates that input is required before progression (a subtle form of inline validation/gating).

The single input field is generously sized with ample whitespace above and below, reducing visual clutter and directing full attention to the one action required. A small "Your data explained" link with an info icon offers a low-friction, optional path to transparency/trust-building without interrupting the primary flow.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is casual, friendly, and slightly playful — evidenced by the informal "Next 👉" button copy paired with a pointing-hand emoji, which humanizes an otherwise transactional moment and can increase perceived brand warmth (common in fintech/crypto or consumer apps targeting younger, digitally-native users).

The microcopy "Enter the email where you'd like to receive the code" is written in plain, conversational language rather than formal instructional text (e.g., avoiding "Please provide a valid email address for verification purposes"). This lowers the psychological barrier and makes the request feel like a natural, low-stakes exchange rather than a bureaucratic form field.

The bold, condensed "EMAIL" header uses a distinctive, heavy typographic treatment that suggests a bold/youthful brand identity distinct from generic corporate onboarding screens.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-field focus: Isolating one data point per screen dramatically increases completion rates versus long forms.

  • Disabled CTA as implicit validation: The greyed-out "Next" button communicates required input without needing an explicit error message, reducing friction and negative feedback loops.

  • Transparent progress indicator: The segmented bar sets accurate expectations about flow length, reducing the "how much longer?" anxiety that drives drop-off in onboarding.

  • Trust-building micro-link: "Your data explained" preemptively addresses privacy concerns without cluttering the primary path, respecting both persuasion and transparency.

  • Playful CTA copy with emoji: Injects personality into a purely functional step, differentiating the brand from sterile enterprise forms.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users going through account creation or identity verification in a consumer-facing app (likely fintech, crypto, or a subscription service given the bold branding and verification-code flow). The design assumes a mobile-first, mainstream audience that is impatient with lengthy forms and prone to abandoning multi-field sign-ups.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the Zeigarnik effect (visible progress bar creates a drive to complete an already-started task), foot-in-the-door commitment (having advanced past step 1, users are more likely to continue), and reduced choice overload (only one input visible, no distractions) to shepherd the user toward code delivery and eventual verification/registration completion.
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any sequential onboarding, KYC, or account-setup flow where you need to collect several discrete pieces of information (email, phone, name, DOB, etc.) without overwhelming the user. It's especially effective for:

  • Sign-up/verification funnels where drop-off at each step must be minimized.

  • Regulated industries (fintech, healthcare) where a "data explained" trust link is needed alongside sequential data collection.

  • Mobile apps where thumb-reachable CTAs and minimal on-screen elements are prioritized.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavily paginated, one-field-per-screen approach when:

  • The overall data set is small (e.g., only 2 fields) — splitting into 5 screens would feel tedious and slow rather than helpful.

  • Users are highly motivated experts (e.g., B2B admin tools) who prefer fast, dense single-screen forms over guided hand-holding.

  • Network conditions or app performance make screen transitions between each field costly or slow, introducing more friction than a single consolidated form would.

screens.name: Cleo Pre-Onboarding 10

Despite being a data-collection step, the layout deviates from Cleo's usual chat-bubble interface, opting instead for a more traditional, form-based UI. This is a deliberate UX choice: for legally sensitive and structured data (like a birthdate required for compliance/KYC), a rigid input field with a date picker icon is more reliable and less error-prone than parsing a natural language chat response.

The hierarchy is clean and vertical: a bold, high-contrast header ("DATE OF BIRTH") sits atop a single, isolated text field, minimizing cognitive load. The redundant helper text ("You must be 18 or over to use Cleo") appears both above and below the input, ensuring the age-gating requirement is impossible to miss before the user attempts to submit invalid data. The disabled state of the "Next" button (grayed out) provides a clear affordance that input is required before progression is possible, preventing premature form submission errors.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The tone here is direct and legally necessary, a stark contrast to Cleo's usual "roasting" personality. The heading uses a bold, blocky, all-caps font ("DATE OF BIRTH") that maintains the app's edgy, high-impact visual identity even in a mundane utility screen. The copy is repeated for emphasis on compliance ("You must be 18 or over"), stripping away any humor to ensure zero ambiguity regarding this hard requirement. The one bit of playful branding preserved is the pointing finger emoji (👉) on the "Next" button, a small but effective touch that maintains the app's fun, human voice even during a friction-heavy signup step.
screens.keyHighlights:

  • Disabled CTA State: The "Next" button is visually greyed out until a valid date is entered, providing a clear system status and preventing invalid form submissions.

  • Data Transparency Link: The "Your data explained" link with an info icon preemptively addresses privacy concerns regarding sensitive PII (date of birth), building trust at the exact moment of friction.

  • Dual Exit Points: Providing both a "Back" arrow and a "Close" (X) button gives users flexible navigation, respecting the user's ability to abandon or revisit the flow without feeling trapped.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users undergoing the mandatory account creation process. Since Cleo is a financial app dealing with money coaching (likely linked to bank accounts or cash advances), collecting a Date of Birth is a regulatory necessity (KYC - Know Your Customer) to verify the user is a legal adult capable of entering financial agreements.

The psychological trigger here is trust and legitimacy. By using a standard, clean form UI (rather than a gimmicky chat bubble) for this specific step, Cleo signals to the user that despite its comedic branding, it treats sensitive financial and identity data with the seriousness and security of a standard banking application.
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any onboarding flow requiring the collection of sensitive, structured Personally Identifiable Information (PII) such as birthdates, SSNs, or legal names, specifically in regulated industries like Fintech, Healthcare, or Alcohol/Tobacco sales where age verification is a hard gate.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this rigid, high-friction form style for casual, non-essential data collection (e.g., asking for a user's favorite hobby), where a more conversational, low-pressure chat input would better maintain user engagement and match the app's core "fun" identity.

screens.name: Cleo Pre-Onboarding 11
screens.uxAnalysis:
This screen is a step within a multi-step onboarding flow, specifically capturing the user's date of birth. The layout is minimal and focused, using a single input field to reduce cognitive load. A progress bar at the top (segmented into 5 steps) sets clear expectations about how much of the sign-up flow remains, mitigating drop-off anxiety.

The core interaction pattern leverages the native iOS action sheet with a wheel/spinner date picker, which is triggered by tapping the text field. This is a well-established platform convention that reduces friction versus a custom-built calendar grid, especially for entering birth years that could be decades in the past (scrolling a wheel is faster than tapping through a calendar month-by-month).

Critically, the requirement text ("You must be 18 or over to use Cleo") is duplicated — once as a subheading under the H1, and again as helper text directly below the input field. This redundancy anchors the reason for data collection right at the point of interaction, reducing perceived invasiveness of asking for sensitive PII (birth date).

An easily dismissible action sheet (with separate "Confirm" and "Cancel" buttons) gives the user full control and an escape hatch, which is important for a financial app where trust signals matter. The persistent close (X) and back arrow in the top nav bar also ensure the user never feels trapped in the flow.
screens.tonalityAndContent:
The tone is direct, authoritative, and slightly bold — using a heavy, condensed display font ("DATE OF BIRTH") that matches Cleo's playful-but-blunt brand personality (Cleo is known for its sassy AI chatbot persona). Despite the playful branding elsewhere in the product, this screen keeps copy strictly functional and compliance-driven.

The repeated line "You must be 18 or over to use Cleo" acts as both a legal disclaimer and a justification for data collection, reassuring the user that this isn't arbitrary data harvesting but a legal necessity (age-gating financial services). The additional "Your data explained" link signals transparency and invites users who are skeptical about sharing personal data to self-serve more information, rather than abandoning the flow out of privacy concern.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-placement justification copy: Repeating the legal requirement both as a subtitle and as field helper text preempts user hesitation about sharing a birth date.

  • Native platform picker: Using the iOS wheel picker for date entry is faster and more familiar than a custom date input, reducing input errors and cognitive effort.

  • "Your data explained" transparency link: A proactive trust-building affordance that addresses privacy concerns inline rather than forcing users to hunt through a privacy policy.

  • Segmented progress bar: Clearly communicates step 3 of 5, setting expectations and encouraging completion (sunk-cost/progress motivation).

  • Two-tier exit points: Both a back arrow and a close (X) give users flexible, low-friction ways to exit or step back, reducing feelings of entrapment common in long forms.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users signing up for Cleo, a financial wellness/budgeting app that must comply with KYC (Know Your Customer) and age-verification regulations before granting access to financial features. The target demographic is largely young adults (Gen Z/younger Millennials) who are accustomed to fast, native mobile interactions and are wary of oversharing personal data with fintech apps.

Psychologically, the screen relies on the justification effect (explaining "why" before asking "what") to reduce reactance to sharing sensitive PII. The progress indicator taps into the Zeigarnik effect
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when regulatory or compliance requirements (age verification, KYC, GDPR consent) force you to collect sensitive personal information early in an onboarding flow. It's ideal for finance, healthcare, alcohol/tobacco, or gambling apps where legal age-gating is mandatory. Also valuable in any multi-step form where you want to justify a data ask directly at the point of collection to reduce field abandonment.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid duplicating the same explanatory copy twice on screen for casual, non-regulated data (e.g., collecting a nickname or favorite color) — this would feel excessive and patronizing. Also avoid native wheel pickers for date-of-birth entry on platforms/audiences where free-text input with masking might be faster (e.g., desktop web forms), and avoid single-field onboarding steps if you have many low-sensitivity fields to collect, as excessive step count for trivial data increases perceived friction and abandonment.

screens.name: Cleo Pre-Onboarding 12

screens.uxAnalysis: This is the settled state of the state-selection onboarding step: rather than auto-advancing once a value is chosen, Cleo surfaces an explicit "Next" button, giving the user a clear, deliberate confirmation point before moving forward in the Setup Wizard. Pairing a prefilled Combobox with a big, thumb-friendly full-width CTA keeps the interaction low-effort while still requiring an intentional action, which avoids accidental advancement if the user was still scrolling the picker.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The headline and subtext are unchanged from the picker-open state and carry the same direct, trust-building framing ("Banking regulations may vary by location" pre-empts the "why do you need this" objection). What's new here is the CTA copy: "Next 👉" — casual, lower-case-feeling despite title case, with an emoji doing the job a plain arrow icon would normally do. This is a small but deliberate personality touch consistent with Cleo's broader playful brand voice, injected even into an otherwise procedural, data-collection-heavy step.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explicit confirmation over auto-advance — requiring a tap on "Next" rather than auto-progressing on selection prevents accidental step-skipping (error prevention).

  • Progress disclosure — the segmented bar continues to set expectations about remaining onboarding effort.

  • Fitts's Law — the CTA is a large, full-width, high-contrast button, making it an easy, low-error target for a one-handed thumb tap.

  • Brand personality in low-emotion moments — the emoji-in-button is a small but consistent way to keep a data-collection step from feeling sterile.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Chime / Current — same explicit-Next-button-after-field-selection pattern in KYC onboarding steps, prioritizing deliberate confirmation over auto-advance.

  • Robinhood — uses full-width primary CTAs at the bottom of each onboarding step, matching this button placement and sizing convention.

  • Duolingo — injects small emoji/personality touches into otherwise functional onboarding CTAs, similar to the "Next 👉" treatment here.
screens.whereToUse: This explicit-confirmation pattern (prefilled field + full-width "Next" CTA) fits best in regulated or data-sensitive onboarding flows where a mistaken auto-advance could mean incorrect data being submitted, and where a large touch target improves completion speed.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for rapid, low-stakes preference selection (e.g. picking a favorite color) where auto-advancing on tap would reduce friction without meaningful risk, making an extra explicit "Next" tap unnecessary overhead.

screens.name: Cleo Pre-Onboarding 14
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen is the final step of Cleo's onboarding Setup Wizard, closing out account creation with a marketing-attribution question rather than a functional or regulatory one. Reusing the exact same visual pattern as the state-selection step (headline, prefilled Combobox, native wheel picker, "Your data explained" link) keeps the wizard's rhythm consistent right up to the last step, so the user isn't confronted with a novel interaction pattern just as they're about to finish. Placing this low-stakes, business-value question last (after higher-friction financial/regulatory questions) is a deliberate sequencing choice — it front-loads necessary data and saves the "nice to have" question for when completion momentum is highest.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "WHERE DID YOU HEAR ABOUT CLEO?" keeps the same bold condensed display headline used throughout the wizard, maintaining visual consistency. Unlike the state-selection screen, there's no reassuring subtext here explaining why this data is being collected — likely because the answer is self-evident (it's an attribution question, not a sensitive regulatory one), so the copy stays minimal and functional rather than persuasive.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pattern consistency across steps — reusing the identical field/picker/CTA layout from the state-selection screen reduces relearning cost at each new step (consistency & standards).

  • Progress disclosure at completion — the fully-advanced progress bar signals "you're almost done," which helps sustain motivation through to the final step (goal-gradient effect).

  • Strategic question sequencing — placing a business-value (non-user-value) question last, after the user is invested, reduces the chance it causes drop-off compared to placing it earlier.

  • Smart Defaults reduce effort — prefilling with the most statistically common answer ("App Store / Play Store") minimizes the interaction to a single confirm-tap for most users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo — closes onboarding with a similarly low-stakes "how did you hear about us" attribution question, using it as the final step before entering the app.

  • Robinhood — uses the same native wheel-picker + prefilled default pattern for late-onboarding categorical questions.

  • Headspace — sequences business-value questions (referral source, marketing consent) after core setup, mirroring this placement strategy.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits attribution/marketing-source data collection placed at the end of onboarding, where the business value of the question is real but the user-facing value is minimal, and where consistency with prior wizard steps matters more than introducing persuasive copy.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit if attribution data is needed for the product experience itself (e.g. personalizing content) — in that case it should be asked earlier and paired with an explanation of user benefit, not treated as a low-priority closing question.

screens.name: Cleo Pre-Onboarding 15
screens.uxAnalysis: This is the settled/confirmed state of the final onboarding step, mirroring the pattern already established on the state-selection screen: a prefilled Combobox paired with an explicit, full-width "Next" CTA rather than auto-advancing on selection. Ending the entire Setup Wizard on this same interaction shape (rather than switching to a distinct "Finish" or "Submit" pattern) keeps the wizard cognitively seamless right up to completion — the user experiences no jarring shift in interaction model between the second-to-last and final steps.
screens.tonalityAndContent: Identical CTA treatment to the earlier state-selection screen — "Next 👉" rather than "Finish" or "Done," despite this being the last onboarding step. This is a minor missed opportunity for closure signaling: reusing generic "Next" copy at the true end of a wizard doesn't reward the user with a sense of completion the way a "Finish 🎉" or "Let's go" label might, though it does keep the flow visually and verbally consistent.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Consistency over novelty at flow's end — reusing the same CTA pattern/copy through the last step avoids introducing new interaction language right before completion (consistency & standards).

  • Explicit confirmation over auto-advance — same error-prevention rationale as the state-selection screen: requiring a deliberate "Next" tap avoids accidental submission.

  • Missed closure signal — generic "Next" copy on the final step is a minor deviation from the goal-gradient principle, which suggests reinforcing completion more explicitly at the last step tends to increase perceived reward.

  • Fitts's Law — large, full-width, high-contrast CTA remains an easy, low-error thumb target.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Chime / Current — similarly reuse a generic "Next" or "Continue" CTA across all onboarding steps including the last, prioritizing flow consistency over distinct completion messaging.

  • Duolingo — by contrast, swaps CTA copy to something celebratory ("Let's go!") on the final onboarding step, illustrating the alternative approach Cleo did not take here.

  • Robinhood — matches Cleo's approach of keeping CTA button styling and copy uniform through account-setup completion.
screens.whereToUse: Reusing consistent CTA copy/styling through the final onboarding step works well when the goal is to minimize interaction learning curve and keep the flow feeling procedural and low-friction rather than emotionally significant.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for products wanting to maximize onboarding-completion delight or reinforce a sense of achievement — in that case, the final step's CTA should diverge from "Next" toward completion-specific copy to mark the moment distinctly.

screens.name: Cleo Pre-Onboarding 18
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen is fundamentally a Copy-driven screen: nearly all of its communicative weight rests on the headline, the two-part message-bubble copy, and the CTA rather than on interactive UI machinery. It exists to disclose a regulatory limitation (state-restricted cash advances/subscriptions) transparently before the user reaches the main app, so they aren't surprised by a missing feature later. Structuring the disclosure as two sequential chat-bubble cards — first the bad news, then the reassurance — mirrors a real conversational pattern (deliver the caveat, then pivot to what's still available), softening what could otherwise read as a blunt rejection.
screens.tonalityAndContent: The headline "JUST A HEADS UP" is deliberately casual and low-alarm phrasing for what is, functionally, a legal/regulatory restriction notice — choosing conversational warmth over a more clinical "Feature Availability" or "Restrictions Apply" heading. The two-bubble structure does real narrative work: the first bubble delivers the limitation plainly and factually ("Due to your state's laws, cash advances and certain subscriptions... aren't available"), while the second immediately pivots to reassurance ("But insights, budget and savings tools are good to go"), using "but" as an explicit contrast marker to prevent the news from reading as fully negative. The whimsical eyeball-candy mascot illustration softens the moment further, reinforcing that this is a minor caveat rather than a serious problem. This tone and sequencing directly serve trust: users are less likely to feel misled or churn when a limitation is disclosed proactively, plainly, and immediately followed by what still works. The CTA "Explore the app" is upbeat and forward-looking, deliberately avoiding words like "Continue" or "OK" that would feel like begrudging acknowledgment of bad news.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive disclosure reduces later frustration — surfacing the state-based restriction before app entry (rather than letting the user discover it mid-task) follows the trust principle that bad news is best delivered early and honestly.

  • Bad-news-then-good-news sequencing — splitting the message into two bubbles that pivot from limitation to reassurance is a copywriting technique that reduces perceived severity without hiding the fact.

  • Illustration as tone-softener — the playful mascot graphic counterbalances the seriousness of a regulatory disclosure, keeping the moment from feeling like a legal pop-up.

  • Forward-framed CTA — "Explore the app" reframes the moment as entering something positive rather than merely dismissing a warning.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Chime / Varo — similarly disclose state-based feature restrictions (e.g., cash advance eligibility) via a plain-language screen before full app access, a common fintech-compliance pattern.

  • Robinhood — uses comparable "heads up" style disclosure screens for state-restricted investment products, balancing legal necessity with approachable copy.

  • Klarna — pairs restriction/limitation messaging with reassurance about what's still available, matching this two-part bad-news/good-news structure.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any regulated product needing to disclose jurisdiction-based feature limitations, where proactive, plainly-worded transparency (paired with a reassuring counterpoint) reduces user confusion and complaint volume better than silently disabling features.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for disclosures involving genuinely serious risk or compliance matters (e.g., fraud warnings, account suspension reasons) — the casual, softened tone used here would be inappropriate where the user needs to register real urgency or take corrective action.

screens.name: Cleo Pre-Onboarding 16
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen handles email verification via a one-time passcode, a standard trust-building checkpoint before account activation completes. The masked email display (partially obscured with only "@gmail.com" visible) balances confirmation ("we sent it to the right place") with privacy on a shared or glanced-at screen. The "Open my email" shortcut button directly addresses a common OTP-flow friction point — needing to app-switch to retrieve the code — by offering a one-tap deep link, while "Resend code" and troubleshooting copy pre-empt the most common failure mode (code lost in spam).
screens.tonalityAndContent: "VERIFY YOUR EMAIL" keeps the same bold condensed display headline used across the app, maintaining visual continuity from onboarding into this security step. The supporting copy is plain and instructional rather than playful — appropriate here, since a verification screen's job is to reduce anxiety and confusion (e.g., "Didn't get the email? Check your spam and promotions, or resend") rather than entertain. This is a deliberate tonal shift from Cleo's usual sassy voice, prioritizing clarity and reassurance over personality at a moment where user friction/anxiety (a stuck verification code) is more likely than in a normal onboarding step.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Reducing app-switch friction — "Open my email" as a direct shortcut reduces the multi-step task of manually leaving the app, finding the email, and returning (minimizing user memory load / reducing steps to goal).

  • Error prevention & recovery guidance — proactively surfacing "check spam" and "resend" options before the user hits a dead end reduces abandonment at a known high-drop-off step.

  • Privacy-conscious disclosure — partially masking the email balances the need for confirmation against shoulder-surfing risk.

  • Visibility of system status — the six empty dots give a clear, familiar visual target showing exactly how many digits are expected and how many have been entered.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Robinhood — uses an identical six-digit dot-based OTP entry pattern with a numeric keypad for account verification, a near-universal fintech convention.

  • Venmo — offers a similar "Resend code" and masked-contact-info pattern during phone/email verification steps.

  • Revolut — includes a comparable one-tap "open email/SMS app" shortcut to reduce OTP-retrieval friction during KYC verification.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (masked contact display + dot-based OTP field + one-tap open-email shortcut + resend/troubleshooting copy) fits any account flow requiring identity or contact-ownership verification, especially in regulated industries like fintech where OTP verification is close to mandatory.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for low-stakes actions where verification isn't strictly necessary — adding this heavier flow (with app-switch shortcuts and error recovery copy) to a non-security-critical step would introduce unnecessary friction.

screens.name: Cleo Pre-Onboarding 17
screens.uxAnalysis: This screen exists purely to close the loop on the previous action (email verification) with positive reinforcement before continuing the flow. Rather than silently advancing to the next screen, Cleo inserts a dedicated full-bleed celebration moment — decorative illustration, exclamatory headline, and a single unambiguous "Next" CTA — which slows the pace deliberately to let the success register with the user. This is a meaningful contrast to the generic "Next" CTA used at the end of the earlier onboarding wizard steps: here, the celebratory visual treatment does the emotional work that the CTA copy itself doesn't.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "THAT TOTALLY WORKED" is a sharp tonal departure from the neutral, instructional copy of the verification screen just before it — casual, exclamatory, almost surprised-sounding phrasing that's much closer to Cleo's signature comedic brand voice. This is a deliberate release of tension: the verification screen was necessarily plain and reassuring (a moment of mild user anxiety), and this screen rewards getting through it with personality and relief. The CTA remains the same generic "Next 👉" seen throughout onboarding, so the celebratory weight is carried entirely by the headline and illustration rather than the button copy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Positive reinforcement after a friction point — inserting a dedicated success screen after OTP verification (a step prone to anxiety/failure) rewards the user and confirms system status clearly (visibility of system status).

  • Tonal pacing — deliberately swinging from plain/instructional (verification) to playful/celebratory (this screen) uses contrast to make the relief and brand personality land harder.

  • Milestone Celebration reinforces retention — even a small win like "your email is verified" benefits from acknowledgment, which can measurably reduce mid-onboarding drop-off.

  • Single, unambiguous action — with no other interactive elements competing for attention, the "Next" button is the obvious next step (minimizing choice/decision friction).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo — uses near-identical full-screen celebratory illustrations with exclamatory copy after completing onboarding milestones (e.g., placement test, streak start).

  • Headspace — inserts similar "you did it" style full-bleed confirmation screens after account setup steps, using illustration-led celebration rather than text-heavy confirmation.

  • Robinhood — uses lighter-weight success toasts rather than full-screen celebration for equivalent verification steps, a useful contrast showing Cleo's choice to go bigger on this particular milestone.
screens.whereToUse: This full-screen Milestone Celebration pattern fits best right after a step with real friction or anxiety (identity verification, a difficult form, a payment) where the user benefits from explicit positive reinforcement before continuing.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for frequent or minor confirmations (e.g., saving a routine setting) — a full-screen takeover for every small success would quickly feel excessive and slow down flows that should stay lightweight.

screens.name: Cleo Pre-Onboarding 19
screens.uxAnalysis: This is a textbook Permission Priming screen: rather than triggering the OS-level notification permission dialog cold, Cleo first shows the user exactly what a notification will look like and why it's valuable, using a realistic mock push-notification card ("You smashed yet another target... Stick to $50 today to stay on track") alongside a benefit-focused bullet list. This pre-permission "soft ask" pattern is standard practice because OS-level permission dialogs are binary and hard to reverse (users must go to system settings to change their mind), so priming increases opt-in rates by building motivation before the system prompt appears. Both CTAs are given clear, tappable, non-punitive framing — "Not now" rather than "Deny" — reducing the guilt/friction of declining.
screens.tonalityAndContent: "NEVER MISS A DOLLAR" is aspirational and benefit-framed rather than feature-framed — it sells the outcome (financial awareness) rather than the mechanism (notifications). The mock notification preview itself is written in Cleo's signature playful voice ("You smashed yet another target 🥊") complete with an emoji, demonstrating rather than just describing the tone of what future notifications will feel like. The bullet list mixes practical value ("Tailored coaching on your spending," "Watch Cleo grow your savings") with an emotionally warm, almost therapeutic note ("Reminders that you're only human 💙") — a notable tonal choice that reframes notifications as supportive rather than naggy, directly addressing the common user fear that finance-app notifications will feel guilt-inducing or judgmental.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Permission priming increases opt-in — showing value and a realistic preview before the irreversible OS dialog is a well-established mobile pattern for maximizing permission grants.

  • Outcome-framed value proposition — "Never miss a dollar" leads with user benefit, not the technical ask ("allow notifications"), which is more persuasive per standard conversion-copy principles.

  • Non-punitive decline option — "Not now" (rather than "No" or "Deny") keeps the door open for reconsideration later without making the user feel they're rejecting the product outright.

  • Emotional reassurance as differentiation — "Reminders that you're only human 💙" preemptively defuses the anxiety that budget notifications will feel shaming, a thoughtful trust-building touch specific to a finance app's notification content.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo — uses nearly identical permission-priming screens with mock notification previews and benefit bullets before requesting push permissions.

  • Headspace — similarly frames notification permission asks around emotional/wellbeing benefit rather than pure feature description, matching Cleo's "you're only human" framing.

  • Robinhood — uses a comparable soft-ask screen with a realistic notification mockup before the system dialog, for the same conversion-optimization reasons.
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any mobile app where push notifications carry real ongoing value (reminders, coaching, alerts) and where the one-time nature of the OS permission dialog makes a pre-ask conversion step worth the extra screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for apps where notifications are purely transactional/low-value (e.g., a single order-confirmation alert) — the extra priming screen would add friction disproportionate to the notification's actual utility.
